lectures.title: How JavaScript Is Executed
lectures.text:
Let's have a look at this interpreted on-the-fly compile thing. How is the Javascript code in our browser executed and not just in our browser but typically in any environment where you run Javascript? Let's say you write your Javascript code and you want it to have some effect on the web page if we talk about the browser as the environment where we run our script. Then you have one important thing built into any environment where you want to run Javascript code and that's a Javascript engine.

It's built into the browser as I said, there in Chrome for example, in the Chrome browser, it's v8, that's the name of the engine, in Firefox the name would be spider monkey and of course other browsers also either reuse these engines or have their own engines. Now the job of the engine is to parse code, so parse, read and understand your Javascript code, then on the fly compile it to machine code because machine code executes faster, so it reads your code but it does not necessarily execute it like that but instead, it now takes that code and compiles it to code which is faster to execute by the machine and then it executes that machine code.

This all happens in the browser with the help of the Javascript engine and then when that code is executed, we have that effect on our web page. Now important, modern engines have a lot of optimizations there, they might start executing your uncompiled code and then compile the code whilst they're also already executing it to get started executing faster and then switch to the compiled code dynamically and so on, so we have a lot of optimizations going on here and we will dig a bit deeper into what the Javascript engine is exactly in a separate module in the course, for now this is all we need to know, the browser has a built-in tool that takes our code, compiles it, optimizes it and executes it and also a bit more technical side note, all of that happens on a single thread.

Now this is very technical but you might know that in a computer, you have certain tasks that are executed, for example the browser you opened is a task or actually might consist of multiple different tasks that are executed together. The Javascript code is also yet another task which your operating system in the end has to take care of and this runs on a single thread. Of course we have multi-threading on modern machines so that they can do multiple tasks at the same time but the Javascript code execution runs on one single thread there, so the Javascript code execution always happens in one single thread on your operating system.

Right now this doesn't really matter, it will become more important later in the course though when I will come back to this concept of single threading and which implications this has for Javascript. But with that we know what interpreted means, what compilation means and how the Javascript code is executed. What does dynamic and weakly type mean then?

lectures.title: Dynamic vs Weakly Typed Languages
lectures.text:
Javascript is a dynamic, interpreted programming language but it's also a weakly typed programming language. Now what does this mean? For one, the dynamic interpreted part as you learned means that it's not pre-compiled, other languages like C++ are compiled during or after development, so before you share them with the end users, Javascript is on-the-fly compiled and that means that the code is evaluated and executed at runtime, it also means that the code can change at runtime.

Now of course not the code you wrote and it won't magically change, of course the code you wrote gets executed but in that code, you can do some things which you are not allowed to do in other programming languages, for example if you're working with a variable, something we will only learn in the second module, for now you can just keep in mind that a variable is a data container, you might store let's say some text in there, text you need in your script to for example output it to the user. In Javascript you are allowed to dynamically switch the type of data there. In a variable, you might start by storing some text and suddenly at a later point of time, you store a number in there instead, in the same variable.

Now again, we haven't really learned about variables yet, we will of course do that but the one thing you can simply keep in mind is that the dynamic thing in Javascript means that it is parsed and interpreted and compiled at runtime and that therefore it is able to do certain things, for example switching the data of a variable other programming languages are not allowed to do. Now it's not necessarily good to switch the type of data dynamically or unexpectedly but you can do that, the main takeaway however is the on-the-fly compilation and interpretation. lectures.title: JavaScript Executes In A Hosted Environment
lectures.text:
Now the last thing we saw on the previous definition slide is that Javascript runs on a host environment, so that means a Javascript engine can be part or can be executed in different environments. The most well known environment is the browser, modern browsers have Javascript engines built in and they're therefore capable of executing Javascript code but you also can run Javascript in other environments, for example on the server side, so right on a computer without having a browser in between, so not inside of a browser but simply execute code like this on your machine.

Now Javascript was invented to run in the browser, to make web sites more dynamic, to be able to change things on a web site without loading a new page you could say because Javascript is able to closely work together with the loaded HTML code, with CSS, you can also use Javascript to send background HTTP requests, so to send some behind the scenes requests and fetch data without reloading the page and much more and it will do all of that throughout the course.

Now there also are certain things Javascript can't do when it runs in the browser environment though, for example it can't access your local file system for security reasons because otherwise every web page you visit would be able to read your file system, maybe delete files on your computer and so on which would be horrible of course and in general it is running in a sandbox you can say, it's not able to interact with your operating system and so on, the browser gives you certain things you can do in this environment and doesn't allow other things.

Now as I said, the browser is only one environment though, the one for which Javascript was invented but not the only one we're restricted to right now, instead the Javascript engine Google developed, v8 is the name of the engine, was extracted by some people to run Javascript anywhere because the idea was if we have the engine in the browser, why don't we take it out of the browser and then make it available as a standalone tool which you can use to execute Javascript anywhere else directly on your machine and this tool is in the end called Node.js.

Now in this course, I'll have a separate module about Node.js where I show you how that works and how it uses the same Javascript syntax you learned throughout the course but which new features it brings to the table. For the majority of course however, we'll focus on the browser side because this is the side where you absolutely need Javascript and it's also the site where you're able to see more because you have a web page where things change and so on.

Now back to Node.js though for a second, Node.js can be executed on any machine and therefore it's also often used to build web back-ends, to build web servers, server side Javascript is also something you often hear as a description for that. Now you might know about server side languages like PHP or also Java and other languages as well, well Javascript with Node.js can also be used to run it on the back-end of a web page, so on the server and not on the client in the browser of your users. Now Node.js also has certain things it can do and can't do, since it runs directly on a machine, in Node.js you're able to access the local file system, so you are able to write files and so on because unlike browser side Javascript, Node.js code has to be executed actively by you, it's not like you visit a web page and then this starts happening, instead it can only access the file system on the machine where it executes which for example is the server where it runs, not your machine and it's also able to interact with the operating system and so on.

However on the other hand since it doesn't have direct access to the loaded web page, it can't manipulate HTML or CSS like browser side. Javascript is able to do, so we basically have even inverse access capabilities here and these are the different environments where Javascript is able to run. Now in this course, we'll focus on the browser side because the Javascript syntax you learned will be the same, no matter in which environment you run Javascript code but in the browser, we simply have more visual feedback and can see what happens.

Nonetheless as I said, we have the separate Node.js module later in the course where I'll also dive into the different things we can do in Node.js and how that works.

lectures.title: Course Outline - What's In This Course?
lectures.text:
So we saw some Javascript in action, we have the basic definition out of the way and hopefully now have a basic understanding of what Javascript is and what this language is all about. Now what's in this course though, what will you learn in this course? You could split this course in two three main blocks I would say - the core basics which you have to know under all circumstances, then the next block where we build up on these basics and build a really strong foundation, you could therefore still call that basics but these would be the advanced basics and then we have advanced concepts which allow you to get to the next level of Javascript development and become a really good Javascript developer.

Now in the core basics block, we get started, this is this module, we learned the core basics about Javascript and its history and so on but once we're finished with this module, we'll dive into all the core syntax, the language basics, into variables, functions, what all of that is, all these core things that make up the Javascript language which you have to know no matter in which environment you want to execute Javascript. We'll dive into efficient development and debugging, how to configure your environment correctly, how to fix errors and how to find them.

We'll dive into control structures, if statements, loops so that you can execute code multiple times based on some conditions. We'll look behind the scenes of Javascript, we'll see what the Javascript engine does in detail. We'll have a close look at functions, a very important concept as it will turn out. We'll have a look at the DOM basics, DOM stands for Document Object Model and this will all be about manipulating the web page we're running on, adding content, removing content and so on.

We'll have a look at arrays and iterables, so at lists of data and how we can work with those. We'll have a look at objects which are super important data structures in Javascript and once we're done with that, you will have a solid basic understanding of the Javascript core syntax and the core features. Now thereafter, we'll build a stronger foundation and if you already know all the core based syntax, this of course might be a great entry point.

You'll find a module, in the curriculum if you check that, about classes and object oriented programming which takes object usage, you learned about objects in the core basics, to the next level. You learned about constructor functions and prototypes, important core concepts baked into the Javascript language. We'll dive deeper into the DOM and how to work with the browser and tap into certain browser features. We'll dive deeper into events, how we can react to mouse clicks and so on.

We'll have a look at functions again, we'll dive really deep into functions and learn about things like recursion and more advanced function usage. We'll explore the number and string types in greater detail and which restrictions we have there and what we can do there. We'll dive into asynchronous code which will be related to that single threading I mentioned and how we can run longer taking operations without freezing our web page. We'll dive into these background HTTP requests, also sometimes referred to as Ajax which I mentioned earlier, which allow us to exchange data behind the scenes without reloading the page and once we did all of that, we will have a very solid foundation, not just the basic core syntax but we'll also know all the important parts of the Javascript language and of using Javascript in the browser.

Now of course then we'll also dive into more advanced concepts, you will learn how to work with third party libraries, how to utilize the Javascript modules and split your code efficiently across multiple files. We'll dive into tooling which allows us to optimize our Javascript code, namely webpack and Babel. We'll briefly dive into browser storage and how you can store data in the browser, we'll have a look at browser support and how you can ensure that your scripts run in all browsers where they need to run, no matter which browsers your end users are going to use.

We'll have a look at Javascript frameworks and there we'll have a look at the React.js library. We'll have a look at meta programming, how you can write code which is easier to use by other developers, really advanced but really important. We'll have a look at Node.js and see how that differs from browser side Javascript and what will be the same. We'll have a look at security and how you secure your code and which security holes you want to avoid.

We'll of course also see how you get your code from your local machine onto a server where other users can use it. We'll have a look at performance optimizations and fixing memory leaks to ship the best possible code and much more. This course is a big course, it has a lot of hours of content because it's simply packed with content. You can simply go from it, from lecture 1 to the last lecture or of course also dive into the modules which are most interesting to you.

I did my best to build the course in a way that allows you to also use it as a reference, so that you don't always have to restart at the beginning if you are coming back to it after a year or so but that you can dive into the sections which are most interesting to you, though if you are new or relatively new to Javascript, my strong recommendation is that you start with lecture one and section one and you go through the course step-by-step, maybe just speeding up playback if I'm going through some concepts you already know.

So this is what's in the course and how you can take it.

lectures.title: A Brief History Of JavaScript
lectures.text:
So now that we know what Javascript is and where it runs, let's have a very brief overview of the Javascript history so that you know how it evolved over time. In 1995, Netscape introduces LiveScript which thereafter was renamed to Javascript. Now in 1996, Microsoft also released its own version of Javascript in Internet Explorer. So same idea, generally same syntax but also differences, so we already had an issue there. Back then Javascript also wasn't able to do a lot of things, it was mainly used for a spammy things, for annoying overlays and pop-ups but another problem was that you had to write very different scripts for different browsers.

In late 1996, people saw that this fragmentation could be a problem and therefore, Javascript the language was submitted to the ECMA committee to start standardization. This simply is an organization which will stand responsible for standardizing Javascript so that you have one standard which then could be implemented by multiple browsers. So then we had ongoing standardization efforts until 2005 roughly and Microsoft did really join the party, well we know how Microsoft was in the late 90s, early 2000s, ultimately they supported the standardized Javascript version.

Still there were differences but we had a more common way of using Javascript. Now the efforts of standardization continue and we had huge progress until 2011 I'd say and Microsoft eventually joined forces and became part of the standardization process and of contributing to building that standard and adding new features because that's important. My timeline ends here, the development of Javascript absolutely does not, I would say especially since 2010, 11, it really picked up and it is under active development.

It's evolving, new features are getting added, it's getting a better and better programming language and whilst it was quite clunky around 2006 and 7 and despite standardization, every browser still did its own thing in some regards. We nowadays really have a uniform language with some small differences but mainly one core language we can use in different browsers. Still different browsers have their own features you can then use but the core language is the same and in the browser support module later in the course, I'll explain how you find out which differences we still have and how you work around them.

But in the end, we now have a standardized language which is really great to use and we have that thanks to this ECMA international organization. Now this organization in the end manages a language called ECMAScript but ECMAScript and Javascript actually have a strong relation. ECMAScript is the actual language which is evolved by the ECMA international organization but ECMAScript is then implemented as Javascript by browser vendors, so by the companies working on the browsers. So it is the most famous ECMAScript implementation, Javascript is that most famous ECMAScript implementation, others would be ActionScript or Jscript and you don't really need to know those. So Javascript in the end is ECMAScript we could say and we have that organization that evolves ECMAScript and with every new standard version you could say which is the end then created and finalized, browser vendors take that and implement it into browsers. So ECMAScript itself isn't directly used but browser vendors implement it into their Javascript engines. Each browser comes with its own Javascript engine though and therefore it's each browser and the engine used by the browser which defines which exact features are supported

and actually browsers also sometimes implement certain features at an earlier point of time than they're really finalized in ECMAScript. So whilst discussions might still be going on over final implementation details, browser vendors could already go ahead and implement a certain feature in their engine already so that you can already use next generation Javascript code earlier in one browser than in the other and that's also something I'll come back to in the browser support module where you will learn how to use next-gen Javascript when writing your code and still ensuring that it runs in all browsers. So ECMAScript is under active development and browser vendors are contributing there as well, are shaping how Javascript looks like and which new features we want there and therefore Javascript is under active development and therefore it's an always evolving language.

Now in this course, you will learn Javascript in the most modern way you can, using all the latest modern syntax and this is important because in 2015, 2016, Javascript saw a major overhaul, a brand new version you could almost say with a lot of important changes and many many tutorials and courses actually teach you the old Javascript syntax which still works but which is not the most recent one and which has certain downsides and then they later switch to the modern syntax. In this course, you will learn the most modern syntax right from the start.

I will also show you the older one because you will still see it in other tutorials and code snippets and you should be able to understand those but we start with the modern one and we stick to the modern one, so you learn all the latest Javascript in this course.

lectures.title: Adding JavaScript to the Website
lectures.text:
So we want to write some script code and as I mentioned already, you got the vendor.js file which you could name however you want, I just named it like this to make it clear that I provide this to you and you don't really need to care about it. So we could add our code in that file but actually, we won't and instead I'll create a separate brand new file next to it which I'll name app.js Now you can also name this file however you want, I'll name it app.js because it will drive our simple front-end browser based application we're building here but you could name it my-script.js or just script.js or whatever you want.

The only thing that matters here is the file extension which should of course be .js because it will hold Javascript code. Now that's the script file we'll work on and that's the file where we will add our calculator logic. Now to get started and see that this works, let's start very simple and simply add in an alert where we say this works. Now you might not fully understand what's happening here, what this alert thing means, what these parentheses mean, what the single quotes here mean and we'll explore all of that throughout this module but just enter this for the moment and then go back to your page and reload and what you'll see is that nothing happens.

Well the reason for that is that of course I added my script file here but the default behavior of the browser is not to scan all subfolders next to my HTML file which I loaded for scripts which it could execute, that would be a horrible default behavior because it would mean that we can't control when which of our scripts runs and we want to control that, So of course it's good that the browser doesn't load and execute our script by default but how can we tell the browser that it should load and execute that script? There are a couple of ways of importing Javascript, now the first way of importing it is to go to the HTML file and in there, like here in the head section let's say, you can add a script opening and closing tag and you can add Javascript between those script tags. So we could write alert, this works between script tags in here, so the alert function just as I used it in app.js but not in app.js between the script tags here.

If we do that and I reload this page, you see before the page loads, I already see that alert indeed and I can click OK and confirm this and now the rest of the page loads. Now that's one way of doing it. Now you can of course throw in some script code here into your HTML file but the downside with that is that the longer your script gets, the longer this HTML file gets and this is not necessarily a technical issue but one issue it might be is that for you, it gets harder to manage your website.

If all your script and all your HTML is in one file, then this file gets very big and if you then ever need to change something in there, be that Javascript or be that HTML, you need to scroll through all the content here and find the part you want to change. So putting your scripts in there is typically not the best idea unless it's a very short script, instead you typically want to import your script and therefore you add a source attribute, src to the script tags and then between double quotes typically, single quotes or no quotes at all would also work to some extent but typically use double quotes, you point at the location of your script file.

So in my case here, I point that the assets folder by adding assets, then a slash to kind of go into that folder or to tell the browser to look into that folder and then there, we want to go into the scripts folder right which is a folder we have in there and then go into that folder and then load the app.js file, that's what we want to tell the browser, it should go in there and load the app.js file. Now important, you still need a closing script tag here, you must not have a self-closing script tag like you have it for the link, that's not supported for script tags, you must have opening and closing separate script tag.

And now with that indeed, you should see that when I reload the page again we see just this works from this file, so if I go back and reload this page indeed we see this works and if I confirm this, the rest of the page loads. So that's how we can import a script. One problem we're facing here is that this blocks the rendering of the page until the script is done and in the case of an alert, the script is really only done when the user confirmed the alert, so when we close the alert. To make sure that the page loads first, we can do one simple thing - we can take the script, take it out of the head here and move it to the end of the body so that the browser has a chance of first parsing all the HTML code and finishing that rendering before it executes our script and later, I'll show you an alternative strategy to that as well but for the moment we can do that. If I now save this and we now reload, you see first everything renders, then we can click OK and then it finishes.

Now actually, the font only came in after but that's something we can work on later, for the moment, this is better than what we had before because at least a majority of this file is now done loading before the script executes and blocks the browser from finishing this up. So that's the basic setup we'll work with, now we will also depend on the code I run here in the vendor.js file and therefore you should import that as well and you should import it before you import the app.js file because the code you write in the app.js file will depend on the code in the vendor.js file and the order does matter in Javascript, so we have to import the thing we depend on before we use it.

So we first import, from our assets folder, scripts folder, vendor.js and then you have your import to app.js so that in the app.js file, we can actually work with the things that are happening in here even though we don't fully understand what's happening in there yet. So that's the finished import setup we need, now with the importing done, we can dive into actually writing some Javascript code.

lectures.title: Introducing Variables & Constants
lectures.text:
So it's time to write some Javascript code in this app.js file and for that, I'll first of all clear the alert code. Now our goal is to write a very basic calculator here where we can enter a number here and add this to the last number we entered up there, so basically a calculator where we can always work with two numbers add add a new number to the old result and so on. So that's the goal here, such a basic calculator. Now for that, we'll need a couple of important pieces that will actually be found in most Javascript programs, for example variables and constants, that's a core feature, not just of Javascript but of most programming languages.

Now what are variables and constants? In Javascript, you define a variable like this and I'll dive into the exact meaning here in a second. Now what a variable is is it's a data container or data storage you could say. In most programs you're going to write, you're going to work with some data, be that a user name entered by the user which you then use to log the user in or as an example of our calculator, be that our last, our most recent result we have and the number the user just entered which we want to add.

So that would be data that we want to store because our program needs that data to work correctly, for example in the calculator we need the old result and the number the user just entered, so we need these two pieces of data to derive the new result. So we need these two variables to get our new third variable, the current result. So a variable is a data container which holds some data and in Javascript, we create a variable by using the let keyword which you see here on the left, then a name of your choice with some naming rules in mind which I'll dive into later, then an equal sign and then the value you want to store in the variable.

Now with a variable created, you can also always reassign it and store a new value in there, so here I'm using the existing variable user name and I assign a new value to it. Now I only need the let keyword, which Javascript understands, if you introduce a variable for the first time. If you then assign a new value to it, you don't repeat that keyword, so you only need the let keyword to let Javascript know hey here's a brand new variable my program will need, if you then use that variable thereafter, you do that without let. So a variable is a data container where the value can change, doesn't have to but often it will. Now you also have a special form of that variable you could say, you have constants, for example let's say you have a total amount of users in your application which is kind of fixed.

Now that's still a data container but instead of with the let keyword, you create it with the const keyword, another keyword which is built into Javascript, which Javascript recognizes and understands. Now the special thing about constants created with the const keyword is that there, you can't change the value, if you try to do that, you'll get an error. So there, the values must not change. Now you might wonder why you would have some value stored in a variable if that's not really variable, if it can't really change and the answer is sometimes in your code, you have values which never change which you still want to store in such a data container so that you can initialize them in a central place, let's say at the beginning of your file and then use them throughout your program, maybe use the same constant multiple times in different places so you will always reference the same single constant and if you then ever, in code when writing your code, you change that value, you change it in one place instead of ten different places but that will become clearer once we start writing some code which we'll do in a second.

For now, just be aware of these two different ways of creating variables, with let and with const, where variables with let can be changed, with const they can't be, the general syntax is keyword name and then if you want to store a value right away, equal sign at the value and also one little hint right away, you typically want to use constants as often as possible, which might sound strange at first because they're restricted in what you can do with them, right?

You can't change them but that's exactly why you want to use them as often as possible, it makes your intentions very clear. If you have a value which actually never changes throughout the lifecycle of your program or of the part of your code where you use it, well then you want to make that clear so that if any other developer ever reads your code quickly understands that this piece of data is never going to change, it simply makes your code easier to understand for others. Now that was a lot of new and very theoretic knowledge, it will make more sense once we use it, so let's use it.

lectures.title: Declaring & Defining Variables
lectures.text:
Back in our calculator, we can already start thinking about data containers we might need in there and there, one value that immediately comes to my mind when thinking about a calculator is the result. So we can create as a result variable with let, so with this special let keyword which Javascript understands and then give it any name you want, like result or current result. Now regarding the name of your variable or constant, there are a couple of rules and recommendations you should keep in mind.

There are certain allowed and not allowed names, so allowed is this name for example, userName, written like this and it's a best practice to use this special naming convention which is called camel case, which means that your name starts with a lowercase character and is only one word, so there are no blanks in there, no whitespace, that would actually be forbidden but every word inside of the word, like name here in userName starts with an upper case character to make that more readable.

So that would be a variable name which is allowed, it also is a good name because it describes what's in the variable, so here we would probably store the name of a user, so that's a better name than what the user entered because it might not be clear if what the user entered should be a user name or a password, so you want to give the variable a name that describes which kind of data you storing in there. By the way, also important, Javascript is case sensitive and this means that it really matters whether a character is a capital character or not.

So userName written the way it's written here on the left with a lowercase u at the beginning and then the uppercase N in there is not the same as if it were written with an upper case u at the beginning and otherwise the same. So the casing in the names you choose really matters and that's important to keep in mind. Now also allowed would be a name like this, It's basically similar to the first example but this also includes a digit because your variable names can be made up of any letters or digits.

You can also use the dollar sign special character and your variable name can even start with it, you can use it anywhere in the variable name but it can even start with it. Similarly, you can also use the underscore character at the beginning of your variable name or anywhere inside of it, so that's also allowed. Now there are a couple of names which are not allowed or not recommended, for example userName like this. This is actually allowed but it's a bad practice, You should use this camel case notation on the left with lowercase starting character, one word and each word instead of the words starting with an uppercase character.

So here, what you see there is actually another convention called snake case which you have in some other programming languages like Python but not in Javascript. So whilst this technically would be a valid name, you can use the underscore here, whilst this would be a valid name, it's not recommended instead use the version on the left. Now what's not recommended but more importantly, not allowed is for example a variable name like this. Whilst I did say that you can use any name that uses letters or digits, you must not start with a digit, so your variable name or your constant name and everything I explained here is true for constants created with the const keyword as well, these variables and constants must not start with a digit. Now there also are special rules when it comes to special characters, you can use dollar sign and underscore at the beginning of your variable or anywhere in your variable but you must not use other special characters, neither at the beginning of your variable nor anywhere else, so dashes or whitespace is not allowed.

The underscore is allowed as mentioned on the left but other special characters are not allowed no matter where you plan on using them. And the last important thing you should keep in mind, in this course you will learn about a couple of keywords like let and const and using these keywords as names is also not allowed because how would Javascript be able to find out whether you want to use the keyword here or your variable, right? It wouldn't and therefore this is not allowed.

Now let me have a closer look at our text here, at our string which we're combining from a couple of substrings. Now for one I mentioned that you can use single or double quotes and the decision is really up to you, you can go for either of the two solutions, I will use single quotes throughout the course but that's just my personal preference, not something you have to use. However, you should be consistent and stick to your choice thereafter. What you can't do is mix your characters, so you can't open a string with a double quote and try to close it with a single quote, this will not work, you always have to close a string with the character, so with double quote or single quote with which you opened it.

So this string here for example is opened with a double quote and then I have no other double quote, therefore this string never gets closed, that actually therefore is invalid Javascript code and hence my IDE already complains here that this is an unterminated string literal so that this string has no end and if we would try to run this code and reload our page, indeed if you look into the developer tools again, you'll get an error. Now the interesting thing actually is if I do close it with a double quote, now everything in between will be treated as one text.

So when you open something with single or double quotes, everything in between the opening and closing single or double quotes will be one piece of text, which makes sense if you think about it. How would Javascript know whether you want to create a new string there, there also is nothing like a string inside of a string? Instead if we now reload the page, we got rid of our error but now our whole we want to create a string code is actually treated as one piece of text and therefore output as such here.

So you always have to close your string with what you opened it and everything in between will be treated as text. Now you can take advantage of this if you for example want to print this single quote character because right now if I use just single quotes and no double quotes and the same would be true if you were just using double quotes and no single quotes, if I reload, we get the output we saw before but what if I actually did want to output a single quote character here?

Well then, you could try to add a single quote inside of a single quote but this won't work, instead what now happens is that Javascript creates a string here and creates a string here and in between, it has this bracket which actually leads to some invalid Javascript code overall here because we're not using any operators that would try to concatenate that and even if we would, a single opening bracket like this is not valid Javascript code. So if you want to output the single quote character, you can actually take advantage of the double quotes and for example wrap your code, your string that contains the single quote which you want to output, between double quotes because now we use double quotes to create the string, everything in between the treated as text and therefore if we save that and we reload, now we see the single quotes here as well.

So that's one way of outputting single quotes if you wanted to, you could deviate from the rule of sticking to either a single or double quotes and make an exception if you really want to output the single or double quotes you otherwise use as your string delimiters. Here of course, I don't really want to print my single quotes so I don't need to do that. Now we'll dive into strings again and again throughout the course because there are more things you can do with them, one thing I want to do right away is restructure this string.

We're building our string here with three pieces of text you could say, with the opening parentheses, with this code thereafter or with this text thereafter and with the value that's stored in default result. Now in such cases, you can actually also use back ticks instead of single quotes. So this is now not a single quote, this is the back tick character which you'll find on your keyboard, get rid of all other single quotes you actually have and get rid of these pluses you used to combine your strings, only keep the plus which you want to output on the page and replace the closing single quote also with the closing back tick or with the back tick.

So now I got two back ticks which surround my text and therefore now if I save this, unsurprisingly here I say default result instead of the value which is actually stored in that default result constant but now back ticks give you access to a special syntax. You can now use a dollar sign in here and then an opening and closing curly brace and now you can put your variable or any expression which yields some result, which can be output as text, so you could also have a calculation like one plus one in here, so you can put that between your opening and closing curly braces now and what this does is it tells Javascript to output the value that's in this constant in this case in this place of your text. So it will not output the dollar sign or the curly brace, instead it will output the value of the expression as it's called, so in this case of the constant you have between the opening and closing curly brace. So if you now save that file and you reload, you'll see zero here which indeed is the value we have in default result. This only works with back ticks, if you used single or double quotes, this dollar sign curly brace thing would be treated as regular text and therefore output as such as you

can see. So this is a really nice feature, using these back tics with this dollar sign curly brace thing, if you have some text in which you want to embed or inject some dynamic value, so the result of some calculation or the value that's stored in a variable or a constant, then this is simply shorter, it saves you the manual string concatenation which we previously had to do where we combined multiple strings with the plus operator, this is simply a bit shorter and therefore how you typically would build a string that includes dynamic values.

This overall construct here is called a template literal, so if you ever Google for Javascript template literal, you'll find exactly this piece of syntax. Now there's actually more to it and we'll dive deeper into it throughout this course but this is the most basic and I would say most important form of using it because that's the form where you will work with it most often to have some text into which you inject or embed some dynamic value. Now some additional information about strings and template literals as we have it here.

One convenient thing about template literals is that you can easily write multiline strings there. Now with multiline strings, I mean strings which really do have a line break in them. So let's say here in front of the asterisk character, I add a couple of line breaks and hence this string looks like that might look a bit strange at first but this is valid Javascript syntax, we opened a string here, we close it here and since it is a template literal with back ticks, this is allowed. For a normal string with single or double quotes, this would not be allowed but I will come back to that. Now if you save that and you reload this in the browser, you'll not see a difference, though if you have the developer tools opened which you can always open with view developer, developer tools and you then click on this select icon there and you select this part of your webpage, you will see that indeed the whitespace is considered here, it's just the browser and the default behavior of the browser and the h2 element that basically strips this redundant whitespace but it's output there and depending on where you output this, in which element and how that element is styled, you might also get that whitespace or the extra line break here in your

webpage. So the fact that we don't see the line break here in the middle is really just due to how this is styled and rendered. If you go down here to the elements style of the h2 element which is selected and you add whitespace pre for example, then you will see the whitespace here as well because this is some CSS styling which does not omit the extra whitespace but instead render it, here in this case that means it renders this extra line break. So you can easily add line breaks here when using the template literal syntax, this can help you with readability because you might be able to read long strings easier or better here in the IDE if you add line breaks but you should always keep in mind that this is not just a visual thing for you in the IDE but that the line breaks really are part of the string.

The same is true if you indent this, for example you could think that if you write it like this, it's a normal string but it's more readable to you as a developer. Well if you save that and you reload, our styling will be lost because we reloaded but here on the right you can see this extra whitespace, it really is part of the string and if we re-add this style here to our h2 element here in the developer tools by setting whitespace to pre, you see we really do have the line break and the extra whitespace in here. So be careful when you use that and really only use the line break or extra whitespace feature here if you want to build a string that has the extra whitespace or that has the line break, don't do it just for readability.

Now if I come back to normal strings, there let's say we have an error message which we don't need for this app or for this website here but just to demonstrate how we work with normal, which means non-template literal strings, then of course you use single or double quotes and you might have a message like an error occurred, something like this. If you would want to split this across multiple lines, you have two options - you can close the string here by adding a single quote and then reopen a new one and combine them with a plus and then add a line break, this is valid Javascript code, you can span expressions that use operators across multiple lines, that would be possible here for mathematical operations just as it is possible for concatenating strings with the plus operator and here you can also indent. If you do this and you would output this somewhere on the webpage, this indeed would not include a line break and also not extra whitespace because this is really just something we do for us here in the IDE to make this more readable. The string that's getting constructed only consists of these characters between the single quotes, so there's no line break in there and there is also no extra whitespace.

Now if you would want to add a real line break here in a string enclosed by single or double quotes, that is possible with a special character or a special combination of characters - you add a backslash and then n. What this will do if it would be rendered to the screen is it will not output \n there but instead it will treat this as a line break. To show this, let's temporarily output the error message here instead of the calculation description, just temporarily so that we can see that.

Now with that if you reload here, we see an error occurred and if we go back and add our good old style here to the h2 element right in developer tools down there by setting whitespace to pre, you see the line break here as well and you can also see it here, there is a line break after error. So with this \n, you can add a line break in a string no matter if you use single or double quotes, you could also use this here in the template literal by the way, it's also supported there but there you don't need it because there you can just add a normal line break and since you're in a template literal, that will add a line break to the string as well.

So there, this is available, here in a normal string with single or double quotes, you need that \n thing. And by the way, using a backslash in a string has a special meaning, it escapes the character that comes after the backslash, which means the character after the backslash is not treated as a normal character with its normal meaning but instead combined with the backslash, it gets a special meaning. In this case here, we escaped the n and therefore we don't just output n here but instead backslash and n combined mean line break.

You have more such combinations and attached, you will find a list of available shortcuts or combinations here in your strings. One other important combination for example is backslash and then a single quote. This is helpful if you want to output a single quote in your string, especially if your string is enclosed by single quotes. Without the backslash, we would have a syntax error here because what happens is we open a string with a single quote, here we then close it and then here in this case, we have a redundant single quote that tries to open a new string which then never gets closed.

So we have to tell Javascript that this single quote should not be used as it normally uses single quotes, i.e. to close that string but instead that we want to output this single quote here as a normal character in our text and adding a backslash in front of it escapes the meaning the single quote would otherwise have and therefore allows us to do that, and of course an alternative always is to use double quotes to surround the string instead of single quotes and then you can use single quotes in the double quoted string without issues and without escaping it because it then won't have that special meaning of finishing your string or closing your string because you can only close a string with the character with which you opened it and since here, we opened a string with a double quote character, we can only close it with such and Javascript won't interpret a single quote as please close my string character, still useful to know that you could escape it like this. By the way if you want to output a backslash in the string, you need to escape this as well because otherwise, a single backslash always tells Javascript that the character after the backslash should be considered or should be escaped.

So if you want to output just a backslash, you put another backslash in front of it to tell Javascript hey the character after this backslash has a special meaning and double backslash then in fact tells Javascript I want to output a single backslash here as part of my string. So these are some of the useful things that you should know about strings, you will encounter them throughout this course and throughout your career as a developer. You don't need to learn all these things by heart, the attached list of escapable characters might be useful, though \n, \\ and backslash single quote are the most important ones I would argue, the ones you typically use most often.

And being aware of the template literal, that you can interpolate content here and that you can easily add line breaks and whitespace in here, that's also something which is good to know I guess. And with that, I reverted all of that, again I'm sending a calculation description to output result and I deleted the extra error message variable because we don't need it here to continue, I just wanted to dive into some of these string specialties and things you should know.

hey the character after this backslash has a special meaning and double backslash then in fact tells

you will encounter them throughout this course

lectures.title: Introducing Functions
lectures.text:
So now we got some core basics out of the way, we're able to work with some basic Javascript, with variables, constants, operators, numbers and strings and we're outputting that here on the screen but the calculator of course is not very responsive, all that's getting output here is kind of hardcoded into the script here, we're not using any user input, we're not really doing something when the user presses buttons here and therefore this is not really a dynamic script, instead it just runs from top to bottom when we load the page and therefore it immediately runs when the page gets loaded and it then does all these steps and outputs the result here, which is nice but again, which isn't really something interactive or dynamic.

So it's time to change that and for that, we need a brand new language feature which I haven't talked about before and that would be functions. I like to refer to functions as code on demand, now what do I mean with that? A function is a language construct which you don't just have in Javascript but also in other programming languages, which basically allows you to define some code which you then execute at a later point of time. You define the code in Javascript like this, you use that function keyword, then you use any name you want for that function, then your function can take something which is called parameters, so some input to the function if you will and then you have the so-called function body between curly braces which is the code you want to execute eventually.

Now as I said, this function can have these parameters, so name in this example would be a parameter and it can also return something which this example function here doesn't but which we'll see an action in this module. Now when you have a function defined, the interesting thing here is that the code in there doesn't run immediately when your script gets first executed, instead Javascript just sees that function and kind of registers it, stores it in memory you could say, you then execute the code in the function by calling that function. You call a function by using its name and then you add parentheses and if that function takes any parameters, any input which this function does and you can have more than one parameter separated by commas by the way but you'll also see that, so if a function takes parameters, you pass in a value for these parameters. Then this code gets executed with the data you entered as parameters and you can call such a function as often as you want, where ever you want in your code with different parameters if it takes parameters. So every function execution then runs independent from the other previous function executions you might have had in your code and the great thing about functions is that this now gives

you way more flexibility because thus far with all the code we write here, we basically write code which always executes from top to bottom when the script is loaded which is the case when the page is loaded and therefore all this code runs immediately. Now with functions, we can define code that should run later and we can then take such a function and actually attach it to the buttons here to make sure that only when a button is pressed, the function runs and this then allows us to write code which doesn't run immediately but which allows us to provide some interaction to our website, to only run some code when something happens for example and of course you're not limited to only running functions when a button is pressed, you can run functions based on a broad variety of events or manually call them in your code whenever you need to do that and actually here, we are calling a function.

I haven't really had a closer look at this yet but output result is a function I provide to you because it's defined here in the vendor.js file with the function keyword, then the name of the function, then in this case to parameters and then some code which is executed when the function is called, in this case this code here simply reaches out to our HTML page you could say, to our webpage and changes some text there, it displays the result of the calculation and this calculation text.

So these two pieces here which are changed in our webpage, that's done by this function effectively because this function communicates with that part of the HTML page with the help of these constants which in turn set up connections to these places in the HTML code you could say. So this function is registered here and we can call it from that file because we import this file after the other file, right, and the order matters of course, and we have access to that function and I'm calling that function here as I explained on the slide by repeating its name, then adding parentheses and between the parentheses, I pass in the values to the function which this function can use.

So here I pass in current result and calculation description, so I pass in the values that are stored in these variables and therefore, this function receives these values and that's important, it receives the values, not the variable names or anything like that, it receives the values stored in the variables and therefore in this function, we can then use these values to, in this case, output it in our HTML page but you could do whatever you want with these values.

So let's write our own function then so that we get a better feeling and understanding for how functions work and what we can do with them.

lectures.title: Adding A Custom Function
lectures.text:
So which function could we write? Well let's say we want to make sure that at some point of time in this module, we can click the plus button and add whatever we entered here to our current result which initially is zero and then if we type five here and click plus, we want to get five. So the new result is then five, if I thereafter type 10 and I click plus, we would get 15, right? So that would be an idea to get started with and for that, we need a function or we could add a function that does just that, that adds two numbers.

So for that we can define a function and it's up to you where you do that, you can actually do it kind of at the start of your script, maybe below your variable definitions or you can actually also do it at the end of your script and Javascript is smart enough to kind of read your entire file before it executes it and it will therefore find any functions you use so that it then automatically pulls these functions to the top so to say, so that if you define a function down there but you then use it somewhere above its definition, you can still execute that code without an error, something which by the way is not possible for variables and constants you defined with let and const but I'll come back to this in a second. For now, let's just add a function here let's say and let's name it add and you can pick any name you want here, the idea for the name here just should be that it describes the action this function will perform. So if its a function that adds two numbers, something like add or add numbers makes sense instead of give me two numbers which describes what it wants to get as an input but not what it does. You also don't want to have something like result as a name because what does this function

do, it doesn't tell us anything, it gives us some results, sure but for which operation? So here, add sounds like a fitting name, it makes it clear that this is a function which will do some addition and then as I said, a function can but doesn't have to take parameters. Now in Javascript and you'll see that throughout the course of course, there are functions which work without any input, let's say you have a function which kind of reads something from the HTML page.

This probably doesn't take any input because inside of the function, you have all the information you need to kind of reach out to the HTML page and get some data from there. On the other hand, a function which should add two numbers probably needs these two numbers which it should add, so we should provide two parameters here and you can give these parameters any name you want. So I will go with num1 and num2 but you could go with a and b or with number1 and number2 or whatever you want. These parameters which you define here are then available in the so-called function body which is the last missing piece on this function.

You add the function body by adding curly braces here, like this and now important, after the function you don't have a semicolon. Now you could add one but typically, you don't do that. You add a semicolon after all these one-line expressions here but after a statement as this is called, which includes such curly braces like this one does here, you don't add a semicolon. You can just keep this in mind, whenever you have some curly braces with some code, some executable code in between, you don't have a semicolon after the curly braces. Whenever you have these short expressions here, you have a semicolon at the end. So here, we have a function, keyword, name, parameters which are optional and then the function body and now in the function body, you can do all kinds of things, for example we can define a constant in here as well, maybe name this result and just add num1 and num2 here. Now num1 and num2 are like variables, though they're never defined with the let or const keyword but they're automatically defined by Javascript but they're only available inside of this function body, not outside.

So if I would try to do something with num1 here after the function definition, this would not work because num1 and num2 are variables only available inside of the function body. Now I used them here to add them together because I expect this function to be called such that whatever I get here on num1 and num2 are numbers and therefore, adding them works and I store the result in a new constant. Now the interesting thing here is that this constant is defined inside of the function, not at the top level of our script and that's something you can do in Javascript and that is actually quite normal.

You can have variables and constants here at the top level of your script, this is also called in the global scope but you can also have them inside of your function and it's actually important where you define that and I'll come back to that. For now, I want to calculate a result which I only use inside of the function and therefore we can declare and define this variable or this constant actually inside of that function. Now inside of the function body, you see that my IDE automatically indents the code, which means it's not totally on the left here but there is some empty space.

This is done for readability, technically this is not required, your code would run even if this would all be written in one line, so if you would move that right next to the curly braces and have that all defined in one line but having the functions split out across multiple lines and having this indentation, this empty space simply helps with reading or understanding your function. Now regarding the amount of empty space you have to the left, you can find a lot of discussions about that on the Internet.

Now here, I indent it by four blanks so to say, so four whitespaces, now you'll find discussions on the Internet whether you want to use four or two, whether you want to use tabs or whitespace, I'm a fan of whitespace and I'll typically use two also later when I do autoformat my document, it's configured to use two whitespaces here instead of four as I have it right now. You can go with whichever approach you want, you then should just stick to it and be consistent and you can also configure your code styling, your code formatting plugin for the IDE you're using to format your code according to your preferences.

Again my tool will later change this to two blanks here instead of four as I have it right now, you can go for either of that, you just should write readable code in the end. So this will now hold the result of num1 and num2 added together and now what can we do with the result? Well we can for example output it with the alert function. This is a function built into Javascript or built into the browser and provided to you in Javascript executed in the browser.

So we don't need to define this function on our own to call it, it's available, it's one of the built-in functions and there are a couple of built-in functions in Javascript, it depends on whether you're running Javascript in the browser or outside of the browser but here we're in the browser and there we have something like the alert function which is built in, made available by the browser. So alert then allows us to output a message and We could say the result is and then this is a string of course, add result here and of course you could have also used the back ticks notation with this dollar sign curly brace embedding here. Now I do create a string here where I concatenate my result because alert actually wants a message as a parameter and you can see this if you hover over alert in Visual Studio Code.

You see this is a function, again provided by Javascript or by the browser and this wants a message parameter, you can ignore the question mark for now, that simply means that providing this message is optional so you could throw an alert without a message which is kind of pointless though and message here is a parameter which actually should be a string because you want to output some text typically. So now I'm outputting this text here, this alert.

Now if I save this and we reload, nothing happens, we see no alert and the reason for that is that we're not calling this function yet. As I mentioned, you need to call a function in order for it to be executed. Now how do you call a function? Well you can just use the function name, so in this case add and if you picked a different name, you have to pick a different name here and then add parentheses like this. So a bit like you defined it here but without the function keyword and without the body because this defines what's inside of the function, how it works, this now calls the function and here I add a semicolon again because here I don't have the curly braces, I don't define the function here, I just execute this as a so-called expression, so I just have this line of code which is executed.

This line of code is also executed but it's executed such that this code is registered and stored by Javascript, so it kind of is made aware of this function, this line then executes and calls that function, it runs that function. Now this function to work correctly needs two parameters, also called arguments. It needs a number one and a number two and now here of course you don't provide num1 or num2, so you don't repeat these names, these are just internal names for these automatically created variables you can use inside of the function, instead here you now provide the concrete values that the function should use for running, so something like 1 and 2 if you want to add 1 and 2 together.

So now, num1 would be set to 1 and num2 would be set to 2 for this function execution and as I said we can now run a function multiple times by executing it again with 5 and 5 for example. Now we would execute the function two times - one with a value of 1 for num1 and the value of 2 for num2 and then the second time we run it, we pass in a value of 5 for num1 and the value of 5 for num2. And now if we save that and we reload this file, you see since this script runs right away, we get the alert with the result is 3 because here I am calling this function with 1 and 2 and if I click OK, I right away get another alert because we're running this function twice and script execution is kind of blocked by the alert which is why the second alert waits until we dismiss the first alert and then in that second alert, I see the result is 10 because I call this function with 5 and 5 and if I dismiss, then we see that page being rendered. So this is how we define a function and how we call it in Javascript.

Now I will emphasize again that a function can have as many parameters as it needs if it needs to have some, you can have one parameter, two as we have it here, three, five, four, as many as you want and a function can also do one other thing which we're not doing here, it can return something.

lectures.text:
Let's have a look at the order. Here, I'm defining my constant and my variable before I use it, right? I define current result right at the top of the script file and then here's the first time where I try to use it because I try to assign a new value to it and then I also use it down there when I forward it or when I pass the value that stored inside of it to output result. Now our code would break if I would move that all the way to the bottom of the script, so if I declare my variable here. Now if we reload this page, you see zero everywhere and if you open the developer tools again, in the console you'll see an error, cannot access current result before initialization.

Now this error message which the browser throws at us is pretty clear, we're trying to use it here and actually the error message even gives us the line number of where this error occurred, it's this number you see here, eight. So you see in line number eight and indeed that's the problematic number here, we're getting an error because we're trying to assign something to the current result variable without defining it first. So in Javascript, when using the let or the const keyword which you should use, you need to declare your variables and constants before you use them and declare is the part where you create the variable with let or const.

Then as mentioned for the same name, you must only declare it once, you can always reassign a value but with let and const, you only declare it once and you need to do that declaration before you first try to read from it or assign a value to it. You don't need to define it, so you don't need to initialize it with a value, if I just set up current result like this, this would actually be valid, if I now tried to execute it, you see this runs because I declared a variable before I then use it and since I use it by initializing it with a value here anyways or by assigning a value here anyways, I don't need to initialize and define it up there.

Now for functions, that's actually a bit different. I could grab this function and move it to the bottom of this file and if I do this, please keep in mind that I do call it up here, so technically before I define it. Still if I now reload this page, we get the same result as before and if we have a look into the developer tools, you see no new error here.

The reason for that is that for functions, we have a special behavior in Javascript. What Javascript actually does or what the browser actually does is that when it loads your script , it runs through it from top to bottom, it parses the entire script and actually it doesn't execute it right away, instead it just reads it from top to bottom and will take any functions it finds in there and automatically pull them to the top and be aware of them so to say. So it automatically registers all functions before it then really executes your script and that's just the special behavior Javascript has there.

Therefore it's up to you whether you prefer to have your functions at the bottom of your script or towards the beginning or is somewhere in between, you just should try to find some consistent code style. Now I personally like to have my functions towards the beginning of the file in most cases because I think if you then read the file as a developer, you kind of see what's in there and if you then later see that I call add, you recall that you did see that function definition above and you don't need to scroll to the bottom of the file to find it but there also are developers who prefer to have their function definitions at the bottom of the file and ultimately, there is no wrong or right is up to you but you should find one approach and then kind of stick to it for this program you're writing.

Of course, you can switch anytime in new applications you're creating or refactor your existing code and move your functions to the bottom or to the top if you kind of decide to go the opposite direction whilst in the project. Here again I'll have it towards the beginning but this is up to you. You also reformat that which I did with the autoformatting functionality I showed you in the first course module.

lectures.title: An Introduction to Global & Local Scope
lectures.text:
So the order matters for variables and constants, it does not for functions. There is one more interesting thing in our code here and that's that we have a constant here in the function and we have a variable and a constant outside of the function. Now when should you use what and what's the difference? Is there a difference? Well there is a difference and generally, if you use some data only in the function, like this result which I use in the function, I return it here, then you want to define it in the function.

I could have said let result here and then just assign a new value here and then we could even do something strange, we could say add like this and set current result equal to result. This code would technically work because what I'm doing here is I'm defining this result variable globally, so in my script, then I assign a new value to it in a function because in your functions and that's one important thing to keep in mind, you can access any variable or constant defined outside of the function, so you can read variables or constants defined globally, so we can interact with this result variable and I'm assigning a new value to it and therefore when I thereafter call the function, I actually don't care about the return value, I let that go into the void but since inside of the function, I assigned a new value to result, I can use that global variable and store it in another global variable or use it anywhere else, whatever you want to do. This however would not be very good code because we have a function that manipulates a global variable, that's sometimes something you want to do but often that makes your functions harder to understand and harder to predict what they're going to do and in addition, that we return this

value here is totally redundant, so not the best code we could write. Instead it's way better if we go with the setup we had before, where we have our contained constant here, we returned this and the function therefore works standalone. It doesn't magically change our global variables, instead we know when we call the function, this function will not alter anything, not anything global, instead it will only work with its internal data and then return us.

This is called a pure function, it gets some input, returns an output, for the same input it always returns the same output and it doesn't manipulate anything global but it is worth noting that functions can access global variables, they can also access other functions you might have defined, so you can call a function from inside a function and that is built into Javascript and it's a good thing which we'll also use from time to time. Now the other way around won't work though, if you define a constant or a variable inside of a function, then this has a so-called local or block scope which means it's available inside of this block, the block is surrounded or marked by these curly braces and we can use it anywhere in this block but we can't use it outside of there.

So if I try to throw an alert where I want to output the value that's stored in result here after defining the function, you will see that if I reload this, nothing happens. You see we seem to have an error and indeed if I open my console in the developer tools again, I get a reference error that result is not defined because I'm trying to use a variable here in line 9, so in this line here, which wasn't defined because as I just explained, you can use global variables and constants and functions inside of functions but you can't use local variables or constants or functions, so variables or constants or functions defined inside of functions and yes you can define functions inside of functions, something I'll dive in later, you can use those from outside of the function.

So using result outside of the function won't work because this is a constant defined inside of the function and it won't work no matter if we use it here or here after we call the function because you could think we only called a function here, so thereafter result has to be defined and now it should be available. Well actually as it turns out, if you now reload, you still get the same error here, now in line 11 instead of line 9 because I moved that code but still, result it's not available outside of the function and that's one important thing you need to understand with Javascript. Functions have full access to their surrounding context, so to all the variables and so on that are defined above them or outside of them but what you define inside of a function is only available in there, the only way of kind of getting it out is by returning it.

Now at this point you might also wonder, what if a variable is defined globally and then we try to create it locally in a function as well? So we have it declared with let or const globally and then we want to do the same with let or const in the function, so not overwrite the existing one but create a new one, is that possible? And the answer would be yes, this is a process called shadowing and in the lecture after this one, I'll dive a bit deeper into this.

lectures.text:
