Now our goal was to make sure that when we click the plus button, we actually take whatever the user entered here and we then use that in this addition and generate a new result which we then output. Now for that, we need to add an event listener to this button and now that's something we haven't learned at all, we don't really know how to interact with the HTML page because that's a bit more complex and I'll have a whole module where we dive into all the depths of this. For now we can take something from the vendor.js file, we can take this add button which the end is a reference, a pointer at this plus button we have here. So in app.js, we can use that, replace this code here with add button and then add a dot here which is strange, we have never seen that before here, let's ignore it for now and then type addEventListener, written like this.

This is actually a function built into the browser you could say which is tied to this button which is why we have this dot in between and we'll dive a bit deeper into what this dot means in just a while. So for now, let's just write this and now this is a function that takes two parameters or two arguments and the first parameter is actually a string which identifies the event to which we want to listen. Now there are a bunch of available events and I'll walk you through them and where to find them all in the dedicated module, for now we can add click here.

Now as a string between single or double quotes or back ticks, though back ticks don't make a lot of sense here because we don't need to embed anything dynamic here. So that's the first parameter, the second parameter and that's now the strange thing actually should be a function. It's not that strange if you think about it though since functions are a code on demand, you want to make sure that you tell the browser, that you tell Javascript which function should be executed if this button is clicked.

So how do we now point at a function here? Well you could do something like add here, right, you could execute your add function here. Now this would actually be wrong and this is one of the trickier things to understand in Javascript or in programming in general, it's not exclusive to Javascript. We want to tell the browser what to execute when a click occurs. Now if we execute add like this, no matter if we add arguments or not which we of course should theoretically though, what happens is that this code gets parsed by the browser when it encounters our script and in the end after registering all functions and so on, it will go ahead, it will add this event listener but then this here tells the browser call this function because we have parentheses with arguments here. We want to tell the browser however or we want to tell the Javascript engine, don't execute this function right away, instead keep in mind that this function should be executed when this button is clicked. The solution therefore is to not pass the function here with parentheses but just the function name. By doing that, you're telling the Javascript engine when this button is clicked, have a look at the function with this name and execute it for me.

So before we manually called the function in our code because we the developer so to say, we're the one executing the function, now we want to make sure that the browser can execute the function when the click occurs and we don't know when that will be the case, so we want to give Javascript the name of the function which it should call for us, we want to allow the browser to call that function for us. Here's a real life analogy, you live in some flat and you have an address where you get your mail and so on.

lectures.title: Working with Code Comments
lectures.text:
Now we wrote some code already, a feature which you can also use in Javascript and many other programming languages are comments. You can add comments to your code to make it more understandable to fellow developers or to yourself if you were coming back to your code after a couple of months of break or something like that. Now a comment in Javascript can be added in two ways, you can add it here, like you add regular code by adding two forward slashes, this is a comment now. This means that this is there for people to read but it has no effect on your code.

If you reload, you don't see an error or anything like that, it's not executed as code, instead this is just there to comment your code, to make it more understandable. If you have a longer a comment to write which should be split across multiple lines, you can of course add another line of comments here with two other forward slashes but you can also add a block comment by adding a forward slash and then a star and now you see everything is green down there because now everything after that is treated as a comment, so this is also a comment and this is and now you have to close the comment with a star and another forward slash, so the opposite combination we had here to open it.

So now this allows you to write a longer comment across multiple lines without starting every line with two forward slashes. Now how will you use comments in your code? You shouldn't comment the obvious, so if you comment this is a function that extracts the user input from the input field, that's not the best comment because for one you don't want to write long text, you don't want to write essays here, instead you want to write short to-the-point comments that add some extra context or understanding that isn't obvious from looking at the code.

So if I look at this code, it's pretty obvious at what it does, we could just add something like gets input from input field. Why is that useful? Because it adds this extra context that this is coming from an input field because it might not be obvious, by looking at the code, that user input refers to input field, so that could be something we could add to make understanding that code a bit easier and simply save the developer who's looking at the code to time to kind of find out what user input is referring to.

Here we could add something like generates and writes calculation log, again this might not really be necessary because that's quite easy to see if you look at this but if you have a first quick look at this, it could look daunting and then this makes it clear that this is in the end just a helper function that outputs some information and generates that information as well. You can also add a comment inline, so after some code, like here, we could say from vendor file to make it clear that this function is not defined somewhere in this file but lives in the vendor file, otherwise this might not be obvious and again if someone wants to follow our code or understand it, this could help with understanding it.

So adding such a short inline comment also sometimes can be useful. In general, you want to comment your code, especially if you share it with others but you don't want to overdo it, don't add redundant information, don't write too long comments because then people will not read them at all and they actually get less out of them than if there were no comments at all and you don't want to comment the obvious, instead provide some extra context, extra information that can help understand your code faster or briefly share your thoughts regarding the code you wrote here.

That's something you could add with comments.

lectures.title: More Operators!
lectures.text:
We got quite a nice application going here, at least for the basics into which we're diving. Now I want to dig deeper into some of the core Javascript features you've got to know because you will need them in many of the projects or the applications you're going to create with Javascript and one important feature if you want to call it like this is a special set of operators which you can also use in your Javascript code. Now we already saw the assign operator, the plus, the minus, the multiplication and the division operator, we used those, now there are a couple of shortcut operators if you want to call them like that.

For example here, what we're doing and not just for adding but also for subtracting and so on, what we're doing is always we're assigning a new value to current result and that new value is based on the current or the old value of current result plus, or minus and so on, a number. Now if you have a calculation like this which is quite common, there is a shortcut, you can absolutely write it like this but if you assign the result to the same variable you're using on the right side of the equal sign, you can omit that variable there on the right side, omit the operator and instead write plus equal, so instead of a single equal sign, use plus equal and that's exactly the same as having, in this case here current result.

equal to current result plus. So you can remove that from the right side and add a plus here and as you will see if I now save this and I reload this, if I enter a five here and I click plus, that still works as before. So that did not change, that still works but now we have a shorter code snippet here, we have less code which we have to write. Now the same is available for all the other operators, so instead of this code here with the minus, we can also write minus equal and the same for the multiplication and division.

So we can take this, multiply this here and also remove that division code here and use this shortcut and with that if we save that, you'll see that now as I reload this, we can add, we can subtract, we can multiply and we can also divide. This all works, now with this shorter code thanks to these shortcuts. Now there also are other shortcuts or other shorthand operators as they're also sometimes called, if you have let's say the case that you want to set a new value to a variable, let's say to current result and that is the current value plus one, so exactly plus one, which we of course don't need here but imagine we had that case, then instead of writing this, you can also write current result plus plus. The same is available for minus, we can write current result minus minus.

It's not available for multiplication or division because, what would that be, multiply the number with one? Well that's the same number and the same for division, right? But adding one or subtracting one, that makes sense and with this increment or decrement operator as it's called, that is possible in a very short way. So if we do that here and I comment out this line for the moment, this by the way is a common pattern, that you use comments to temporarily remove some code which you then can re-add later but since comments are ignored, you can kind of temporarily remove code by commenting it out as it's called.

So if we do that and we therefore only reduce current result by one, if we click add, you will see that now if I don't enter anything here because I'm not using the value anyways right now, if I add a plus, you have a result of minus one, we can ignore this NaN thing for now, here the result is the thing that matters. So this gets lower and lower, always by one each time I click the plus button because we're decrementing this here. Little side note, you could also write minus minus or plus plus in front of the variable, and it will actually have a small impact or a small difference, not if you just use it like this to change the value but if you're interested in the return type of this operation, if you add plus plus in front of this, it will actually add it to current result by adding one, just as it does if you add it thereafter. If you have plus plus or minus minus in front of this variable, then this operation returns the edited value, if you have it after the variable, well then this returns the value of the variable before it was changed.

Now here we're not using the return value but if we would alert that return value, it still changes current result always in the same way by adding one but this operation returns a new value which you can or cannot use, depending on whether you want to use it. So here for example, I'm using it by outputting it with the alert and if we do that and I reload here, you see I get one here, so I get the result after the change. If I add the pluses at the end here and I repeat here, save this and reload, then I get it before the change. So this plus plus and minus minus operator return something, it returns the value before or after the change depending on where you add the pluses and minuses.

Again in many cases, that doesn't matter because the variable itself is always edited in the same way, it just makes a difference regarding the value which is returned. Now of course here, I'm not interested in incrementing this so I'll just remove that line and comment this back in, by the way in case you're wondering how I did this so quickly, I use the shortcut here in my IDE, under edit, you can use toggle line comment to add or remove a comment and to quickly comment code in or out.

So these are some additional operators which I recommend that you keep in mind and that therefore completes our list of operators which we are aware of for now with these shorthand operators and the increment and decrement operator.

lectures.title: More Core Data Types!
lectures.text:
Those extra operators which you have are good to know because sometimes you can save some extra code by using these shorthands, these abbreviations. Even more important than that however are other data types you can work with. We learned about numbers where you have numbers with or without decimal places, numbers without decimal places are also called integers, numbers with decimal places are also called floats. Besides numbers and text or strings as it's called, you also get other core data types which you have to know when working with Javascript, for example there are booleans. Now booleans are a bit strange and a bit hard to understand right now but they really shine once we learn about controlled structures, if statements which we'll do in a separate module soon. Booleans are effectively values which have one of two possible values, true or false.

So where you can, as a number, have any number or as a string, have any combination of characters, booleans are exactly one of two values, true or false. Now you might wonder when you need such a restricted data type and the answer is quite often, because quite often in code, you have some condition, like is the user currently logged in, which is either true or false and then you want to run different code based on that condition maybe and that's what I meant, booleans shine if you have conditional code and we haven't really learned about this yet but we will learn about this in a whole module as it's such a core feature.

So already keep booleans in mind, we'll dive deeper into them a bit later and then very deeply though. More important and something we won't see right away are objects. Objects are an extremely important type in Javascript, maybe the most important type if you would have to choose one, of course you need all of them but objects are really important. Objects allow you to group data you could say, something like this. Now you create object with curly braces and of course we already saw curly braces when we wrote a function and that of course was not an object, that was the function body but without the function keyword and so on, in the place where you could also use a number or a text, you can create an object by adding curly braces and then you have key-value pairs in there.

Now as I said, you use that for grouping or relating data, let's say you have a little program where you work with persons, where you have user data that you kind of need in your Javascript code. Now each user might have a name and an age, of course you could have standalone separate that variables for that but having an object makes it much easier to understand that this data kind of belongs together, that it's related, that you use it as one piece of information if you will and therefore objects are really powerful, you can also do way more with them than just group data and we will do way more with them throughout the course but the data grouping functionality on its own is already pretty amazing and very important.

Now and speaking of kind of organized or grouped data, another core data type are arrays. Now arrays are created like this with the square brackets here, also in the same place where you would create numbers or text or whatever you need and an array is simply a list of data. So arrays are always great if you need to store a list of data, let's say a list of transactions, a list of maybe calculations in our calculator and you can store any data in there.

It can be an array of integers, so of numbers without decimal places like in this example but it could be an array of text, an array of floats, an array of objects, even an array of arrays is possible and you can also mix data in there, you can have an array that has numbers and text elements and so on. Elements in an array are separated by commas, as are the key-value pairs and objects but I'd say it makes way more sense to understand and explore these objects and arrays by simply working with them, so let's do that in the scope of our project.

lectures.title: Using Arrays
lectures.text:
How could we introduce arrays and objects here? Well let's say we want to log every operation we do, so when we add, when we subtract, when we multiply, we kind of want to log this, we want to store this in an internal log which we theoretically could send to a server or anything like that. In Node.js, we could write it to a file, in the browser we can't because we don't have access to the filesystem there for security reasons but we might want to keep track of that, right, because we want to store it on our own analytic server for example.

Now in such a case, we want to keep track of a list of operations because we're not just interested in the first click on the add button but we want to store every click on every button and therefore we need to have a list of data that gets bigger and bigger over time. For that, we can add a new global variable here and I will create it here with the let keyword and name it log entries, the name is totally up to you of course, again it should be a name that kind of gives an idea of which kind of data you're going to store and it's a plural name here because I'll have multiple elements in there because it should be such an array as I mentioned.

Now you create an array by adding square brackets and it can either be an empty array or of course an array with some initial data and there, each element is separated from the other elements by a comma. Typically you also add a whitespace to improve readability but that's not required, the comma however is required. Now here, I want to have an empty array though because initially we have no log entry, so therefore we can create it just like this.

Now if we want to add a log entry, let's say when we click the add button here, we could say we go down there and now we want to edit this array and add a new entry. Now how can we do that? Well we can refer to log entries and now previously we always assign a new value by setting this equal to a new value. Now of course, we can set it equal to a new value here as well and here the new value would be a new array because I want to overwrite the existing empty array and therefore of course we could also leave this uninitialized with a new array which now includes let's say the entered number, right?

So now, we set this to a new array, a new list of data with one element and that one element is this entered number which we have. Now that's one way of editing an array, we basically overwrite the array stored in the variable with a brand new array and sometimes that's just what you need but sometimes you also want to edit the existing one and for that, let's reinitialize this to an empty array up there, let's say we want to add a new element to this existing array, for that we can reach out to this array and not assign a new value with the equal sign but instead use a dot to use a function that belongs to the array so to say and there, there's a specific function built into Javascript and that's the push function.

Now actually, arrays have way more than just a push function and I have a whole module dedicated to arrays where we dive way deeper into them, for now let's focus on the push function. The push function does what the name implies, it pushes a new element onto this array, so it adds a new element to the list and there we could say that should be the entered number. Now it would be kind of neat to see that array and for now we can do something which you will often do during development, you can add console log here and that's a built-in functionality built into Javascript, a built-in command which the browser understand which allows you to output something into that development console, into the console which you see in the developer tools where we previously saw some errors.

Now here we're not outputting an error but an information log message and here we can for example log the log entries, so the value that's currently in that variable, which should be that array with one extra element if we run this for the first time and after the second click, it should have two elements because we always push a new one. Let's see, let's save that, open the developer tools in your browser and go to the console there, reload the page and now enter any number you want and click on the plus and of course you see the result down there but more interesting than that, you see this thing on the right here, that is your array and if I add another value, so if I click the plus again, you see now this is the new log, this now is a new array or the old array with an extra element to be precise.

You see we have two elements and they're separated by commas, in this case two numbers but again you could store any data in the array and therefore that's what we have in there and this is a great way of keeping track of multiple items, multiple pieces of data that are kind of belonging together and that should be managed as a list of data. Now if you want to read from the array in the sense of not logging it entirely but let's say you want to extract the first element that's in there, so the five in this case, well then you can also do that. If you want to access a specific element in the array, you do this by adding square brackets after the variable name if you access the variable, so in a place where you want to get or read the variable, you can also add square brackets thereafter and now in there, you add the index, so the position so to say, of the element you want to extract. Now you could think that you add one here if you want to read the first value but this will actually not work because and that's just something you have to know but thankfully it's the case in pretty much all programming languages or in most programming languages, arrays are zero-based or their index is zero-based, which means the first element in an array has

an index of zero. So if you want to access specifically the first element, you want to retrieve that, to work with it, then you do this with this square bracket notation and then with index zero. Index one would refer to the second element, index two to the third, well and so on and index zero therefore to the first one, that's just how it works in many programming languages. So now what we should see when we log this is that we don't log the entire array but a single value of the array, to be precise always the first element in the array.

So if I now reload this and now I add let's say six here, you see a log six, not as an array so without the square brackets but just a number because that's what we're retrieving and retrieving by the way does not mean that we destroy the array, it's still there, it's still managed in memory, I'm just reading a single value from there because that's also something you need quite often in programming, that you have a list of data but then for a specific operation, you want to work with one specific entry of that list and again as so often, we'll of course also see examples for that throughout the course.

So that's how you can add a new element to an array, by the way if you would try to read the second element, so the one with index one here, we would actually get an error here in this code because when I reload this, when I add a new element here, you see I now get undefined, so not an error technically but also not the value we expected because of course this already fires, for the first element we add it, so when I clicked the button for the first time and there we simply have no second element in the array yet because we only added one value, so we pushed one value into the array, so there only is one value in there and as you learned, that one value has the index of zero, only after the second button click, we have two values in there and then we can retrieve a value with index one which is the second element.

So now if I add another element here, now this gets logged and if I had a third one, I of course still get eleven logged here because I still extract the second element and that's still the element we added on the second click. So that's arrays, we can manage lists of data with them, there is way more we can do with them than just push and access single elements but again that's also something we'll gradually learn throughout the course because we also need some other things, some other pieces of knowledge before we can fully unleash their power.

There are already quite nice like this though to manage lists of data.

lectures.title: undefined, null & NaN
lectures.text:
With arrays, booleans, objects, numbers and strings, we had a look at the most important or almost all of the most important data types you have in Javascript but there are two additional important data types and one strange value which looks like a data type and that would be null, undefined and NaN. Now what's that? These are kind of special values, though null and undefined are both values and data types. So what's the idea behind that? Undefined is the default value uninitialized variables have, so if you create a variable and you don't assign a value at the beginning with the equal sign, then this variable is undefined.

We also saw undefined in the log when we try to access an element in the array at an index where no element was created yet, then we tried to access an element which wasn't there and therefore we got back a value of undefined. So that's a value, it's a value that indicates that nothing's there but at the same time, it's also a separate data type. So just like numbers and strings are a data type, undefined is also a data type actually. Now you should never assign undefined to a value on your own, so never write equals undefined because that's just a default value you have if something has never been assigned a value.

Now you could have cases in your code where you indeed get something, where you're not sure if it's undefined or not and later you will learn how you can check whether a value is defined or undefined but it's already important to be aware of this type. Now related to this, there is the null value and type. Now it's very similar to undefined, it means that there is no data but undefined is the default value for variables and so on where you never assigned a new value. Null is never a default value on the other hand, instead you have to set something to null to use that value and that's often used if you want to reset or clear a variable, let's say you have some user input and you want to reset this, you could set it to an empty string but you could also set it to null for example, to make it clear in your program that there currently shouldn't be a value because no value has been entered or whatever.

And again this is especially useful later if we can also run some checks, some conditional checks with if statements to find out if a value is set and then do something or if it's not set. So undefined and null are important to manage empty data, either because it never was set or because you want to set it to empty, to null. They're very similar but they're not entirely equal because of the reasons I explained. Now there also is one other special value and that's NaN, that stands for not a number and technically, unlike undefined and null which also are their own types, this is not a type, instead it's of type number, it's not its own type and you can therefore use it in calculations where you work with numbers.

Now the idea behind NaN is that it's kind of like an error code if you run a calculation with something that doesn't include a number, so if you have let's say a multiplication with text or anything like that, then you would get not a number as a result and if you use the not a number value in that calculation, you also get not a number as a result. So this yields not a number if you use it in calculations and it's the result of calculations that are invalid.

Now you might wonder why you would ever run an invalid calculation, keep in mind that Javascript allows you to write highly dynamic code. So like in the case of our calculator here, you could have a calculator where users can enter any value, where they are maybe not forced to enter a number and where therefore you could run a calculation with some user input which is not a number and then you could get such a not a number result. Again this is most useful if you also have the abilities of comparing it or of checking it with some if statement to run some code if you get such an invalid result but it is worth being aware of this type. Now to quickly give you an idea of these types, let's clear that Javascript console here because here we also can type some Javascript code which runs immediately, which is immediately evaluated and here I want to show you these three types I just talked about. Let's create a variable here, userName maybe and not set this equal to anything, just like this, so we declare it but we don't initialize it.

If we now hit enter, you see undefined here because that's the return value of this execution here but if you now write console log userName or actually here in the console you can just write userName and it will automatically log into the console, you'll see the value that's in there and that's also undefined. Now of course if I now assign a value like Max and I print this, you see Max here, it also showed it here. So that's one thing, we got undefined if we haven't set this to a value yet.

Now if we would want to reset this, as I mentioned you should never do this, technically this would work but this is not recommended, instead you should set this to null now, this other special value and if you do that and you have a look into userName now, you see this indeed is null. Now for the not a number example, if you run three times hi here, you see the result is not a number. If you run three times not a number which is also a special value written like this, you also get another number.

So these are the special types which, for now, you should just keep in memory somewhere and which we'll come back to throughout the course when we'll be able to check for whether a variable has a value or not, for now just loosely keep these values in mind.

lectures.text:
Now that we had a thorough look at these basic and very important types you can use in Javascript, these types of data, I want to show you a little keyword which you can use in your code here of course as well and that's the typeof keyword. The typeof keyword lets you evaluate the type of a variable at runtime. Now we could use it here but to quickly see the result, I'll just do it here in this console. You use it by typing typeof and then the name of the variable which you want to evaluate or of course just the hardcoded value like this string here.

So here if I run this, you see I get back a string which contains the name of the type I used, so here it's a string with the name string in it and indeed that is the case here, right, that is a string. Now of course we could also use our userName variable which we initialized earlier, set this to Max and check typeof userName here and we'd also get string, right. So we can also use a variable here and you'll get the type of the value that's stored in the variable.

Now we can of course also check the type of a number and you see it is number then, it's a string which simply contains that description of the type, so in this case number or the name of the type, so in this case number and that's the same no matter if we use an integer as here or a floating point number as we do here. We also can check typeof true, now we haven't really worked with true or false yet but these are these booleans I mentioned and hence of course it prints boolean here. We can also check the type of an array, like this and you see here we actually get object and that's interesting, an array is a very important feature, very technically though it's of type object, so there is no special array type.

It's a special type of object if you will but the overall type is just object. So thus far, we saw a string, number, boolean and now object. Now if we check undefined, we see as I mentioned that this has its own type, undefined, on the other hand null is also just of type object, so it also has a type, a special type which is not the same as undefined but it's not type null but instead type object, so another special kind of object if you will. If you on the other hand check not a number written like this, we see it's of type not a number, so this is not an object, this is not undefined, this is not its own type, this is a number instead.

So typeof, quite nice here to get an understanding of which kind of data you're working with, of course we'll see all these different types of data in action throughout this course and all the examples where we need to work with numbers, with strings, with arrays, with objects and so much more.

lectures.text:
I already outlined it in the introduction video, there are effectively three parts that we'll have a look at in this course module. The first part I want to have a look at is how you can write code efficiently and with that, I don't really or don't necessarily mean that you can write code as quickly as possible but I mean that you are able to really get a lot out of the tools you're working with, that you know how to write code without too much copy pasting or manual work.

Now the next block we'll then have a look at is how you can find help because in programming, even if you took many courses, even if you've been a developer for many years, you'll always encounter scenarios or use cases where you're not sure how to solve something or where you know there was a feature in Javascript, some built-in function that allows me to do that but I can't remember that function, I don't recall how it worked in detail and that's totally normal.

So don't take this course or any other resource as a I have to learn it by heart to resource, rather learn how a language generally works and how you have to think about writing code and then also know where to find help and where to dive deeper if you need a specific feature or a specific command and that's also something I'll explore with you in this module.

It means that you should work in a productive environment, now with that, I'm talking about the environment on your machine, not the environment you're working in. Of course that should also be productive but that's something you'll have to figure out, where you work, in which office and you might also not be able to control this if you for example are employed.

So I'm talking about the IDE, the editor and about configuring it such that you like working with it. lectures.text:
Now of course the look and feel of your editor and your IDE is one thing but it doesn't stop there. There I could mark log entries and if I now hit the shortcut for this or I choose the option here of course but using the shortcut is simply faster, so if I do this, then it selects the next occurrence of this same word if you will in my code. So now I have this selected and this selected and that's great for renaming for example, if I want to rename this, I can just hit the shortcut until I have all occurrences selected, I also get a hint here on the right in the scroll bar where all these occurrences are and then I can give this a new name and now it's renamed in all the places where I did use it.

So that allows you to change and refactor things much faster and this is also a crucial shortcut and all these selection shortcuts can be really helpful, for example for moving something up a line or down a line, that makes restructuring your code which you will ultimately do a lot in development. way easier. Now not all shortcuts might work for you, maybe you want to change one and you can do that under code preferences and then there, keyboard shortcuts. If you can't find a shortcut otherwise, you can search for this here on Mac by just typing command D and now it shows you all shortcuts that include the command key and the D key, of course also the control or the shift key is supported, same for space and so on. So you can also search for keys and find the actions that are bound to these keys.

So that gives you a lot of power to really find all the different commands you might need and then of course it's needless to say that you can change them by just right clicking on this and then change key binding. So really make sure that you adjust these shortcuts to your requirements and that you simply have a look at the menu up there, the menus up here, to find some actions that might look useful to you and bind these to shortcuts which you can reach and as you work and as you grow as a developer, you'll find more and more shortcuts to work with.

So the goal is not to stop developing for two days now and just explore all possible shortcuts, you can do that if you like but my recommendation would be that you just have a brief look at the options you find here in the menu and experiment with these options and then as you continue with development and as you write code, you will automatically reach situations where you think that would be really nice if I could fix it with a shortcut and then you can go to this shortcut changing menu, to the keyboard shortcuts menu here and simply search for the action you want to do and see which shortcut this has and if it doesn't have a shortcut yet, you can assign one.

lectures.title: Working with Auto-Completion & IDE Hints
lectures.text:
Now all the shortcuts don't help you if you write bad or incorrect code but here again modern IDEs or editors like Visual Studio Code have you covered, you get a lot of autocomplete here. Let's say here, with our create and write output method, if I want to use this method, let's say I would want to call it here, I can type create and write or just create in my case and I get suggestions. I get suggestions of functions or variables that I could use here that basically includes the words create and they don't just have to start with it, they include it anywhere.

It doesn't even have to be one word as you can see with the suggestions down there, all properties or functions that includes the characters I just typed in the right order will be shown here and then the suggestions are narrowed down the more I type. So that's really useful because that allows you to write code quicker, for example here, I can just type create, the IDE intelligently guesses that I probably mean create and write output, otherwise I could select a different option and then all you have to do is tap enter or tap to use that and to complete that word, which of course saves you the hassle of writing it all on your own, so that's much faster. Now in addition, you'll also find a short description of what you are going to use here on the right, here for example you'll see that this is a function, that this is the name and that this function will take a couple of arguments which of course allows you to find out if that is the function you really want to use here.

Some functions and properties, especially the built-in ones even have short descriptions attached to them which you then also find here in the panel on the right to learn more about it and learn more about what this will do for you. So this is very important and really helpful. You'll also get something similar if you for example add a dot after an object or in this case here, after an array which turns out to be an object. If you add a dot here, you get this auto completion that offers you a list of all the properties or functions you can access on this object, like the push function here which allows us to add a new entry, then you get a short description of it here on the right, you see the arguments it takes, this syntax might not fully be clear at this point but that's not a problem, we'll dive more into arrays later and you'll see that an array for example has way more methods or way more functions attached to it and I'll dive into way more of them in a separate module focused on arrays.

So this dot notation also comes with great auto completion and by the way, if this menu ever closes or you accidentally close it, if you want to bring it back, of course you can delete the dot and add another one but you can also just use a shortcut which by default should be control space and this will bring up this suggestions menu again. So this is another core feature which I would recommend that you use. You can also hover over the things and you'll get a short description of what this is and what this does for example that pushes a function, it's called method here and I'll come back to what the difference is but it's essentially a function and you see what it does.

So this is also helpful, you can hover over the things to learn a bit more about it. And when you call a function, like let's say create and write output and you enter the parentheses, you by default get this parameter help here where you see all parameters and the value which you now need to provide for the first parameter is even highlighted here, so that you know that whatever you're going to type now will be received on this operator parameter and once you enter this and you add a comma, you see that now the next parameter is highlighted, now that's really convenient. If you ever close this menu for some reason, you also get a shortcut for this, so let's quickly check this and maybe just type parameter here.

What we see is we got this trigger parameter hints shortcut which is this combination - shift command space in my case, so if I now type shift command space here, you see this menu reopens so that's all the really convenient. So these are the core features you should be aware of and you should experiment with and you should leverage because that helps you write correct code faster and without errors and that's always something you want to do of course.

lectures.title: Debugging JavaScript - An Overview
lectures.text:
So you know how to write your code and how to dive into external resources and find support, now you're writing code and you're having errors in there and that will happen. That doesn't make you a bad developer, that's just totally normal, you will always also encounter errors when writing code. Now we need to learn how to find and fix them and that there also are different kinds of errors. So when we think about debugging our code, there are different kinds of errors you can get, you got errors which basically show you some error message, where your app maybe crashed, where it doesn't work at all and you've got logical errors. Logical errors don't make your app crash, they also don't result in an error message but your app behaves incorrectly.

Now I will show you both kinds of errors in this module and show you how to find and fix both. Now if you're getting an error message, read and utilize it, seriously. So many people see an error message and they just go into panic mode and that's it, so many people don't even bother reading error messages even though many error messages are quite clear regarding what's wrong. So by just reading it and diving into the line of code which typically is included there, you can fix many errors. If you got an error message which you don't understand, you can Google it because guess what?

You're probably not the first person who got an error message, so put it into google and you'll find many solutions there. But sometimes that alone doesn't do the trick, sometimes you need to look into your code whilst it's executing to get a feeling for how values of variables change over time and where something might be going into a wrong direction. For that you can use console log which I already showed you, this is a built-in command which outputs information in this developer tools console.

It's invisible to the users of your page, unless they open the developer tools, then they can see it and that's important to keep in mind. Everyone can see what you output here not just you but it doesn't show up on the page itself and it allows you to log whatever you want, log whichever variable you want to log and this can be really useful for getting a first look into certain things or values of your code. You can also have multiple console log statements to see how things change throughout your program execution, so the kind of output, the flow of your application. But writing these console log statements can also be cumbersome, especially if you have a more complex error to fix.

You might need to throw a lot of console log statements into your code, change them, configure them correctly and that can be annoying over time, so therefore also leverage the debugging tools which are built into modern browsers, I recommend the Chrome debugging tools which are really amazing but Firefox also has debugging tools built in for example. Same for Edge and so on but in this course, I will go with Chrome and show you how to work with those.

Last but not least, your IDE can also help you with debugging and with fixing errors and we'll have a look at all these things now in the next lectures.

lectures.title: Next-Level Debugging with the Chrome Devtools & Breakpoints
lectures.text:
Now what are breakpoints? Breakpoints allow you to tell the browser to stop code execution when a certain part in the code is reached. So for example here we can go to the add function and place a breakpoint right here so that we stop code execution when we reach this line, so that we can then look into our code and its current state during execution and that's what we'll be able to do. Now to place a breakpoint, you just need to click on a line number here and you see this mark, you can also place multiple breakpoints by the way.

Now if you placed that, what will happen is that if you now run your code, in this case when I add 10, you see now this gets frozen, you see this message here paused in debugger, you can resume by clicking this play button but let's not do that now and here on the right, you see this line now gets highlighted in blue which means this is where the code execution stopped and now you can for example hover over things to see their current values, for example since code execution always stops before this line where you placed the breakpoint is executed, you see that entered number is currently undefined.

Makes sense because as I mentioned, it stops before this is executed so this is all undefined. Now you can step through your code with these controls down there, you can always resume which means that it will continue running until it hits the next breakpoint if there is any. You can step over the next function call which basically means you move to the next line, I'll show this later, you can also step into a function call, that would be nice here because here we are calling a function and by stepping into it, you see we now jump to that code which is executed in that function and now here again I can hover over this, here since user input refers to an element in my HTML page, I even get it highlighted on the left which is another convenience feature and here since user input is a quite complex object, I can even find all the properties of this object and get the value that's in there, also by hovering over a value and we see this is a string, 10.

This might already allow us to fix this error at this point but let's say we haven't fixed it yet. So we see that's a string, okay, we're now done, we can now step out of the current function back to the code where we had our breakpoint and we're now in the next line and we now see entered number is that string. Now we're not interested in this line so we can just go to the next line with step over next function call or this button, the difference is that this will always step over the next line and if a function is executed there, it will not go into that function but just call that function and go to the next line with the result of that function call available. This on the other hand will always go to the next step and if that's inside of a function, it will go into that function, so it kind of combines that this button and this button and we can go through our code with these buttons therefore. You also see I got this nice the output shown by the developer tools here which shows me the values of entered number and the initial result even without hovering over them and that for example should already allow us to kind of fix the problem here because now we see this is a string and this might allow us to see that that might be the problem with our addition,

that we're working with a string here. If I go over this line, we see current result is this concatenated string and now it should definitely be clear that the problem is that we're kind of working with strings here, this would probably allow us to fix the error. Now before we fix it though, let me show you what else we got here in the debugging view. At the bottom for example, I haven't really talked about that, besides these buttons, you see your call stack. The call stack is essentially a list of all the functions that have been called. Let's say here we go into create and write output, if I do that, you see now this is on the call stack as well and below that is the add function, you can also click here to jump between the lines that are connected.

What this means is that the topmost thing is always the function which is currently running and below that, you'll find other functions that were responsible for calling that function, so that kind of shows you the order of your code execution if you will. There, you also see the variables that are available, local variables and global variables. There by the way, we have a lot of dummy variables because in the browser, we've got a bunch of general information about the window available globally but that's also something I'll dive in later. Local variables here would be the variables available in this function here and that are essentially all the different parameters I'm getting and calc description and we can ignore the this thing here for now.

So that can also be really nice, that you see which variables are available there and which values they currently have. You can even change the values here, for example here we could change this to a number and change initial result to a number to see whether this now executed correctly and if it does, you would see that the problem is not our addition logic but the logic where we get the input. So changing these values here is also something useful you can do.

You can also set up a watcher here, there you can add an expression where you want to watch certain values. You can either just enter the value name, like entered number and now you always see the value of this variable here as it changes throughout your function execution but you can also add a more complex expression, like entered number plus current result and now you will always see the result of this as your code executes, so this can also be really nice for keeping track of how things changed during your code execution. Now needless to say that all of that is lost and cleared when you reload the page or when you're done with the function execution, so this is really just temporarily there in memory to help you debug your code.

So that were normal breakpoints and how we use the debugger here. Now there also are other breakpoints which I want to show you before we ultimately fix this error here, for example you got conditional breakpoints. Let's say you have some error which you noticed only occurs if you entered numbers greater than 100 here. So let me resume this here, I clear the breakpoint by just clicking on it again and now of course our error here doesn't occur just for numbers greater than 100 but let's assume that would be the case. In such cases if you right click here, you can also add a conditional breakpoint which allows you to write an expression like only pause here if get user number input is greater than 99.

So now we would only pause here if a number greater than 99 is entered, so therefore here if I enter 100, you now see this pauses here. On the other hand, if I resume and enter five here, this doesn't pause. So conditional breakpoints can be nice and also very nice if we increase this at the bottom again are the event listener breakpoints. Now we know if something goes wrong when we click the plus button, it also will go wrong on any other button though, so we might not be interested in manually adding breakpoints here to add and subtract and to multiply, instead we might be interested in just pausing code whenever a click happens and you can do that with the event listener breakpoints. There you can expand mouse and there, click. If you click this, if you check this, now you will pause whenever a click occurs, for example if I click here, now execution pauses in the first line of the function which is handling that click and now we can navigate through that here.

So now you see that pauses no matter where I click. Now important, it does not pause if I click anywhere else in the document, really only on event listeners I registered for click events, there it will pause. Let me clear this now because we don't need it anymore, we already found the error but that's also important to be aware of.

lectures.text:
So now that we're able to find the error, let's fix it and let's say we think we know what the problem is but we're not sure yet. Of course we can always go back to our code and change it here and reload the page and try it again but you can also change your code here in the sources tab. There we have the suspicion that fetching our user input is the problem, so that this is a string instead of a number. So we could add parseInt here, like this to see what whether that does the trick.

Now you just have to save this by pressing command or control save so that the star disappears up there and you get a warning that this only was saved locally, so only here in the browser, not to your filesystem, so the code we have here still is untouched. If you go to get user number input here, you'll see that's untouched. So you don't change your local code but you change it here in the browser so that you can test changes here in the browser without facing the danger of changing your real code and maybe breaking things there.

So now if I add five again, now this is looking better because now you see this is not getting concatenated but instead, this really changes here at the end, it really adds five as a number. So now that we validated this fix, we can just take it and bring it to our real code and then apply it here, save and now reload and now we have the code we wrote and now we see this is now really working the way it should. So this is how we can work with the debugging tools.

Now you've got more tabs up there, we'll explore them later in the course, for example the elements tab once we work more with the DOM and the performance and memory tab, these are tabs I'll dive in later once we optimize performance and memory usage of our application. For now, the sources tab, breakpoints and the console here, these are your bread and butter tools for finding and fixing errors.

lectures.title: Debugging Code directly Inside VS Code
lectures.text:
Now the Chrome developer tools are pretty amazing and as you saw, you can do a lot there and I personally prefer working with those but you can actually also use your IDE to set breakpoint and so on. Now for that here in Visual Studio Code, you just need to make sure that you got a special extension installed and for that you can search for Chrome debug and you should find the debugger for a Chrome extension which I have installed, if you haven't, make sure you do install it because this will allow you to connect your Visual Studio Code editor to the Chrome debugging tools.

So with that installed, let me go back to the explorer view here and let's say we have the same problem we had before, so we want to debug this here and now we want to be able to run this code with the help of the Chrome debugger but also connect it to our editor here, so that we can set breakpoints here and we can indeed set breakpoints here. Let's say we have the suspicion that something goes wrong when we click the add button and this function executes.

Now you can set a breakpoint here by clicking on the left of the line number and now we got the red dot here which means this is a breakpoint. Now we just need to run this application, this website here with the help of our editor. So instead of manually opening the browser and opening our index.html file in there, now we need to go to debug here and then start debugging. Now the first time you click this, you might be asked in which environment to run, though this probably is only the case if you've got other environments installed, so it might also just automatically pick Chrome if you don't have other environments otherwise choose Chrome here and now it adds such a launch.json file in vscode.

This configures how it launches your application in the browser because it will open up a new browser window. Now here, this is generally OK but this URL is wrong. This would be right if you had a local development server which we don't have here so that will not work for us here, I'll dive into local development servers later, for now we should just copy and paste this URL which we opened in the browser and basically paste this in here, using the file protocol and then the path to your index.html file ultimately. With that if you save that, the rest can stay as it is, you can now press debug, start debugging again and what this will do is it will now launch the app here, enter this debugging view here which you can always switch with view, go back to the explorer or go back to the debugging view which we have here and we can also back to our code now, have the breakpoint set here and go to that window which it opened which in my case is this browser window.

Now if I now enter something here and I click plus, you see it goes back to the editor and pauses the code execution here. Now just as in the Chrome development tools, here we also see which variables are available in this execution context, local and global variables, we can add watch expressions here just as I showed it to you in the Chrome developer tools. We see the call stack and we see it's getting paused here, we can hover over things to see their result and we also get controls to step into a function for example and see the updated call stack, see values if we hover over them and of course step out of them, resume execution, stop debugging and close the debugger with this red square and so on.

So you can essentially do the same as in the Chrome debugger but now directly in your IDE, which you might or might not find more convenient. Now I, as I said, personally like the Chrome debugging tools, also because some of the extra features we have here, that we can change the code without really changing the code but that's up to you, if you like to use your local editor, this is how easy you can get started with Visual Studio Code. Now you can always clear breakpoints here by just clicking on them again.

So this is how you can leverage the IDE for that in case you prefer that and once you stop debugging by the way, which you do by pressing the red square here, this will automatically close the browser window which it opened for you. You can also start the app in non-debugging mode here if you prefer to do that but you can also just double click the index.html file in your explorer or finder as we did. One note about the console that opened down there, this debug console opened during debugging, it outputs log messages here and you can also evaluate expressions in here at runtime to run some quick calculations or get the value of a certain variable.

So whilst the debugging process is running, you can use that console here to see what's going on in your code.

lectures.title: Module Introduction
lectures.text:
After covering variables, operators and all these core basics that you need to know in Javascript and actually in most programming languages, there is another important block or set of features which you will also need in basically any programming language you are going to learn, Javascript included, and that would be control structures. Now that's kind of a strange term, what does control structures mean? It means that when you're writing code, you don't always want to execute exactly the same code top to bottom. Sometimes you have some condition that should be met for some code to be executed and execute some other code if the condition is not met or you need to repeat some code execution and instead of writing every cycle on your own, you can use some built-in features built into Javascript to run through a code snippet multiple times until some condition is met or until some data is exhausted, so that's exactly what we'll have a look at in this module. To be precise, we'll have a look at conditional statements, if statements, you might have heard about if statements if you worked with some other programming language in the past and we'll also have look at conditional expressions. We'll therefore also have a look at another very important related topic and that would

be boolean values and operators that help you generate boolean values, which turn out to be rather important in if statements and conditional expressions and we'll also have a look at loops and how you can run the same code with different data maybe multiple times with help of the many loops that are available in Javascript. Last but not least, after having a look at loops, we'll also dive into error handling and that will be different from what you learned in the debugging section as you will learn, here I'm talking about errors which you can't avoid, that might happen in your program as it executes and how you can then react to them and what you can do to still fail gracefully, maybe show an error message to the user or even fall back and make sure that your program works even though an error occurred.

So these are all very important control structures and with that, let's dive right into them.

lectures.title: Introducing "if" Statements & Boolean (Comparison) Operators
lectures.text:
I want to start with conditional code execution which is super important. For one, there are certain, quite a lot of cases, of scenarios which you couldn't really solve or couldn't really handle without the availability of conditional code execution, so without features that help you run code based on certain conditions. The app we built thus far could be built without conditional code but that's not the case for all apps and in addition, even if you can build an app without conditional code execution, like our basic calculator, you can still opt to write cleaner code, shorter code if you can run certain parts of your code conditionally.

Now what does conditional code execution mean? Imagine that you have a function and conditional code execution is not just available inside of functions by the way but consider that you have a function and in there, you have two code snippets that you could execute, for example you either add two numbers or you subtract two numbers. You do that in the same function and of course you could write two separate functions but even then, you might want to call one of the two functions based on some condition and that's exactly what conditional code execution is about.

You might have some program where you either want to run option A, so want to add two numbers or you want to subtract two numbers. So you have some condition that needs to be met and for this you can use a so-called if statement. If statements are a core construct, not just in Javascript but actually in any programming language you can learn. Now if statements require conditions, you specify a condition that must be met and a condition is in the end just a boolean value.

You remember that strange boolean part I mentioned earlier in the course? Well that's becoming important right now. This was this special kind of value which could only be true or false but that's exactly what you need in a condition because a condition executes code A if it's true or code B if it's false. Now since a condition in an if statement was in the end just true or false, you can always pass in a variable that holds true or false into that condition part, so you can always add if and then just check that variable and the value in there. That is possible but you will not always have a variable that holds true or false, you will need to create that and more often than not, you'll work with different kinds of data, let's say you have some user input which is a string or you're working with some numbers, the result of a calculation and therefore often you need to dynamically derive a boolean value and you can do that thankfully with the help of some boolean operators, also known as comparison operators because these are operators built into Javascript, just like plus, minus, the times operator and so on which don't yield a new number or a new string as a result but which instead return or yield true or false

and there, you for example have the equality operator. This double equal sign operator and that's important, these are two equals signs, the single equals sign was used for assigning a value to a variable or constant, the double equals sign operator is used to compare two values and then return true or false and you use it to check for value equality. So for example, you compare the variables a and b and if they hold the same value, this would yield true.

So you could use that comparison here in the condition or as a condition in an if statement. Of course you also can check for values not being equal, you do this with the exclamation mark in front of the equals sign and important here, you only have one equals sign, so the other equal sign is basically replaced by the exclamation mark here. This checks for value inequality and therefore you could check if a and b are not equal and only execute some code if that's the case. Now there also is a special form of these two operators.

You also have the equality operator with three equal signs and therefore also the not equal operator with an exclamation mark and two equal signs. Now what's the difference to the first two operators I showed you? Well, the triple equal sign operator checks for value and type equality or with the exclamation mark, for inequality. Now what's the difference here? To find out, let's just dive here in the console, in the browser developer tools on any web page of your choice, like our calculator but that really doesn't matter and in there, you can quickly play around with these operators.

Now let's start with the double equal sign operator, let's see what the result is if I compare two to two. Now of course, we get true as a result because these two values are equal. Now needless to say that in your program of course, you won't hardcode a comparison like this, that's redundant because that will always yield true, instead you might be comparing two values entered by the user, for example with the input like this where you don't know the value in advance, I'm just using hardcoded values here to show how these operators work.

So this yields true but you also get true if you compare two to a string that holds a value of two and that's what the double equality operator does. It checks for value equality only, it doesn't care whether the two values you are comparing are of the same type. That would be the case with triple equal signs though, there for two numbers being compared, if they have the same value, we get true but if I compare this to a string with the value two, I get false, so that's the important difference here and the same, just the opposite of course is the case with the negation, so with the exclamation mark. Now typically in Javascript, you should prefer the triple equals sign or not equal operator over the double equals sign or not equal operator simply because it forces you to write better code.

You should care about the types of values you working with, for example if you're checking some user input and you're comparing it whether it's equal to some number, well you should first convert the user input to a number so that you can use the triple equal sign operator. It makes your intentions clear and it also avoids cases where a user might not enter a number at all, it would be better to then handle that case before you use the number instead of just getting a false result in a condition here.

So typically, you want to use the triple equal sign operator just because it forces you to write more explicit and clearer code. Now of course, you can also not just check for equality or inequality, you can also compare numbers for being greater or smaller, so that's also available where you can check if number a or input a is bigger or smaller than input b. Now both the equality and the greater than and so on operators can be used with numbers but also with strings, obviously you can compare two strings for being equal but you can actually also use the greater than operator for example with two strings to check if one string is greater than another string in a lexical graphic way which means c would be greater than a because it's greater than a in an English dictionary.

Now besides greater or smaller than, you also have the combined greater than or equal or smaller than or equal operators which allow you to compare values for being smaller or equal or greater or equal, which of course makes sense because sometimes you want to include the value in the comparison and not just check for whether the other value is greater or smaller. So these are the core boolean operators you have. The exclamation mark operator is also important to highlight, you saw it of course here with the equality checks, there we can combine it with the equal signs.

Now you can also use it on a value where you already know that it holds a boolean, so on a variable where you know that it stores a boolean let's say to negate it, so to check if that is not true. This might sound a bit strange right now because you typically create booleans with the other operators and if you wanted to negate it, you could just use the unequal operator but you will find cases also throughout the course where you have some value which you derive as a boolean in some part of your code and then in some other part of your code, you need that value again, so which already is a boolean and you just want to then run code a if that was true or code b if it was not true and then you can just use that exclamation mark operator to do that. Now again, we'll see all of that in action in this course and in this module here already, this is just the overview and with that overview out of the way, let's actually see a concrete example for how we write an if statement and how we use some of these operators in there.

lectures.text:
For this, I want to reuse the calculator and attached you will find my version of that calculator, the one we finished in the basics module, you can of course also use yours or just download and use mine to have exactly the same code and in there, I want to give you an example of how we could use conditional expressions to optimize this code a bit more because of course, this works without any if statements, clearly because we haven't learned about them yet but you might notice that in the add, subtract, multiply and divide functions, we have a lot of code duplication.

We always start by getting the entered number, then we set the initial result, that's always exactly the same, then we have our calculation which is always different, then however we again just write the output or write to the log and yes, we do pass different information in there but actually the only information that is different is the operator that we used and description of the operation we did, the other parameters are always the same. So there is a lot of code reusage but without conditional statements, without if statements, there really wasn't a way around it, well now this changes.

Now we can for example add a new function here, maybe just name it calculate result, something like this and there, I'll bring in my code that I have in the add function but here I now want to write this in a more flexible way, here I can now expect a parameter, let's say calculation type and I expect this to be a string that describes the type of calculation we want to perform. Now we can add an if statement here by just adding if, this is a keyword understood by Javascript, then parentheses where we place our condition in and then important, curly braces.

Now this here, the parentheses here, that will take our condition, the parentheses here will in the end take our body, our code that should be executed if the condition is met. Now you don't add a semicolon after this, just as you didn't do it for the function here and now we need to add a condition here. Now the condition could be that calculation type is equal, with the triple equality operator here, equal to let's say add. If that is the case, then I want to set current result equal to current result plus entered number and now I also want to provide an alternative to that and we do that with the else keyword.

Now you add that right after your closing curly brace for the if blocks, so the if the condition is met block and then you add another pair of curly braces that now marks the block of code that should be executed if this condition is not met. So if the condition is met, we make it into this first block and therefore this code gets executed, the other code is ignored, so the code in here is ignored, if this condition is not met, then we'll ignore this code and instead the code in here will get executed and therefore for now, let's say we want to subtract, later I'll also cover the other cases but for now let's say I want to subtract here, so I will just move that subtraction code in here.

Now you can also by the way write this like this for example, so move on onto a new line, if you only have one expression you want to execute, you could also omit the curly braces here, that would be allowed but for readability sake, I recommend that you always add curly braces even if you have only one expression in there and you also most often will find the style where the else statement or the else keyword then is on the same line as the closing curly brace.

So whilst this would work, my code formatter even moves it back to this line if I autoformat the code because this is the most common way of writing this which you will find in most resources you find on the web and therefore this is the style I would recommend to you. We also use indentation here to improve readability, technically that's all not required, technically just as with the functions, you could write this all in one line like this but of course, that would be super hard to read which is why we split this across multiple lines.

So now we're doing, we're performing different calculations based on the calculation type we're getting, now I also want to write my output here based on that and for that, let me actually check for add here, all capital case, so now calculation type could be forwarded here, now this all of a sudden is way more dynamic, it has no hardcoded values in there, instead this is now fully reusable because all these values are dynamic, we therefore get a different result by just tweaking these values and now here for the plus operator, we just have to introduce a new variable here, math operator for example which by default has no value but then here in the add case, I set this to be equal to a plus and now just with one equals sign because here I'm not checking two values, I'm not comparing two values, instead here I want to assign this as a value to the math operator variable and in the else case, math operator simply is a minus, so that's just a string of course and I'm using that because now I can use math operator down here and now these two lines are fully reusable, they have no hardcoded values in there and therefore they work for whatever the calculation we're performing, we just have to make sure we set these values correctly.

Now calculation type should be received from outside and therefore what we can now do is here in the add case, we can remove all that code and instead call calculate result and pass in add as a calculation type and for subtract, we also remove all of that and I pass in subtract or for now actually, any other value than add will do the trick because if we pass in add, then this function will be executed and calculation type is set equal to add which means we make it into this block here, we make it into this block, this code gets executed and therefore we do the same which we previously did in here in add - we add the numbers, we set math operator to a plus and therefore down here, we forward add as a value for calculation type and a plus here for math operator. If anything else, then add is received, we currently always subtract the values here in the else block and math operator is set to a minus, so here we'll pass in whatever value calculation type held and the math operator will be a minus.

So if we save that and we reload our calculator, you will notice that it works exactly as before for all these operations and most importantly also for plus and minus where we now reuse our code with help of this if else statement.
