lectures.title: Beware When Comparing Objects & Arrays for Equality!
lectures.text:
When comparing values in Javascript, there is a strange behavior you might notice if you start comparing objects and arrays to each other because these don't work like numbers or strings do. Consider this example - you have an object which has a name property which holds Max as a value and you have another object which has the same value. Now these are not the same object, we're not talking about one variable here which I want to compare to itself, that would be redundant but instead let's say these are two different variables with two different objects but of course the objects themselves regarding the values that are stored in there are kind of equal to us humans. Now still, if you compare these, no matter if with the triple or the double equal operator, you will find out that the value is not true as you might have expected but instead that it's false.

Now why is that? Because objects and arrays and for arrays, it's indeed the same, if you had two arrays with the same values, they would not yield true if you compare them with the equal sign operators. For objects and arrays, you have to understand that they're kind of special in Javascript. Now I'll dive deeper into what exactly is special there later in the course where we have a closer look at the technical details of Javascript and some of the core things you also have to be aware of, for now let's just keep in mind that these two types of data, objects and arrays, are special. Now we can again check this by opening the console in the developer tools, here again in the calculator but that does not matter and in there, let's create two constants or variables, doesn't matter, person1 which is an object with name Max, so with a name property that holds a string and then person2 which basically now holds the same data.

Now if you now compare person1 to person2 with the equality operator, again it doesn't matter if you use two or three equals signs here, you see you get false as a value here, so this generates a boolean of the value false here not true, even though to us humans, this looks exactly the same. Now it has something to do with how that is stored behind the scenes in memory but again we'll dive into the details of that a bit later, for now just keep in mind that two objects stored in different variables will never be the same.

It's different if you have an object stored in a variable or constant and then you create a new constant or variable, let's say a person3 which you set equal to person1, then you will see the person3 is indeed equal to person1 but if you have another constant or variable where you assigned a brand new object which you created like this and then assigned like this, then this will never be equal to an equal looking but differently created object in another constant or variable.

So that's just something to keep in mind, again why this is the way it is is something we'll have a detailed look later. It's also the same for arrays as I mentioned if you have your hobbies array here and it includes sports and cooking, like this and then you have more hobbies and that has exactly the same values written in exactly the same way, then here also you will find out that hobbies in this case is never equal to more hobbies no matter how many equal signs you use, just as it was the case with objects, now also because arrays behind the scenes are objects as you learned earlier.

So again why this is the case will be covered later, for now just keep it in mind, equality comparisons won't work like this for object and arrays. You would have to compare individual values, so for example person1.name equal to person2.name since you then get access to the string that's stored in there, this again would work so this is a comparison you can make but the overall object or array, that can't be compared.

lectures.text:
Now sometimes when writing an if statement, you want to combine conditions. There is not just one condition which has to be met to execute some code but maybe two or you got two alternative conditions. So let's say we have three conditions in our code that should be met in an if statement - the first one is that name is equal to Max, the second is that the age is 30 and the third one is that the isAdmin flag is set, so this could be a boolean value which is set to true, for this user it's always set to true for example.

Now maybe you want to combine these conditions, maybe you want to say if condition a is met and b is met, then I want to execute the code, alternatively if the user is an admin, i don't care about a and b, so I always want to execute some code if isAdmin is true. So then you could say A and B should be met together, hence the and or condition C is met and translated into code that you can write in Javascript, and is represented with double ampersand operator, or is represented by the double pipe operator.

So in that case, the condition A and B would be evaluated together and only if both yield true, this combined condition here yields true and the alternative with the or is evaluated separately and therefore this overall condition where you combine these three conditions together would only yield true if part 1 or part 2 yields true, so if isAdmin is true, the code would always run no matter which age or name you have, if isAdmin is false, then you would only run the code if the name is Max and the age is 30 for example, so if then both A and B are true, then you wouldn't care about C, if C is true, you don't really care about A and B, that's how this concrete example here would work.

Now sometimes, you also want to combine conditions differently, you don't want to have a and b combined, instead you maybe want to say if condition A is true and either B or C is true, which is not how this currently would be evaluated, but if you would want to say this, then you can always use parentheses around your conditions to control it, so let's have a look at that. Remember, if you call return, if you use the return keyword in a function, that means that this function returns a value, doesn't really matter to us here, we don't expect a value, we don't store it, we don't do anything with it but it also means that code after the return statement is not executed and this is indeed a common pattern, that you check some condition and if it's not met, you know running this function, running the rest of this function doesn't make sense because it won't work with the values you're giving me and therefore you might want to return.

So these are things we had to look at and in addition, we also had a look at these boolean or logical operators which we used to derive true or false.

So roughly you can say where these arithmetic operators - plus, minus, the asterisks, the multiplication operator and so on, where those operators helped us with numbers and in the case of the plus, also with strings which we could concatenate, these logical operators produce true or false which we then in turn typically use in conditions. Now with that, we have a solid list of operators but then we also have these and and or operators and these actually also are operators.

Now as you already see, not all operators produce the same result, some operators produce boolean values, true or false, other operators produce numbers or strings. Now there's more where we dive into but one thing that already is important to understand is the concept of operator precedence and for that attached you find a link to this web page on MDN which talks about operator precedence. Does Javascript check this and then check the result of this comparison or does it check is this true and this true or this true?

That of course matters because if we change this a little bit and we say is 10 greater than 5, so this is true but here we check if three is greater than six, then the result of this first comparison, if this would be executed first would be false because yes this is true but this here, this comparison is false. So if the and operator where both has to be true to return true, this would actually return false. Now as you can already see here in my IDE, we will get true as a result , o this already indicates that this is evaluated first and then this and if either one of these two blocks returns true, the overall condition will return true and that's in case what's happening here.

Instead if it would be the case that this is evaluated and then this would have to be true, then it would also work like this but not for example if we check if that is not equal. Then if we say this has to be true and this has to be true, we would have a problem because this first part wouldn't be true. So what I'm saying here basically is that and has a higher precedence than or and indeed that is what we see here in the table, the logical and has a higher precedence than or which means that first Javascript connects these two pieces and evaluates them and then this operator kicks in and considers the second condition as well, which means that if this is true, we overwrite the fact that this yields false.

In general, common sense is what's happening in Javascript or what's getting applied there and the one thing where you might not have an intuition is maybe that and and or thing, well there and takes precedence over or which means first this is evaluated and then it's compared to this and there, the or operator simply means if one of the two is true, the overall statement returns true, the overall expression returns true and therefore this overall returns true because this is true and therefore thanks to the or operator, this doesn't matter, the fact that this is false but still important to know, this was grouped together because and takes higher precedence.

So instead of grouping together this, this was grouped together.

lectures.title: Beyond true/ false: "Truthy" and "Falsy" Values
lectures.text:
Now in Javascript, you also have a concept which is called falsy and truthy values. Now we learned about false and true which were these boolean values, now what's falsy and truthy, is this kind of a strange, special extra data type? No, it's actually just how Javascript under the hood evaluates conditions. Generally, Javascript conditions work with booleans, true or false but they also work with these falsy or truthy values, here's an example. Let's say you have a constant name input which holds a value of Max, here it's hardcoded into the code but of course that could be fetched from an input field on the web page let's say and then we use this in a condition where I compare the value in name input to the hardcoded value of Max, well we know that name input stores Max and therefore this of course would work, to be precise this condition yields true in this example here, so it yields a boolean value and therefore this of course works, that's what we saw thus far.

Now consider this code snippet here. We again have name input which holds Max, in this case hardcoded but could be fetch from the input field on a web page but now in the if condition, I don't compare name and put to any concrete value, I just have if name input here and this name input constant here of course holds a string, not a boolean, right? We initialize it one line above it, so this holds a string, not a boolean and still this works and this works because Javascript tries to coerce values to a boolean value if a boolean is required as it is the case in an if statement. So yes, if statements work with booleans but Javascript tries to convert a value to a boolean if it doesn't get a boolean comparison and also not a boolean itself.

So for example, if you have a variable which you pass into an if condition which you don't compare to anything but you just say if that variable and that variable holds a value of zero, then this will actually be treated as false, so zero is treated as false in a condition. Any other number, including negative numbers on the other hand are treated as true, so zero is kind of a special case which Javascript treats as false. Now when might this come in handy?

Let's say you're doing some division and you don't want to divide by zero. Now let's say the value is provided by the user, the user enters a value in the input and you want to make sure that you don't divide by zero. Of course you could check if user input is equal to zero and if it is, you return or you just use that shortcut of just plugging in the variable name and actually again, our calculator is a great example. It actually never makes sense in our calculator if the user enters 0 here - adding 0, subtracting 0 or multiplying or dividing by zero doesn't really make sense, you could say multiplying resets it but let's say we don't want to have that case and dividing would even be illegal, it's not allowed to divide by zero.

So what we could do in the calculator here, in the calculate result function, besides checking our cases here, we could also make sure that we return if and now we can actually use the or operator here if the entered number and for that, we just have to extract it before we run that code here. So if the entered number here is equal to zero, of course we could do that. What this would now do is it means we would return right away if either the calculation type is not add, not subtract, not multiply and not divide or if the entered number is zero, so let's test this. If we reload this page, of course everything works here but if I enter a zero here, you'll see our output doesn't change down there, so that works.

Now again we can do that but we can also say if entered number or to be precise, since this would be treated as true, if it's anything but zero, we can add an exclamation mark in front of this. Now this might look strange at first but what this says is if not entered number. You might remember that slide at the very bottom here, the exclamation mark operator, that's what we're using here. This negates a value and checks if it's not true. So in this case, entered number if it's 0 is treated as false by Javascript, it's falsy and therefore by adding an exclamation mark in front of it, we kind of invert that value, we say if that's not the case, then we want to make it in here.

Now since zero if the user entered zero is treated as false, this means if not false which is true, then execute this code. So if entered number is a falsy value, then not falsy will return true and if we return true here, well then we make it into this if block and therefore we return from this function and we don't execute the function. If entered number is any other number but zero including negative numbers, then it's truthy and then with the exclamation mark in front of it, it's converted to false, so if false will never execute the code in there right because this code only executes if this first condition is true and therefore we don't make it in here and we don't skip function execution by returning early.

This is how this works and this is the idea behind the truthy and falsy values, you don't always have to make an explicit comparison with the equal or greater than operators, you can also just throw in the variable or the value which you're interested in and then just take this as a condition itself and if it doesn't hold true or false, Javascript tries to convert it to true or false and there, zero is treated as false, any other number is treated as true. Now for strings, an empty string is treated as false, any other string is treated as true and for objects and arrays, it's important to understand that all objects and arrays, even empty ones are always treated as true.

So an empty object is not treated as false, it's always treated as true no matter if there is data in it or not. Null, undefined and not a number by the way are always treated as false. So these are the truthy and falsy values you can keep in mind, you can take that slide, it's attached and kind of print it out and put it next to your desk, these are the special cases in Javascript if you just throw in a single value or just a variable with a value in it into an if condition without a comparison operator, so without the equal sign or the greater than operator, so just the variable like this, then Javascript will look into the variable or look into the value and if it's not true or false already, it will try to convert it to true or false and this is how it then does it.

Now that's it for our calculator and for the basics about if statements, before we advance to loops I'd say it's definitely time to work more with if statements to get a better feeling for them, for the comparison operators, for booleans and for all these things which we used a bit here but which is still brand new and therefore definitely needs more practice so that you feel confident using if statements in your code.

So we can attack the monster normally, we can launch a strong attack, we can heal, we get various checks and they're also to see whether we won. Now let's maybe start with the bonus life. The idea behind the bonus life is that if we're low on health and we would die, like now if I click attack and the monster hits us, we would very likely die, then we actually don't die but instead we consume this bonus life and we got time or an opportunity to come back. OK, so I didn't die, now I should die, I lost and here we shouldn't lose but instead consume the bonus life, freeze our health, so don't reduce our health for this turn and thereafter, we have a chance to heal back up or if it was close, maybe now launch an attack towards the monster that kills it and therefore we have one chance to recover throughout the entire game even if we then restart it later.

So this is the idea behind the bonus life, where should this bonus life come in therefore? Well the and round function makes sense because this is where we check whether we lost and here actually before we check this, we should check whether we have a bonus life. lectures.text:
Now how can we let the player of our game choose that initialMaxLife here? For that, Javascript has a nice little built-in function, so the browser has a nice little built-in function I should say and in Javascript in the browser, you can therefore use that and that's the prompt function. It's a bit like alert which shows a message dialog, this also shows a dialog but it shows a dialog where the user may enter something. So here, first of all we have some text which is displayed to the user, for example maximum life for you and the monster, to tell the user what you should enter and then you also can define an initial value which should be a string, so for example 100. Now if you save that and you reload this page, you're presented with this prompt where you can enter a value, for example 70.

Now if you hit okay, nothing happens right now because we're not doing anything with that entered value, the prompt function actually returns the value the user entered. So here I got my entered value constant which holds that value the user chose here. Now that will be a string, not a number, that's important but I want to have a number here to do my calculations correctly and not start concatenating strings or anything like that, so I want a number here and therefore we should convert this to a number.

Of course you learned how that works, we can simply use parseInt, either wrap this right around this prompt function here which would work or for readability sake, do it right here on chosenMaxLife where I then use parseInt on my entered value, so the entered value here which is a string is forwarded to parseInt. Now of course, the user could have entered any kind of garbage here, for example a string which is not convertible to a number and therefore here we can add an if check and you can do that here as well, not just inside of functions but also directly in the script and check if the chosenMaxLife here is maybe not a valid number and for that, you can use another function built into Javascript and that's the isNan function which checks if that is not a number and parseInt will yield not a number, szo this special NAN type if you remember, if the value you pass to it, so entered value in this case is something that can't be converted to a number, then it will spit out NAN as a value which is then stored in chosenMaxLife and with isNan, we check if that's the case, so if chosenMaxLife happens to be not a number, so this NAN special value. If that's the case, I'll set chosenMaxLife to my default of 100

so that we still have a working value for the game, we then don't use what the user entered because that was unusable, instead we use our default value here. I also want to step in if the user sets the life here to a negative value or to zero, so we'll add the or operator here and check if chosenMaxLife is smaller or equal than zero, that means that I also reset this to 100 if the user entered a too low life. Now one important note regarding the order of evaluation here, Javascript works such that it first checks this here if you have the or operator and if this yields true, since or wants one of the two values to yield true, to yield true overall, it doesn't even look at that second check here.

So if we have chosenMaxLife which is not a number, it won't even try to do that comparison which is great because for this comparison, we need chosenMaxLife to be a number but it will not even try to do that if this already tells us that it is not a number so that's really good, it will stop for the or operator after the first sub condition that returned true. If you had and here, it would always look at both because obviously for and, both need to return true but for or, it stops after the first one that yielded true.

So if we don't have a number with which we can work, it will not even try to do this check here. Now in either case, we set chosenMaxLife to 100 and therefore now we give the user a chance of initializing the values here. So if I save that and I reload, now we get that prompt and if I enter 80 here and I then inspect these health bars, you will see that indeed max and value is set to 80 here. If we now attack, you see this decreases to lower values and at some point, we won and then we can start another new game and we won again because I'm spamming the strong attack, obviously this game is not really balanced, by spamming strong attack you will very likely win every game but it's more about practicing if statements than building the next best amazing game which will win you tons of money, you will have to do that on your own unfortunately.

So that works, if I reload and I set a different value like let's say 200, you see it takes 200 as a value here and therefore of course, the game takes way longer, the health bars take way longer to shrink. lectures.title: Utilizing Global Constants as Identifiers in Conditional Code
lectures.text:
So our game is taking shape, the login functionality is still missing and we'll add it soon, before we do that I want to show you one pattern which you also sometimes see in code or which you might want to use if you're having an if condition where you are using some kind of identifier as I'm doing it here with the mode in attack monster. There we get attack and strong attack as values for which I check here. Now that means that in this case, since we receive that here as a parameter in this function, we need to make sure that whenever we call that function, we do pass in attack or strong attack written exactly like this and a simple typo like this already will break our function.

Now obviously, we can always find and fix such a typo thereafter but you might want avoid code where you use string identifiers like this, where you then can mistype. Now that does not mean that you should avoid string identifiers altogether, there is just a more elegant way of handling them and that's exactly what I want to show to you now. What you can always do is you can create some global constants, let's say here at the top of our file, doesn't technically have to be there, it just should be done before you start using these constants but having such global static constants at the top of your file quickly makes it possible for other developers to understand which key-values this file uses, which key static values this file uses and there we could create something like mode, attack and store a string value of attack in there or alternatively, a number. So you could also have mode attack equal to zero, let's say and also have mode strong attack where you then store strong attack in there or if you work with numbers instead of string, mode strong attack might be one, so a different number then for general attack.

Now what's the idea behind these constants? The idea is that you can use them in your if condition down there and also when you call the function because now instead of comparing mode to a hardcoded string here, we can compare it to mode attack, so to this constant which of course holds such a string. The idea is that we have for only type the string once up there and even if we do mistype here, that doesn't really matter therefore because thereafter we only refer to this constant in all the places where we want to use this identifier and therefore we avoid that danger of mistyping.

So here I refer to mode strong attack and therefore now when we call the function, we pass in mode attack and mode strong attack and it's way harder for us to mistype the variable or the constant name here because here we get some IDE support and therefore we avoid this extra error source. So with that, our code still works exactly as before, it just should make it easier for us to ensure that we avoid dumb mistakes or dumb typos which might cost us minutes or hours to find and fix.

lectures.text:
There is one special conditional expression which we haven't seen and used thus far and that's the so-called ternary operator or the ternary expression. It's important to understand that if statements themselves return no values, right, you just dump them into your code to then execute code conditionally, it's not like a function or a calculation with some operators, an if statement doesn't return any value which you could store somewhere. Therefore this for example does not work, you can't assign an if statement to a constant because this will not return anything, an if statement won't return anything and this will actually be a syntax error therefore, this is not allowed. But maybe you have code where you want to use a different value in let's say user name or any other constant or variable and the concrete value you do want to save in that constant depends on some condition. Actually that is something which we have in our code already, there here in attack monster, we have max damage and log event and these are variables that hold conditional values, they either hold, for max damage, attack value or strong attack value based on this condition and thereafter we use that variable.

So in the end here, we have a variable where we store data that depends on some condition but I do so by first setting up the variable and not assigning any value and then we have an if condition which we don't try to store in any variable or constant because that wouldn't work as I mentioned and then inside of the if condition, we assign values to max damage in this case and to log event as well. This is valid code and this works but this snippet here doesn't work but it would be convenient to have some kind of if statement that would work like this where we kind of return a value in it and then that returned value get stored in a variable, would save us some extra lines of code.

Well there is a solution for that, you can use the so-called ternary operator in such cases. It allows you to have an inline if statement if you will, without the if keyword because that can't be used inline but with the question mark and colon operators here and together, they make up that ternary operator. Now the logic here is simple, you first put your condition which you want to check and there you can have any condition, you could have an if statement, including multiple conditions combined with and and or, then you have the question mark and thereafter you have the value you want to use if the condition is true and that's important, you have a value here, so something which could be stored in a constant.

You don't put more complex code here, not multiline code, not multiple expressions, you can't use an if statement here or define a new variable here, instead here after the question mark, you need some value that could be stored in a constant or a variable in any other place as well, so which you could direct assign with the equal sign to a variable or constant, and then you have a colon and then you have your else value and you need to specify this.

So omitting that else value is not allowed, that would be a syntax error as well. So here, we have the isLogin condition which probably is a boolean or as some truthy or falsy value and if that is true, we store Max in user name, if it's not true, I store null in user name. This is a ternary operator in action and we can actually use that in our code as well, we can change that code to not use this if statement and let me make it very clear that there is nothing wrong with using an if statement like this, in some cases using explicit if statements like this might also lead to more readable code than using ternary operators but in some cases, you also can save some extra code by using ternary operators and for example here we can comment out the if statement and set max damage here equal to and now I check if mode is equal to mode attack and then if that's true, separated by a question mark, I assign the value to max damage that should be used if mode is equal to mode attack, so basically attack value here and otherwise, separated by a colon, I use the else case, so in this case strong attack value and now we set that variable to either attack value or to strong attack value based on this condition,

so on this condition, if mode is equal to mode attack. Now of course, since i therefore never really assign a value here, previously we did do it because we assigned values in the if statement, now we initialize this variable with a value right away thanks to this ternary expression, we can also switch this to be a constant because I never assign a new value, we never use the equal sign after max damage again in this function here and of course we can do the same for the log event.

We can also switch this to a constant and now assign a value based on this check here. So check whether mode is equal to mode attack and if that is the case, then we have a value of log event player attack, otherwise we have a value of log event strong attack here and we can also structure this across multiple lines, like this. I did this with the auto formatting shortcut, as you see it's no problem, as always in Javascript you can write your code along multiple lines here, Javascript then finds out where this ends with the help of the semicolon here.

So with that, we remove that if statement and we saved some extra code here, we are able to initialize these constants right away and therefore we are able to use constants instead of variables and as I mentioned, this is now not strictly better than using the if statement, absolutely do use the if statement, especially if you had more complex conditions here and more complex values where you may be also run some calculation first of all, so where you then all of a sudden have very long lines of code, then you might actually prefer having an if statement where this is more structured and readable. If you have relatively short conditions and value assignments as we have it here however, then using the ternary expression is a fine alternative that can save you some extra code. Well and with that we should see that if I reload here and I start my game, that still works as before but now with the help of that ternary expression. It's also worth noting that a ternary expression can also have nested conditions, so here where a value is expected, you can have some other check and then have a nested ternary expression where you then have the nested value and the nested alternative value here

but you should use that with caution because that can quickly lead to very hard to read code and using a real if statement with else if blocks often is the better alternative to deeply nested ternary expressions. One important trick is how you can convert or coerce a truthy or falsy value to a real boolean, you do this with the double exclamation mark, also called double bang operator.

Now we learned about the exclamation mark operator which is there to negate some condition or a value and by using two exclamation marks, you basically negate the negation which kind of reverses the negation but there is one important thing, the exclamation mark, so the single exclamation mark already converts a truthy value into a real false value and if you then convert that false value back with another exclamation mark, you could get a real true value, so a real boolean.

So for example if you use double exclamation marks in front of an empty string, you will get a real false boolean instead of that falsy interpretation which Javascript normally uses. If you use double exclamation marks in front of a one, you get a real true value. So it's basically a type conversion trick which can convert an empty string to false or any number to true, things like that and sometimes in code, in more advanced programs, typically you might need that and then this is a convenient and handy approach. lectures.title: Working with the "switch-case" Statement
lectures.text:
Now last but not least, to conclude that if statement part, I want to introduce the switch case statement, which is a new statement but kind of related to if statements. It's great in situations like this, where you have multiple equality checks because that's where it really shines and where it is the most helpful and where you want to execute different code based on the condition that was met. Now you can also use switch case statements with other conditions where you don't check for equality but there, you save less code and they often are harder to read.

lectures.title: Introducing Loops
lectures.text:
After all these if statements which are extremely important, which is why I spend so much time on them because you will basically need them in any program you write, so after the if statements, it's now time to come to another very important construct in Javascript and in actually any programming language and that would be loops. In programming, you often have the scenario that you need to execute certain code multiple times. Now you might think okay we have functions for that, we can have reusable code in there, we can call a function multiple times.

Sure but in your code, you have to write every function execution, right? Of course you can attach a function to an event listener and then whenever that button for example is clicked, the function executes but if you want to control that a certain snippet of code runs for every item you have in an array or runs ten times, then you would have to put ten function executions for example into your code and loops allow you to write such code repetition in a more dynamic and flexible way.

Now in Javascript, we have four main loops and that's the for loop, the for/of loop, the for/in loop and the while loop and for the while loop, we also have one variation which I'll also show you. Now what's the idea behind each of these loops and when do you use them? The for loop together with the while loop is the oldest loop, it's been in Javascript forever and the for loop allows you to execute code a certain amount of times and you use a counter variable for that which you typically increment or change with every loop iteration.

So that means that with a for loop, you can easily define that a certain part of your code should run 10 times, 20 times, a million times. Here's an example, this is how for loop looks like, you have the for keyword, then between parentheses you initialize or you set up that loop and that consists of three parts - a begin phase where you initialize variables you can use inside of that loop, so between these curly braces and that's important, the variable set up there are really only available inside of the loop, then we also have separated by a semicolon, so not by a comma, not by colon but a semicolon, we have a condition, an exit condition which basically defines when we stop executing that code between the curly braces and then we have, separated by another semicolon, the code that should run after every loop iteration and there, you could do whatever you want but typically, you just change that variable which you initialized and which you also use in your exit condition.

So this loop for example would initialize i and i is a name which is often chosen, it stands for iterator, so you choose i and you set it to 0 initially, then after every loop iteration, so after this console log body ran, it's incremented by 1 and then before the next loop iteration, before every loop iteration actually, this condition i smaller three is checked and the loop body is only executed if that condition yields true which of course means that in this example here, we would print the values 0, 1 and 2 but never 3 because after the third loop iteration, i gets incremented to three, before the next iteration this condition checks if i is smaller than three which of course is not the case if i is equal to three and therefore it would stop executing that and move to the next line of code after that for loop, that's how a for loop works and of course, needless to say, we'll see that in action right after this lecture. Now another loop you have which is a bit newer but now also very well supported in Javascript and that's the for/of loop. Now that executes for every element in an array, it allows you to execute code for every element in an array.

It looks like this, kind of like the first for loop but a bit different, between the parentheses we don't have these three parts, instead here we have the of keyword and we create a constant, could also be a variable but typically you create a constant which gives you access to one element of the array at a time and then this body between the curly braces is executed for every element in the array and l in this case then refers to that element in the array for this current iteration and this is convenient for for example doing something with every element in the array or outputting it to the console or whatever you want to do.

Now for/of helps you with arrays, we also have for/in and that allows you to execute code for every key in an object. This is how it looks like and there we basically have the same syntax as in a for/of loop but with the in keyword instead of the of keyword and an important difference is that for of is built to work with arrays, for/in is built to work with objects and there, you get access to every key in the object, so that's the part on the left side of the colon when you create these key-value pairs and objects and then this second line you see here, console log object, square brackets key, that's actually a syntax we haven't used before, this is a way of dynamically accessing key-value pairs in an object when you don't have the key name but instead you have a variable or a constant that holds the key name, then this gives you dynamic access to the values stored for that key in the object and of course, we'll also see that in action in this module. Now last but not least, we have the while loop.

The idea behind the while loop is that you execute code as long as a certain condition is true and only if that condition is somehow set to false, you exit out of the loop. It looks like this, the idea here basically is that you don't really work with a counter, though you could also do that here if you check the counter in your condition but that you maybe have some boolean which you then change at some point of time inside of your while loop and you can continue executing code until this is done.

So these are the different loops, let's now have a look at them and see how we can integrate them into our project or generally work with them.

So for loop is created with the for keyword, then with parentheses and then you have these three parts in there. The first part is a part where you initialize things for the loop.

You could run a lot of different code here, basically any expression, so anything but an if statement or another loop can be executed here, you could call a function in here but typically what you do here is you initialize a variable, you could initialize multiple variables but in most loops, you'll need one and that's that helper variable which you change after every iteration to execute code. So we print that nice separator here three times even though in IDE, we really only see it once but theoretically we create it three times, now let's say thereafter we really want to output something for every item in our battle log. Now as I explained, we can do that with the normal loop here and here we can reuse i because it really only exists for that loop, so not even for the entire function but only for that loop here so we can reuse it in another loop, that is possible and then here we can go all the way up to the length of our battle log array, increment i and then here, we could console log battle log and then you learned that you can dynamically access an element in an array with that square bracket notation and then you provide the index of the element which is zero based but of course here we don't hardcode the index but instead we use i as an index because that allows us to access to i'th element for every loop iteration.

So for the first iteration where i is 0, we access the element at index 0 which is the first element, then we increase this to 1, assuming that we have a length that is greater than 1, so more than one element, so then we have i equal to 1 so we access the element at index 1 which is the second element in the array and so on. There you work with a constant instead of a variable with let, you could use let but using const is better because unlike this for loop, i will not change, instead you get a new constant for every loop iteration.

So we're also not redeclaring an existing constant but we're really just getting a brand new one and the old one is dumped.

Technically it has something to do with the scope where this is created but that's something we'll have a closer look at in the next course module. So for now, just keep in mind that this gets dumped after every execution and we get a new one. So here, we go through battle log through this array and log entry now as a constant which as I said gets created for every loop iteration, so between the curly braces we can now use that and here again, we can output log entry for example and if we do that, if we output log entry like this, what happens is that if we reload this app and we attack and strong attack, we get the same output as before unsurprisingly because we're going through all elements in our array, get access to it in the log entry constant which exists for the lifetime of this iteration and then output it.

So it's basically the same as we had here but of course it's a bit shorter and it takes advantage of this special for loop that was built specifically for going through arrays and getting access to the elements in there. Now one important side note here, with this approach, by using the old for loop, you automatically have access to the index of every element as well because i is just the index. With this syntax, you have access to the element but not to the index, you don't know which index this is at.

You could manually get access by defining a variable outside of the for/of loop, which starts at 0 because your index starts at 0 which you then increment in every iteration and then here, this would be your index but you have to manage this on your own with an extra variable, the for/of loop like this doesn't give you access to the index. So now here, you will see if I add some entries and I log this, now we have the index being printed after every entry but again, we have to manage this manually if we need it.

lectures.title: The "for-in" Loop
lectures.text:
Now we saw the for loop and the for/of loop, now there also is the for/in loop for going through all the key-value pairs in an object. Now, I also want to do this here in the printLogHandler because there in the for/of loop, log entry actually is an object, right? It's this here and this is a Javascript object and you can have loops inside of loop, so you can have such nested loops. You can't have a normal for loop in a normal for loop, you can have a normal for loop in a for/of loop, you can have a for/of loop and a normal for loop, so you can mix and match them as you need.

You can also have if statements inside of for loops and for loops inside of if statements and the same is true for while loops. So you can combine these structures and these concepts as you need to, that's also very important to understand. You are not limited to only using for loops or any loop on the top level of a function. You can use some outside of functions, inside of if statements, inside of else blocks of if statements, inside of other loops and if statements inside of loops and so on as I said, so you can nest these structures as deep as you want.

So here for example, I want to adjust my output here and I want to console log a little string identifier where I use the back tics to dynamically inject a value, then I'll add a hash symbol, a hashtag and then this dollar sign curly brace syntax to output the index, so that's basically just giving me the number of this log entry starting at 0 and then I don't want to console log the entire entry like this but instead, go through all the entries in there, all the key value pairs in there by adding such a for/in loop. It looks a lot like a for/of loop, you create a constant because just like with the for/of loop, this variable, this constant is recreated for every iteration and then here, we get access to the key, you don't have to name that key, you can name it whatever you want, you could name it property, whatever you want to name it, I'll go with key, then you use the in keyword and then your object, either created in place just as you could create an array in place here if you wanted to or more often, you refer to some variable or constant which holds an object, so in this case to log entry and then you have curly braces and your loop body.

Now of course, the implication of having a nested loop like this is that this outer loop will run and then for every iteration of that outer loop, that entire inner loop will run and only once this is completed, the next iteration of the outer loop will kick in, so that's how these two loops will work together - inner loop has to complete for the next outer loop to continue and then a new inner loop is started and so on. So now here, we can console log the key-value for example and key here really is the name of the key, so event, final monster health, final player health target and value, these are the keys and that's what is stored inside of the key constant and if we now also want to get access to the value for that key, well then we have to use a different syntax. Then we can also console log this but here we need to refer to our object, so log entry and now the dot notation won't work because if we type .key here, Javascript will try to find a key, a property named key in here and there is no key property, we only got these five properties here, event and so on, so there is no key property, no property with the name key because key is the name of this constant, not of a property in the object but the value of that key constant then is the name of a property

of this object. So the value here key will be event and for the next iteration, final monster health and thereafter, final player health and so on. So for our object, we want to access the property with the name event and with the name final monster health and so on and these names are stored in key, so what we want to tell Javascript is that it shouldn't use key as the name but the value stored in key as the name and we do that by using a different syntax for accessing properties which we haven't seen before for objects and that's that we use square brackets here.

Now we don't use it as we use it on an array where we use 0 and 1 and so on but instead here you can enter a property name and you could hardcode it like this, to access the property with the name event, so this would be similar to .event but you can also pass in key here and Javascript will then extract the value stored in this constant and then access the property with that name on log entry and therefore now in this inner loop, we will now log the name of the property and then its value.

So lot of talking, let's have a look at that, let's reload, strong attack and attack and show the log and now what you see here is a lot of output. We have this #0 which means it's the first log entry and then we have event and its value and then the value property and its value and the target property and its value and so on and then because I never change i as I just see, we would need to increment this, forgot that, accidentally deleted it, so therefore we still have #0 here, that should be #1 with the updated code here but then we have the next log entry with different values for the properties.

Now of course, that's not super readable but of course we can change this, for example we could add string interpolation here to output a readable string where we then first output the key and then maybe such an arrow here with an equals sign and a greater sign, so this is just some text, so not something Javascript tries to pass, it will just create some text here and then output the log entry value for that key here and now that should be more readable. If we do it like this and we reload and we attack and strong attack and show the log, now here if we maybe expand this a bit with the first log entry here, then event with its value, value with its value and so on, second log entry with index 1 and so on.

So this is how we could now output our log, if that's more readable or not, I'll leave that up to you but it shows you how you can use different loops here and how you can also use loops inside of loops and how you can use a for/in loop to go through all keys in an object and still get access to the values that are stored for these keys.

lectures.text:
Now what about the while loop? I have no great place to squeeze it in here, though I will say you can also use a while loop to replace a for loop, so if you would want to replace this, we would have to manage the variable manually. Now since I use i down there, I now have to use a different name because now we're initializing it in the function and there we must only use each name once, so here I'll go with j, initialize this to be zero and then we can add a while loop with the while keyword, then a condition between parentheses and then your loop body.

Now if you put something like true here, this is obviously always true and therefore this would give you an infinite loop which you want to avoid because it will crash your application. Instead here we could check if j is smaller than 3 and then here we can console log our code from up there, so these dashes here and then simply increment j and now we manually replicated this behavior, though I will say if that's what you want, you would go for the for loop, this is just so that we can have a first look at while.

So with that, if I reload strong attack and show the log, we see our dashes here three times just as before but again, you wouldn't really use while for that, you would go with the for loops, so let me quickly comment that back in and comment out the while loop. Let's say you're generating random numbers and I'm doing this in the browser console, so I create my random numbers variable and you have another variable finished which initially is a false and then you write your while loop where you check for it not being finished, so with an exclamation mark because this has to return true to make it into the body and then you place your cursor between the curly braces, you hold shift and press enter, now you can write multiline code here because pressing shift without enter executes the code.

If I repeat this code by pressing the up arrow here which quickly recreates the code we just wrote, so the up arrow key on your keyboard, then hit enter, well now it doesn't even execute because finished of course was set to true, so let's set finished back to false here actually and then thereafter by pressing the up arrow key multiple times, go back to the while loop, hit enter again, now it took five tries, we have five elements here, though that's not entirely correct of course, it used the old array and just added one element so it actually took only one try.

We increment this, value now is three, this is not fitting our condition anymore, so we exit by that time, so this works as expected. Now let's say you actually always want to execute your loop body before the condition is checked because at the moment, the condition is checked before the loop body is executed, maybe you want to do it the other way around, well then you can use a do/while loop For that, you can cut your body here and then add the do keyword and add your body here and then typically you move while right after the closing curly brace, though technically it also works if it's a new line.

What this does is it now executes the body first and thereafter checks the condition. If you now save that and you reload and you press show log, you see we print the same as before because we still exit after this is equal to three but you'll notice a difference if you for example set j to three initially. The reason for that is that three of course is not smaller than three and here we check the condition first but with do/while, in which case by the way it's also common to add a semicolon after while, not a must do but you typically do it in this notation, not after the normal while loop but that's just a side note but the important thing here is here, this code runs first and thereafter this is checked, so that's why we here see three being printed if we initialize j to be three because this condition which actually finds out that we don't want to continue for j being equal or greater than three is only executed after we first ran this loop body.

So that's while and do/while, you typically will use for loops more often, while loops are kind of niche, there are some use cases where they're really great but for the majority of use cases, you typically work with for and for/of and for/in loops, that just happens to be the case the way we write programs and what we want to do in there but it's good to have while loop especially if you have some condition which changes inside of the loop and you don't know in advance how often you want to execute that loop, then while loops can really shine.

lectures.title: Controlling Loops with "break"
lectures.text:
Now to conclude that part about loops, I want to dive into two important keywords which can help you control your loop execution and that's the break and the continue keyword. We saw the break keyword already in our switch statement, there we have break to avoid that fall through mechanism, we can also use break inside of loops to leave the loop execution, to stop the loop execution earlier than it normally would, so to kind of cancel loop execution. How does that work?

Now let's say we only want to output one log entry. Well of course there are various ways of achieving this but one way would be to simply add a break keyword here, maybe after this i++ thing, doesn't really matter for this example though. Now what this will do is it will tell Javascript and it works in any loop by the way, not just in for/of loops but in all loops I showed you, it tells Javascript stop this loop execution of the loop, I'm calling this in.

So if you're calling this in a nested loop, it will stop that nested loop execution but continue with the outside one, which of course means that for the next iteration of the outside one, a new inside one is started and that will then run but the currently running inside nested loop will stop when you call break. If you call break in the outside loop, well then this outside loop is finished and therefore there also will be no next run of the inside loop because that only runs for every iteration of the outside loop and since we break out of that and we finish that outside loop, there is no more inner loop execution too.

So break stops the loop in which you call it, so in which you call it directly, so you have to not have it in a nested loop but directly in that loop as we do it here, this break call here will stop this outer for/of loop. The result of that is that if we save that and we go back to our program and I then attack and have a strong attack and I then click show log, we only see one entry here. We see our attack, we don't see the attack by the monster, we don't see our strong attack or the response on that by the monster, we only see that very first event we wrote to the log, so that very first attack we launched, that's how break works.

Now we could actually use that to make sure that whenever we pressed the show log button, we only output one event at a time but of course not always the same one, that would be great and for that, we can add a new global variable where we keep track of the last event we logged. So for that, I'll add a new variable up there, last logged event or last logged entry and initially that's not even zero, that's minus one or just not defined let's say and then we can use the last logged entry down there in our loop where we log the entries to set last logged entry equal to i, so in this case to zero. Now we can add an if statement here and say if last logged entry is not set, so we'll add an exclamation mark here, so if this is undefined or falsy at the beginning which it is or if last logged entry is set and it's equal to i, then I want to log my event, so we move that code into this if statement and then since we now logged something, we update the last logged entry to that i number and thereafter we increment i and we break. This is still not the finished logic, now if I save that and I go back to the web page and I attack and strong attack and I click show log, we see that entry and if I click show log again,

we see that same entry still. So we can add that same entry multiple times, so we haven't changed a lot here. The reason for that is that we set last logged entry here to i, so to zero for the first run and here we check if we have no last logged entry or if last logged entry is equal to i but we always start at i zero, so this is always true and therefore we always log this. Now the trick is actually to change this here to look for last logged entry to be smaller than i and if we do that and we go back to the page, I can click attack and strong attack and then show log and we have one entry but if I click it again, we still keep on printing results.

The reason for that is that this change here will actually yield true if last logged entry is undefined but also if it's zero because as you learned, zero is a falsy value, it's treated as false. So this here with the exclamation mark actually yields true and therefore executes this code if last logged entry is zero. So I'll combine this first condition here with another condition that last logged entry is not equal to zero. So if this is falsy but it's also not falsy because it's equal to zero or last logged entry simply is smaller than i, then we want to log something.

So now with that, if we go back to the web page and we attack and strong attack and I click show log, we have an entry here but if I click show log again, now you'll see I only print my stripes here, my dashes but I don't print any real log entries anymore and the reason for that is that we don't make it into the if block anymore and that makes sense because i always starts at zero when printLogHandler is executed which is the case for every click, so that's not incremented across clicks, for every click it restarts at zero.

Last logged entry however does change with every click, it starts uninitialized and then after that first log we printed, it is set to i which is zero, so it's zero after the first click and thereafter this code never runs again due to the logic we wrote here. So now the next step is to move break into this if statement so that the loop actually continues and has a chance of reaching a new i. So now if we save that and we reload and then we attack and strong attack and now we click show log, we have that first event player attack with index 0, if I click show log again with index at 1 which is the monster attack and now if I clear that, we can still continue pressing this button, now we have some logic that allows us to log event by event with every new click until we have no more events which is when we only print our dashes.

Now of course, you could add another if check here to make sure you don't execute any logic in here if we have a last logged entry that is greater than the length of our battle log in the end which means we have no more entries, you could do that. So that's the break keyword, it allows us to break out of a function execution, for example to do something like this but you can do it for whatever reason you have in your code. It allows you to break out of a loop execution earlier than it normally would finish, so before the loop really finished, in this case whenever we printed something to the console but of course you can use break for whatever reason you have, doesn't have to be because you only want to log one thing at a time to a console, could be any reason why you want to stop a loop iteration before it really is done, so that's break.

Now I mentioned we also have another keyword and that's the continue keyword.

lectures.title: Controlling Iterations with "continue"
lectures.text:
The continue keyword is a bit like break, it also stops the current execution of this code in your loop but it doesn't stop the entire loop, so instead it just moves on to the next iteration. I can best show how it works, here in the console if we add a quick for loop here, a normal for loop with i equal to zero, i smaller than 5 and i++ let's say, curly braces and then shift enter to write some code between, and now of course if I console log i here, unsurprisingly we print 0 to 4.

Now press the up arrow to be able to edit this again and now let's add a little if check in there where we check if i is equal to let's say three which is one of the values we're printing here. If that's the case, for whatever reason I don't want to print it here, well then of course we could use break, right, this will stop the loop execution. If we hit enter, now we see 0, 1, 2 but we don't see 3 but also not 4 because we cancelled function execution with break.

This might or might not be what you want because I actually only wanted to skip this three value, I didn't want to cancel the entire loop execution and that's exactly what continue does. If you use continue instead of break, you just skip this loop iteration, so all the code after continue will not be executed but for the next iteration it will continue as normal, so it will not break out of the loop, it just continues to the next execution. So if I now hit enter here, we see 0, 1, 2, 4, we don't see 3 because there we continue and as I said, this means this code is skipped for this loop iteration, subsequent iterations like the 1, 4, 4 are executed.

So break and continue give you some extra control over your loop execution, you definitely don't need them in every loop you write but sometimes, you have some code where you want to break out of a loop up on some condition being met or you want to skip an iteration based on some condition and then break and continue are your friends.

lectures.title: Error Handling with "try-catch" - An Introduction
lectures.text:
Now after all these if statements and all these loops, I want to conclude this module by diving into error handling, another form of controlled structure you'll need in your Javascript code to build code that runs under different and also under harder circumstances. Now what do I mean by that? In the Javascript applications, in the programs you're going to write, you can't always avoid all errors. Some errors can't be avoided and with that I of course mean errors that are beyond your control as a developer.

So I'm not talking about bugs which you introduced into your code or about syntax errors, you should have a look at the debugging module in this course to learn how you can fix and avoid such errors, I'm talking about errors which you can't rule out when you're writing your code, for example user input errors, that a user enters text like hi in a field where you expect a number or network errors, that you're maybe communicating with some server, something we haven't done yet but which we'll do later down in the course and that server is offline or something like that, so basically things where you have no chance of ruling out that this problem occurs because you can't control what a user types into the input field.

You can do your best to kind of restrict the options to user has but ultimately, users might always find a way of breaking your code so to say and the same for network errors, you can't rule out that a server might be offline when you're trying to talk to it. So the best you can do in these cases is that you throw your own errors and catch errors to fail gracefully, which means maybe at least show the user a nice error message or in the best possible case, maybe you can write some fallback code so that you can recover and you don't even need to show an error message to the user and you can do that with try catch, another control structure which Javascript exposes to you that allows you to try a certain code which might fail and then catch potential errors thrown in that code to then do something with them or to do something indicates that such an error occurred.

lectures.title: Working with "try-catch" to Catch & Handle Errors
lectures.text:
The idea is that you wrap try catch around the code that might fail. So you might think, great I'm going to put my entire program into the try block, right? We put all that code here, all of that, we move that into try because then we catch any error that might occur and even though we don't know yet what we can do then, this sounds good, we catch any error and we'll probably be able to do something great and have our script not fail. This is not what you should do, don't wrap your entire script into try, it's not good for performance and it's also a very bad programming style.

You want to write code that doesn't yield errors and you can use the debugging section to find and fix logical and syntax errors, you only want to move code into try where you can't control whether it throws an error or not, as it's the case here, we can't control whether the user enters something valid or not. So in the end, we move this line in here but since I want to be able to use chosen life thereafter, I will actually create and declare the variable before the try block, like this and then only assign a new value to it inside of the try block.

So now we have that try block which tries that code but just like that, it's not valid, it's not helpful and it's also not valid syntax, you also need to add a catch block. So you add the catch keyword and then you add parentheses and in there, a parameter which you can give any name you want, tpically you name it error. This now is like a function, so you add curly braces thereafter and inside of these curly braces, this error which was caught is available.

So this is called like a function by Javascript and error is the error which was thrown, in this case it's your own error object, if it's some system error, like with the network request I already mentioned, then it will be that error object which Javascript created for you. So here for example, we can now console log that error to have a look at it, to see what's inside and we could now say okay chosenMaxLife in this case is 100, that's our fallback logic. If this fails and if it succeeds by the way of course, this will not execute but if this fails, if we get an error here, then this will not execute successfully but this here will and therefore here we can now set a value with which the rest of our code works.

This is not always possible, sometimes the best you can do is show an error message to the user, for example if a server is offline and you can't save data on a server, there's little else you can do, you can just tell the user about that and tell him to not leave the page and try again later. In other cases like this, you might be able to use a fallback value and fall back without the user even noticing. You could of course also tell the user that you entered something wrong, default value of 100 was used so that you fall back but you let the user know about that, that's totally up to you.

So now with that, if we save that and we reload, now if I enter hi there, I get that you entered something wrong, I get that console log which please note, now is not an error anymore, we don't have that red background so this is not a system error anymore, instead it's just the normal log message and our app works just as before with that value of 100 being used. So that now all works and we can play with this game just as before but now with our own error handling logic, in this case with a graceful fallback, in other cases showing an error message might be the best you can do.

Now just to make this really clear again, of course the logic we had before where we had just this if check and then also assigned a default value of 100 wasn't bad, I wanted to show you try catch which here isn't bad and in other cases is absolutely necessary because in other cases, you get an error if you want it or not and you need to be able to handle it, that's why it's a good time to already practice with it here even though in this exact case, since parseInt doesn't throw an error, you could have absolutely kept the old logic and avoided this try catch block.

Now I'm not entirely done with try catch, you can also add another element to try catch and that's finally. Now you add finally like this, you add the finally keyword after try or after try catch, you don't need to have catch, you can just have finally here, you need to have try though, try catch without try doesn't exist but you can also have try catch finally and the idea is that the code inside of finally will now always execute no matter if you had an error or not.

Now you might wonder what the idea behind that is because the code after try catch, so all the other code also executes here no matter if we had an error or not. So why would this be helpful? Well you can use finally to do any cleanup work if you for example have a case where another error happens inside your try catch block and be that only because you maybe throw the error again, that's also something you will sometimes do the more advanced you become, this is called rethrowing an error and we might do some error handling here, typically not some fallback as we're doing it here though but we might just be sending that error to our own analytic server for example so that we are notified of that error we had in our application.

Maybe we can't fall back as we can here but maybe we can just show the user an error message and we also want to log the error to our own analytic servers. So we might be sending that request to our own servers here and then we rethrow that error. We rethrow that error here so that in some other part of our code, we can then handle it and show that error message to the user. Again, that's a little hard to imagine here, I'm aware of that because this is some basic project, some basic program but you could have multiple try catch blocks in different places of your app and here, you only have the first one which sends it to your own servers and then you throw that error again.

Now in that case, still maybe you want to do some cleanup work here, maybe release some data which you save, maybe clear some variables, do something like this and then you could do that in finally. Now I will be honest, in a lot of scenarios, you will not need finally, especially in this example you definitely don't need it because we can perfectly fall back, so the code after this will execute, there's no reason to rethrow the error. If you would rethrow, the code thereafter doesn't execute and only finally will, that's the difference then, that's the advantage of finally, it executes even if you do throw an error here, the other code will not because your script will crash if you then don't handle it somewhere else but here, we don't really need that because we have a perfect fallback.

It's good to know that finally is there though in cases where you will have an error in catch, you rethrow or you get another error and therefore you know the rest of your script will not be able to continue, well then finally can be used for some cleanup work and that can be helpful at times. Now just as with the other construct shown here, we'll also see try catch in action again later in the course and especially when we work with network requests, it will make more sense because then we really need it, then there are things we can't do without it but since it is a control structure, now is the time to introduce it, keep it in mind, keep its general functionality in mind, that you try code and then you can react upon an error and fall back or show an error message and you'll get more and more practice with it throughout this course.
