lectures.text:
Now before we actually start to work with any HTML elements, let's have a look at that document and that window object. Now for that, attached you find a very basic starting project, essentially an empty HTML file and an empty app.js file which is imported into that HTML file here and if you open up that HTML file and you open up your browser developer tools and go to the console there which allows you to also run some Javascript commands as you learned, then here you can simply write document and this gives you access to this document object.

Now by default, you'll see you get this strange representation which looks like HTML code here, that's a little feature by the chrome dev tools, this is actually a Javascript object but since it's tied to the loaded document, to that loaded HTML code, it gives you this presentation where you can even select different parts if you hover over them but to get a feeling or get a look into the real Javascript object, you can type console.dir document and you can use console.dir in any cases where console.log gives you this strange output in the dev tools and now you get access to the real Javascript object with all the properties that are in there and you see, there are a lot of properties in there.

Now most of them might never matter to you but for example, the body property here if you expose that gives you access to entire new object which in the end reflects your document body and everything that's attached to that and this will also allow us to get access to all the HTML content rendered in there. There are other properties which you can dive in, for example document element here is basically your entire HTML content, so the body gives you access to everything that was rendered in that body part age, HTML holds everything that was rendered or set up for your entire HTML code which was rendered, so that's also another important property.

We also have a couple of other important properties, head for example unsurprisingly gives you access to everything that was rendered as part of this head, so together they kind of make up that entire HTML code as well of course and so on. So there are a bunch of interesting things in there and we'll work with a couple of them but there also are a lot of them which you will never really need but of course feel free to browse through all of that in that document here, this in the end is one of this important topmost objects which are made available to you by the browser to allow you to interact with your loaded HTML document.

Now let's clear the console and let's also output window here, so you can type window here and you get access to the window object. Now this is that real topmost object and this gives you access to all the core APIs that the browser wants to expose to you and for example here you also find alert, a function which we already used a couple of times in this course to throw such an alert. The important thing is that with window, you by default if in your Javascript code, if you're running, if you're typing some code here, you by default have access to everything in window which is why you can just type alert like this. Totally correct would be window.alert as you see because window is this topmost global object which is exposed to you by the browser and there, you have the alert functionality but actually browsers always parse your Javascript code such that window.. is automatically added in front of some function if that function can't be found anywhere else, so the browser always looks in the window object if you're calling or accessing something, which is why alert works just as well as window.alert would work here, so that's really great.

So that window object is a really important global object giving you access to all these browser APIs like alert, a bunch of other things which we haven't worked with yet and which we'll see later and also the documents here. This is the document I just output a second ago, it's part of that window as I mentioned now but as I also just mentioned, if you enter something just like this, the browser automatically looks in the window, which is why we could use console.dir in the dev tools and we could also use it here because that will automatically look in window.document. So you could use window.document but you don't need to, the same for the alert.

So that's document which we have in here, a couple of other nice features which we'll see throughout the course here to store data in the browser and so on, a couple of events which are exclusive to the window though which fire when certain things happen in the window and these on something events here by the way are just alternatives to using add event listener, something I'll dive deeper in the events module of this course where we learn all about events and how to work with them and so on.

Now what the browser does in that case is it of course renders all the pixels but it also kind of parses the HTML code and creates an object representation of that because behind the scenes, the browser doesn't work with text which HTML is in the end but with these objects that are stored in memory and there for example, the HTML tag is translated to an HTML node as it's called and this is an element node to be precise because that in the end is a node and these objects are simply called nodes which represents an HTML element, an HTML tag and therefore it's called an element node and such element nodes are created for all the HTML elements you see on the left. lectures.title: Nodes & Elements - Querying the DOM Overview
lectures.text:
Now to query elements or nodes and I kind of use this term interchangeably, though I will come back to the difference in a few seconds but to query content let's say in your HTML page, I mean in your rendered HTML page so in the DOM, you have a couple of methods which you can use on that document object I showed you a few minutes ago, most importantly you got query selector and get element by ID. These methods will select one element at a time, you also have query selector all and other methods like get elements by tag name which will select multiple elements. So you can get access to single elements with query selector and get element by ID and these are simply different ways of querying elements. Query selector takes a CSS selector as you could use it in a CSS file, even pseudo selectors are supported and gives you therefore a lot of flexibility and power when it comes to selecting elements with complex query in your DOM. Get element by ID on the other hand takes an ID which you might have assigned to an HTML element and selects an element by that and since ID should be unique on your web page, this is a method which returns one element. The query selector method takes any CSS selector and

therefore this might be a selector that matches multiple elements but in this case, query selector, this method will always give you access to the first matched element on the page, so in the DOM. So this gives you a direct reference to the DOM element which it found, now query selector all, get elements by tag name and there are other methods as well which I'll show you give you access to collections of elements, array-like objects, typically a node list, though that also is not always the case but typically it's such a node list which is not a real array but array-like, so which supports certain behaviors of an array but not all of them.

You have different ways of querying elements, you can for example use the above methods - query selector all takes a CSS selector as query selector but unlike query selector, it does not return the first element which it matched but all elements that match the selector. Get elements by tag name give you all the elements that have a certain HTML tag and then there are other selectors to select by class name or by the name attribute which you might have assigned, though the query selector all method is the most flexible one where you have the power to select anything you want by CSS selectors.

Now one important difference here which I want I mention right away which often will not matter but still is worth being mentioned is that query selector all will give you a non-live node list, so a snapshot of the currently rendered DOM, whereas these get something by something methods like get elements by tag name return a live node list which means that if you then add or remove elements which we'll also learn throughout this module, you'll see that reflected in the list which you loaded through the get something by something method, it will not be reflected in the data returned by query selector all but again, that's something we can come back to later once we learned how to add and remove elements, for now let's ignore that. Before we try these methods though and play around with them a bit to get a feeling for how you select things, let's dive into nodes and elements. I kind of use these terms interchangeably but actually should be careful and you should at least understand what the difference is.

So you have nodes and elements and nodes are the objects that make up the DOM, everything in the DOM is a node. HTML tags are just element nodes as I mentioned, I will also refer to them as just elements but in the end, these are element nodes to be super precise. We also have for example text nodes and there are other nodes as well which aren't really that important though and which with you'll not really work. Attached, you will find a thorough document about all supported nodes but text nodes and element nodes are the important ones.

Now elements therefore are in the end just element nodes as I just explained, so elements are really just the nodes which are created off of HTML tags which were rendered, not the text in there. Now why does this matter? Because on element nodes, on elements therefore, you have special properties and methods to interact with the elements, to change their style, to change their content and so on. You also have special properties on methods and text nodes but you simply don't work with text nodes as often as you will work with elements because typically you want to add a new HTML element, you want to remove one, you want to change the style of one, you want to edit it in any other way. For text, you typically just want to change the text and then you typically just go to the elements that holds the text and change the child content which is the text of that element, which is why you don't work with text nodes as often. So which exact properties and methods are available on every element, so on every rendered HTML tag depends on the kind of element though, for example on the input where the user can enter content, you have ways of reading that input, on other elements where users just can't edit the content, you don't have access to that of course and you have

different ways of selecting elements, as I mentioned we'll learn about different methods that give us access and you can also create and remove them with the help of Javascript. So that's the difference between nodes and elements, elements are the important thing for us here, text nodes are most of the time just created automatically when you set the text content of an element to a new text content for example but again it is something we'll come back to.

Let's now try out some of these query methods to get a feeling for how they work.

lectures.title: Exploring and Changing DOM Properties
lectures.text:
So we selected an element in the DOM or multiple elements, now we want to manipulate them. That is not something we have done too often in this course, sometimes like in the monster killer when we change the health bar that's rendered on the screen but it is something you typically want to do a lot in Javascript heavy applications where you want to provide that good user experience to the user, where you change things in the rendered user interface without the need to reload a new page with that changed HTML code, instead you want to change it in the already loaded page since that is just faster and provides a smoother experienced than loading a new page.

So let's say we have a paragraph here with an ID and a CSS class and some text in there and we selected this, for example with get element by ID which we can of course do with that welcome text ID it has and store that in a constant and now, what can we do with that? Well for example, we can read its text content, welcome in this case and we do this with the text content property which this exposes. We can also read the ID by accessing p.id and gets ID as a string that's stored in there or the same for the CSS classes with the class name property. So important, not .class but class name to get access to the CSS classes that are assigned as a text here on the element.

So that's how we can read data from there, something which you also want to do a lot. You don't always immediately change things, sometimes you also just want to find out in which current state is this element, which CSS class does it have but then you can also change this by for example assigning a new value to class name. Not all properties of an element are writable but a lot of them are and then you can assign a new text here and this will be reflected back in the DOM which the browser rendered and will of course be updated on the UI, totally automatic by the browser, so let's have a look at that.

So back here in our playground, let's say on that header here, on this h1 element, I want to change the text color and the background color and maybe also the text which is shown in there. Well then first of all, we can get access to it, I reloaded the page for this and now I'll create my h1 element with document and to mix things up, I'll use query selector h1 here, we could have used get element by ID and use the ID which this h1 tag has, the main title and now this is stored in h1, this is storing a reference to that DOM object which the browser exposes to us. Now here for example, we can read text content and get the text which is in there or a class name to get that CSS class string which is assigned to it, which currently is an empty string because indeed we have no classes assigned here and of course other things as well.

Now let's say we want to change the text and for this, you can simply write text content equal and then some new text for example and if you do that and you hit enter, this changes here on the screen and what this does behind the scenes is it removes the old text node that was in there. Remember it's a node, just a text node and instead created a new text node and replaced the old one with it, so that's what happened behind the scenes. Now we can also assign a new CSS class by setting class name equal to title for example and if we do that and we go to elements, now we see the class title on there and if we now had some CSS code that would assign a certain style to that, we would see that but since we don't have that, let's change the style in a different way by reaching out to h1 and then there is a style property which in turn gives you access to a huge object with all these CSS styles you can assign to an object just now translated to Javascript properties you could say. So for example there you can set the color to white or to hex code and now the text is white which makes it quite hard to read.

So let's also change the background color by going to h1 style and then import it here, background-color would not work because this is not a valid property name, you must not have dashes in there, so instead all these CSS property names that have a dash in there are translated to Javascript property names which are generally the same but where the dash is removed and to make it more readable therefore, the first character after the dash, so in this case the c, is replaced with a capital character, so background-color becomes background color, like this and now we can either read it, well there's nothing in there because no value has been assigned or assign a value, for example red. If you do that, you indeed see the red background, the white text and so on.

So this is how you can work with the properties on these elements and also manipulate them. Now of course you might wonder, how do I know which properties are available? Well for one, don't forget you can always console.dir h1 and then simply dive into it, that is something I would recommend that you absolutely do because whilst there are many things which you won't fully understand yet, you can just ignore them, There are many things which you will understand and where you have an idea of where this value might be coming from and what changing it might do and you can also just try changing certain things, if it doesn't work, you can just reload the page and start from scratch, nothing can go wrong there, so simply just play around with that but of course if you want a more official documentation with some explanations, you can always search on MDN, for example for h1 element and find an article on that with detailed explanation about that element of course and there important, you'll find the DOM interface, in this case a HTML heading element, this is in the end just the kind of object that is created automatically.

You don't need to learn these heart of course, I'll dive into the relation between these different types of elements a little later once we learn more about objects, for now that doesn't really matter to us. What's important here is you'll find that list of properties which it has and the methods it has. Now what you see here for example is that a heading element doesn't really have any specific properties or methods, instead the HTML element which is kind of like an element or an object type this object type is based on, that's the one you want to have a look at.

So if you go into that, here we find a more extensive list of properties that is available with descriptions of what they do and so on. So this is something you also always can dive into learn more about it but again, good old console.dir and looking into it is also something I would strongly recommend that you also give a try to get a feeling for what's happening there. Now really important here by the way, whatever you change here in Javascript will be lost whenever you reload the page because what you do in Javascript is only stored in memory, it of course doesn't affect the underlying files which were loaded which typically lie on some server on the Internet, so that of course changes. If you reload the page, you load these original files again and your Javascript changes are lost because whenever you reload the page, this essentially resets your Javascript application, it clears the existing application from memory in the end and starts a brand new application so your Javascript file is parsed again and any changes you made are not kept around, that's just a side note.

lectures.title: Attributes vs Properties
lectures.text:
When speaking about manipulating elements, it's also important to understand the difference between attributes and properties because it's easy to confuse these two things or to not even be aware of these two different things because often, indeed attributes are mapped to properties and some live synchronization is set up and I'll show what l mean in a second but that's not always the case, for example here we have an input element with an ID, with a CSS class and with a value and it's interesting because there we have three different kinds of attributes which behave in different ways when it comes to the DOM object that is created and how the properties of that object are initialized.

So these are all attributes here placed in the HTML codes, so what you write in the HTML code is named an attribute, what you add on the HTML tag, that's an attribute of that tag. What the browser does with these attributes is it creates such a DOM object based on the tag name, input in that case and preconfigures it and preconfigures some of its properties based on these attributes because the important thing is that the attribute is the thing in your HTML code, in your HTML text in the end. The property is a value stored in the object that's created based on your HTML code so to say, right? Objects in Javascript have properties, no matter if there are some DOM objects or not.

So of course for DOM objects, we also have properties and these simply reflect the configuration and setup and positioning and so on of that rendered DOM node, of the DOM object and the idea of attributes is that you, if you're writing HTML code, can provide a certain default configuration to this to be created DOM object. So that's what you do with attributes and how they are translated to properties and here for example, we see that if we get access to this input element and store it in a constant, let's say we name it input, then we can read the ID from it but also the class name and the value and the properties as I mentioned are automatically added on the created DOM objects.

Now here, it's important to understand that not every attribute has a one-to-onemapping in properties though, input ID has it, there we have an ID attribute and an ID property and if we change the value of the attribute, the property updates, if we change the value of the property, the attribute will update, so we have some live synchronization going on here. Input class name is different, there we also have live synchronization, so if we change the property, the attribute will change, if we change the attribute, the property will change but the names are not equal so we don't really have a one-to-one mapping. Class on the input, so on the HTML tag is translated to a class name property here on the DOM object and of course the browser does this automatically, it's just important to know that not always the attribute name is equal to the property name and for value, we have yet another different behavior.

There we have a one-to-one mapping, it's called value as an attribute and value as a property but we have no real life synchronisation going on, only one way because what you have here is actually that if you change the input value, this will not be reflected back to the attribute, only if you change the attribute, the value properties value will change again and that makes sense because you have to keep in mind that for example this input element is there to hold some user input and if you would always reflect this back to the attribute, then that would mean that if you ever want to reset the input to its initial value which the developer writing the HTML code at some point of time stored in that value attribute, that this would not be possible if we always reflected the latest user input in the value attribute because then we could never reset it because we lost the original value we wanted to assign there.

So that's why when the user types there, the users input is stored on the value property but not reflected back into the HTML code. So let's see that in practice here and for that, I'll add an input element here actually with a value of default text here and after saving this, we can reload, of course the color here is gone by the way. So here we have that input element with the default text and again of course, we can store a reference to it by using for example query selector and here then just the inputs tag selector like this and we can of course console.dir input here to get access to it.

We find a lot of properties which we already know but if we scroll down to v, we will also find one which is not available on all elements and that's the value property which in this case holds default text. Now if I go to the input here and in this elements tab here, we change default text by adding an exclamation mark for example, if we go back to the console, you'll see that if I reselect this, so const input2 document query selector input and I now console.dir input2, you will see that if we scroll down to the value at the bottom here, we have this exclamation mark in there as well.

So if I change the attribute that is reflected in the DOM object, so that is reflected. Now if I go ahead and we reset input to .value equal to some other input the user might have entered and I hit enter, you see this this reflected in the user interface, right? This is set as a value here, so that's great but if we now inspect this again, we see there the value is still the default text we had in the attribute before, so there this is not reflected back.

Now as I explained before, for CSS classes and ID for example, that's different. If I select my h1 tag here with get element by ID main title and I then set the ID equal to new ID for example, I don't lose my reference here by the way because here we set up this connection and thereafter, this is mapped to the address in memory, so the address in memory is stored here, so if I change that ID, this doesn't clear that connection, just the same command would of course not work again because in elements we now see this has a new ID and this is now also reflected here in the HTML code, so there it is reflected back into the attribute. The same would be true for class name by the way. Now important, if you do want to change an attribute, then you also have a method for that, you have a set attribute method.

So on the input for example, we could call set attribute and this takes two arguments, two parameters and the first one is the name of the attribute, so here we could set value, should be a string and the second is the value you want to assign to that attribute, so here some other default text and if you do that and you hit enter, this does not update UI because actually, changing this value here will not overwrite any existing changes that might have been made so that you don't accidentally get rid of the user input but you do clear that value here, you do indeed change that attribute here but since we have no live sync, indeed if I go to the value that's stored in there, I still have the other value which was set and not the new attribute value here. So value indeed of course is one of the more complex properties you can work with due to the way how it updates under which circumstances but generally of course, it's pretty straightforward regarding how this value attribute and property behaves, it behaves such that you don't accidentally clear user input and that your changes you made to value aren't easily dismissed but that you can still have that attribute around and either assign a new value or of course if you would

want to reset the input, you could always just set value equal to input.getAttribute to get the value stored in the attribute, reach out to the value attribute and since this doesn't reflect the current input but instead whatever you set here or originally in the HTML code, you can run this code here to reset the content in there to that starting code. That's what I meant with that resetting and why this is kept around. So this is how you can work with attributes and properties with set attribute and get attribute and dot notation to interact with properties like this and this is therefore how we can evaluate values stored in DOM objects and also change them if we need to.

lectures.title: Traversing the DOM - Overview
lectures.text:
We had a look at how you can select elements in the DOM with query selector, with get element by ID and so on, we also had a look at how you can then use these elements to manipulate them or to simply read data from them. Now there is another connected concept, connected to selecting elements which is typically known as traversing the DOM and what does traversing the DOM mean? It means that once you selected one element, one node therefore, you might be interested in diving into all of its child nodes, for example to add it all list items in a list or anything like that, so rather than manually selecting every element you might be interested in with query selector or so on, you could take an element which you already did select and then move to its children or its siblings and so on based on that element, that's what's traversing the DOM means. Now for that, I first of all want to clarify a couple of terms which I'll use - children, descendants, parent and ancestors because it's important to understand what these things mean.

So let's have a look at what child or children means, what descendant or descendants mean, what parent or parents mean and what ancestor or ancestors mean. Now when I say child, if I speak about a child element when talking about these DOM traversal methods you learned about, then this always means a direct child node or an element, so an element node and with that I mean that here in this small example, the paragraph is a child of the div because it's a direct child element, it's directly below the div, one layer below it so to say, the em tag, the emphasized tag however isn't because whilst the em tag is still kind of nested inside of the div tag, it's not a direct child, the paragraph, the p tag is in between, so the p tag is a child, the em tag is not a child of the div in this case. Now descendant on the other hand is a direct or indirect child node or element, so when we talk about a descendant, then in the same example both the paragraph but also the the em tag would be descendants of div.

So p, the paragraph tag is a child and a descendant, the em tag is not a child but a descendant of div in this example. Now a parent and ancestor are kind of the opposite - a parent node or element is the direct parent node or element of another element, so in this example here still, the div is a parent of the paragraph but not of em for the same reason as em is not a child of the div and the ancestor on the other hand, if I talk about an ancestor element or node, then this is a direct or indirect parent relation, so there for example in that same example, we have div as an ancestor of both the paragraph and the em tag, so that is important, that's an important differentiation, it will be important to keep in mind when talking about the DOM traversal and what you can do there.

Now as i said, DOM traversal means that you have a selected element, a selected node, let's say this div element node here and now you want to dive into some of the surrounding or nested elements or nested nodes and there, you've got a couple of directions into which you can go. You can always go up, so find a parent element or node with parent node or parent element, so with these specific properties which every DOM object will have, so every element object which you can select no matter if it's a div or a paragraph or whatever, it will have this parent node and parent element property, the difference being that parent node selects any parent node whereas parent element only selects a parent node that also is an element, so only parent HTML elements.

There also is the closest method which you can use, to not just take a direct parent but take any ancestor that matches a certain CSS query and I'll show you how all of these work in action in the next lectures of course. Now of course, you can also go the opposite direction and instead of reaching out to a parent or ancestor element, you can also reach out to a child or descendent element. There you have child nodes and children, child nodes to select all child nodes including text nodes, children to only select child element nodes, so only HTML element objects and of course as I also showed you already, you can use query selector, get elements by a class name and so on on any selected element node as well, so these are also methods which are always available on any selected element object and therefore you can always use these to dive deeper into all the descendants you might find there in that part of the DOM tree based on that element which you already selected.

Now there also are special properties you can use to get the first child which selects the first child node and first element child to select the first element child node of a given element and the same is available for the last child, the last child node and the last element child node which you can select for a given element. So that's for going up in the DOM tree or going deeper into the DOM tree, so into nested elements, now maybe you want to stay on the same level and want to select sibling elements. For that, you've got the previous sibling and previous element sibling properties on any DOM object which allows you to get the direct sibling of an element and that of course works in both directions to get the sibling before or after the currently selected element and previous sibling and next sibling give you the next sibling node, previous elements sibling and next element sibling give you the next element node that is a sibling of the selected node. So that's the theory, let's have a look at it in practice.

lectures.title: Traversing Child Nodes
lectures.text:
Here's the same example we already worked on where we already do select things and now here let's start simple and let's select a list item here. Now of course, you learned about different ways of selecting it and I want to select this second list item actually. Now for this second list item, there are a couple of ways which will not work, since it's the second list item not the first one for example, you won't be able to select it with document query selector li because that selects the first matching element, so the first list item in this case that is found and that would be this list item, not this one.

What would work is if you take the class, so .list-item here like this because since this is the first element with that class, it would work but maybe you have a setup where this is not the case, let's say and let's actually change it as such, on this first list item, you have the same class, now all of a sudden, this way of selecting also won't work anymore as soon as we reload this page because now this will select the first match and now that we change this, the first matching list item is this list item here now that I reloaded the page.

So, what can we do to select this item then? Well we can use some DOM traversal techniques which I already showed you. Of course in reality if you are building this page, you could also add an ID attribute or find other ways of making this uniquely selectable with the query methods you already learned but it's important to also be available to interpret the DOM. So one way of accessing it would be to get access to the parent unordered list element here, to this element node and then have a look at its child nodes or child elements and then select the second child here because that would be this list item.

This can be done here in the console by getting access to the unordered list for example with documents query selector ul, that gives us the first fitting element so since we only have one unordered list in the document, it will give us access to unordered list here and now on this unordered list, of course we can use the query selector to select any elements nested in there but we will have the same problem as before. If I search for list items, I get the first matching one which is this, not this, the same if I use a class so this won't really help us here but what we can do is we can use some of the things I showed you on the slide, for example you can output children here. If you look at ul children, this gives you a so-called HTML collection which is an array-like object in the end, so it's not a real array but it supports looping and so on, so what I already showed you and there we know the second element is the one we want, so with ul children and then index one to get the second element, we would get access to exactly that list item I was talking about and you'll see it selected here on the left, right?

If I type this here even without hitting enter, it is already selected. So this would be one way. This also is a great place to understand the difference between child nodes and child element nodes in case it's not fully clear yet. Here I'm using children and this gives me access to all child element nodes, so only child nodes that are based on HTML tags, HTML elements, text nodes are excluded here. Now please keep in mind that as I mentioned earlier in this module, text nodes are also part of the DOM tree, of that tree that is created here by the browser to reflect your HTML document and that there, even the whitespace which you add in your HTML file for readability reasons is treated as a text node because it is text in your HTML file, right? So therefore, actually in our HTML code, here of course I also have a bunch of whitespace in front of the body and in front of the header and of course also in front of the list item here, I also have a line break between the unordered list and the list item.

So here the difference we can actually see is that children gives me this collection of element nodes that are direct children of this unordered list, so no other descendants and also and no other types of nodes. If we use child nodes instead, now you see instead of this HTML collection array-like object, we now have a node list array-like object and if we output this, indeed we see there's way more content in there. There are a bunch of text nodes as you can now clearly tell and of course also our element nodes but also the text nodes because child nodes selects all child nodes, whereas children only select child element nodes and child nodes therefore also includes text nodes and here this text for example, in front of this first list item, that is exactly this whitespace which you in the end have here.

So if we have a look at this text here, data here is actually its text content, we haven't learned about this yet but where you have text content on element nodes to assign a text and automatically create a child text node for an element node, data on a text node sets the text of this text node and here this is the line break character and then we have a bunch of whitespace thereafter, so a bunch of empty whitespace and that's just what we have here.

We have a line break after the unordered list and then we have 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 pieces of whitespace here and that's exactly what we have here we have the line break and then we have 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 pieces of whitespace here. So this is this text node, now why is this not rendered here? It's not this whitespace in front of the bullet point in case you're wondering. Well it's not rendered because we have no style that would render it. The default for HTML in most tags is or the default for the browser for most tags I should say is that it basically omits empty whitespace that has no purpose, so whitespace like here between item and one is of course rendered but whitespace at the beginning or at the end of the content of an element is typically omitted. You can change this with a special style though if we expand this down there and you go to styles for the unordered list which holds these elements we just had a look at, so which holds all these child nodes, there if we add whitespace pre, now you see it here in the left as well, you see there's a bunch of whitespace and the line breaks because this is some specific CSS styling which overrides the browser default of basically ignoring, leading

or excess whitespace and it renders it instead, so now instead of ignoring all that extra whitespace, it is getting rendered which is why the list item is still as big as before but of course we can see there seems to be some extra content in front of it and whilst we don't see that here in the elements tab or whilst this is not displayed here as a text node, we can see it here in the console, it's just this text node, if I hover over it, it's now selected, this is this extra whitespace that is getting rendered, a line break and then also all the other extra pieces of whitespace we have in there.

So that's children and child nodes which allows us to select child nodes, often you want to work with children because in most cases you're interested in getting access to the child element nodes but if you need access to all nodes, you can use child nodes like this and this by the way is then also how you can get access to text nodes, for example with child nodes and then by using the right index. Now besides children and child nodes, we also have two other useful properties, let's say you select that the unordered list with query selector ul and there, you want to get access to the first or the last list item.

Now again, of course you can always do query selector li last of type or first of type, that will work but for one, this will cost a little bit of performance because query selector has to scan the entire page and then scan this quite complex CSS query and find the fitting elements and it also just might be redundant if you already got access to the unordered list any ways. If you then know you want to work with the first list item, you can use first child to get the first child node, which in this case is a text node or first element child to get the first element child node which would be the first list item here and of course the same is true in the opposite direction.

One important node about all these DOM traversal techniques here by the way - it's super important to be aware of them and as I mentioned, for example if you want the first list item for unordered list and you have the unordered list selected anyways, it might be best to just use first element child to get access to the list item than to run a brand new query with query selector, both for performance reasons but also save some code. Here, it also makes sense because a list item is pretty guaranteed to always be a child of an unordered list and therefore even if you later go to your HTML code and you change things around, it's to be expected that this relation between unordered list and list item will be the same.

So if you have code where you select the first element child on an unordered list, it will probably always be a list item. That might not be true for your entire page, let's say here in this example page, we write some js code and for that, I'll clear that old code which I don't really need here and I select my unordered list by reaching out to document body and then here in document body, in the end it's of course the sibling of this header, right?

So here on the first element child which is the header, we could now call next element sibling, so that would work because this here up to this point, this selects the header, so on the header object, we can of course call next element sibling to get access to the next element sibling which is our unordered list.

So now if we want to get the first li, I can of course say ul first element child and if I console log first li here and we save that and we reload this page, go to the console and reload, we see that works. The problem with that is, for one this is a bit hard to read. If I'm reading your code, it's not immediately obvious for me that you are selecting an unordered list here. The bigger downside is that here, maybe as you work on this app, at some point of time you decide oh, I need an extra section element here, a section tag and you move your unordered list into this section.

Now if you do that and you don't adjust your app.js file which is easy to overlook, then you might get unexpected behaviours in your app because now if we reload, we of course get the unordered list selected here and not the first list item anymore because we didn't adjust the selection code and we select the header and then its next element sibling which now no longer is the unordered list but which is this section. So if we then select the first element child of the sibling of the header, that's not the first list item anymore but the unordered list because the sibling of the header was the section, the first child is this unordered list.

So using these DOM traversal properties can be very powerful but you should do it with care, use it in cases where it's likely that the relation you're traversing will stay the same, even if you move code around, list items will always been in an unordered list. In cases where this can't be guaranteed, carefully check your js code and adjust it if you adjusted the HTML code and also of course, don't be shy to use the query methods, they're not bad or anything like that. Just because this could yield a better performance does not mean that the other approach yields horrible performance, you'll not even feel the difference.

Just try to be smart regarding what you use and that is also something that will come with experience, there also is no strict wrong or right, it's important to know both and in cases where the relation is always the same, DOM traversal properties like this one can be nice for general selection things, like generally selecting an unordered list. Using query selector might be better than trying to do that by traversing the DOM but that's just a general hint or just a thought I wanted to put out there to make sure that you are able to write good code that doesn't suddenly and unexpectedly break.

Now that we know how to select elements both with the query methods, get element by ID but also with the DOM traversing techniques and that we also learned how to evaluate and manipulate elements, let's have a look at one specific way of manipulating elements and that is changing their style. I already showed you how that works with the style property but turns out there are other ways of doing that as well. So of course you can use that style property with which we already worked, with that you directly target the individual CSS styles applied to that element, it's like using inline styles on the element in your HTML document.

So if you know a bit of CSS, you'll also know that this has the highest specificity, which means styles assigned on the style property will overwrite any other styles that might be assigned to an element by a class or anything like that. Now important here as you learned already, the style property names are based on the CSS property names but they are adjusted, for example background color is written like this and not as it is in CSS with a dash.

Now that's one way of setting styles but there are other ways and it's kind of obvious if you think about it, you of course can also manipulate the CSS classes that are added to an element. So with the class name property, you can set the CSS classes that exist on an element to dynamically change these classes, remove them or add new ones and that of course means that you adjust the styles that are applied by these classes because you control the classes on an element. With class name, you set and control all classes at once, class name is a string and it's a string of all the classes that are added, so you can manipulate that string to manipulate the classes. By the way, you of course alternatively could also change the ID or some other attributes of an element if you are using an ID selector or attribute selectors in your CSS code but CSS classes are of course the most common way of spreading styles across multiple elements.

Now when it comes to CSS classes, you actually also have another way of editing classes on an element. Class name takes one string, which is simply a string of all the classes that should be added and therefore if you want to toggle a class there, you have to manage it manually, that you keep classes which you don't want to remove and only remove the classes that you want to get rid of. To make that a bit easier, all these element nodes also have another property, the class list property which is in the end a Javascript object and not just a string like class name but an object with a couple of built-in methods that make it easy for you to add, remove or toggle CSS classes, so that it's easier for you to manage individual classes and not having to do this string micromanagement that you have to do with class name.

It gives you finegrained control over the classes that are added and you can even use it in conjunction with class name, though you should be careful that you don't overwrite each other and typically you use either of the two. Instead of using this, you can use this class list object I was referring to. So class list is another property you have on every element node and there you've got a couple of nice methods, you've got a contains method to quickly check if a class is set. So for example here you could then easily check if the visible classes is set and don't worry about the entire string, you don't have to worry about other classes that might be set, you can simply check if that is set.

You can also call add to add a new class or remove to remove a class, so that's all nice, you can replace a class and you can also toggle a class and here we can toggle the visible and the invisible class. Now I just have to go to index.html and initially here, I'll add visible as well and now class list will automatically check whether visible is set when we call toggle visible and we'll remove it if it is and add it otherwise and the same for invisible and the result of that is that if we now reload, this toggling works just as before but with less work from our side.

Now of course here actually adding visible is totally irrelevant because invisible is the one that does the main work here and that sets display to none, so we can actually even comment out this visible part and only add invisible but I hope it becomes clear what the power of class list is, it makes managing CSS classes much easier and that overall allows you to dynamically add or remove or change classes, CSS classes on an element and therefore that in turn allows you to dynamically change styles because while you sometimes might want to change inline styles, more often than not, you want to add more complex styles to an element and instead of setting them all as inline styles in your Javascript code which also is hard to find for other developers, you typically want to take your CSS code and dynamically add or remove classes.

That also makes it easier to work in a team where you might have one colleague working on the CSS styles and you working on the Javascript. If you have to set styles in Javascript with inline styles, then you have to know CSS and you have to align with your CSS colleague. If you use class list or class name but better class list for more flexibility, then your CSS colleague can give you the CSS code and you can dynamically add or remove classes from that code based on your logic, which simply makes working on that easier as well.

lectures.title: Creating Elements with JS - Overview
lectures.text:
So now we have an understanding of how you select elements with different selection methods, most importantly get element by ID and query selector, we have an understanding of how you traverse the DOM based on an element which you selected with parent node and so on, we have an understanding of how you can read values from a DOM element and how you can manipulate DOM nodes or DOM elements, now let's have a look at how you can create and insert brand new elements because that's something we haven't really covered thus far.

Now for that, we have basically two different ways of doing that - we can and that might sound surprising but we can write some HTML code in Javascript and tell Javascript and therefore the browser that it should take and parse this HTML code and render it in a certain place of our documentary in the end or we use the create element method on the document object to create a brand new node and manually then insert it somewhere in our document. Now the HTML string can be added with the innerHTML property which you find on element nodes and that indeed adds and renders an HTML string, so some HTML code in that place where you add it.

Alternatively, you also have insert adjacent HTML, a method you can use if you want to add some rendered HTML content next to existing content instead of replacing that content with it, so that's also supported or as I said, use create element to create single DOM element nodes instead of a bunch of HTML at once. Such created elements or element nodes can be added with append child or append and I'll come back to the difference throughout the next lectures, so this appends such a new DOM element or node inside of another, the new parent element or node then. You also have prepend, before, after, insert before and so on to be more specific where you want to add it, instead of adding it at the end of the existing child node list, you can add it in front of it and so on, so that can help you be more specific about the position where it should be added and you can also replace an existing node with that, with replace child or replace with, that's also possible and allows you to basically remove an existing element and replace it with a new one.

So these are different ways of manipulating the document, let's now have a look at them and understand their differences and when to use which.

I want to start with innerHTML and for that, let's select this section again and let's say we want to entirely change its content. You saw text content before which in the end gives you access to all text in there, by the way that might be interesting, you see this is all the text of all the list items, so not just direct child text but any nested text and you can also set new text content here, like this which by the way will also replace any existing HTML content in there if you now inspect this, so that's also interesting to see. So that's what innerHTML does, it really just swaps the entire nested HTML structure, all nested nodes with your new content. Sometimes that is exactly what you need and want, then this is great but sometimes you just want to add a single new element and keep the old content and then innerHTML is not that great. Now one workaround you might come up with is that you append content to innerHTML. This has two important implications, for one it's not great for performance. You are forcing the browser to re-parse and re-render a lot of HTML which didn't change at all. So innerHTML is useful whenever you want to change everything, all the HTML content of an element, it's not so good if you only want to add something to the existing content, that's one thing to keep in mind. Therefore a better way of updating this, to keep the user input here which I just typed would be to use div insert adjacent HTML, this allows you to target a position and then define which HTML you want to enter. For that as so often, it's good to Google for js insert adjacent HTML and find the respective MDN article and there you find the different values for position where this should be inserted, before the element, just inside before the first child, at the end of the element just after the last child or after the element itself and here you also see a visual representation of where stuff is entered.

So we basically have four values - before begin, after begin, before end and after end and hence here, we could say before end, so inside of the element, inside of the div but after its last child, so after the input in this case, I want to enter this paragraph, something went wrong. So now the same HTML code as before but inserted with insert adjacent HTML. The result is if I now it enter, this is kept and not reset, instead we just added this new paragraph, in this case after the last paragraph which I entered with this code here and now this does not re-render everything but really just insert this code and render this new code since you explicitly tell Javascript and the browser that this should be added next to the existing content.

So this is one way of adding new content to an existing element with some HTML code which you write in Javascript and this is therefore a great way of manipulating this. Still whilst this might seem perfect, there are scenarios where you don't want to do it like this.

lectures.text:
Do you have an idea when using HTML code like this or even with the better adjacent HTML method might not be great? Performance is not an issue here with this adjacent HTML method and also not that we would lose user input, so that's not the reason. Well a downside of this approach is that you tell the browser which element to render or which content to render and that can be any HTML content, doesn't have to be a single element, can be any as complex as you want HTML code. The downside just is you have no direct access to the newly rendered content. Let's say you would want to later reach out to this paragraph and change it or you inserted a button and you want to add an event listener, well then you have to do good old div query selector and query for a paragraph for example, in this case, we of course fetch the first one because we have to but you get the point, this would allow us to get access to this paragraph.

Now the more complex the HTML code is you inserted here, the more complex is to query for the right things so that you get the objects with which you can work, where you can add event listeners, where you can change the properties and so on. So the missing direct access to the inserted elements can be a problem. Of course it's not if you don't plan on doing anything with the inserted elements in your Javascript code but as soon as you need to add event listeners or change styles or read some values or do anything else with them in Javascript, this approach has the downside of not giving you direct access and if you find yourself inserting content like this and then querying for it thereafter, you're basically running two steps to get access to a newly added element when there actually is only one step required and that's the case with create element, with this other approach of adding new elements. So here I reloaded this page on which we worked all the time and now let's say here in the unordered list, I want to add a list item at the end on which we can click. Now for that, just as before we can now get access to the list with document query selector li, not li, ul like this and now of course we could use innerHTML or insert adjacent HTML but now I'll do something else.

I now want to create a new element node here in Javascript and then append it at the end of the list and this can be done with document.createElement. Now you always call create element on the document, you don't call this on any other DOM node or DOM object, it's always document.createElement. This creates a new element, a new DOM object, just like you could select it but it creates it from scratch and it takes at least one argument here and that's the tag name you want to create, so the tag name of the element you want to create, in this case li because we want to create a list item, without the brackets, so without the angled brackets, just the tag name which you find between the angled brackets, so li here to create a list item element.

In case you're wondering about the second argument here, we don't need that here, this is actually an object with exactly one property that is supported, the is property and that is related to custom elements, a very advanced topic which we'll not cover here, this is the form in which you use this pretty much all the time. So here we create a list item and I could hit enter but then we create it and we just let it go into the void and it will actually get garbage collect because I'm not saving it anywhere.

It creates a new element and it actually returns it, so now we can store it in a constant maybe which is maybe named new li, of course the name is up to you and this curly brace has to go of course. So now we have the new li available, if I output it here, here it is but of course if I hover over that, that's not getting highlighted in on the left here because it hasn't been inserted anywhere but now we can do that. Now we can reach out to our list which we got access to earlier and we can insert li here with append child for example.

This takes any node, actually you could also pass a text node here but you typically don't create text nodes in Javascript, you just set text with text content because you rarely want to add a text node next to existing element nodes, so therefore it is not really a use case, so instead here, you use append child and pass in this new li. If you do that, you'll see this bullet point here and of course no content next to it but since we have access to new li, we can now also set text content equal to item 4 for example and you'll see it up here on the left. Typically of course, you would first finish up configuring this and set the text content and anything else and then append it instead of first appending it and then completing it because you only want to append it once you are done configuring it and you can set the text content and the style prop and so on even if you haven't added the item to the DOM yet because it's already there in Javascript memory, you can work with it.

So this is now how we can add it and the big advantage is now that we already have this object now where we can add event listeners or change the style or do whatever you want, that is all possible now thanks to this way of adding it.

lectures.title: Inserting DOM Elements
lectures.text:
So we saw document create element which is really useful for creating DOM objects with which we then can interact and we did insert it with append child, nothing wrong with that but there also is append. The difference is not only that append is shorter but that append also does not only take our new li which we created but that here you can also add a string, some text for example which is then inserted as a text node next to the other element nodes, so if you want to insert a text node you can conveniently do it like this. Another difference by the way is that you can add multiple nodes here, simply separated by commas as multiple arguments to append to add multiple nodes at once in that place, that's also a difference to append child.

Now it is worth mentioning that if you google for js append to find the MDN entry on that, that if you scroll down to the browser support table there, that Internet Explorer, no version of it supports append. Edge does and Safari and all other browsers but if you need to support older versions of Internet Explorer, you might prefer append child but that really depends on the user base you're targeting, if that's not an issue for you, then you can absolutely use append instead of append child, otherwise append child has been there for longer and is simply safer to be used. In the browser support module later down the course, you'll also learn how to make features like this work in older browsers, like Internet Explorer which would normally not support it.

So that was append and append child, we also got more. So again let me get access here to our unordered list and let's create a new li, a new list item, however you want to call it with document create element as you learned, li is the tag name and now there, we can add a text content of item 4 since I reloaded this page, the old one which I added is gone and now we can of course append new li as you learned, but let's say we want to insert it as the first element, well then we can use prepend. So we can call prepend, new li, hit enter and now item 4 is actually the first element.

Now just as before, searching for js or MDN prepend is helpful to get the official article and scroll down to the browser support table to learn that here again, Internet Explorer does not support this, so with the same thing as with append, this is not necessarily supported. Still, to show you a couple of other methods and one other interesting behaviour, let's say we decide we actually want to use it somewhere else, we want to add it before the currently last list item. Now we can get access to that with list and then last element child, right?

That gives us access to the last list item in the list and now I want to add the new list item, item 4 which I already did add but I want to add it again let's say in front of item 3. Now for that, I can now call before here and I can pass a new li here or as many nodes as I want to insert before the selected last element child, so item 3 in this case. If I hit enter, item four is added there but the interesting thing we see here is that item 4 is now actually removed from the beginning of the list and basically moved into this place.

If you have an element selected, either because you selected it in the DOM with query selector or because you created it with create element and that element is already part of the DOM, so it is already rendered, if you then insert it somewhere else, this is not copied or anything like that, instead the existing element is detached from the place where it was and moved to the new place and I guess this actually makes a lot of sense since objects are reference values as you learned and the DOM objects you're working here are nothing but normal objects in the end and therefore if we do something with it and we add it somewhere else, we always work with the same object, so of course it's detached from the existing place and moved to the new one, it's just something to be aware of. If you want a brand new one, you have to create a brand new one with document create element. Now and of course, you don't just have before, you also have after to insert it after this selected element unsurprisingly and you also have replace with, so if I select let's say in this case the first element child and then I use replace with and replace this with new li, then you see item 1 is now dropped actually because replace does not swap it, it just replaces the

element with it, which means it gets rid of the old one and replaces it with a new one and therefore the old item one is replaced with item four. So these are different ways of inserting this in different places, important - append, before, after and so on, they all take multiple nodes if you want, so you can absolutely say append new li and some other item which you might have created. They also take strings, so text nodes if you want to but most of the time, you'll use them with single elements and then they simply give you a lot of flexibility and control over where this element should be inserted, just keep in mind that inserting the same element multiple times will move it because we're working with objects here and not with some automatically copied things.

Now one word about before and after, if you search for it on MDN and you again check the browser support table, you'll see that here we actually also have a problem with Safari. So whereas append and prepend work on Safari and only don't work on Internet Explorer, before and after also have problems on Safari, so there you want to be even more careful for whether you want to use that or not and maybe find different ways of inserting elements than with before and after.

Now what would be such a different way of inserting an element in a specific position if you want to insert an element let's say after item 2 which you can't really do with append child or so on or anything like that. Well for that, you might want to select the element you're interested in, in this case my second list item, that could be found on children and then index 1, right, that gives me the second item, so second li is now stored in there and now if I create a new list item and I reloaded this page so that I can create that all again from scratch and I create a new list item here and I set new li text content to item 4 and I want to insert this after this second li, well then of course the most convenient way would be to use second li after but again, support for that on Safari is not that great.

So if we want to avoid it, then you have another useful method, list.insertAdjacentElement. If we have a look at this on MDN, then we see, just like insert adjacent HTML, these are the strings we can use and browser support is way better. So now here, we could insert this inside of the list or since we want to insert it next to the second li, we can just go to that and call insert adjacent element where is after end, if we want to insert it after this one because as you can see here in MDN, after end inserts element after the element you selected, so after the second li and then here, it's the new li which we want to insert and now item 4 is inserted after that second element. So insert adjacent element, whilst being a bit longer than after and before is the safer way of doing this, of inserting elements after or before other elements since it has better browser support. So that's also something you should be aware of.

lectures.title: Cloning DOM Nodes
lectures.text:
So you learned that inserting an element more than once will move it and not copy it, if you would want to copy an element, well then you can do this with another method which is available on every DOM node object, so let's say on our new li with clone node this will clone this node and will really return a brand new one. It takes one optional argument and that's a boolean which can be true or false which by default is false, which simply determines whether a deep clone, so with all child and descendant elements should be done or not.

If you pass false here, which is the default, then only the list item itself is cloned but no nested elements you might have in there. If you pass true here, then not only the direct child element but also all child elements of that element and all descendants in general will be part of the clone. So now if we do that and we have newLi2 where I store this clone, now I can of course go ahead to my list and let's say append new li and newLi2 and the result of that is of course that item 4 is moved to the end because I appended new li which already was part but I also appended the brand new li 2 which is why I have another item 4 here added to the end.

So this is how you can also copy elements if you need to instead of recreating and reconfiguring it, this might simply save you some time if you want to take most of the settings of an existing element or all of the settings and then just insert this brand new element into your DOM as well.

lectures.title: Live Node Lists vs Static Node Lists
lectures.text:
So now that we have a feeling for how we can insert content into the DOM, let me come back to that live node list versus non-live node list thing. So we have this list here, we worked with it many times, I reloaded this document so let me again select this like this as we did it many times in this module already and now here, I used query selector, this gives me access to this unordered list. Now I also want to get access to the list items in there and for that, we can use document query selector all li and this will select all list item elements on this entire page.

So of course not just in this list but on the entire page, if we would want to restrict it to this list only, I would have to run this on the list instead of the entire document which of course also works for this example here. So now I got my list items here and if I output them, you see it's a node list with a couple of list item objects in there unsurprisingly. Now I will also fetch my list items in another way, list items 2 here by reaching out to list and then here I can use get elements by tag name for example and pass in this li tag name here.

That's one of the older query methods which is built in and if I do this, list items 2 is a HTML collection actually as you can see. So it's still an array-like object as I mentioned, supports a couple of the important array methods but as you will learn later in the course in the array module, not everything you can do on arrays but most of the things and it looks quite similar. Well let's now add a new element, so I'll add a new li here with document create element, like this and create a list item element and so that we can see it really good, I'll also add a text content of item 4 again.

Now it's up to you how you want to insert this, you learned about different ways of doing that, here I'll just reach out to the list and use append and append my new li, you could use append child or target a specific place with after and before or insert adjacent element and so on. Here I'll just insert it like this and once we did this, we of course see it here on the screen, now to the interesting part. We got our two list items constants, list items and list items 2 and on list items, you can already see this still is a node list with three items.

So our most recent addition is not reflected here, that's what I mean with non-live array or non-live list. This is taking a snapshot of the DOM, of what we select there when I run query selector all and does not update that array when that part which we queried in the past changes. Now, that's not necessarily a disadvantage from a performance perspective, from a memory consumption perspective, this might even be better and I also want to highlight that of course the individual objects in there are still reference values, so an object in there is still of course a live reference to the DOM objects that are responsible for what we see on the page.

So if I go to let's say the first item there and I change the text content to item 11 here for example, that gets reflected on the screen because the items are reference values, these are pointers at the objects, at the DOM objects in memory, just the overall array is just a snapshot of list items when I ran that query selector all command. Now if we have a look at list items 2 however which is this HTML collection I got with get elements by tag name, we can see this indeed is a live list which also includes our most recent addition.

So all these get elements by something, not get element by ID because that only gets a single element which always is a live connection so to say but get elements by something, this always gives you array-like objects with live lists which will change when the items you queried in the past change, so when the number of these items changes I should say. That can or cannot be an advantage, often it will not matter to be honest. It could lead to a higher memory consumption if you're managing a lot of such collections which change all the time but again, that will also probably only matter in rare niche cases but for the most part, query selector all simply should be used because it is more flexible, supports richer queries and therefore often is a common choice if you want to query for multiple items.

I just wanted to highlight this difference again which sometimes can be an advantage, sometimes can be a disadvantage, well and often to be honest, it will probably not matter that much.

lectures.title: Removing Elements
lectures.text:
Now being able to add elements is of course nice, sometimes you also want to remove them. Now with replace with, we are able to remove them but of course only to replace an element with a brand new one. To just get rid of it, we of course also have ways. Now for that, I reloaded this document and here, let's say we want to get rid of that entire list. So I'll again select it with document query selector ul, ul as a string and now to get rid of it, there are two ways.

One is to use list.remove and this will just do what it sounds like, it removes the list from the DOM, so from the rendered page. Now good old MDN, if we check the remove method there shows us however that Internet Explorer again is not too fond of this method so if you want to ensure that this works there as well, you can't really use remove there. All other browsers have great support so you can definitely use it there but if you need to support this like this in Internet Explorer, then another way of making this work is to select the item you want to delete and then you reach out to the parent element, so the element node above the item you want to delete and there you have a remove child method and to that, you pass the item which you want to delete, list in this case and it will also work. Remove child is supported in all browsers, just like append child and therefore, this is the safest way of removing an element, reaching out to its parent and then remove child and then passing the item you want to remove but again, remove also has pretty good support.

If Internet Explorer support doesn't matter for you, then just remove on the item you want to remove just like this is of course the shorter and the recommended way.

lectures.title: Insertion & Removal Method Summary
lectures.text:
So we learned about a lot of different insertion and removal methods, let me now summarize the important ones which we used here. Now I'll not dive into the innerHTML and insert adjacent HTML methods which I also showed you but focus on the ones where we created a new DOM object programmatically in Javascript. We can then add such an object with append child, with insert adjacent element, replace child or remove child. Now I haven't shown you replace child, in the end this also just is a convenient method for replacing one element with another one. Now attached you also find a detailed summary document which you can have a look at to find an overview over all the methods you have available and when to use which, I strongly also recommend having a look at that.

We also had a look at some of the more modern methods - append, prepend, before, after, replace with and remove. Now the main difference here is really browser support, also a minor thing might be that you find more examples on the Internet using these older methods which have been around for longer than for these newer methods because these have also a good browser support as you saw but some browsers are not supporting all methods, for example Safari doesn't support before and after, it supports the other methods but Internet Explorer is a big problem there.

So this might be an issue if you need to support these browsers and you will also see them a bit less often used in some of the other tutorials you find on the web which is why I find it important to learn all of them. If you want to be super safe regarding support and so on, you want to use the left ones but the right ones also are pretty good, mostly if Internet Explorer users are not that important for you and as I already mentioned, later down in the course, you will also learn how you can actually ensure proper browser support even if you are using features that are not supported in all browsers out of the box. So you will even learn about ways of making these methods run in older browsers as well later down in the course, in the browser support course module.

Now again, check out the attached document as well, there you find a full list of all the methods you have available for that, what they do and when to use which and with that, that should be all, super clear. Now still, that was a lot of theoretical knowledge now, now it's also time to apply at least some of these methods and features in a simple project so that we can see how we would use them in a more realistic app.
