lectures.title: Selecting the Modal and "Add" Button
lectures.text:
So here's our skeleton, our HTML page and right now of course, no interaction is possible. Now the first thing that would be great if it worked would be that if I click add movie, we actually display an overlay, a so-called modal here which is like a pop-up but not this alert which is controlled by the browser but a pop-up which we create visually in our web page which allows us to enter some movie data and in the HTML code, we actually already got everything for that.

This div here, this one here, this in the end is such a modal, has some CSS classes to look nice, has an ID, add modal which might come in handy for selecting it later and there I also already added a couple of inputs which allow us to add a movie title, an imageUrl and a rating which we then enter here and then some buttons to either cancel adding that movie which I also want to support or for completing adding that movie would should then add it both to a Javascript array but of course also output it on the page.

If we scroll down there, I have an unordered list with no entries at the moment, I want to populate that list once we add movies. So the goal is to show this div and of course therefore an important question is, why is it not showing at the moment? Well actually because if we have a look at the CSS code, in there I added a style to this modal class which is the class I'm applying here to this div which sets display to none which basically means it's not added to the document flow, it's not visible, it's not clickable, it's like it wasn't there.

It's actually part of the DOM as you can tell if you go to the elements tab, there you find that modal but you don't see it anywhere on the screen, if I hover over it here, if I select that, it's also not selected on the left because it's set to display none it's not part of the document flow, just of the DOM, that's an important difference because that means we will be able to select it from Javascript and then we can toggle this display style to show it. Actually there even is an easier way, there is this visible class which we can add to a modal which will set display to block and also play a nice little animation to fade it in and to slide it in.

So actually our goal will be to make sure that when we click the add movie button, we reach out to this div here with the ID, add modal and we then add this visible class. These are all things we of course learned, so here already is a great place to pause and try this on your own but of course after this short pause which I give you to pause the video, we'll do it together. So let's try it together and we got two steps with which we should start, we need to get access to this add modal div and we can do this with the ID, we could also try to do it with a class selector, though you should be careful because we also got another modal here, another div with the exact same classes.

So since is the first div with these classes, we would be able to use query selector to select by class because query selector selects the first matching element but later when we need to access the second modal for example, we'll definitely need to use the ID or come up with some other unique selection criteria. So here I will actually go for the ID and select it by that and you also mustn't forget that we also need to get access to this button so that we can add an event listener and for this, if we scroll down, we can have a look. Here's the header and there is this add movie button, so we also probably want to select this. Now we'll have to see how we can select it because this button has no ID or anything like that.

Now of course, we can always add an ID and that might be a good idea, give this some unique ID which we haven't used anywhere else on the page but also to practice the different ways of selecting stuff, I will also use a different approach of selecting this button. Now let's start with the modal though and let's go to app.js and in there, I'll assign a new constant because I'll never assign a new value and I'll give it a name of add movie modal, the name of course is fully up to you but it should describe what you store in this constant and here, I'm in the end storing a reference to my modal, so to this overlay which you can add and it is the modal for adding a movie, so I will name it add movie modal, seems like a fitting name to me.

Now we can select it with document and now, we can use get element by ID because our modal here has an ID, add modal so that is probably the most reasonable way of selecting it. As an alternative to that, just to also show this, we could also use query selector and then we just have to add a hash here because a query selector wants a CSS selector here. This would work as well, would also select it, this tends to have a bit better performance, though for this app it really won't matter, for most apps you'll probably not feel it but it's a little bit better to use get element by ID than to use a query selector if you really just want to get access to an element by ID, so that's just a side note and another way of getting access of course also would have been to use other techniques, for example we could dive into the body and then have a look at all its children, so all the child element nodes and then pick the second child because the first child is this strange backdrop thing which will become important later, second child would be that.

So another way of selecting this would have been to use document body and then there, children and then there, the element at index one which is the second element, All these approaches select this movie modal, just to prove it, I'll quickly output it here, comment out the first two steps so that we don't get errors because I'm using the same constant over and over again and now with that, just go to the console here, reload, now we see that selected this modal and that's also true if I uncomment this and comment this back in and then reload, add the same modal here and also for completeness sake and this is the approach which I will use if we use get element by ID, we also lock that modal here.

So these are just some ideas, of course there are more ways of selecting it, just to give you an ID for that but I will go with this approach because if you have an ID, you typically should strongly consider using that ID at least, this also will be very fast from performance perspective, so there is little that speaks against using this. So with that, we selected the movie modal, now as I said, we also need to get access to this button here, to the add movie button and for that, I'll add another constant here, add movie button or actually I'll name it start add movie button. I'll name it start add movie button because later, I will also have a button inside of that add movie modal, so inside of that modal which we just selected, there we also have an add button and I want to give this the add movie button named later because this will be the button when we press it that really adds a movie to our app, the button in the header starts this whole addition process which is why I will call it start add movie button.

Now how can we select that? Of course there are different ways of selecting it, we could for example say document query selector and then reach out into the header and then to the button. So here I am using tag selectors because I only have one header on this entire page, it's this header here and then this is a normal CSS selector, we select a button inside of a header element. So we only have one header element, we select the first matching button which in this case also is the only button in this header and therefore this would give us access.

So that's one way of doing it, another way of course and I will not always show all alternatives, no worries but here I do want to show it and so another way would be to use query selector header and then for example, last element child because if we have a look at our header, here we see the button is the last element child inside of the header, so that would be another way of selecting it. The downside of using this, just as before with using document body children one for the movie modal is that whenever we change something in the structure, whenever we add something in the header, some other content here after the button, some other title or anything like that, then this way of selecting it here will not work anymore because it always selects the last element child and if we change that in the HTML code, our Javascript code will select the wrong element.

So therefore you should be careful with using this selection technique in places where the HTML content might change, where you as a developer might change it later. So therefore, I actually prefer this approach, as I mentioned earlier an alternative would have been to add an ID to this button but also to mix things up, let's use this query selector.

Now with that all selected though, let's add an event listener to the start add movie button because that's what we all came here for, we want to make sure that we can open that add movie modal and that should happen when we click that button.

For that, you can define a function whichever way you want with the function keyword and the declaration approach, with the expression approach where you stored a function in a constant or with the expression approach where you use an arrow function.

So this will actually hopefully show our modal, we just have to connect it to the click listener by pointing at toggleMovieModal without parentheses here of course because we don't want to execute it immediately, we just want to point at this function.

We could therefore do it in this toggleMovieModal function but actually I want to create a new function because we will need to reuse this backdrop, also in another place of this application later so I don't want to tie it to this function.

Now this again is a great challenge for you, try it on your own first and in the next lecture, we'll implement this together.

lectures.title: Which Data Can You Store In Arrays?
lectures.text:
Now that we know how we can create arrays, I also want to emphasize what you can store in arrays. You can store numbers as you see, you can store strings, you can store objects, these are all things you did throughout the course. It's really important to understand that arrays can be of the same type, like hobbies where we have cooking and sports which are both strings but can also be of mixed types, like personal data where we might have the age as the first element, then the name as a second argument and then even an object with more details which might even be another array as a third element. So you can have arrays which are uniform or which have different types of data in there.

You can also have nested arrays or multi-dimensional arrays as they're also called, for example you could have some analytics data which is in the end an array of arrays where you have 1, 1.6 and then another array, -5.3 or 5.4, 2.1 and so on. So where you have an array, where each element in the array is another array and of course you could for example also loop over such an array, const data of analytics data. This will go over the outer array, so now data will be these elements of the array, so the nested arrays. So you can have a loop in a loop and go through the data points here for example of data, so data is this data which is just one of the elements, which in turn is an array and then console log data point here, that should be data point because we'll always have a look at one element at a time.

So that's also something you can have, if I reload here, we see the data point is being logged here. So multi-dimensional arrays are also a thing and of course you could have even more dimensions, you could have an array in an array in an array. You can also have a mixture of an array with arrays and then still have another element which is an object or a string, so you can also have mixed data in multi-dimensional arrays. So what I want to say here is you're really flexible there.

Of course if you would have an array with nested data and then you have some other element which is just a number let's say, it's still not an iterable object, well then code like this would break because there we loop over this array with this outer loop and we have a look at each array element and then we loop over that array element again which works for iterables but not for numbers. So you have to be careful how you can use your array but in general you can store whatever you want in there, nested arrays, nested arrays and nested arrays, mixed data, strings, numbers, whatever you need, arrays are really flexible regarding the values you store in there. Also important to know about arrays and something we of course had a look at already but it's something which sometimes gets messed up is that arrays are index based, so you can access data by index. If I would want to get my name from personal data which is that second element, I would do so by accessing personal data one because it's index based and the index starts at 0, so the first element in an array has an index of 0, second element has an index of one, third element has an index of two and that's simply important to keep in mind, it's a common mistake because the length of that array would be three,

the highest index value would be two. That's something you learn earlier already and what we used already but since it's easy to mess up, I just wanted to repeat it here. Index based, index starts at zero, the length of an array is max index plus 1 though.

So if I call slice here and I store the result of that slice call in stored results, I store a copy of that array in stored results, so a brand new array is created and stored in memory based on that old array, it has a brand new address which is in the end stored here and therefore now if we added test results here, this will not affect stored results because that stores its own brand new copy.

So here if we save that and reload, in test results we see 5.91, in stored results which is this first array, we don't see it, there we don't have that sixth value. So that's one use case of slice for copying arrays but actually slice is also really nice for selecting ranges of an array. You can select a single element of an array with the index based access here, 0, 1, 2 and so on but what if you want to select two elements at the same time? So you want to select a part of your array, not the entire array but a part. Well slice helps you with that, you can use it like this and it will give you the full array but you can also specify a start and an end number and these are indexes of the array, start is included and is not. So if I specify 0, 2 here, I tell slice to give me a new array which is based on the existing array, starts add the first element, index 0 and then goes all the way up to the element with index 2 which is the third element here but does not include that. So slice here with this configuration should give us this part of the array, 1 and 5.3.

Well let's have a look at that. If I now reload this, indeed we have 1 and 5.3 in that first array which is my stored results array. Though what you can use are negative indexes but then both have to be negative. So you can start at the third last element, this has negative index 1 because there is no negative 0, so in the negative indexes the first element from the end has index 1, negative index 2, negative index 3 and then going up to 2, you might think you select this part but this is actually not supported, this is not how it works but you can for example go to -1 and this will then select from the third last element all the way up to the last element so these two should be selected.

lectures.title: Adding Arrays to Arrays with concat()
lectures.text:
There also is a useful method for adding elements to an array and returning a brand new array which again can be useful in situations where you want to create a copy of an array, maybe after adding new elements to it, let me show what I mean. I'll comment this out and instead create stored results here by using my test results and now here, there is the concat method which we can call. The concat method allows you to concatenate, so to add elements at the end of an array.

Now therefore it's of course a bit like push, with push you can also add items to an array, by the way also more than one item, they will be added at the end but concat actually here takes an array or multiple arrays but not individual numbers or items in general but arrays, one or more arrays and combines these arrays with this array. So it does not add these arrays as new nested arrays, that is what would happen if you pushed an array, that would add this as a single element in the existing array hence creating a nested array, concat on the other hand will pull out all elements of the array you are passing here and add them as new elements to the existing array and it will then also return a brand new array. So it will create a copy of the array, add these items and return that copied brand new array, hence creating a new place in memory and a new address.

So here for example, if we have 3.99 and 2 and I concatenate this here, what you'll see is if I reload, here we get the array with 3.99 and 2 at the end which are the two values I just added. And of course please also note that when I push 5.91 to test results, this does not end up in my stored result which is the first array I output here because concat returned a brand new array. So you see no 5.91 here in the first array, only in the second one.

So that's also useful, concat can be really useful if you have array data and you want to combine it with an existing array and the fact that you get a brand new array is also quite convenient because that often avoids problems where you manipulate an existing array when you actually didn't want to do that.

lectures.title: Retrieving Indexes with indexOf() /& lastIndexOf()
lectures.text:
Thus far when we worked with arrays, we always talked about adding items or selecting single items or a range of items. Now you also encounter use cases or scenarios where you have an array of data and now you want to find out at which index in that array a certain item sits, so that you can use that index to replace the item or for whatever reason you might have. Let's say we want to find out where in this array this item with the value of 1.5 lives.

You can do this with another method that is available in Javascript on every array, let's run it on test results here and that's the indexof method. Now as the name suggests, this returns the index of the value you're passing as an argument here. So for example here we could search for 1.5, you also have an optional second argument that would allow you to specify a starting index so that you for example only start searching on elements with index 2 or higher.

Now I will search the entire array here and hopefully, get a result of 2 which is the index of this 1.5 value here. So if we reload this, indeed I see 2 here. Now there are a couple of important things to understand, for one if you have the same value more than once, like I do here now that I added 1.5, then this will stop after it found the first matching value, so it will return you two, it will not return you all indexes of all items that have that value.

So if I repeat that code with that new item added, you'll see I still get to here even though I have another item of the same value at index four. So that's one thing, indexof stopped once it found the first element that fits this description. Now if you want to start searching from the right, there is last indexof, you can use that to search from the right and therefore it will now stop at this index, so it does the same as index of, just starting from the right.

So if I now reload, we see an index four here because it started from the right. Another important gotcha regarding index of and last index of is that it works fine for primitive values but not for reference values. Let's say we had our person data array here and there we have an object with name Max in there and another object with name Manuel, so it's an array of two objects. If I want to find out where Manuel is, then of course we could try person data index of and pass in that object, right?

We could try that. If we do this and I reload my page, we'll get -1 though, -1 is the return value of index of and last index of if it couldn't find any entry, then it always returns -1. So it doesn't throw an error, it doesn't return false or anything like that, it returns -1 if it didn't find anything. Now the reason for this behavior of course is this reference value thing. Objects are reference values and therefore in the end here, I'm creating a brand new object and I'm passing this to index of and behind the scenes, index of is of course comparing all values to the value I passed to index of and because two objects even if they look similar are never similar, it doesn't find any match and therefore it returns -1.

So index of won't work if you have objects in there but no worries, we'll have a different method that does work if you do have objects in there.

Now this is a typical use case for an anonymous function, though of course you could also define a function somewhere and then just pass in a reference to that function, so the function name but since this often is a function which you only need to run in this place and which you never call from anywhere else in your code, this is a perfect scenario for an anonymous function. lectures.text:

Now we had a look at find and find index which was really nice for finding single elements but what if you want to basically reduce the amount of elements in your array based on some filter, let's say here we only want to have prices that are greater than 6, so that only 6.59 and 10.99 are included.

Well for that, we can create a new constant for example filtered array and then use the prices array and call the filter method on it. Now just like all these other array methods, filter will return a brand new array, so it will not touch the original array but instead return a new one which we then store here and which I therefore want to output down there and the filter method also takes a function and this function here works just like the function you pass to find and to map and so on. You get the value it's currently looking at because this function which you pass to filter is again executed for every item in the array on which you call filter, so on every price in this example. You get the index here and you get the original array if you're interested, though you will rarely use that last argument as you already saw here.

Well and then here again you need to return something, so the filter method is a method that expects the function which you pass to it to return a value, to be precise it wants true or false. It wants true if the item on which this function is currently executed should be kept in the newly created array and false if it should be dropped. So here I want to keep everything where the price is greater than 6, so I will return price greater 6. This boolean comparison here will return true for any item where the price is greater than 6 and therefore any item where the price is greater than 6 will be kept, other items will be dropped from that newly created array, the old array is not touched, so the prices array itself is not touched.

So if we save that and reload, filtered prices here indeed only has two values which are my two values greater than six. So filter is also really useful for filtering an array as you can guess and therefore this also is an operation you'll find yourself do quite frequently.

lectures.text:
Now there is one last important array method which you absolutely have to know and that's the reduce method. Now I'm diving into it last because it's one of the more complex or challenging functions but in the end, it's also pretty straightforward and I will explain it step-by-step. So let's assume here with your prices, let's say the unfiltered, unchanged prices, you want to sum them up. Now of course what you can do is you can create for loop or you can use ForEach and you could create a sum here, let sum, set it to equal and then you could go through your prices, let's say with ForEach where you have the value of each price and then here in the end you say sum plus equal price, right?

And if you do that and you console log the sum thereafter, we should have the sum of all prices. So that's not too much code and if I reload this, this probably is to sum. Again let's ignore this strange output here, I'll explain it later, it's not a bug or an issue, just related to how computers work with floating point numbers. So I added these values together and I got a sum. Now of course that's not too difficult or not too problematic here, it's a quite short code snippet but we can actually write this with less code.

Let me comment this out and instead, create a constant sum and set this equal to prices.reduce. Now the reduce method is another built-in method available on arrays and the reduce method takes a function. This function as you can see takes a couple of arguments, it takes a so-called previous value, okay, it takes a current value, okay, it takes a current index if you want to and it also accepts this original array on which you are running it. Now I will say that current index and that array again are the arguments you don't use that often here, the index maybe sometimes, this original array pretty much never.

I'm just adding all arguments here for completeness sake, the first two arguments are the really important ones here though. Now the reduce method itself also takes another optional argument or parameter. So the first argument or parameter is this function and you must never forget, we're always passing functions here as arguments, as parameters to sort and so on. So here I'm passing a function to reduce and then reduce itself does not just take this function as its first parameter but another optional second parameter.

Now what does reduce do to begin with? Reduce, as the name suggests, reduces an array to a simpler value, for example it can reduce an array of numbers to the sum of these numbers. Of course that's not the only kind of reduction it can do, you can reduce any array to any value you need, so the idea always is that you reduce an array to a simpler value. Typically an array to a single number or a single string or whatever it is. Now the second argument you pass to reduce is the initial value with which you want to start, so here if we want to get the sum, we would start with zero probably here.

Now what happens is reduce executes this function on every element in the array, just like map and find did and previous value for the first execution is this initial value which you set here if it's set, otherwise it will be undefined. Current value is the first element of the array, so generally the element of the array it's currently executing on. So for the first execution, current value is the value of the first element in the array, previous value is this initial value. Now here in this function, you have to return your updated value, so your currently reduced value, so that in this case here would be previous value plus current value.

So for the first execution, previous value is zero, current value is the first element in prices, so current value would be 10.99. So now for the second execution, this function here is executed on the second element in the array which in this case is 5.99. Now on that second execution, previous value no longer refers to that initial value but instead, to the value you returned in the previous execution, so in this case since we're on the second execution, previous value will hold the value of the first execution, so the result here of that first execution.

Now remember in the first execution, we had 0 + 10.99 and the end here because 10.99 is the first value, so in the second execution we'll get this 0 + 10.99, so 10.99 in total value as a previous value and now, this 10.99 value is what we use in this calculation here to add our current value which for this second iteration is the second elements value, 5.99, so now we add 10.99 + 5.99 and so on for all elements in the array. Here's a graphical representation of what happens, let's say we have an array with the value is 1, 2 and 3 and we want to reduce it. We might start within initial value of 0, of course you can start with any initial value but let's say we start with zero and now the reducer function executes.

Now this means it has a look at the first element so to say and it returns this initial value plus that first value which is 1. Now does this fed in into the second execution where we have a look at the second element, so the reducer function returns three, 1 which was the result of the first execution plus 2 which is that second element we're looking at and then we repeat that one last time, where we have a look at the last element of that array and hence we get six because we had three as a result of the last execution, three also is our last element in the array, so we have 3 + 3 equals 6.

Now of course the original array is not emptied or anything like that, I'm just removing the numbers we worked with here to make this slide clearer. The original array is not edited in any way, instead this only executes this logic on all array elements to gradually build up a value which you in the end return. Well and for the last execution if there are no array elements left, well this value is returned overall and is stored in this case in this sum constant which we can therefore log and hence what we see here if I log this is this same result as before which makes sense, it would be bad if we had a different result. Now just as before, you can also shorten this, thanks to arrow functions, we only need the first two arguments so we can get rid of the other two, we need to keep the parentheses here since we have more than one argument but we can get rid of the curly braces like this, then have to get rid of the return value and just write it like that, get rid of the semicolon and have a very concise reduce function which really just reduces this array of numbers to a single number. That's just one use case but reduce can be really powerful for combining values in an array to a single value.

lectures.title: Arrays & Strings - split() and join()
lectures.text:
So that's basically it for all these special array methods. Now there are two other special methods which are related to strings and they're also quite handy. Let's say you have some data which you maybe read from some csv file which looks like this, New York; 10.99; 2000, whatever value that might be but you have that value. You might want to transform this to an array where you have three separate values instead of one single value like this, actually this of course shouldn't be an array, it's just a string.

So instead of having a string with this combined data which to us humans is clearly recognizable as three different pieces of data, you might want to split it into three real elements with which you can work on the computer as well. For that, the transformed data can be created by running data.split. Now that's a string method, not an array method because data is a string not an array. Now split splits a string into an array of multiple segments and as an argument, you specify the separator by which you split, that could be a whitespace, so blank, underscore, comma, any arbitrary character or of course also a semicolon and this will now split that string into three elements after every semicolon, it will pull out a new element and split therefore returns an array with these elements into which this string was split.

You can also specify an optional second argument to limit the number of elements which is created but here I don't want that, I just want to split it like that and therefore here if we console log the transformed data like this and we save that and we reload, we indeed have our array with these three data pieces. Now of course if you would want to transform numbers to real numbers, you would have to do that as well with parseInt by then diving into that transform data and for example using the map method to transform some elements or targeting them by index and setting that equal to plus transform data, one for example to replace it with a real number if you wanted to.

These are things you can do as you can tell but the split method is the main thing I wanted to focus here as it allows you to split a string into an array. Now you also have the opposite kind of operation, let's say you have the name fragments constant here and that has Max and Schwarz so that could be a first and a last name and you had this as an array because maybe you pulled this from two different inputs on the screen and now you want to merge this together into one string which you can use in your user interface to greet the user or anything like that.

Well then merging this into a string is very easy by using another special array method now because name fragments now is an array, not a string and there you have the join method. Now join also takes a separator which you can use to join these things together. Now let's first of all join without a separator to then see the difference and console log name. So this should now join the elements of this array into one string and it will always generate a string, even if you had numbers in here, it would still work but it would convert everything to a string.

So if we now save that and we reload, indeed we see Max Schwarz and you see by default it separates the values by a comma. Now that might or might not be what you want, if you want some whitespace for example, you simply add this as a separator here, so as an argument to join and if you do that, now the elements of this array will be joined together into a string with this as a separator between the individual words in the string in the end. So now if we reload, we see Max, Schwarz like that.

So join and split also are very helpful for transforming strings to arrays and arrays to strings and making sure that you got machine readable data and human readable names, that's the idea here.

lectures.title: The Spread Operator (...)
lectures.text:
More about arrays. Now here for one I noticed a little typo, of course that should be fragments not fragements, sorry about that and now let's dive in two more interesting Javascript features related to arrays. to be specific into two syntax features which help us work with arrays. Now one is a feature which I already briefly introduced but didn't dive deeper into, well now is the time to dive deeper into it and that would be the spread operator.

In case you forgot it, the spread operator is an operator that in the end pulls out all elements of an array and gives them to you as a standalone list of elements. So if I for example do name fragments and pulling out all the elements of that array but using it like this is actually not supported, here I'm pulling out all the elements of the array and I'm not doing anything with that. I also can't assign it to a constant like this because that would just be as if you had Max Schwarz here like that and that would be an invalid syntax, this is is not a supported operation, what would you do with just a comma separated list like this? Instead where you use this spread operator is for example to copy an array. So if I have my copied name fragments here, then I can create a new array with square brackets, an empty array but now populate it with the elements of name fragments but not by adding name fragments like this, this would insert this name fragments array as the first and only element in the copied name fragments array so we would create a nested array in the end but instead we add these three dots which make up that so-called spread operator, which is liked that rest operator you saw in the function's module but simply used in a different place. In the functions module,

we used these three dots, the rest operator in the argument list of a function. Here I'm using that in a place where I need multiple elements, for example when we initialize an array. This will then pull out all the elements out of the name fragments array and add them as individual elements to that newly created, otherwise empty array and then copied name fragments is a new array because we created it with square brackets with the values of the old array, so with these strings here in that case and the consequence is that if I log name fragments here and I log copied name fragments here, we'll of course see that if I reload, we get the same array here but it's interesting that if I now go to name fragments and I for example push a new fragment here, Mr for mister let's say and I reload, we see that this mr element is part of the first array output here which is the name fragments array which is the one where I push that to but it's not part of that second array which is my copied array where I indeed created a brand new array and just added the existing elements.

Therefore if I added array one, name fragments, this array two, the copied name fragments array which is a copy and therefore a brand new array is not touched at all. So that's one advantage but you don't just use this spread operator for copying things. If we go back to our prices which we have up there, then you see this is an array full of numbers. Now you also have some functionalities in Javascript, for example on the global math object which we'll have a closer look in the numbers module later where you have a min method.

The min method takes a couple of arguments, it does not take an array, instead it takes values like 1, 5, -3 and then it will return the smallest value, so if we console log that and reload, we of course output -3 because that is the smallest value. Now if you would want to find the minimum value in your prices array,then you would have a problem normally because that is an array, not a list of values, not a list of arguments so to say. So if I pass in prices like that and I save that, this doesn't work, I get not a number because indeed I passed it in array, not a number and it only works with numbers.

So here, again we can use the spread operator to pull these elements out of the array so that we have a comma separated list of elements and that's exactly what the min method here requires. So also for situations like this where you are working with some function or some method that requires a list of standalone values, the spread operator helps you get these values out of an array and therefore now, this indeed returns us the minimum price here.

Now one important note about the spread operator and especially about copying arrays with the spread operator like this. When you copy such an array, indeed when you added the original array, the copied one is not affected as I showed you. Now one common mistake is that you copy an array of objects. So for that let's create a person's array here maybe, where we have objects with name Max, age 30 and another object, name Manuel, age 31. Now let's say we want to copy that, so copied persons of course can be created by adding square brackets and then using the spread operator on persons like this.

Now unsurprisingly if we console log persons and copied persons like this, you will see that if I go to persons and I push a new person into this array, let's say Anna, age 29, that this will be part of persons but not of copied persons because copied persons as you learned is a brand new array and therefore changes to the original array are not reflected in the brand new one and indeed that is what we see here, the second array doesn't hold this Anna object.

Now a common mistake is to think that the objects in the array which are also reference values are also copied and that's not the case. We're copying all the elements of the array which means we're copying the addresses of these objects at the end. So whilst we have a brand new array, the objects in the array, the objects in that brand new array are still the old objects because in the end, you must never forget you're working with reference values and therefore in the end, this is an array full of addresses to the places in memory of these objects, so you are copying all these addresses here.

Hence if we would go to persons and there let's say to the first element which is Max and change the age to 31, you will see that this change is also reflected in copied persons. If I reload this, we have a look, expand this, this is copied persons and you'll see the age is 31. Now that happens because I copy the address of the place in memory and here I then added this object in that place in memory. So since we here only copy these addresses and create a new array but no new objects, of course any edits to these objects also affect our persons in a new, in a copied array and that's not a bug or anything like that, this is the intended behavior.

If you would want to avoid that, you would have to copy every object here as well which you could achieve by using the map method for example. So here on persons, we map that to get a brand new array and then we pull elements out of that returned brand new array and now in there, we get a single person and now we can return a new object for every person. So then here, we could return an object and side note, since I returned something in curly braces to tell Javascript that this does not mark the function body but should be my object, I have to wrap this in an extra pair of parentheses, this will then tell Javascript that this here is the single expression function body, so I just return something immediately and this here does therefore not mark the function body but instead marks the object which I'm returning.

So here I can then return a brand new object where name is equal to person.name and age is equal to person.age. So I keep all the data of the original person but I wrap it into a brand new object, so the same logic in the end as I do it for this array, I create a new array and keep all the original objects. Now I don't really do that, instead I map all objects in the original array into new objects which therefore have new places in memory and then map gives me a new array as you learned and I pull out all the elements of that new array that map returns and merge them into this yet another new array with these square brackets and therefore actually, here you could omit that, you could just save the result of map here because map already returns a new array, so now we would have a new array with new objects in there but even then, if one of these persons had a hobbies key which is an array, then you would have the same problem. You would clone the object, you would clone the outer array but any inner reference value fields are not copied.

Now this is not necessarily a problem, of course you could now find ways to then clone the hobbies as well, right? So that's the spread operator, another very nice syntax feature is the array destructuring syntax which you can use. Now for that, let's go back to my name fragments here with Max and Schwarz here. This is a perfect example for where array destructuring might be useful. You could be getting those from some other function let's say that reads some values from some inputs you have on your web page and now you get this as an array but you want to split it into two separate variables with which you continue working.

So you have your name fragments and to make this easier to read, I'll comment out all of that here actually so that we have less output in the console and recreate my name data, name fragments, however what you want to call it. So it's Max and Schwarz and this clearly is my first and my last name. Now in the rest of your code, you might not want to work with this array but with the individual values, of course you can always access the individual values by their index but always writing name data zero, name data one just to access these values is a bit cumbersome.

So of course you can store that data in new variables or new constants, first name could be name data zero and then the last name could be name data one and that is absolutely fine, it works, nothing wrong with that. Now there is a shortcut for that though and that's exactly what array destructuring is all about. You can write this a bit differently, you can add square brackets here after const, so on the left side of the equal sign which is something we haven't done before and point at your array and now what you put between these square brackets are variable names for these elements in the array on the right side.

So this array has two elements, so here we can add any names of your choice, for example first name and last name like this and what Javascript will do is it will pull out the elements here and store the first element in a variable or in a constant in this case of this name and the second element in a constant of this name. So therefore now if you console log first name here and last name and you save that and reload, you see Max Schwarz is getting logged here but this is now really stemming from these two individual variables which are output.

So that's a very powerful syntax for a splitting an array into variables with which you want to work. Now sometimes you also have more data in the array than you want to pull out, let's say we also have a Mr. identification element in name data and I'm only interested in first and last name, if I save this and I reload, this works so we can leave it like this and if you maybe also want to collect all other information which you have, let's say we also have the age here, well then you could add another variable here, other information or however you want to call it and add that good old rest operator here.

Now here, I'm calling it rest operator because what it will do here is it will collect all remaining elements of that array which are not assigned to variables and store them in one brand new variable which will be a new array that is in the end created. So here, other information, if I output that as well and we reload, now we see other information indeed is an array with the two remaining pieces of information which we don't assign to separate variables.

So you can also do that if you want to kind of collect the remaining data and store that in some array that holds all the remaining data. Now needless to say, this destructuring syntax is read and assigned from left to right, so first element here gets the first element in the array, second element gets the second element, third element the third or if you use the rest operator, any elements after this element, so all the remaining parts here, are merged into this array.

So array destructuring is a really neat feature if you want to split up an array into variables or constants which you then can use throughout your code. It simply saves you the extra work of doing this manually and therefore can speed up your development process.

You also have no index based access, instead you just have an access that allows you to get a specific value if you looking for it and then you can see whether it's in the set or not.

Now maps are yet another data container where you store key-value data of any kind in length and that's a bit like an object where you also have key-value data, one important difference is that in an object, you may only have strings or numbers as keys or symbols but we haven't learned about those yet, in maps you can use anything as a key. Duplicate keys are not allowed but values can be duplicated throughout this map and you access values by key.

So let's now work a bit with these data structures and then get a feeling for when we use them and how we use them.

lectures.title: Maps vs Objects
lectures.text:
So as you can tell, maps in a way are pretty similar to objects, which of course raises the question, when should you use which? So let's compare the two. Maps can use any values and any types as keys, so you can have an object as a key, a string, a number and in the same map, you can have mixed key types. Objects on the other hand can have mixed key types but you are restricted to using strings, numbers or symbols, we'll learn about symbols later, so you have less flexibility there.

You can't use a boolean as a key and an object, you can't use another object or an array. For large quantities of data and with that I mean more than 10 entries, really large quantities, maps can provide better performance than objects do. So that might be one possible use case if you're working with large amounts of key-value data which you need in your application and in many applications, you might never really have that much data but if you do have that, that might be a place where you want to use maps, whereas objects are perfect for small or medium sized sets of data.

And with that, I really mean medium sized not in the sense of five key-value pairs but still pretty big, 30, 40 key-value pairs, that's certainly not a problem for an object. Objects by the way will also have another advantage which we'll see once we dive deeper into objects in the objects deep dive module, you can have methods that interact with the data in the object, that's not really possible on maps. So if you have methods that need to do something with the data that's part of the object, that's a strong reason to use an object.

Now maps also can yield better performance when adding and removing data frequently, so if you have some operation which adds key-value pairs and removes key-value pairs multiple times per second, then a map might be worth a look. Objects on the other hand in general are easier and quicker to create, not just because you have that shorter syntax with curly braces but also from a performance perspective, new map takes a bit longer than creating an object with curly braces, though as always, with all these performance things, it's always important to keep in mind that we're talking about differences which you won't feel in the majority of apps you're building.

So in general, the summary I want to give you here, not just about maps versus objects but about arrays sets and maps and objects in general is that in probably around 98% of cases, you will work with arrays and objects. Sets and maps have their niche cases where they can shine for unique value which has to be unique in the case of sets, for large quantities of fast changing data in the case of maps or if you have some use case where you have some data, let's say an object, where you kind of want to attach extra data which you don't want to merge into the object, as we did it in this example I showed you in this module, then you could also think about using a map to use the object as a key and add the extra data as part of the map instead of as part of the object.

But again in the vast majority of cases, you can focus on arrays and objects but since sets and maps exist and you might encounter them in other code and you might personally also end up in some application at some point of time where you can benefit from them, it's of course important to be aware of them and to know them. Well and with that, they're actually also are two specific versions of sets and maps which are also quite interesting.

So here persons now is my new weak set which now requires objects to be stored in it, that means you can also store arrays in there since they are objects in the end but you can't store numbers or strings in there. So here I'll actually initialize this to be an empty set and now I can add a new entry with the add method and add person. Now right away, when you type persons., you see there are way less methods available, only add, delete and has. There is no method to get all the entries for example and the reason for that is that weak set, just like weak map which I will also show you internally works such that it can only store objects so that it can actually clear these objects for you, release them to garbage collection which I covered in the behind the scenes module, if you don't work with a certain piece of data anymore. Conveniently if we console log persons here, the browser dev tools console still allows me to look inside of that, if we reload here, we can actually have a look into our set and see the value here.

Now you might wonder, why would I need this strange thing? Well if you have an application where you store data, let's say in a set, object data in a set or other arrays, where you eventually will let go of data, then you want to make sure that this data can be garbage collected. Now if we work with that person here let's say and then we do some operations with it and we needed it in the set for these operations and we still need the set thereafter, maybe for other operations but this person is not really required anymore, then we can set person equal to null.

This means we set this variable to null, so this object no longer has anyone who is interested in it. This person variable, which stored its address is now reset to null, so the address is released from there and the Javascript engine then is able to pick this up and eventually clear this object from the heap, that's what garbage collection does, it clears that data from memory. Now if you would use a normal set here which you can normally, then the person you created here would still be part of that set.

So even if you cleared your variable here, you added that object, that pointer at this object to this set and Javascript thankfully detects that and will not clear the object because the set still holds a reference to it and that's good because Javascript would expect that you plan on working with that and deleting it therefore would be bad. Now let's say you eventually never end up working with that person again, then with a normal set, you have that unnecessary data stored in memory because you have that data in a set even though you don't need it anymore.

lectures.title: Special Key Names & Square Bracket Property Access
lectures.text:
So we know how we create an object, how we can dynamically add properties, how we can delete properties, how we can read properties and how we can call functions in objects. Now let's have a closer look at the property names we're using here, so at these keys. Thus far I always use keys like this, basically as I would use them for variable names, anything which you can use as a variable name can be used as a key name and keys are even more flexible than variables, so everything which you could use on a variable can be used as a key but not everything which you can use as a key name can be used as a variable and here's an example. Let's say I don't want to have name here as a key but first name but also not written like this but let's say written like this.

Now as you already can tell, my IDE gives me an error here because this actually is not a valid Javascript syntax, having two separate words here, Javascript doesn't know what you mean by that, it tries to understand how these two words work combined and it sees that first is neither an operator nor some other keyword, so it doesn't know what first should do to name and that makes sense because if you had a variable or a constant, you could also not use first name like that, that's not supported, right?

You must not have a whitespace in your variable name, it always has to be exactly one word without whitespace, without dashes and so on. Now the same is generally true for these object properties, first name like this for example is also not allowed but you have a way around that. You can use any string as a key in an object and actually any key you enter is automatically coerced, which is this behind the scenes automatic conversion you could say, to a string.

So even age is kind of converted to a string in Javascript, so an object really just is a dictionary you could say of keys which are string values and of then values which can be of any kind of value. And for first name, Javascript is not able to automatically convert this for us because before this code runs and Javascript has a chance of converting it, it already breaks because it first of all tries to interpret this in another way which is not valid.

Now therefore for names like this, we have to tell Javascript that no we want to use this as a key, it's not some calculation which you should perform or anything like that, it should just be a key name and how could we tell Javascript that this should be a key name which in the end is just a string? Well we just wrap it in quotes, single or double quotes, doesn't matter, either way works, so you can just use any string here as a key name, with a dash, with a whitespace, with multiple words, whatever you want, these are all valid key names.

Now I will say that names like this are the exception though, you typically use names which you could also use on variables because on variables, this does not work, that's just an important side note. You can't have const first name, this does not work as you can already see in the IDE, this is really exclusive to objects and again, whilst you can use it there, it's not so common to use it like this. But let's say we have first name like that, now we have a new problem, how do we access this?

Well you would say okay person.firstName but we have pretty much the same problem as before now, Javascript tries to parse this as an expression and in Javascript, this is never a valid syntax, having two words after each other only works if one of the words is an operator or some keyword, like here with delete person.age, with this delete keyword, this delete operator here, well Javascript understands this and then it can have a look at the thing after that keyword and see how that is affected by that keyword, by that operator.

Now it tries the same here and it sees I don't know first, it's not a built-in keyword, it's not some operator which I know so I don't know what to do with that and what to do with the thing after it, therefore this doesn't work in Javascript. So how can we now access this key name, which I told you is valid and which we see, we're not getting an error here, with this notation? Well the answer is with this notation, we can't but there is an alternative way of accessing properties on Javascript objects and that's the square bracket notation.

Now we know this notation from arrays, in arrays we could also use that to access the elements at certain indexes. In the end, that makes sense because arrays are just objects and this is basically just a general object notation. For array objects, we just have that built-in special behavior that we have certain methods to add elements to the array and they automatically get the indexes assigned and so on but other than that, we have this square bracket notation available on any object.

Now what we enter here is now not an index number because this person object doesn't have indexes, it's not an array but instead here, you can enter any key name but that's now important, not like this, this would look for a variable age outside of the object and then try to read that variables value and find a key with that variables value in here, instead you pass in a string here. So here, you can then type first name and this is now how you can access the first name of person with that square bracket notation.

So now if we save that and we reload here, we see Max being printed here and that is that result of that property access with square brackets. So this is really important to know, that you have this alternative and that this allows you to use key names which you normally could not use without the quotes around them. By the way, this is also pretty interesting because you might remember that on DOM nodes when we worked with the styles, for the things like background color, we had to use this camel case notation.

Let me quickly show you what I mean. We have a bunch of stuff here in our HTML file and let's say I want to select that movie list for now, that's in the end an unordered list where I later want to output the movies we added. So right up here, I'll add movie list with document get element by ID, that's something you learned. So now we have access to the movie list and here, we can access the style object to work with the different CSS styles and as I said, we can for example access background color, color written like this and set this to red and we have to use this notation because background color like that would not work and therefore Javascript automatically gives us these translated property names if we want to call them like this.

So now we could see that, however for this movie list we'll also have to set the style of display to block because by default it's hidden at the moment. So with these two lines added, if we save that and we reload, we got this red background down there. Now the interesting thing is with the square bracket notation, we can of course also access background color like that, however not exactly like that but with quotes around it as I mentioned, without quotes this here would lead Javascript to search for a background color variable in our other code and use the value inside of that variable to then look for a key on the style object with that variables value.

So we have to wrap this in quotes and this will also work if we save that and reload but the interesting thing now is that actually the style object does not only have these translated property names but you also find the original CSS property names in here because if you wrap your property access in quotes and you use the square bracket notation, you can of course use background color like this because your key is a string and in the string, you can have any characters you want - dashes, whitespace, question mark, whatever you want, it's all possible.

So therefore now actually we can set the background color like this and it will also work as you can tell. So that's also nice to know I guess and it shows the power of this square bracket access feature and also of the flexibility we have since we can use any string as a key name and just again because it's important, all non-string keys here which I have, like age and hobbies are kind of automatically converted to strings, coerced to strings by Javascript.

We had a look at this square bracket notation, to access key names which we couldn't access with the dot notation, you actually can do more with the square brackets. One cool feature is that you can also dynamically access properties with this notation. Here I hardcoded first name in here, now what if that would be stored in some constant, key name or whatever you want to name that constant?

So this constant holds a string and now I know I want to access the property with that constant value, so with this string, in person. With square brackets, we can dynamically look up values and we can work with key name values which are actually stored in other constants or the result of any other expression, could be a function call, could be a ternary expression, anything that yields a value can be inserted here to then access a key with that yielded value.

Now of course in this little example here, it's still the same as if I would have hardcoded first name here because I hardcoded it into this constant but you will have cases in this little demo app we're going to build in this module already actually where this is derived dynamically and then this is really useful. Now here, we know all property names in advance, now what if that's not the case and we'll see an example for that in this app we're about to build too. So you can not only use square brackets to dynamically access properties but also to dynamically set them, which is of course really powerful and again a concrete example will be shown in this little app we're building.

lectures.text:
So the movies which we have in our array should be output on our page and for that I'll add a brand new function here and you can of course name it however you want, I'll name it render movies, like this and in render movies, I will do something which is not the most ideal way of doing it but which is good enough for this demo. I'll reach out to my movie list, so to this unordered list here in index.html with that ID here with document get element by ID movie list and then there, I want to render all my movies into this movie list.

Now the ideal approach would be that for every movie you add, you append one item to the already existing list, this is also what we did in an earlier module. Now here to save some time and focus on objects which is of course the core of this module, I will actually do it differently and I will reach out to movie list and set innerHTML to an empty string which will clear it, so that if something was rendered into it, it's now completely deleted.

This is not ideal because now this means that whenever we add a movie, I clear the entire list and re-render it from scratch which of course costs unnecessary performance but again I'm doing it here to save some time, you saw a different approach of appending one item after another in an earlier module. So here I am clearing this, I also want to make sure that we can see the movie list to start with because by default if we quickly have a look at our styles here, we can see that movie list by default has a display style of none and it only gets a display style of block if we add the visible CSS class to it.

So therefore here whenever we call render movies, I want to check if movies, so my array up there, if the length which I can access with the dot notation here because length is a property of this array object, if that is equal to zero which means there are no movies because if there are no movies, then I will reach out to the movie list and class list and there call remove and remove the visible class if it's on it, else I will reach out to movie list, to class list and add the visible class and this should then show it. Now we can also return here after removing the visible class and therefore this innerHTML clearance can also happen after this if check.

So now with that, we have this logic in place, now let's make sure we actually output the movies here whenever we call random movies and we don't just toggle the visibility of the list. So I clear the current content here by setting innerHTML to an empty string, now I want to go through all my movies and output them there. So now whenever we add a new movie, it should be rendered. So it's time for the search logic then because adding movies works and I'll not work on making them deletable here, not really the focus of this module but instead let's make sure that we can enter some term here, something like that complete for example and then we can click search and we would find this but if I had another movie which doesn't include complete in the name, I wouldn't find this. So to achieve that, we need a new function here which I'll name search movie handler because it will be connected to an event listener and this function here in the end, I want to read whatever the user entered here and then also trigger the render movies function but then I want to tell that function here that it should not render all movies but only filtered movies, so step-by-step. Let's first of all read the user input and if we have a look at the index.html file, we can see that it's this input here with that ID that's interesting to us, that is where the user will enter the search term.

That shouldn't always be all movies, instead I want to have my filtered movies here. So I'll add a new constant, filtered movies and now that will either be all movies if filter is falsy, if it's an empty string or any other falsy value or it will be my filtered movies if filter is string other than an empty string.

So we can check filter, so this parameter here, if it's not true-ish, so if it's not truthy, if it's falsy, then if it's falsy I want to use all movies because then we have an empty string or anything like that and I want to use all movies because no filter was set in that case basically, otherwise finishing this ternary expression here, otherwise I want to use movies.filter and you learned about the filter method in the arrays and iterables module. Now let me reformat that and with that, we're filtering all movies for only movies where the movie includes the filter term, however of course looking at the entire movie does not make sense, I should look at movie.info.title and check if the title of the movie includes the filter term, that's what I want to check. So if my movie, if the title there in the info object, if that includes my filter, then I will add it to movies, otherwise I will not, if no filter is set, well then I always use all movies and now we can use that filtered movies constant here to go through it here with ForEach because that will now be the movies that respect my filter I might have set.

If I just search for s, new courses is shown because it's a lowercase s and Javascript only has an uppercase s here, if I search for a, both is shown because we have a lowercase a in both. So that's how this, of course basic but nonetheless, how this search works and how we can enable it with our Javascript knowledge here and even bring some array magic to this example.

lectures.title: Understanding "Chaining" (Property & Method Chaining)
lectures.text:
With this example finished, there are more exciting things we can dive into when it comes to Javascript and object syntax or Javascript features that help us work with objects. One important thing which I again want to emphasize is the concept of chaining, here we're doing something which is called chaining. We're having multiple dots in one and the same line or to be precise, in one and the same expression because we just prefer multiple operations on objects or on values returned by prior operations, for example movie.info returns an object and therefore we can access .title on that object.

We don't have to split this across multiple lines and store the result of movie.info in a variable and then use .title on that variable, we can all do it in one line. This concept of chaining is not only available on properties but also on methods, for example here with the ID. Math.random uses this built-in math object to generate a random number. Now it turns out that numbers in Javascript also have a method you can use which is called toString, actually everything in Javascript has this toString method.

Now what I'm doing here is I'm chaining the toString method on the result of math.random, so random is called on math and gives me a random number and toString is then called on that number. So this concept of chaining and this term, this special word, chaining, that is something you should memorize because you'll see it a lot in most programming languages and especially in Javascript, it is a common thing to do, it simply saves you the hassle of splitting code unnecessarily across multiple lines with helper variables in between.

lectures.title: The Object Spread Operator (...)
lectures.text:
We also have another nice feature in Javascript which we don't really need in this app but which we will need in general from time to time in Javascript and that's the spread operator in combination with objects. Now we saw the spread operator in combination with arrays but we can also use it in combination with objects and I will actually show this here in the console because there isn't really a great place to apply it in this dummy project. So let's say here we have an object, good old person and that person has a name, Max and maybe has some hobbies which is an array where I have sports and cooking, close the array, close the object and we're done, so that's my person here.

Now if we want to copy that, for example into a new person, so another person here, then we can try it like this but as you learned, objects are reference values so if I now set person.age equal to 30 and I add this new property, another person will also have have it because it points at the very same property in memory. Now we can avoid this if we want to by using the spread operator. For that if I create yet another constant, person2, however you want to name it, you can create a new object with curly braces and then use the three dots just as you do it on arrays and then add that other object you want to spread into this object.

What this does is it takes all key-value pairs of that object you pass after the spread operator and merge these key-value pairs into this object. So it creates a new object but copies over the values you have in the keys of the old object and not only values but also the key names. If you do that and I set person.age to 31, you will see that person2 still has that age of 30 and didn't get that new value because now we created a copy. Now beware, just as with the arrays example earlier in the course, if you have other reference values inside of your object, like the hobbies array, an array is an object and therefore is also a reference value, then this will not be copied, instead well it's of course kind of copied over into the new object but the object is not cloned, it's not copied, it's still the same array object in memory.

So if I go to person.hobbies and I push a new hobby of coding, you will see that person2 also has that on his hobbies if he expand this, here we also see coding now and that's just something which I explained in the arrays section already. This is normal, this is how reference values behave and the spread operator does not do a deep copy where it goes through all level of nested reference values you might have in this object or array and then copies it from scratch, instead it just copies the top level key-value pairs into a brand new object and any nested reference values are kept, the addresses there are kept, there are no hobbies created. If you would want to copy those as well, you would have to do it manually by assigning a new hobbies array where you copy over the old array and that's actually quite interesting to see so let me show you how that would work.

We have person3 and again, I copy person let's say but I want to make sure that hobbies is actually overwritten with a new array and we can not just use this technique if we want to overwrite another nested reference value but whenever we want to overwrite a value. So let's say we also want to overwrite age, well then we just add age here and set this to let's say 30 or 29 and what this will do is it will pull all key-value pairs from person, including age but since then you again add age after this finished, the age that was pulled out of person will be overwritten with this value and the same of course can be applied to hobbies. I set hobbies here to a new array and now we can use a spread operator here in the array which you also learned and for example spread everything we find in person.hobbies, so all the array elements in person.hobbies, into this new array and therefore we now create a clone of that old array as well.

So now we create a brand new array here instead of copying the old array address and hence now we would have a new object with a new array in there. Now it's not a must do that you always do that if you have nested reference values, you don't always need to copy everything, it's just an option that you can do that if you then plan on changing hobbies for example on person and you don't want that reflected on your copy persons, then you would have to use that approach, if you don't plan on changing hobbies ever, then you of course don't need to create that deep copy because ultimately, every operation costs a little bit of performance.

So if I now hit enter here and we have a look at person, we see there age is 31, hobbies is an array of three items, person3 also has an array of three items but age is 29 because we overwrote it here and if we then go to person and there, to hobbies and we pop off the last element, we see that for person, now hobbies has two elements, for person3, we still have three elements in the array because we did create a brand new array and copy over the old array values as well. So that can be a nice feature, being able to use that spread operator on key-value pairs in objects as well, perfect for creating copies and then as you see copies where you can still overwrite certain parts of the things you copied.

lectures.title: Object Destructuring
lectures.text:
So that's it for the spread operator, another nice feature which I can show you here in our little app is object destructuring. You might remember array destructuring which helped us pull out elements of an array and store it in variables, well you can do the same for objects and we have a great example here actually where we render all movies. I go through all my movies here with ForEach, right and I go through my filtered movies there of course and in there, I then have this for/in loop where I go through movie.info and I also extract the title from movie.info and the key from movie.info, so I always repeat movie.info.

So in the end here, you could say I'm really just interested in the info property of movie, I'm not interested in the other properties of movie or the other property of movie which would be the ID. So here, we can use object destructuring to pull out that key-value pair and store it in a new variable, for example here we could add a constant and now just as with array destructuring, a syntax you haven't seen before where you in this case have curly braces on the left side of the equal sign, something we didn't do before and now on the right side, point at the object where you want to pull something out of it, so in this case movie. Now between the curly braces on the left, you now enter a key name which exists in that object on the right, so for example info and of course you have to enter a key name here which exists there. In array destructuring, you could use any names between the square brackets you had there because in arrays, you access values by index and not by name and therefore you could assign any name because the order was important there for pulling elements out of the array. For pulling properties out of objects, the order does absolutely not matter, instead the key matters. So you can only use info here if you have an info property name, an info key

in your movie. Just as with array destructuring, you can also use a rest parameter, three dots, and then in this case any name of your choice, other props or however you want to name it and this will now collect all properties which you didn't pull out by name and give you a new object with all these collected remaining properties. So here if I console log other props, you'll see this will be an object which in our case should only include the ID because that is the only other property we have in there.
