Now there is nothing wrong with accessing it like this and since this is the only place where I access the title here, it would be perfectly fine to keep the dot notation but to practice this object destructuring a bit more, here we could also use it on the info constant here which holds an object right because info is just an object here, if it wouldn't be an object we couldn't use that but info is an object, so of course we can destructure that as well with the syntax and in info, we have the title and then whatever the user entered here. So here, I can also pull out the title from info and store this in a constant.

Now we can still then use a for/in loop on info because this doesn't destroy the info constant or anything like that, it's still available so if we then want to use info in other parts of our code, we can do so but I can also pull something out of it here and then use just title here if I wish to. Now you can actually also assign a new name here, you have to pull it out by name because that's how objects work, you don't pull out by order but if you want to use a different name because maybe otherwise you would have a clash with another variable name you're using or anything like that, then you can assign a new name to that pulled out value by adding a colon here.

So inside of the curly braces on the left side of the equal sign, inside of this destructuring syntax, you can add a colon and now not to create a new object where you have a key name and a value but instead to assign a new name to that extracted property, for example here, movie title and now we could use movie title here because that will now hold the title value, so the value of that title property in that info object and hence if I reload this one more time and we try adding this, we should see that that still works just fine, as you can tell everything is output correctly here and we're taking object destructuring to the max.

So a really useful feature to shorten code, write short and concise code and also be able to get exactly what you want out of an object, especially useful if you use the same property over and over again in multiple places.

lectures.title: Checking for Property Existance
lectures.text:
Often when you write code, you can of course be sure about the existence of certain properties in your objects, for example here, I know I will have an info property in every movie because I myself wrote the code that adds it. Now depending on how dynamic your program is and how much of the data that you're working with has been entered by the end users where you can't predict at the point of time you're writing your code what will be inside your objects, you might want to validate whether something is present or maybe you have some part in your code where this info property would be deleted and you're not sure whether that ran already or not.

So sometimes you want to check if a property is part of an object and you can do this in Javascript as well, for example here in an if check, you can use a special keyword that helps you find out if something is part of an object, you can use the in keyword. It works such that you check if, then the property name you want to check as a string, info, then the in keyword and then your object. So we can check if info is in movie, if this yields true, we know movie has an info property and now we could write code that should only run if we have that info property.

if we want to check the opposite, we can wrap this into an extra pair of parentheses and add the exclamation mark operator here to check if that returns a false value basically. So that's the in operator, of course here we could have also checked if info has a truthy value after setting it here because that will hold undefined if there is no info key, so that would have been a perfectly viable alternative but if you have some other code where you don't plan on using object destructuring and still it matters to you to know whether a property is part or not, you can use the in operator. Another way of checking this is to just use movie.info and compare if that is equal to undefined.

You know that a property has a value of undefined if it's not there, if it was deleted or if you manually set it to undefined or if it never was defined in the first place. So if this is equal to undefined, then you know this property does not exist, so if this is equal to undefined, we have no info property, that's another way of determining whether you have that property or not. Now here, I don't need that check but this is how you could check for the existence of a property in case you need it in your code to avoid errors where you try to work with a property that's not there or where you maybe want to assign some dummy default value to a property if it doesn't exist yet.

lectures.title: Getters & Setters
lectures.text:
Enough about this for now, there's one last nice feature which I want to introduce here and that are getters and setters, now what's that? Now we have normal properties here, info for example and sometimes we want to control how a property can be set, so how a value can be assigned or how you can get it, so how you can retrieve it. Let's say here on our title, here I'm checking the validity of the inputs and then I'm assigning these properties all in one go when I create the new movie object.

Well let's say for the title, so for properties where we know in advance that they will be part, I want to do that differently. I remove the title check up there and remove it from down there from info, instead what I'll do here in info is I will add a special keyword, get, then the property name of my choice, in this case, still title, then the parentheses as if this were a method and then curly braces for the method body. Now what this will do is it will create a so-called getter, so Javascript detects the special get keyword and in combination with a method thereafter, this can actually be accessed like a property, so without adding parentheses to call it in quotes but still execute some logic to retrieve the value and the same can be done for setting. We can add the set keyword, then the property name and then again parentheses in curly braces.

Now here for setting, we also have to accept the parameter and that's the value parameter, of course you can give it any name you want which holds the value you're trying to set. Now inside of the setter, you can now target a property with this which refers to new movie if you call new movie.title later and for example set another property here, not the same so not title but often you use something like _title to make it clear that this is like the internal value and for the outside world, you have title with your getter and setter and set this equal to val for example but here you can now also perform an extra check and see if val trim is equal to an empty string and if that is the case, maybe set this to another default value, default like this and then return to not continue with this line here.

Now of course the result will not be the same as before, before we stopped the entire function execution for an invalid input, now I continue and I just set a default value but that's exactly what I want to show. If you have such a scenario, you can use a setter to do some validation when a value is assigned to the title property and either accept it or set any other value, well and for a getter, you now have to define what you want to do if people tried to access title. You can also omit it, then you have a non-readable property, by the way if you omit a setter, you have a read-only property but here I added both and here I will just return this._title, so referring to this internal property which I create here on the fly.

So how do we now use that? Well you can simply go to the line after this new movie creation here and then call new movie.info and then in there, title. You use it like a property, so you don't add parentheses here, instead you can assign a value like you assign it to a property because setters and getters are a special kind of property, a special syntax understood by Javascript and you can for example assign this title here which we got there. So now if that title is empty, we'll not stop here because I'm not checking for an empty title anymore, instead the setter which will be triggered whenever we assign a value to this title property because the setter is on title here will then check the value we try to assign, this value here which we assign is automatically passed in as this single parameter here and then we either accept it or if this happens to be empty, we set a default and the getter is triggered whenever we access the property, for example like this. When I access it and want to read from it, then the getter runs, so then Javascript looks for this title property and again even though this looks like a method, we don't execute it as one because combined with the get keyword, Javascript allows us to access it like

a normal property and it will execute this function for us and here we could also do additional transformations, additional checks and for example here we could add our to uppercase transformation and we wouldn't need this method anymore, I'll keep that method for reference though but this would be an elegant way of always converting this title to uppercase when you retrieve it even if we saved it in different casing but again I'll not do it here to keep that code and hence here, I'll just return the unchanged code.

Now let's have a look at this and reload here and if I now enter Javascript here and enter the other fields here as well and click add movie, Javascript is getting logged here, that's from line 74 which is where I access my getter, so that works and setting also seemed to work otherwise we wouldn't be able to get it and otherwise you wouldn't get the output down there. Now side note, you'll also see that internal variable now being reflected here as well, the _title thing, you would have to exclude this now here in your if check by also checking if key is unequal to _title so that this is not output. So this should be added if you plan on using this pattern here so that we don't output the _title when we go through all properties. So getters and setters can be nice if you want to add some extra validation, maybe a fallback or add some extra transformation when getting a value and as I mentioned, what also is nice is of course that it allows you to also work with kind of read only values. If we wouldn't have a setter here, if we tried to assign it like this, we'll actually get an error if I reload here and we try to enter Javascript here and then any values here, you'll see I get an error because I can't set a property which only has a getter.

So this allows us to add read-only properties and make sure you can only assign it here initially maybe but never thereafter by adding a getter but no setter. You can also add both or none of that, you'll not need getters and setters for every single property you use in your projects, actually you will only use them sometimes but it's nice to know about them and to be able to create read-only properties, to add extra validation with fallback values and to also set up some default transformations for when you're reaching out to some data for example.

lectures.title: What is "Object-oriented Programming" (OOP)?
lectures.text:
So what is object oriented programming, also often abbreviated as OOP? It's an approach, it's a way of writing and of structuring your code in the end, it's a way of thinking or reasoning about your code and planning your code and the idea behind object oriented programming is that you work with kind of real life entities in your code. Now I already mentioned this before when I talked about objects, so that's not that new. We use objects to group data together in the end and we do so to for example create a movie object so that we can work with such a movie in our code and we can think about our code in terms or in a way that's easier to think about to us humans. Now object oriented programming is just that, it's all about embracing that logic, that we work with objects, that we work with objects only almost in our code and we put all our code into different objects, so into different methods of objects in the end.

Now here's an example, let's say we're building a very simple online shop. There we might have a list of products and hence we might build such a product list component which in the end holds all the data and in methods, also all the logic that is related to outputting such a list of products. So it holds the logic for rendering a list of products but also for fetching that list of products and it probably also has a property or a couple of properties which help us store that loaded product data.

So it's an object that holds the rendering and fetching logic and all the data that's related to it. Now we might have another object which reflects a single product, this object might be responsible for rendering the details about a single product and maybe it also renders a button and it holds the logic to add a product to a cart. So that's the responsibility of this product and therefore of course in this example, this product would be kind of linked to the product list, so inside of methods of the product list, we might be working with this product object. And then we might have a shopping cart object which is also kind of linked to our product because we trigger the addition to the cart from inside the logic stored in this product object and that shopping cart is responsible for let's say outputting all the products that are part of it and the total sum and it may be also offers a button to the user or renders a button to the user and holds the logic that is executed when the button is clicked to order the items.

So that's a theoretical example, it is actually the example we'll have a look at into some module to learn about object oriented programming and to also learn about another important feature, classes. But let's first of all start with this object oriented programming approach, let's start with this way of thinking about it because for that, we don't really need classes.

lectures.title: Defining & Using a First Class
lectures.text:
So I mentioned this concept of using classes and we haven't worked with classes at all in this course yet. Classes allow us to build objects in an easier way or to build objects based on some blueprint to be precise. So we have objects and we have classes and the idea is that objects are the things we work with in code and we worked with objects a lot in this course already. Now classes are something we can create in Javascript too, which do not replace objects but instead which allow us to define blueprints for objects so that we can easily recreate objects based on these classes because indeed objects then are also called instances of classes. So we can create an object based on some class thereafter and therefore a class is just a definition of how the object looks like, which properties and methods it has, the place where we store our logic and then the object is the concrete thing we build based on that class with which we work in our code. So this class based creation which I'll show you in this module is an alternative to using object literals.

It's not always better, object literal notation is great if you will just want to quickly group some data together but it's awesome to use classes if you have reusable logic which you wanted to define in one place and then create multiple objects based on it. So classes can make the creation of multiple, similar looking objects where the data differs but not the structure much easier. So let's translate this code which I wrote here into a class-based system and let's start with this object in this array. This object always looks the same and as I mentioned, we could create a function that builds us such an object, well a class in the end is such a function, it's just a different more powerful way or an easier way of writing such a function.

You add a class in Javascript by adding the class keyword just like this, it's a reserved keyword and then any name of your class, the convention is to start that name with a capital character, so here for example Product, like that. If you have a word that consists of multiple words like product item, you would write it like this every sub word starts with a new capital character, there must not be any whitespace or dashes in there, that would all be syntax errors.

You could theoretically also name your class like that starting with a lower case character but the convention is to start with an uppercase character. So now I got my product class here and then you add curly braces to define what's inside of that class and what's inside of that class is basically your blueprint of how an object created based on that class should look like. So you define which properties such an object should have and which methods it should have.

Now for that, you go into your class here and there, we can add a property or here we would call it a field and I'll come back to the difference in a second, it's not that big, by simply adding it in here, for example title and then you can assign a default value here because keep in mind the product class will always act as a blueprint, that's why I'm saying default because typically you'll assign a new value but we can create a default value of let's say default here.

Now one important note which you can see right away, inside of this class definition, you assign values with an equal sign, not with a colon which you would do an object literal but with an equal sign and you end a line after such a field with a semicolon, not with a comma. That's one important difference and classes do not replace objects as you will see, instead as I mentioned multiple times, we build objects based on classes. So we might have a title, an imageUrl, which could be an empty string or you just don't set any value at all, then it will be undefined initially and also a description and also a price.

Now this would defined that objects based on product will have these four properties thereafter. Now I mentioned, I call in fields here once we create an object, based on such a class every field will be translated to a property in that object, that's how that's related, we just call it field here because the class is not the concrete thing with which we work here, instead it's just a blueprint, it's just a definition of an object and what becomes a property in an object is just called a field here, however for the rest of this course, I'll also use these terms interchangeably because in the end they're closely related.

So now that's how a product would look like. Now the question is, how do you now create an object based on such a class? Well you go to the place where you need it, that could be here in your global script or here in this array of products and then you refer to the class name, product, you execute it like a function and very important, you add a keyword in front of it, new and we've seen this new keyword before in this course, I sometimes showed it. New in the end is a keyword Javascript understands that together with such a function execution which is based on a class, it's not a real function but still, should basically create a new object, that's what new together with this function execution does. Neither of the two alone works, we have to combine them.

So now this gives us a new product object, this returns a new object which has this structure and therefore indeed if we comment this out for a second and we just go here and we console log new product to have a look at how this looks like, such an object, let's save that. Since I added this globally, it should execute right away when a script runs and then reload this page, also make sure you're using Chrome because classes are not supported in old versions of Internet Explorer for example and I'll come back how to still make them work there in the browser support module. So reload your page thereafter and what you should see is this object which is getting logged here which has a title property with a value of default, please note that this is a regular object with a regular property hence we have a colon separated key-value pair and then we have the three other properties which are part of the object but which have no value because we haven't assigned one here.

So that's the first step towards classes, we now know how to define one but it's not that useful yet. When we create a product based on such a class, it would be nice if we could create it with some initial values. We could of course assign all values in here but then all products which we create based on the product would have the same values. Instead I want to make sure that when we call new product, we can kind of pass our initial values here to new product so that we can create a new object with some initial values.

Of course by the way, we could of course create a new product like this and then just assign values with the dot notation but that's not what we want to do, we want to create it in one go, so let's have a look at how that works in a second.

.imageUrl because every product object has an imageUrl property. Now we get two possible solutions for that, solution A is that the render method accepts an element, a DOM object where we can call append and append this to or that in this render method, we instead return the created product and wherever we call render, we have the responsibility to then use that returned object and append it and that's the approach I'll go for, I will return prod el in here, in render and now we can just go to the product list and in here where I go through all products, we can now create a product with new product item, let's also maybe name it product item here, so by using the product item class we just worked on and constructing an object based on it , to that as you learned, you have to pass a product, that's what we expect in the constructor and that's what we pass between parentheses when we create

a new object with the new keyword and prod here where I through all products in product list conveniently is just such a product object. So now we can append product element again because prod el is such a DOM object created by render but by render in product item and now we might be able to see the advantages of this object oriented approach become clearer. Now we already split our logic in some classes and yes of course it's still in the same file but if you are now coming to this code, if you're a new developer working on the project and you want to find out where's the logic for rendering a single product, then you don't have to scan through all the file, you just have to find this product item class and it will be pretty clear that yes here, this is what's responsible for rendering a single product element and you don't have to worry about the other code. lectures.title: Static Methods & Properties
lectures.text:
When you work with classes in Javascript, you have these properties and methods and fields which you already learned about which are all instance properties thus far, well turns out you also have something called static properties and methods. Now let's have a look at what the difference between static properties and fields and methods and instance field property and methods is. Now static properties and methods are defined with the static keyword in front of them.

The difference to the instance properties is that the static properties and methods are only accessible on the class itself, so you don't need to instantiate the class, you don't need to use the new keyword to create an object based on that class and we typically use this on helper classes or for some global configuration, etc. And instance properties and so on are instead defined without the static keyword, that's what we did thus far in this module and they're only accessible on the instances based on that class.

So we use that for all the core reusable logic, for example in our code thus far, we only work with instances, we always use all these classes by using new because we need different product items which have the same structure but hold different data, with static properties and static methods, we have a class which is not instantiated and which therefore always works on the same data for example but that's exactly what we can utilize here. Here we could add a new class, maybe name it app because it holds our overall app, which is created like a regular class, nothing special there but in here, I add a new method, init where I now add the static keyword in front of it and that's new.

Now we can move that code here for example into init, we can execute any code in there, just be aware that if you would use this in here, you would always refer to the class itself not to an object instance based on the class and now you therefore also don't create a new app like that or at least you could do that but to call init, you don't do it, instead you can just call app referring to the class itself like this, .init like this and this will execute this init method directly on the class itself.

Now again, we therefore have no app object we work with, instead we directly operate on that class and hence this will work but it's a different approach. Now the advantage can be seen if we now solve our cart problem. Remember that on this cart here, we got this add product method in the end, this accepts a product and then should update the rendered cart. Well what we can do now is for example on the shop which we initialize an app, we can store this reference to the cart object in a property, so this cart is equal to shopping cart.

So now this is a property of shop, with this cart of course that means that here where I refer to cart, I also have to use this cart and the advantage of this is that we can now go to our app class here and in init, we get access to that shop right and that shop is in the end an object based on the shop class which holds this cart property, right? So here we can also add a cart property by referring to that cart property on shop, like that. Now if we save that and we reload, this should still work.

Now why am I doing that though? Because now here in app, I can also add another static method, add item or add product to cart, expect my product here and now refer to this cart and call add product on that because this cart, don't forget, refers to an instance based on our shopping cart class and there we have that add product method and then call add product there and forward that product. So we kind of use this app class and the static method as a proxy because and that's the advantage and the whole idea of using these static methods, since we always operate on the class and not on instances, we don't work on different objects which we would do if we would not use static and instead create different apps in different places of the app but instead the app I'm using here to init my app, this class is the same I can now call from inside product item.

So here in add to cart, we can get rid of that instead just call app add product to cart, this product, referring to the product stored in this product item. So here I am utilizing static methods and the fact that we're not working on objects based on classes but on the class itself to share some data, share the cart instance for example. Now of course that's not the only way of solving this, you would be able to find other approaches too but it's a nice case for static methods in this case.

Now important here I'm calling add product to cart on app and I'm forwarding this product, referring to my product in product item. Now here however, we'll have a problem. If I save the code like this and reload and click add to cart, we'll get an error, cannot read property add product of undefined. So it can't find an add product method on cart because here, I'm trying to store cart which I get from shop cart before calling render, if you watch closely, you see that it's in render where I create the cart.

So this won't work in this order, instead we have to swap that and first render and then we got access to the cart. So now if we save that and we reload, it will still not work because I made a mistake earlier as I recognized, here in shopping cart where I assign a new value, that of course shouldn't be total output equal, it should be innerHTML equal because I want to update the HTML content in there, not the value stored in total output. And with that, if we reload, now you see that changed to 1, still not the real value because we haven't added the logic for that yet but at least we see a change so that works and now we connect it to classes with the help of static methods.

Now one side note, it's optional but still I would say it's a good practice, you can also add a static field here to the app class which is named cart so that we make it clear that we have these static cart property. We refer to it here with this cart and if you use this in a static method, it always refers to the class itself, doesn't try to refer to an object based on the class, so it adds a static property implicitly and accesses this static property and implicitly therefore but still this makes it clear hat we expect to have that static property, not needed technically but I think it improves readability and as a side effect, it also allows me to show you how a static method or property would look like.

Of course you can also initialize this to some value if you need one, here we don't need that and therefore the code is good like this.

lectures.title: First Summary & Classes vs Object Literals
lectures.text:
So now we had a first look at classes, we're using some classes to split our logic and we're also using classes in different ways. We have our class with the static properties and the static methods to glue together some of the other classes and that's just one possible use case, static methods and static properties are always a good idea if you want to share some functionality across different parts of your application or like in this case, if you want to share some data or use this as kind of a communication interface you could say.

Now of course that's not all you can do with classes or that's not all that's to classes. Before we dive into more things we can do with classes though and before we can work on this app a little bit more because right now for example this cart total of course is not behaving correctly, let me take a step back and go back to the relation between classes and the objects you work with in Javascript. For one of course it's important to realize that if you're not using a class in a static way like this here but instead by instantiating with new, what new shop in this case here returns, so what's stored in the shop constants here is a regular Javascript object or a reference to that object to be precise.

So it's in the end the same as what you get with that object literal notation, I really want to emphasize this. As a result, you can of course use all the things on these objects as you can do on normal objects because these are just normal objects. You can for example use destructuring to get the cart out of shop if you wanted to do that, something like that is possible, it's really important to understand this relation. It's also important to understand when to use classes. You might think that with classes, the old way of creating objects with the object literal notation is obsolete and that would be wrong, It's not obsolete, it's great to use that object literal notation if you have some data collection, a couple of variables which you in the end want to group together and where you only want to do this once or in one place of your app, of your code and you don't plan on reusing that.

So not as we're doing it with the product where we need that in different places, where we want to ensure that they always have the same structure but where you quickly want to create such an object on the fly, that's a perfect use case for using object literals. They're quick and easy to use, you have no extra overhead and you also have a small performance benefit versus this class based instantiation which is quickly made up for though if you would unnecessarily create multiple objects with object literals instead of using classes and therefore sharing code, just to also say that. So classes in general are a good idea if you have some logic which you want to reuse, if you want to recreate the same type of object with the same structure and the same attached logic over and over again like in that demo application we worked on. You have a little bit more overhead initially because you need to write that class definition but thereafter, you have that easy object duplication, of course not really a duplication instead new objects are created with that same internal structure but with different data, depending on how your class works of course.

So both is important and both has its place in Javascript and it's simply also something that comes with experience and with you working with Javascript, that you get a better feeling for when to use which. In this example application here, classes make a lot of sense because that allows us to cleanly split our code and we are actually reusing quite a lot of these classes or the logic attached to these classes in different places of our code. So here, having classes makes a lot of sense.

lectures.title: Getters & Setters
lectures.text:
Now before we move on to more exciting features about classes and how we can improve that code here, let's first of all dive into another nice thing you can add to classes where you already learned about when we talked about objects and that would be getters and setters, you can add them to classes as well and the shopping cart here is a perfect scenario. There, I am editing my items and I then want to update my but my output here in the end, right? Now we could use getters and setters as an elegant solution for that, we could add a getter, maybe name it total amount like this and we do this with the get keyword as you learned in the objects module, then any name of your choice and then like a method, like this method shorthand and in there. you have to return a value in the end.

Now the value I want to return here is the cart total and for that, we can use a technique we learned about in the arrays module where we simply reduce our list of cart items to a single number. Now since we in the end just store products and items here, every product has a price property so we want to reduce that. So here we can calculate a sum with this items reduce, items is an array so we can call reduce on it and as you learned, reduce takes two arguments - a function and here I use an anonymous arrow function and then an optional second argument which is our initial value and there I'll start with zero.

Now that function which we pass in is a first argument itself also receives multiple arguments and there are two important arguments which I want to accept here, that's the previous value and the current item, you can name the parameters here however you want. Inside of the function, I then want to return previous value, for the first run this will be zero, thereafter it will be the value returned by reduce plus current item which will refer to an element in the items array and therefore that's a product, .price because we'll have a price property on every item and items. If the array is empty initially, then this will automatically return the initial value which is zero.

lectures.title: Introducing Inheritance
lectures.text:
In this application, we get a couple of classes - product item, product list and also shopping cart and what they all have in common is that they have a render method and in that render method, we do different things but we always create a new element, we then add stuff to that element, for example with innerHTML, we then return that element. Now we duplicate that logic, of course the exact configuration, for example the class name and the tag, that differs but the general logic always is the same.

So whilst we do have different logic for what we then add to this element, the creation and configuration basically as I just said multiple times is the same and in such cases, we can use a concept called inheritance, which we can use in many programming languages and Javascript is no exception, to conveniently share code amongst classes. Now let's explore that concept. The idea behind inheritance is that we have some base class, let's say a post if we're building a social network, which holds a couple of properties and/or methods, in this example three properties, which we also need in other classes. Let's say we have a specialized version of that post which is an image post which also has all these properties but also in addition has an imageUrl and an image description and then we also have another specialized version of a post you can make, a video post which also has title, text and creatorId but which then also needs a video URL and let's say a rating regarding the age you've got to have to watch the video. So we can of course build multiple classes but that's suboptimal because we duplicate a lot of code, all that purple code - title, text, creatorId, these properties we duplicate them all the time.

So instead it would be nice if you could extend that base class and of course you can do that in Javascript and therefore inherit all that purple stuff. So you can extend that class and then you get this shared purple content automatically in the specialized classes and you can still add your old extra properties or logic in these subclasses here, you can also override things shared in the base class if you would want to do that. And now that's something we can utilize here, this concept of inheritance is something we can utilize here in our project as well.

lectures.title: Implementing Inheritance
lectures.text:
Back in our project, there we could add a new class and I'll add it here above my other specialized classes so to say which you can give any name you want and I'll name it component because in the end, this will be a class I use to output different, you could say, components, parts of my web page. Now such a component class will have a method which I'll name createRootElement which receives three arguments - the tag of the element I want to create, so I'll use that later to basically replace this line here, so I want to have the tag, I want to have any CSS classes that should be added and any other attributes that might need to be added to that element which is created here. Inside of createRootElement, we can then create that root element here, you can of course give that constant any name you want with documents create element and pass in that tag, then check if we have that CSS class constants set, so if that is a truthy value, if CSS classes is a truthy value. If it is, then I'll go to the root element and set the class name equal to CSS classes, so I expect CSS classes to be a string of CSS classes that should be added, else I'll do nothing so no need for an else block. After this if check,

I'll add another if check and see if attributes holds a truthy value so that's basically something we can work with and also it's not just truthy but also if it's an array with a length greater 0 because this should be an array and if both is true, I'll go through my attributes here with a for/of loop, you could of course also use a ForEach loop if you prefer that and then on the root element, I will set an attribute with the set attribute method, where I expect to have a couple of objects in this attributes array, where every object has a name property and also a value property. To guarantee the structure, we can add a new class, an element attribute for example which has a constructor where I get the attribute name and the attribute value and then here I say this.name equal attribute name, this.value equal attribute value, so we stored the data we got on the constructor in properties of the class and then here, I essentially expect attributes to be an array full of objects created based on that class so that we can set attributes on the root element. Well and then thereafter, I also want to append that element to the DOM. For that I need a place where we can add it and for this I'll actually add a constructor to component, where I expect to get a render hook value

as a parameter and then store this in some property of component, so in a property for that component class and this hook property holds the data passed into the constructor and of course I'm just coming up with one possible way of implementing this, you can definitely build this in a different way as well, this is just one example, let me really emphasize that. So here once we created that root element, that HTML element with that given tag, I want to add it to this hook, so to this element I got on the constructor and to be precise here I expect that hook should not be the element itself but let's say the ID of that element, so maybe rename it to hook ID so that down here, we can say document get element by ID for this hook ID, so for that ID we got here in our constructor and then call append and append that root element here, that's the idea here. Thereafter we can return this root element here.

So now we have this component, how can we now use this? To inherit from this component class which I want to do on shopping cart, product item and product list, since these are all methods that render something, to inherit from that class, I go to for example the shopping cart and there we now add a new keyword after the name of the class before we add the curly braces that mark the class body and we write extends here. That's the keyword, extends and then we write the class from which we want to extend and you can only extend from one class, so inheriting from multiple classes is not available in Javascript.

Some programming languages have it, most modern languages don't really have that, Javascript certainly doesn't have it, you can only inherit from one class. Now what does this mean now? It means that shopping cart now still creates normal objects if we instantiate it but all these objects don't just have all the logic we defined in here but also all the logic we defined in the base class, so also the createRootElement method for example, this is available in every object we create based on shopping cart.

The implication of that is that we can go to the render method now and instead of creating our cart element like this, we can now refer to this createRootElement and my IDE even supports this here because this here, when we call render in this class on an object created based on that class, this will refer to this object and as I said, this object will hold everything or will have access to everything that's part of the parent class as well, so createRootElement is accessible via this in the subclass. So I can call createRootElement here, now as a tag I'll pass in section, as a class name I'll pass in cart and therefore here we can get rid of this line and createRootElement of course returns an HTML element, the element that was added to the DOM, so I'll still store this in cart el because I need it here and render to define what exactly I want to do here. I can't move that code here into the base class because this differs for every class, this here is specific to the cart, we don't need that on the shopping list. So it's only that part where we create and append the element to the DOM that can be outsourced and that is now part of a separate class.

The specific rendering for this cart item, that's still part of this cart class, that's how this works. So now with that, if we save that and we reload this page, we get an error, now do you know why? Well we get an error because we can't depend on null, so we basically have a problem when it comes to appending the created element and that makes a lot of sense because let's revisit createRootElement. There, I need that hook ID to append my root element. Now hook ID is set in the constructor of the component we inherit from and the question now of course is where do we call that constructor?

When we call new cart here in the end, new shopping cart, we call the constructor of shopping cart. So when does the constructor of this component we inherit from get called? Well when it comes to constructors, there are a couple of rules, if your subclass, so the class which extends another class, does not have a constructor, the constructor of the parent class is automatically called. The problem here just is yes this is getting called as I can prove if I just output something here, let's quickly add that and then reload.

So this is getting called but of course render hook ID is not passed in because how would Javascript know what to pass in there. So it's getting called but without any values. Now if you add a constructor, maybe below the getters and setters, to your subclass, so to the class which is extending, then this constructor will be called and the parent class constructor will not be called, so also not what I want. What I in the end want here is I want to call this constructor and from there, call the parent constructor, so the constructor of the parent class which is the class we're extending from and we can do this with another special keyword, the super keyword, execute it like a function and this will call the constructor in the parent class and you want to do this in your own constructors if you're a parent class also has a constructor that should be executed, which typically is the case if it has a constructor.

Now one important note about super - when you add super to your constructor, make sure you're not relying on any field in that super constructor method, that will become important later and also if you plan on adding properties in your constructor with this something equals something else, you have to do that after you called super and you always have to call super, so the constructor of your parent class, of your base class first before you start using this inside of your subclass constructor.

So now we can call super here and forward a value for that render hook ID, so an ID which we find in the DOM. Now for that, here let me go down to shop where I also have a render method and the ID where I want to add cart to for now is just app, right because that's what I'm doing in shop here essentially, I get access to that render hook in my document and then I append the cart element and so on. So in the end here in shop, I no longer need cart element, so I can get rid of that line as well and instead here to shopping cart, I want to forward app as a string, so that value of that ID here which I want to use as a hook to render that item and then in shopping cart, in that class, I now expect that render hook ID or however you want to call it as a value here on that constructor method and then I simply forward that, so that value I'm getting here to the super, to the parent constructor so that this constructor has access. And now as a side note, render here in my shopping cart also no longer needs to return anything because I'm not interested in the cart element anymore, I don't need it anywhere in the place where I call render.

So now with that if we save that and we reload, this looks a bit better but we get another error, cannot set property innerHTML of undefined, this simply is an error here however because I'm returning this root element in createRootElement, that's wrong, it's just root element, so that's simply an error I have in my code. We're creating root element here and we're storing it in a constant, I should return that constant, we're not storing it in any instance property here because we don't need to.

So with that fixed, if we now reload this, now that works and it behaves in the same way as before but now we're taking advantage of this base class. Of course we're not there yet, I now also want to adjust the other classes so that they extend from component as well.

lectures.text:
Now we adjusted all classes to use this concept of inheritance, now we can also improve that code a little bit and I will definitely say there are tons of different ways of implementing this, so if you want to try this on your own and also experiment with that and maybe find another or a better solution, a shorter solution, definitely try that. One thing I want to do here is these render calls here right are kind of redundant, we create a product list and then I manually call render, well that should be done as part of the creation process I think because I'm always doing it thereafter manually.

So I'll say product list render gets removed, gets removed here for the cart hence here, I'm not even interested in storing the product list anywhere, same for the shop, can simply remove that, I need to store to shop in a constant though because I need it here but I don't want to call render and if we go to the product list class itself where I render all product items, I also don't want to call product item printer and therefore we don't need to store the product item anywhere.

Instead now what we can do is we can of course call render here in the constructor or this render to be precise of course as my IDE corrected it because we were referring to this method on this object but even that would be redundant, we would add this logic to every constructor of every subclass. So since we are calling the parent constructor anyway, since since we're sharing this parent, let's just do it in the parent. So in component here when we construct this, I will call this render.

The only thing I will now also do there is I will add a render method here and this is an empty method, so it doesn't do anything useful here. I'm adding it so that if someone looks at this class, this person doesn't wonder why we're calling render here, so that we at least see that such a method exists. Now we can still do something which is called overriding it because in all the parent classes, I basically implement a special version of rendered thereafter.

So when we do this in a subclass, when we override a method that's defined in the parent class, this will fully replace it. So if thereafter in the parent class, we call this render here, it will not refer to this render method there but instead it will do this in the subclass and this can be counter intuitive but there is one simple rule and it's a rule you already learned actually. Always remember that this refers to what called the method and for the constructor, that basically is always the object you are creating. That can get bit strange because in the end you're creating an object by calling new, right, here new product item but in the end what the new keyword does is it make sure that a new object is created and that this inside of the constructor is set to that object, so that's a little bit of magic the new keyword does for you, that's something you can memorize, inside of a constructor, this will refer to the object that is being created, that's what new does for you so to say. And therefore this always refers to the object which is being created and the object which is being created is always product list or product item or shopping cart, it's not the base class. We're calling the constructor of that but we're doing that in the process of

creating a shopping cart or a product list and only one object is being created and that is the subclass or an object based on that subclass. So when we call the constructor of shopping cart, a shopping cart is getting created, an object based on shopping cart. The parent constructor of component is also getting called but this in this parent constructor will refer to exactly the same as this in the child constructor, in the subclass constructor, it will refer to that object that is being created. And therefore since that object which is being created has its own implementation of the render method, this render in the parent class will refer to the render method in the to-be-created object which is based on the subclass.

So now with that, we're almost there, the only thing that's missing now is in the shop because if you now reload, you'll see an empty screen and that is because when we create our shop here, the shop class doesn't have a constructor where we would call the parent constructor due to the way shop works. So in the end, here in shop, I want to add a constructor and in that constructor, I want to call super and we don't need to pass an argument to super actually because that render hook ID is not required for the shop, the way render works here, we're not calling this createRootElement here, so we don't really need a render place for shop, though we could also certainly restructure this code to make it work as such but we definitely need to call super to make sure that the render method is getting triggered.

Now of course that also means that we need to extend component here however, otherwise there is no base class which we could trigger with super or where we could trigger the constructor with super. So now, now that shop also extends component and calls super, we can reload here and we'll actually get a different error but at least we can already see the cart is getting rendered. Whatever approach you chose, let's now make sure we understand and fix this error.

lectures.title: super() Constructor Execution, Order & "this"
lectures.text:
This error is related to a little specialty regarding fields. In the end it's just a case that these fields are created as properties automatically when the constructor gets called but only after the parent constructor which you call with super has been executed and by the way, you would also not be able to create your own properties here in the constructor with this something equals something before super has been executed. So all your fields are basically translated to this this field name equals field value syntax here in the constructor but they're magically added after the super call so to say which is why inside of the parent constructor or inside of methods triggered by the parent constructor, you can't access any of these fields but as I just explained, you also wouldn't be able to access any of the other properties of this subclass here because you can only add properties, you can only use the this keyword in your subclass constructor after the parent class constructor finished execution and that includes any methods that might have been invoked by that parent class constructor. So that's the problem we're facing here with this render method being called by the parent class constructor. In a constructor, we already go ahead and we execute

render and we rely on data which hasn't been created yet. Now it's just important to be aware of that, there's no huge issue with that, it's just something we have to fix here and here, we can fix that by taking that array and let's say we initialize products to be an empty array, we could also remove it and instead set this products equal to the array here then which means we create this instance property during the constructor. Now with that if we save that, it would still fail because the order is wrong, I'm calling super before I do that and inside of super, we call render.

So here is a case where we should move super after we initialize our local data which we know the parent component will in the end depend on because it will call render for us which then needs that data. So after we switch that order, you see that is gone. Now the problem just is that we're not allowed to call super there, indeed we have to call it first or at least before we do anything with this in our subclass, so that's not allowed. So how can we solve that issue then?

Well this is a quite common use case, you might wanna do something with some data which might just not be there yet when you get started and indeed, the products data would probably not be hardcoded into our code here but we might be fetching it from a database, so indeed it might really not be loaded when we try to render everything here. So to simulate that, I'll cut that code and add a new method here, fetch products and here we could be reaching out to a server, we'll learn how that works in a separate module later when we learn how to make HTTP requests, for now I'll just set my products there. So I simulate that in this method, I then have access to these products before I didn't.

So here I want to call this fetch products inside of the constructor. Now of course, render will also be called but here we simply know our render method depends on something where we don't know yet if it's there. So we could add another method here, render products and move that code where we go through all products into render products and here in the main render method, we can check if this product, if it is set and if this product's length is greater than zero, so if we have something to render, then we call this render products and in our example here, this will not be the case when render is called for the first time and that's fine, we'll just create that root element and we're done but I also want to call render products here in fetch products, so also call it here once I got my products. And now with that we have a setup for a solution which solves a problem you'll encounter quite often, that data arrives after you want to render some initial content and here we do render that initial content, we do render that list, it's just an empty list initially but then we add the product as soon as we have them.

So now if you save that and we reload, we'll find a similar problem, now it's stemming from line 97 and this is from inside the product item. There we also call render in the end as part of the constructor and we only store our product thereafter and we need that product to render it right. Now we can employ a similar solution there or to show you an alternative, go to the base class and since we have problems with it rendering too early, maybe accept a second argument, render or should render and set this to true, so use a default argument and then here we check if should render is true and if it is, we call render but now we can override this when we call the parent class constructor and that's an alternative strategy.

So here where we know I want to call render myself, like in the product item, we could pass in false as a default value for or as a new value for that default argument, so for should render so that the parent component will not render and we instead call render manually after we know that the product was set. Of course this is an approach we could have used down there as well but here I also wanted to show how you could deal with data that actually is loaded at a later point of time, so where we don't just talk about different sequence steps but where we might have a bigger delay if we are reaching out to real server. Here it's just this sequence which is wrong and with this approach, we could fix that and therefore get rid of that and now we would render everything and we get the same behavior as before.

So that was quite a lot of work with the base class and with the subclasses and some different use cases you could encounter and how you can work around them, overall it just takes some practice and of course experience to get a feeling for how you split your code and when you use which approach. The great thing about programming is that you can be flexible and that there are different solutions, different approaches you can take as I hopefully showed you thus far.

lectures.text:
So that's almost it for classes for now, obviously we'll see classes in many places throughout the course so there are plenty of other opportunities to practice with them. There is one additional, very new feature which I don't want to hide from you though. It's extremely new, browser support is pretty slim right now but will get better and since this is a future oriented course, you'll learn it right now already so that we can use it in the future and in Chrome thankfully, already today and that would be private fields, properties and methods, so that private term might not tell you much.

Until now though I can tell you we only worked with public methods and public properties and fields but we can actually also work with private properties and fields and methods. Now the idea behind public properties and methods is that we can access them from outside of the class and object and that's what we did in some cases already. You typically want to make everything public which needs to be accessed from outside, so the things you worked with in your other code. An example would be if you have a product and there you have a buy method, which we don't have in our example but if you have another app and that should probably be triggered from outside the product object because the place where you work with your product object is probably the place where a user can buy it.

You also on the other hand have some logic, some methods or some properties which you need inside of an object but not outside of it, so the things which you need to make your object work and which you don't really need to trigger or work with from outside, some hardcoded fallback values or some class specific logic. Now that's very abstract, here are some concrete examples in our code, for example products here in the product list. It's only used inside of that product lists class or in the object created based on the class and not from outside of it. The place where I create my product list here, I don't even store it in a constant or in a variable because I'm not interested in it, so I don't do const list and then set list products to something and actually I also don't want to allow it because if this would be possible and it is possible right now, then if another developer works in our project, he might think that setting products like this should be reflected here on our page but it turns out that setting it like this will only change the products stored in the object but will have no impact on the rendered HTML because in the product list, we have no setter on products that

would trigger a UI update as we do it on the shopping cart, instead if you would set products from outside the class, nothing would happen. Fetch products is the only method inside of the class which actually changes something there and which then also updates the UI by calling render products. So I want to make sure that we can't even set the products variable or property to be precise from outside because it could lead to cases where you think you changed something but it's not reflected on the UI.

That's a perfect use case for a private property, product should only be available from inside product list and we can achieve this in Javascript by adding a hash symbol in front of that. Now this is such a new feature that my IDE doesn't even support it, it will work though despite my IDE complaining though because normally indeed, that would be an invalid character, you can't add anything but dollar signs and underscores to your variable or property names. Well the hash symbol is a new exception with this specific meaning inside of a class or inside of an object where it then turns this or it sets this to a private property.

You then also have to use the hash symbol when you access it, so here for example this hash products is set equal to that or then also here in render products, we refer to this hash products and also down there, this hash products and this hash products length and again you can ignore the errors for now and with that, we'll now have a situation where if I would store the list here and I would try to do console log list hash products, like this and I save that and I reload, I get an error that a private field must be declared in an enclosing class, so essentially I can't use it from outside.

So this fails now, if we remove that code however, you'll see it now generally works but I get a different error and that error is related to our base class calling render in the end, that base class of course does not have hash products, instead only our subclass here has it and private properties are only available in that class where you define them, not in some base class or in some subclass and therefore here when I call the super constructor, I'll also set rendering to false and manually render and I'll just call this render here, important do that before you fetch the products because there, we'll then try to render the products so we need to render the list first and yes therefore of course refactoring that and making sure that render is part of the base class doesn't make much sense here because I override it in most cases anyways but it was a good practice and when we introduced it, it made sense, now however it of course doesn't make that much sense.

I'll leave it there though for reference and use this approach where I tell the base class that it shouldn't call render, instead I call render myself and therefore I do that from inside the class where that is defined, so where hash products is defined and with that if we reload, this again works. Now again this shows you how you can add private properties, very new feature, will of course be supported by IDEs in the future as well and can also, even though it doesn't look like it here with all these errors but can also lead to clearer and cleaner code which makes your intentions clearer, where you can avoid that some fellow developer or maybe you in the future if you come back after a couple of months accidentally change code or change parts of objects or classes from outside of them as I showed you before when you should only work with them from inside the class, when you have a property that really only can be used from inside that class and therefore from inside the object that's built based on the class.

Now you will also be able to have private methods in the future, for example fetch products is a method we only use from inside there, so we can also add a hash symbol in from that and call this hash fetch products but that's not even supported in Chrome yet as you can tell and therefore here I can't show this to you, in the future, this will be available as well. So it's also something following the same logic as with private properties, methods which should only be called from inside a class, from inside an object can be marked as private by adding this hash symbol in front of their name.

I structured it like this to show all these class features you have available and when you might want to use them, showed you a couple of different approaches and ways of thinking about that and hopefully could show you why classes allow us to split our code into logical units which we then can use to compose our app together because that really is the idea behind object oriented programming and behind classes and behind working with objects everywhere, that you have your logic and your data grouped together and then you just use these bundles of data and logic to put together your application.

Now there are a couple of other things related to classes and to objects which are also useful to know and for that let's go here to the console and let's create a class here which we can do, let's say a person class here with class person, place the cursor between the curly braces, hold shift and press enter to write across multiple lines to make it more readable and there for example let's add a field of name name with a value of Max and if we now instantiate that class by calling new person like that, p of course is an object of type person with a name of Max and it's this type person which is interesting.

lectures.text:
There is this term, this concept called prototypes in Javascript and it's super important to Javascript, it's been around forever and Javascript indeed is a prototype-based language which uses prototypical inheritance. So these are a lot of strange terms, what does it mean? Well in the end the class syntax, that's important to understand, just is syntactic sugar for constructor functions and also for working with the prototypes because working with them can be confusing, classes make that easier but it's still important to understand what they do.

So constructor functions and these prototypes power Javascript objects, but what are prototypes then? Consider this constructor function as I just explained it, a function which we can call with new, the equivalent roughly would be such a class where we then build a person, a concrete object by calling that constructor function with the new keyword. Now this object which we build based on that blueprint, based on that class or this constructor function has all the properties and all the methods defined in that constructor function.

So coming back to this example, when we create a person based on this constructor function, this p object here has an age property, a name property and a greet property which holds a function and therefore effectively that's a method because all of that is defined in here. Now you learned about that idea of being able to inherit from other classes and therefore this has to be possible for other constructor functions as well. In order to share functionality, to provide some methods or some properties which are available in all objects based on this class or constructor function or some subclass or subconstructor function in quotation marks because that's not an actual term. In non-class based Javascript and also in class based Javascript but there it happens behind the scenes, this is implemented with the concept of prototypes.

Every constructor function you build has a special prototype property which is not added to the objects you create based on it because it's not part of the function body but a property of that function object, keep in mind that functions are objects and that prototype is there by default, you can also edit it, something we will do and it is then automatically assigned as a prototype to the object which is created when you instantiate that constructor function.

Now a prototype is an object itself, there are objects and every object has such a prototype OK but what exactly is the idea behind a prototype, why does every object have a prototype? It's how Javascript shares code in the end and you can think of prototype objects as fallback objects, objects Javascript has a look at if it searches for a certain property or method it can't find on the object it started looking at. Let's say we have a person object which has a name property and a greet method and then you have some code which calls person.sayHello.

lectures.title: Wrap Up
lectures.text:
So that is it for constructor functions and prototypes. A core concept, you won't have to write this code a lot or actually that depends on the job you're on, the project you're on, you might end up in jobs where you have to write that code but in modern Javascript you typically work with classes, you can extend other classes, still under the hood as I showed you, this embraces this prototype concept and you need to know that, you need to know that because it helps you implement performance optimizations like this one or use the proper syntax there, at least be aware of it, that's already a plus and it also helps you ace your interviews and in general get a feeling for the language you're working with.

You don't just want to copy and paste snippets, you want to understand what's happening behind the scenes and in this module, you learned that classes are in the end syntactical sugar for prototypes and constructor functions. Though very important, let me come back to that slide I showed you earlier regarding constructor function versus classes, there also are differences, differences which you at least should be aware of. Constructor functions are these functions which you can call with new, so that they don't behave like normal functions but differently.

Now classes actually have to be used with new, if you try to call a class without new, it'll just fail. Another difference is that when you create an object with the help of a constructor function, all properties and methods are enumerable by default. Remember at the end of last module, I had a look at object descriptors and I showed you this idea of enumerability and how you can turn it on or off and how that affects what gets used or what gets output in a for/in loop. For objects based on these old school constructor functions if we want to call them like this, every method is treated as an enumerable property. For classes, that's different, there methods are non-enumerable by default.

One other difference which I want to highlight is that constructor functions by default don't use strict mode, you would have to turn it on, classes on the other hand do use strict mode. So all behaviors you have in strict mode, you have that turned on in classes out of the box. Now these are all not the most important things to know, the thing regarding methods not being enumerable is probably the most important one but still for completeness, combined with all the other things, this is what you should take away from this module and with that, you're well prepared to work with classes, to inherit, to extend, to work with properties and methods and you also have the theoretical foundation to understand what's happening behind the scenes.

lectures.text:
So to also practice inheritance again, let's add a base class and you can name it however you want, I'll name it component, I like this name for a class that in the end is related to controlling parts of the DOM but you can name it however you want. I'll name it component and I will take detach and attach, cut it from the tooltip and move it into component, though the attach method here now doesn't really look the way I want it to look, it should look a bit different, it should in the end just be concerned about appending something, so we'll actually cut this part here again from attach, go back to the tooltip and there, add a create or render or however you want to call it method where I now add this again and now in the tooltip, I want to call this create from inside the constructor so that this always runs when this class is instantiated. There I then build my tooltip, the only thing which I don't do here is I don't attach it but I store it here in this element property and that's also important because I'll be referring to this element property in attach here and now I just need to extend component here on my tooltip class so that we have access to these two methods here and as you learned, this inside of these methods will then always refer to the subclass,

so that will work fine, this element will be set there when detach is called, same for when this method is called. Only adjustment here is of course that we need to append this element because that's the element we're setting here, that is our tooltip element and therefore with that, we only have to do one more thing, we have to call super in here to call the base class in our own constructor, if you added your own constructor and you're extending another class, you need to call super in your own constructor and once you did that, we can reload and click on more info and this should still work as before, also the prevention of opening multiple tooltips works fine and therefore, this now works and we have more generic class. And in addition, insert before can be used, we can store this also in a property, so store insert before in this insert before and now we can use this in attach to not always use document body append but instead use this host element to begin with and then use insert adjacent element actually and check if this insert before is true, if it is, use before begin here, otherwise use before end for example

In addition if I add true here as a second argument, we would add it at the beginning so if we now reload, it would be added here before our active projects container and actually that shows me that it's not entirely what I want, I should change this here to after begin because I want to add it at the beginning of the container, not outside of that container, so not before that container but inside of the container but there, right at the start and that is what after begin will do.

So with that, let's reload and retry, now this is getting added inside of this active projects container, at the very beginning but inside. Now again, this is not what I want here, so I will remove both from my super call but for testing this, it was useful and now we have this more generic component which also allowed us to practice inheritance again.

lectures.title: Module Introduction
lectures.text:
We already worked with the the DOM, we created elements, inserted them, we queried for elements, you learned how to work with elements. Now in this module we'll take it one step further, we'll have a more detailed look at what we can do with DOM elements, we'll work with their coordinates, their sizes, we'll learn how to attach data to them and we'll have a look at what else the browser offers us when it comes to working with what the user sees and experiences in the browser window. In detail in this module, we will have a look at how we can attach data to DOM elements and why we might want to do that.

We will work with element coordinates and sizes so that you learn how you can use Javascript to find out where an element sits and which size it has and how you can also modify these values. We'll also have a look at a concept called templates and I will also show you how you can add scripts dynamically, so how you can load scripts and create scripts with Javascript, which is pretty meta I guess and as I mentioned we'll have a look at what else the browser offers to us and there, we'll have a look at the navigator object, the location object and window.history and you will learn what these things are, what we can do with them and why they exist. For most things in this module, we'll use this little application we worked on in the last course module which was optional, so if you skipped that last module you'll find a finished snapshot attached and you can use that.

I would recommend that you go through the code and get acquainted to it, one thing which I want to highlight which you learned about earlier but which we haven't used in a real project before is that in this project I actually pass functions around as callback functions, for example here to make sure that in this project where we got two boxes with projects, we can move projects between these two boxes and for that, we pass functions around into our two project list objects which are two instances based on the same class to trigger different actions in different instances of these classes.

So just have a thorough look through this code and if you want to learn how we wrote this and why we wrote it like this, check out this last course section. With that, let's dive right in and let's have a closer look at what we can do in the DOM and with all these cool DOM elements.
