lectures.title: Using "dataset" (data-* Attributes)
lectures.text:
I want to start with attaching data to DOM elements and why we might want to do that. Now in this project we worked on, we do display a tooltip. We got this tooltip component here and right now what this does is when I click on more info, it adds a tooltip at the very bottom of the page which of course is something we'll change with some dummy text in there and when we click on it, it is deleted. Now the dummy text is displayed because I am setting this here and the problem I have is that I don't know which text should be displayed for which project.

Now we could be managing data like this in our Javascript code in an array of projects but here we actually got to some HTML code which for example could be precreated on a server and sent to us on a client like this and therefore, we don't really have that tooltip data available in Javascript. lectures.text:
Now of course though, the tooltip still is in the wrong position, here at the bottom of the page, that's not where we want it, it would be nice to displayed here below this button for example, so below this DOM node to which it belongs and for that we need to find out where exactly that sits on our page, which coordinates this has and we'll need to find some information about its size as well as you will see and for that, we first of all need to understand how items are positioned, well that happens with the help of CSS and simply based on how the browser renders a page but we also need to understand how we can get the exact coordinates, the exact calculated width and so on because as you know with CSS, even without being a CSS expert, you probably know you cannot just assign pixel values, you can also use something like rem which is dynamically calculated, you can use percentages, you can use media queries to use dynamic different sizes and therefore if you want to find out the exact size as it was rendered, you need Javascript and you can indeed get coordinates and so on of any DOM element you want to and that's exactly what we need here. For that attached you find a zip file with two files in there and that would be the sizes.html file and the

sizes.css file. If you extract these files, drag the sizes.html file next to your index.html file and the sizes.css file in the styles folder and with that you can go to your page here and temporarily replace index.html here at the end with sizes.html and you'll find this page here. If you load that, you'll get an error regarding a missing sizes.js file, you can simply add one, should be empty anyways and this is simply a basic dummy file here, dummy setup where we can practice with sizes, positions and so on.

Now for that, to get access to this box here, we can select it by the ID or here in the dev tools, you can also select it and then when you select it here on the right, if you mark this div here, you can also use it in your console with $0. This is just a shortcut the browser developer tools offer to you and then you have direct access to the DOM node and you can work with it. Now which sizes and which properties do we have available that help us with understanding the positioning, the width and so on? Well for example, there is a method you can call, getBoundingClientRect, if you execute this as a method, you get back an object which gives you some useful information about this box and you can run this for any element on the page.

Now what this gives you is a couple of coordinates and sizes, to understand these values, you need to understand that the browser basically renders the page in a two-dimensional coordinate system with an x-axis from left to right and a y-axis from top to bottom and that's important. It's not like a traditional coordinate system where the y-axis would go from bottom to top and x from left to right at the bottom but instead it's all starting in the top left corner and that makes sense if you consider how a web page is rendered, it's rendered from top to bottom, not built up from bottom to top.

This coordinate system also thinks in pixels and therefore in the top left corner, we would have the coordinate 0 0, x has a value of 0 and y has a value of 0. All the way on the right here, we would have y still equal to zero but x would be basically the width of your screen or the width of this document. All the way on the bottom left here, x would be 0, y would be just as high as your document and in the bottom right corner, x would be as big as your width and y would be as big as the height of this document.

So this is how you can read this, therefore if you see x y here, this basically means that this box which we selected has its top left corner at a position of 100 pixels down and 100 pixels from the left. So the x coordinate on the screen is 100 and the y coordinate is 100 from the top left corner and we have that positioning because if you check out the sizes.css file, indeed I have a margin of 100 pixels set for the body which means any element in the body and this div with this ID is in the body is moved in 100 pixels from top and left because that's reserved as a margin for the body, so that's how we get there.

We also got the top and the left value and that's the same as x and y here as you can see and most of the time that will be the case, if you have a negative width or height, that can differ depending on the exact positioning and your CSS code but left and top simply gives you the coordinates of the leftmost and the topmost point of this box in the coordinate system and typically that's the same as x and y. More interesting is bottom and right, well that in the end is just the combination of left and top or x and y with width and height. So bottom and right basically tells you where the bottommost and the rightmost point is indeed coordinate system that starts on the top left and therefore width and height are also important of course, should be pretty self-explanatory, width gives you the total width of the box, height gives you the height of the box. So this is some rough general information you can get about this box. Now you can also dive into more specialized properties though if you only need a single value there or if you want to have different values for some of the sizes based on whether you want to include a border or not and so on.

So let's have a look at that as well.

lectures.title: Working with Element Sizes & Positions
lectures.text:
So we saw getBoundingClientRect which gives us some general data, now you can also get more specialized data by diving into your DOM element with special properties, for example there is offsetTop. offsetTop gives you the distance of the topmost point here to the top of this coordinate or to the start of this coordinate system and of course you don't just have offsetTop, you also have offsetLeft, makes sense I guess. So these are basically your x and y values here or your left and top values from that object we saw before.

You also however have clientTop and clientLeft and now that's a different thing as you can tell, where offset gives you the outer positioning, so the position of the box in the coordinate system, the client properties give you the inner positioning and specifically clientTop and clientLeft tell you how far it is from your left and topmost point to your left and topmost point of the content of this box and the content of the box is basically the entire box without any borders and potential scroll bars that might be rendered in there.

So at the moment, there is no scroll bar here but I have a border of 15 pixels and therefore that's exactly that value which we see here for clientTop and clientLeft. You can also get some of the sizes for that, you can get the offsetWidth and you can get the offsetHeight and that's the entire width and height of this box, including all borders and scroll bars. Now unsurprisingly, you also have clientWidth and clientHeight and that's again the inner width and height without borders and scroll bars, therefore for the width, it's basically the width of 300 which we saw just a second ago minus the border times 2 because we got a border on the left and on the right and if we had a scroll bar, that would be deducted as well, the same for the height.

Also interesting, this content here is scrollable as you can see, the scroll bar here on Mac is only temporarily rendered and therefore not included in that calculation I just showed you but regarding the scrolling, we can also get some interesting data, we can for example get scrollHeight. Now what scrollHeight gives you is the entire height of the content including the part which is currently not visible in the box, so which is outside of the box at the bottom here for example or now at the top.

So scrollHeight is the entire height including the non-visible parts because they're currently scrolled out of view. You also have another interesting value, scrollTop, scrollTop gives you information by how much you scroll that content in the box. So if I scroll the content all the way to the bottom for example, you see now I have a value of 240 there because I basically scroll the content up 240 pixels you could say. If I scroll somewhere in the middle, that obviously shrinks, if I go all the way to the top so I haven't scrolled at all, I got zero again.

Now you don't need to memorize all these properties of course, on MDN, you can check out the HTML element article and there, you'll find all the properties there and on the element article to be precise and there you can read more about that and then of course also just play around with them to get a feeling for what these values do and what they offer. Attached you also find this simple slide where I just summarized the key values for you and what they mean and which values they give you.

One note about the entire document width, if you want to get that, you got two options, you can use window.innerWidth and window.innerHeight and that should give you the width and height you have here inside of your window, so without the dev tools, without that URL bar at the top and so on but the problem with that is that if you had a visible scroll bar on Internet Explorer for example or on Windows in general, you might have that, then this will actually include the scroll bar and not subtract it from the width and height and therefore actually give you more width and height than you actually have available for your content. Hence a better way of getting the real available width and height is to go to document, document element which is your root element including head and body so to say and there you use the clientWidth and the clientHeight. Here, this gives me the exact same values as window.innerWidth and innerHeight simply because I have no scroll bar here but again for the reason I just mentioned, if you had one, these values are more reliable because they will deduct any visible scroll bars and give you the real width and height that is available.

lectures.title: The DOM & Prototypes
lectures.text:
Now before we continue working with width and height, one short extra lecture regarding MDN and the element docs we find there and the HTML element docs we find there. Now that we understand how inheritance and prototypes works, this picture here actually also makes more sense or should make more sense. Javascript or this DOM API exposed by the browser in Javascript I should say simply alsi works with multiple constructor functions, with multiple classes if you want to call it like this and this is how they are related.

The way you should read this is that every HTML element is inheriting basically from element, so has an element prototype, any element prototype has a node prototype and that in turn has an event target prototype and that makes sense because if you remember earlier, I explained that elements are just specific type of nodes, so it makes sense that they have a node prototype but then they bring their own properties and methods as well and you even have more specific types than just HTML element because you have specific types of HTML elements.

If you scroll down a bit further on this HTML element article, you find the more specialised versions and there are a bunch of them as you can see, for example there is the HTML input element. The specific thing here is that it has all the properties or it has access to all the properties and methods of HTML element, of element, of node and of event target but it also adds its own special properties and methods to which only an input element has access.

Here for example, the labels property, a property other HTML elements don't have access to but HTML input elements have access to it. Now how do you create such a HTML input element? Well you don't have to create these objects or these instances, instead when you select a HTML input element from the DOM, you will automatically get such an object of that type With all these properties and all these methods and thanks to how prototypes and the prototype chain works, we then also have access to everything from HTML element, from element, from node and from event target.

So this hopefully now also makes a bit more sense now that we had a look at object oriented programming and at prototypes in earlier modules.

lectures.title: Positioning the Tooltip
lectures.text:
Let's now go back to our main project here by again changing to index.html. Now there, we want to position this tooltip here. If I click on more info, I don't want to render it is here at the bottom, instead it would be nice to kind of position it near this element. To do that, we need to tap into Javascript, into the app.js file and there, work on the positioning with some of the properties and tools we now learned about. It's in the place where we create the tooltip, so therefore inside of the tooltip class in the create method where we can configure it and where we can position it. To position that tooltip, we also need to know where the host element, so the element that is responsible for showing that tooltip, lives in.

So in the end, where this project item, where we clicked on more info, where this can be found and for that on the tooltip when we create it here in the constructor, I expect one extra argument, I also want to get the host element ID here so that I can actually pass this to super host element ID because in that component which is our base class, we expect that host element ID and then we use it to select that host element and store it in a this host element property which we'll of course therefore can then also access from our subclass because we can access any property which we have in a base class or therefore in a prototype also from a subclass or an object using that prototype and hence here in tooltip, we now pass this on to our base class component and therefore we'll have access to this host element property.

So what can we do with that? Well here in create where we create our tooltip element, before we add the event listeners maybe, let's console log this host element and then getBoundingClientRect, this method we saw earlier before just to see whether that all works and where we can get that information about that host element positioning and so on. So now to test this, we just need to make sure that we actually do get a host element ID here on the constructor of tooltip because at the moment, we're expecting this but we're not sending this when we create a tooltip.

So here in project item where I create a new tooltip as a third argument to the tooltip constructor, we should now forward the ID of this project which we can get under this ID, that's the property of this project which holds the ID of that project and with that if we go back and reload, let's click on more info and indeed we get our object here and there we get the coordinates of this project DOM node and its size and width. The tooltip now also is created here based on the logic we have in that component class where we now use the host element now that we got it to insert our tooltip there and whilst this doesn't look too bad, it's not exactly how I want to position this, also because I don't want this to grow and shrink when I add a tooltip but we'll come back to that. For now let's focus on the coordinates and there we see to the left, we have 63 pixels in the end here, to the excuse me to the left, to the top it's 161 and the exact values here are of course not values I set up like this in the app.css file, instead that depends on how the browser renders this from top to bottom, on system specific settings, you might have for example regarding the font size because I'm using rem in here to set my sizes and hence these are the

calculated values which are of course exactly the values I'm interested in because I want to have the current position I have on the screen to position this tooltip. So now back in the script, we can position this tooltip in the tooltip create method here with some information from that bounding client rect or to also practice with some of the other properties I showed you, with some information from those properties. So for example I am interested in the host element position left and I'll name the constant like this therefore and we get this by accessing this host element and then offsetLeft.

Remember that's the distance from the start of our coordinate system on the page to the leftmost point of our element. Now I also want to get the host element position top and this can be fetched with this host element offsetTop. So now I know the x and y coordinates of my element, so the top left corner of the host elements so to say, which coordinates this top left corner has. Now I also need the height because I want to position the tooltip, at the end at the bottom of this element and not in the top left corner. So I can get my host el height here with this host element and now the height is the client height, that's the height of the content, I could also get offsetHeight to get the full height including any borders but here I have no borders so that should be the same. With that information, we can try positioning our tooltip, for that let's calculate an x and a y position for the tooltip.

x could be the host el position left and then maybe plus 20 pixels, and if you work with values here, these are now always pixels because what you fetch here are also pixels and let's get a y coordinate and here I want to use my host element position top, so the position of my top border in the coordinate system so to say and to that, I want to add the height. Now important, when I add something to that since my coordinate system starts in the top left corner, we push elements further down.

So if I have the coordinate of my mouse cursor here and then I add 100 to that and we render an element at that new position, it will be rendered 100 pixels down from that point because the coordinate system goes from top left to bottom right basically, that's how the browser lays out the web page and that's how you have to think about that, so we have to add to height here to go down on the page. Now I'll actually then deduct 10 pixels to not go down the entire height but only height - 10 basically and now let's try out these coordinates for rendering tooltip. Now to position an element, you don't do this by accessing tooltip element and then offsetTop and setting this equal to a value. All these top and left coordinates are just read-only values, if you want to assign a new value, you do that with CSS instead.

So here we can access the style property of the tooltip element and then we can set left equal to x and now important, really important and a common mistake, if you're assigning a style and we need to do that here as explained, it's not enough to just set this equal to some number which is in the end what we have here in x and y but you need to set it up as you would write it in CSS code which means if you work with pixels here, you have to add px after the value.

So here in app.js, I need to add +px, so we in the end set this to a string which is now made up of my number and pixels and therefore this gives me something like 500px, just an example and we do the same for tooltip elements style top and set this to y + px. If we now do that and we save this, let's reload and click on more info and you will see no difference and the reason for that is that we can set left and top but due to the way CSS works and you can't magically change this with Javascript which is good, you also first of all need to set one other style on the tooltip element, you need to set the position style to absolute and then you can really position the element in the absolute coordinate system on the screen, otherwise it's always positioned relative in the document flow, this is how the browser and CSS works.

So now by setting position to absolute, we can make that work and now if we reload, indeed you see now the box doesn't grow anymore and we render the tooltip in this position. Now that's great, you will encounter a strange behavior if you now scroll to the bottom project in the first box and you click on more info here, you see the tooltip is totally in the wrong position now, now what could be the reason for that? Well if we take a closer look and we scroll this element down again, I would say this tooltip is roughly in the same position as the tooltip is here for the first element, just ignoring that we scrolled it.

So the scroll distance here, that's the problem. It's not taken into account here when we calculate our top and leftmost position and indeed that is what's happening, when we get coordinates of an element, these coordinates ignore whether the element has been scrolled somewhere or not. Now to include the scrolling information, we just have to find out by how far we scroll the content in this box and we of course can find out how far we scrolled it, I showed you how that works.

So we can get our parent element scrolling or however you want to name it by reaching out to this host element, then to the parent element of that to get the entire box, the entire unordered list and not just the single project item and then the scrollTop property. Remember, this tells you by how far you scrolled in that container and in the end, this parent element scrolling, that is something we have to deduct from our calculation here, so we have to deduct it from there so that we move the tooltip up a bit and don't position it at the original position or the original coordinates of that element but the actual position which is adjusted by the amount of scrolling we did basically.

So now by deducting this, if we reload again and I scroll up this box here, this project that and I click on more info, now this is in the right position. Now it's not sticky if you scrolled, that would be a bit more advanced, you would have to set up event listeners, listen to scrolling and I will dive into event listeners and so on in the events module where we can learn way more about event listeners but for now, this is not the focus, the important thing here is that we are able to now position this correctly with the help of the coordinates we're getting and with the help of the width and the scrolling we're getting.

lectures.title: Handling Scrolling
lectures.text:
Speaking of scrolling, we can not just find out by how far the user scrolled on the entire page or inside of a box but we can also actively scroll the user somewhere and a good example would be when I add buy groceries to finish projects. It gets added there but of course it gets added at the bottom and therefore I can only see a part of it. Now maybe we want to scroll in this box where we add an element to, to make that element visible and we can do that, you can actively control scrolling through Javascript.

Now let me show you how it works here in the developer tools. Let's select this section here and in there, to be precise, let's select the unordered list. If we now expand the styles, you see that there I kept the height and I make sure that we can scroll to see the content which doesn't fit in the unordered list, so that unordered list is scrollable. Now with it selected, let's go to the console and use $0 again to interact with that unordered list and now there, you got a couple of methods you can call, for example scrollTo. scrollTo takes two coordinates - x and y, where you can define how much you want to scroll to the left or right and how much you want to scroll to the top or bottom.

Now here we can't scroll left to right so there's nothing we can set there, if you set this to 100 on x for example, it wouldn't have any effect but we can scroll on the y-axis. Now if I set zero here, then I tell Javascript that I don't want to scroll at all, not that helpful. If I set it to 50 however, then this might be better because now I tell Javascript that I want to scroll down to 50 pixels. If I hit enter now, you see indeed this changed right, it scrolled there.

Let me show this again, let's repeat that same command, boom, it scrolled. If you set it to a very high value, well then it just goes as far down as possible. Now you can also not just scroll to absolute values, you can also scroll relatively with scrollBy. With scrollBy I tell Javascript by how many pixels I want to scroll down. So if I enter 50 here, I'll have the same effect as before actually but you'll see a difference now if I am at 50 and I repeat this command, now I scroll down 50 pixels more.

If we would do the same with scrollTo, scroll to 50 here, you will see I scroll to 50 pixels and if I repeat that and I am at that position, nothing changes. So you can control whether you want to scroll to a specific position or by some amount of pixels and combined with the fact that you can get the coordinates of any element on the screen, you could of course then also use this to tell Javascript to scroll to a specific element by getting the coordinates of that element and then scrolling to it. If you want to make a specific element visible with scrolling though, there is an even easier way.

You can also go to that element, for example the project item which we added here with the help of this add project method in the project list class and make sure that this element, when we move it, gets scrolled into view and to make sure that this happens, we can go to this place where I move the element here and then on that element which you want to bring into view, there you can call scroll into view as a method and this will do just what the names suggests.

So if you now save that then reload, you will see that if I add buy groceries to this finished projects box, it gets scrolled into view automatically and of course the same if I add something to active projects. So this can be useful to make sure that it scrolls into view. Now of course what you might notice is that scrolling here always means jumping, it immediately is there, we have no animation. Well you can in some browsers at least, Chrome and Firefox support it, you can set up how scrolling should be performed.

By passing in an object here to scroll into view where you can set the behavior to smooth, the default is auto which just jumps there but with smooth, you'll get a tiny animation. So if you set this to smooth here for example and you reload and then you add groceries here to finish projects, watch the bottom box, you'll see it scrolled there with a nice animation and that might be nicer than just jumping there. Again, it's not supported in all browsers, specifically Internet Explorer and Safari don't support this feature but you can still add it to your code and on these browsers, it will just not have any effect, on the browsers that do support it though, you get this enhanced behavior.

You also have this configuration available by the way if we select the unordered list again on scrollTo and scrollBy, there you can pass in the coordinate pair or alternatively pass in an object where you set top and left, top by how much you want to scroll from the top and left how much you want to scroll from the left, so I'll ignore left here because I don't want a scroll from the left but I'll set top to 50 and then here you can also add the behavior and set this to smooth and now here you'll also get that animation, same is available for scrollBy as I mentioned, like this.

So this is how you can scroll and how you can control scrolling from inside Javascript, a feature which of course also can be helpful to make sure users see the content you want them to see.

lectures.title: Working with <template> Tags
lectures.text:
So enough of the positioning and sizing and scrolling, let's come back to working with content and there, one thing we did a couple of times throughout this course because we had no better way was that when we wanted to set up some HTML code that should be rendered or some content, we always did this here in our scripts. Now in this example here or in this project here, I actually have no HTML code in my script but it would be easy to add some to the tooltip for example, you could say that when we create the tooltip here, we don't just set some text content but we set some innerHTML here which for example includes a h2 tag where we say more info and then below that, a paragraph where we output the actual text here with string interpolation like this and if we do so and now reload and I click on more info, we get this kind of tooltip here.

Now of course you could adjust the styling but the core idea is here that now I have this HTML code in the script and this is not ideal because you might be working in a team where other people are responsible for the markup and so on or you're not working in such a team but you don't want to have all that HTML code in your Javascript code. Now obviously, this is a very simple HTML code right but if you had longer HTML code, lots of HTML code in there, this could get more and more cumbersome and thankfully the web has a solution for this.

We can use a special HTML tag in our HTML code to kind of setup such to be used HTML code which we don't want to render right from the start but which we want to eventually use from inside our Javascript code and for this we can use a special tag, the template tag here. Just add it in your HTML code, in your body and the special thing about the template tag is that its content by default is not rendered but it's part of the DOM, so you can query it and use it and then use it in your Javascript code but it's not getting rendered by default at the beginning.

We can add an ID to the template, we can for example assign tooltip here and then move this HTML code from our Javascript file into this template. Now this string interpolation will not work here, so for now I'll just have my empty paragraph here, we'll have to insert content there from Javascript in a second. So now we've got the HTML code in the HTML file which makes sense. Now in Javascript we can use such a template of course, for that here, we can get access to our tooltip template with document get element by ID and then looking for the ID we assigned to the template and now we get access to this template element. Now to utilize this template, we can create a new constant here, tooltip body for example and there we can use document import node to which we then pass tooltipTemplate.content and this in the end gives us the content of our template tag, so the h2 tag and the paragraph we set up there and essentially creates a new node based on that, that's what this line does.

We should set up true here so that we do a deep import which means we really import everything in the content of the template which is exactly what we want and now we got that body available which we can add to our tooltip element. lectures.title: Loading Scripts Dynamically
lectures.text:
With this, this project is pretty much finished but there is another cool thing you can do with Javascript which many people wouldn't expect or which might be strange when you hear it the first time. You can also create and run a script with Javascript, now let me show you how that would work. In app.js, let's go to init, so to app init here at the very bottom, this static method and in there, you can create a script dynamically in Javascript. How would that look like?

Well let's create a new constant for example, some script and we create it with document create element like we always did but now we create a script element. Remember, there are script tags in HTML and then of course you can create such a script tag as well with create element. So now, some script is in the end a script tag which we created. Now we can insert some text content here and for example enter alert Hi there to throw an alert, this is valid Javascript code right.

Now we just need to add it to our document and we can do that by going to document and there in the head maybe, append our script which is stored in the some script constant. The result is that when init runs, our script here should be added. Let's save that and reload and indeed here is my alert and if I save this or click OK, then we're done and we see the content because if we now inspect the render DOM in the head, indeed we have that script here, so you can create and add scripts dynamically. Now for scripts like this, this might be nice but I'm not sure you really need that because if you just want to execute some script code, you can just write it like right here, right? It's more interesting if you have some other script file which you only want to download at a certain point of time, so where you want to control when the browser loads this script from inside your Javascript code. So let's say we had another script here, analytics.js where we just send some analytics data.

So for now I'll just console log sending analytics here, very simple script. Now if we go to our HTML file and we import this here with script source, then we of course run this right away. Of course I can add defer here but that means once the parsing is done, this script executes. Now maybe you have some app where you only want to run your script after something happens, so for example after the user click the button or anything like that. So for that, I'll add a new static method here, start analytics and in there, I now want to dynamically load that script. For this we can again add a new script element with document create element script but now I don't add any text content to it, instead you can set analytics scripts.source, you can set the source property just as you can set the source attribute here and this will basically tell the browser where to find that script.

Then here, you should set up a path as you would do it here in your HTML file, so not seen relative from the Javascript file but really just as it would be added to the HTML file because that is where it will be executed in the end, so that would be assets/scripts/analytics.js. in this case and then also maybe add the defer attribute or the defer property and set this to true so that this is only loaded after all HTML parsing has been done. Now I just need to add this here to my head with document head for example and then append my analytics script and now whenever we call start analytics, this script should be loaded and executed and now we could do this of course in the init method here but we could also say we want to do that whenever one of our buttons here is clicked, then we just should make sure that we don't add this same script multiple times.

So here to keep it simple for now, I'll just do it when init runs, so here I'll call this start analytics and if I now save that and we reload and I open the console, you see sending analytics here. Now of course this executes right away when the app starts because I call it here in init, nonetheless this script was actually added dynamically through Javascript and you could have added it at any point of time, not just when this page loads. For example you can go to the index.html file and in there at the very bottom, add a footer where we can add a button where you could say start analytics.

Now of course you typically wouldn't add such a button to your application because most users will probably not start analytics on their own but it can be useful for us here to prove that this script really only is added and executed when your Javascript code runs. So I'll give this an ID, start analytics button and with that ID, we can go back to app.js and then in here, in init, not do this here, don't start the script like that but instead, reach out with get element by adding to our button so that whilst the start analytics btn ID which I assign here and then add an event listener to this button so that upon a click, we execute this start analytics.

Now if we save that, you will not see it send analytics when I reload but you'll see it once I click this button here at the bottom, now you see that as soon as I press the button. Now the button is a bit strangely positioned here simply because I'm zoomed in that far and I have given it an absolute positioning at the bottom, if I would zoom out a bit more, this looks better but it's not so much about the styling here, the behavior is the important thing. In the developer tools, you can also go to the network tab and in there, you see all the files that were loaded.

If I now reload, you'll see everything is loaded but the analytics Javascript file is not one of the loaded files. If I click on start analytics though, you see now it's getting downloaded here, super fast of course because it's a small file but only once I click the button. So this is pretty neat and this is how you can add and run scripts dynamically from inside Javascript. Now one important note about adding scripts dynamically like this, it's a powerful feature but of course you want to do it with care, you should especially be careful when it comes to dynamically rendering user created scripts because that opens you up to some attacks here and it is something we'll have a closer look at in the security section later down in the course, where we talk about attacks like cross-site scripting attacks which in the end try to inject malicious code into your code.

So if you dynamically add a script, make sure you don't do it based on some user entered content or at least validate that content and sanitize it before you execute it but again we'll have a closer look at this topic in the security module.

lectures.title: Setting Timers & Intervals
lectures.text:
So now with the dynamic script added, I'm pretty much done for the interaction with the DOM which I wanted to cover in this module. However, there are some other nice features the browser exposes to you in Javascript that also allow you to influence the user experience and one of these cool features is a timer which you can set or actually two different kinds of timer as you can set in your Javascript code. Let's say instead of starting our analytics here, when the user clicks a button, we want to do this three seconds after the page was loaded and for that indeed you can set a timer.

You do this with the built-in setTimeout method, under the hood this exists on the window object but as you learned you can omit the window and just call anything on it like this and setTimeout does just what the name implies, it sets a timer. Now setTimeout takes two arguments, the first argument is a function which should be executed when the timer expired, this can be an anonymous function, both an arrow function or a normal function or of course you point at a function like in this case, this start analytics so that this method is executed when the timer expires.

The second argument then is the amount of time you want to give the timer, so for example here 3000 means 3000 milliseconds, so that would be three seconds, so this is a number in milliseconds this timer should take until it then executes this method. Now this also by the way is an example for some asynchronous code execution in Javascript, a topic we haven't really had a look at yet but as you will notice is when this timer is set, it will not pause your entire script execution, you will be able to click all buttons and have your script to work as expected, instead this is registered by the browser somewhere in the background, the browser manages the timer and also just registers that this function should be called when the timer expired and then once the browser sees that the timer expired, it will come back to your script and execute this function for you.

So it's important to understand that this will not pause script execution, instead the browser will manage all of that for you in such a way that your script can continue to run, it will not pause. Another side note, you can also pass a third argument here and that would be an array of arguments you might want to pass in to that function when it executes. This function here, this method however needs no arguments, so we can just run it like this and hence now if we reload, we should see sending analytics here after 3 seconds, here we go, start analytics of course doesn't do anything.

So that's the first kind of timer I wanted to show you, this is a timer which runs once. Sometimes you also want to have a timer that runs on an interval, so that runs every 3 seconds, every 5 seconds, every 100 milliseconds, whatever you have and you can do that too, let's maybe do that in the analytics.js file. In there, instead of logging this right when the script is loaded, let's set a timer because we might want to send analytics data to our server every 2 seconds let's say. For that, we can use setInterval, an alternative to setTimeout which does something different though.

Here, I pass in an anonymous function, again can be an arrow function but doesn't have to be and in here I'll say sending analytics data, like that. Now the second argument to setInterval then is the time when this should be sent and it will be sent every x seconds or milliseconds, so if we entered 2000 here, this function here will execute every 2000 milliseconds, so every 2 seconds. You also can pass in a third argument which would be an array of arguments which will then be fed into this function when it is executed for you.

Here we don't need that, so I'll just set it like this. The result of that is that if I now save that and reload, for 3 seconds nothing happens but thereafter, every 2 seconds, therefore initially after the first 5 seconds, we got this information being sent which is why this slowly increments here, every 2 seconds this is getting sent to the server. Now if you want to stop a timer or want to stop an interval, you can also do that. Let's say we change our button here at the bottom to stop the analytics so that no more data is getting sent, so we can set this to stop analytics button.

This should either stop this timer if it still is running or if we already are on the interval, it should clear that. So to start with this timer, here after setting the timer, I will add an event listener, document get element by ID, stop analytics btn was the ID I assigned to this button here at the bottom and there, I want to add an event listener, a click listener where we can use an anonymous function, you could of course also set up a method but I'll just use this and here I want to stop this timer if it still is running.

For that it's useful to know that this timer will actually return an ID so to say, so we can store this in a constant, timer ID and here you can then run clear timeout, another function provided by the browser in Javascript and to that, you pass the ID of a timer, of a timeout which you want to stop. So now if I save that and I reload, if we click on stop before the 3 seconds expires, you'll see we'll never see any analytics data being sent. On the other hand of course if I reload again and we wait until this is sent for the first time, if I now click on stop, this will not stop the interval.

It will also not throw an error because the timer already expired so that's OK but the interval of course continues because we're not saying anything about the interval here, though we can also clear the interval if we want to. We can go to the analytics.js file where I set up this interval and I'll copy that code in there and essentially just store my interval ID here because just like setTimeout, this returns an ID for that interval and then instead of using clear timeout here, we would use clear interval and pass the interval ID to it, though little fun fact, you could also use clear timeout and it would also work but since we have it, it's better to use clear interval because it's clearer about your intentions and simply more descriptive. So clear interval for clearing intervals, clear time out for clearing timeouts and with that in place if we now save that and we reload and wait until this starts to send data, here we go, if I now click on stop analytics, you'll see this will not increment any further because no other data is sent because we cleared the interval.

So these are timers in Javascript and how you can control them, what the browser does with them, it manages them behind the scenes so that your code execution is not stopped, as you see, I can interact with everything just fine even though there is a timer going on and intervals and timers are therefore a crucial feature which help you time things or do things on a regular basis, something which you actually need to do quite often in Javascript.

lectures.title: The "location" and "history" Objects
lectures.text:
Besides timers, the browser also has a couple of other nice objects or features it exposes to us in Javascript, for example and I'll show you this in the console here, there is the location object, it's on window.location and therefore as you learned, you can just access it like this and if we have a look into it, we see that's an object with a couple of properties and methods and they're all related to our URL and the page we're on. lectures.title: The "navigator" Object
lectures.text:
Now besides location and history, there also is the navigator object, also quite interesting. This allows you to interact with the browser and the operating system of your user so to say, of course only in a limited way, not unlimited access. If we expand this, we can find some information about the browser the user used for example and here, you might see something strange. This here says something about Mozilla even though I am using Chrome here, even more interesting is a specific property which is often used to check which browser the user is using, the user agent property.

If we access this property, navigator.userAgent, you might expect information about the browser the user uses, though if I use it we see information about Mozilla there, AppleWebKit and then yes, also something about Chrome but also about safari. Now what's up with this? This actually looks the way it does look for historic reasons, browser vendors in the past used to fake this to make sure that their browsers could have access to all features website might be using in their scripts because in the past, browser support was pretty different for different web features and hence, some programmers working on websites used user agent to find out if the user is using let's say Internet Explorer and therefore they wouldn't run a certain script if that browser was used. Now as browsers evolved and maybe Internet Explorer 7 included a feature which version 6 didn't include, that script that prevented Internet Explorer from getting access to certain features of the website would still block access even though support might now have been added to the browser.

Therefore browser vendors started to put basically all browser names into this user agent string because this is set by the browser, so the people building the browsers of course can influence what shows up in there and hence, browsers basically faked to be another browser so that they could get full access to whatever the script wanted to do, so that the users of that browser had no limited or restricted user experience. Hence this is not really that useful.

Now attached you find a link, how you can still parse this, a certain way of reading this that should still give you mostly reliable information about which browser your user is using but if you really need to know which browser your user is using, you should not rely on this string in the end but instead check if a couple of features are available because by checking for feature availability, you can narrow down which browsers users are using in a better way and you should also check out the browser support module in this course where I also dive into techniques that allow you to write scripts which work in a broad variety of browsers or that fall back to some behavior if a certain feature is not supported.

So I just wanted to show this because I find it kind of amusing to understand how this evolved over time, as I said with the attached link you can parse it but do it with care. Now navigator also exposes many other features, for example it also exposes access to the clipboard API which allows you to add something to the clipboard or paste something into some input field for example. It gives you access to geolocation which allows you to locate your user with get current position which allows you to get the user position, you would do that by then passing in a function which executes once the position was fetched and in there, you can console log the data which you will get automatically as an argument, so this function will be called for you by the browser once the location was fetched and then here if you enter this, you have to allow that the browser fetches your location and eventually, you'll get that position object with your coords object in there where you can find out which coordinates the user has and there's more in navigator.

Now it's impossible to cover all features in a course, so as always, I strongly recommend also using MDN and just playing around with these features to learn more about what you can do there, we'll also see some of these features being used throughout the course, so that will also be a nice way of learning about what you can do there. And with that we had a look at location and history which allow you to move your user around and find out where the user is on and so on and navigator which allows you to interact with the machine, with the browser itself so to say, for example to get the position or to get some vague information about which browser the user is using.

lectures.text:
Now to come to an end in this module, there's one last built-in or global constructor function you could say that helps you deal with dates and that's the date object and constructor function. You can use date in a broad variety of ways and attached you find documentation that allows you to have deeper into date. You can for example create a new date object like this and what this gives you if I hit enter is indeed the current date and timestamp here, so that's the current date and time at which I'm recording this specific video here, this is what you get with new date.

Now actually, this is really an object you can work with though. If we store it in a constant, then on this constant, so on this stored object, we get a couple of methods, for example we can call get date to get the day in month, 24th in this case, we got get day to get the day in this week and so on. So there are lots of methods that allow you to analyze this date, get the time for example since the beginning of time in Javascript land which is January 1st 1970, so since then, this is the time of milliseconds that has passed and this can sometimes be helpful for calculating differences and so on and much more, so there are a bunch of methods you can call to work with a date.

You can also construct a date with new date by passing an argument to the date constructor, if you don't pass anything, you get the current timestamp but you can also pass in a date instead which Javascript then tries to parse. Now for one, you can pass in an existing date object, this would simply store that date as a new object in date2 but you can also pass in the string to describe a date and of course then Javascript will do its best to pass this as a date, for example I could pass in 07/11/19 and now what Javascript derived is July 11th 2019 from this date.

Now again, the attached resources allow you to dig deeper and find out which formats you can use there, how you can also specify minutes and hours and so on and much more. Now these date objects can be really useful because for example if you would want to calculate the difference between this first date, which is today and date2 which is in July, then we can just execute date minus date2 and this gives us the difference in milliseconds and therefore if we take that difference and for example divide it by 1000 to have the difference in seconds, divide it by 60 to have a difference in minutes, divide it by 60 again to have the difference in hours and then by 24, we get the difference in days since that date, so that's just one example of what you can do there.

So definitely check out that date object also with help of the attached documentation if you need to work with dates in your application, if you need to store a date, run some date calculation or anything like that, this object has got you covered.

lectures.title: Introduction to Events in JavaScript
lectures.text:
So let's explore events in Javascript, we already worked with some events, well mostly with the click event but we didn't do much with it. Now the core idea behind events does not just exist in Javascript but pretty much in any programming language. Most programming languages have some kinds of events architecture built in because the idea is that you can run code upon certain events and that could be a user clicking a button, an upload finishing, a video playback starting or finishing or being paused, there are a lot of events you could think about that should trigger some code to run.

We could also think about more abstract events that could happen on a server, like an incoming request or some scheduled task which should run every x hours and is triggered by some timer. So the exact implementation of course differs between programming languages but also inside of Javascript, it differs between the browser side and for example the server side with Node.js. On the browser side, we saw we can use add event listener to add an event listener to a DOM node, in Node.js on the other hand, you often see on or once as methods you chain on some object which then allow you to listen to certain events.

Even with that different syntax though, the general idea is the same and the idea also is that events often or typically transport data. We haven't really utilized this yet in this course, we always worked without utilizing it. Now in this module, we'll have a look at which data is being transported and you will get that data and object that is created for each event automatically as an argument passed into the function you register as an event listener and thus far we always ignored that argument, we always ignored that object but we actually do get it automatically, so in this module, we'll also learn how to use it and what's in this object and that's by the way not just the case for browser side Javascript, for Node.js or for any other programming language even, it's typically the same, an event typically comes with some data which describes the event, which might hold some metadata, which basically helps you interact with that event and run some code based on it.

Now as I mentioned in this module, I'll focus on the browser side simply because that's easiest for us, we can immediately see something there but the rough idea, the general idea of why we use events, that's of course always the same and as I also already mentioned, in the Node.js module, we'll also see how we would work with events there. So in the browser context, it's important to understand that we have different kinds of events we can listen to - a click on a button or a click on anything else, a right click or a double click, hovering over something or moving the mouse button away from something, these are all different kinds of events and indeed in Javascript for the browser therefore exposed by the browser into the Javascript we run in it as you learned, we have an event constructor function, a core event object you could say with some core functionalities which all events share but then we also have specialized event constructor functions which are based on that core event with the help of prototypes as you learned which hold additional information that only makes sense for certain events, for example we have a mouse event which also might yield the coordinates of the event, so the coordinates

of the mouse button when the event occurred and in addition to that, might also hold an event target which describes the element in the DOM on which this event was triggered or which was responsible for this event. One is a way that is pretty old and which you shouldn't use anymore, still for completeness sake, I want to show it to you. You can go right to the HTML node in your HTML code and on there, you can add an attribute, on click and this is not an arbitrary name chosen by me, there are various on attributes for different events this element supports. Now it's strongly discouraged that you use this approach, it makes your project very hard to maintain, it's completely unexpected that we suddenly find Javascript code in our HTML code, especially when we have separate Javascript files and it just makes working on your project, especially on bigger projects much much harder, so don't mix HTML and HTML attributes and Javascript code, it's absolutely not a recommended practice.

Don't execute it right away, instead as with the event listener, point at it like this. If you do that and you now reload, we'll again see that alert. Now this is better than using an attribute in our HTML code because at least now, it's in a Javascript code and actually this is fine to use especially in smaller projects but it has one major downside,

we can only add one handler for this kind of event to this element. So if you want to for example run two different functions upon a click, let's say we have another function, another button click handler and here I want to console log this was clicked, now if I want to add both functions on this button, we can't do button on click like this twice, well we can but you'll see that now the first function will never run. So this is not added or appended as a listener, it's simply overriding the old listener. Now of course the workaround could be to create a third function which calls these two functions but that quickly gets cumbersome because then you have no finegrained control over when you want to use which handler, maybe you want to remove a handler at a later point of time, that's all pretty tricky. lectures.title: The "event" Object
lectures.text:
So now that we know how to add events or how to listen to events and how to remove event listeners which can also be quite handy, let's have a look at that event object which is generated automatically, by the browser in this case and passed into our event handler and which in general though, even if you're not working in the browser is a core idea behind event driven code. Whatever causes an event typically also provides you some data along with such an event to describe it, to give you some extra metadata or to give you methods to control how the event behaves thereafter, important for some more complex events for example.

So therefore here on the button click handler, instead of just showing an alert, let's accept the argument. You can name this argument however you want, often it's named event or ev or just e because it is describing the event we're getting but since it's your function, you can name this whoever you want of course and then here I want to console log that event object, it will be an object so that we can look into it. So now when we click our button, this will be logged. For now by the way, I will also change this back here to directly point at the button click handler down there.

So if we save that and we then reload and click on this button, we see we get a mouse event here and we see it has a bunch of properties and it actually also has a bunch of methods which we just don't see here when it's output like this. Now we have a bunch of properties which in the end describe the event. This for example tells us if the alt key was pressed whilst we clicked and that can be interesting for building certain user interfaces where you maybe want to do something else if the alt key was pressed while the user clicked somewhere versus when it was not clicked, you'll have similar properties for the control key for example. We see which button was pressed, zero is the left button, if I right click this by the way, nothing happens because I haven't registered this, only a left click works and you will have to reload to click again because we still remove this here, right?

So back to the event here then, we see which button was used, left button. We then also have client(x) and client(y) and that would be the exact coordinates of where my pointer was, so the mouse cursor was when I clicked. You can see if I reload and I click again somewhere else, these are different coordinates than before and so on. Now in general, check out the MDN documentation to get detailed explanations of all properties and what they do and of course also simply play around with that to learn more. As you see, for a mouse event, you get various coordinates, here these are the general coordinates inside of the window, here for example we would have the coordinates inside of the button itself.

So if I reload and click on the top left for example, you see that would be pretty small because coordinate system starts on the top left and I clicked very close on the top left and therefore I get these very small coordinates. Now if we scroll down further, we see one very important property and that's the target property. Every event has this and this describes which target, which element in the end caused this event, so where, in this case where you clicked on. lectures.text:
Of course we have more than just click events though. Back on our buttons, we can also register other events, for example mouse enter. Mouse enter is triggered whenever our mouse or a cursor enters this button, so if it is moved above this button. Now let me disable this disabling code so that we don't disable the button anymore and now let's have a look at that. If we now reload and I move my cursor above this button, you see that event triggers, if I keep the button on it, if I keep the cursor on the button, nothing happens, if I leave the button and re-enter it, we again trigger this.

So of course you can also add a listener to listen for when the mouse leaves this button and so on. Now please also note that if we now inspect this, we got a lot of properties which we knew before too, client(x) and so on, so these coordinates, what we also have now however is a related target and that's quite interesting. We have this property for mouse enter, mouse leave and so on, this tells us which element the cursor was on before the mouse enter event trigger, so from which element we're coming basically and that in this case was this div which surrounds the buttons.

So that's quite handy, also good to know there if you are very fast with your cursor and you move your button very fast, your cursor, you see in this case related target actually is the whole HTML document and not the div because I moved my cursor so fast over the div into the button that the browser basically didn't get that the cursor was on the div in between as well because the browser does not check the cursor position multiple times per millisecond but quite often but still only periodically and therefore if you move your cursor in a very fast way, this will not always be the direct neighbor of the button in this case that triggered the event.

So that's just good to know, nonetheless it's a useful property which can help you understand where the mouse cursor is coming from. Now of course we have way more events and as I mentioned MDN is the place to go to learn more about them and in general simply throw some elements onto the screen, register some listeners and play around with events there, that's the best way of diving into them on your own and learning more about them, it's really what I would recommend for learning more about events, event objects and which events you have.

Of course you're also not limited to registering events only on buttons, you can register events on basically any DOM elements, on any HTML element you want to listen to, whatever you want to listen. You can also register events on the overall window, for example you can listen to scroll events there. Now to demonstrate this, let's go to events.html and now below this div here, I'll add a section, give it an ID of long one or whatever you want to call it and in events.css, I'll just add a selector, long one, an ID selector and give this a height of 3000 pixels so that this simply is a big invisible section.

lectures.title: Working with "preventDefault()"
lectures.text:
So let me comment out these two event listeners here or these two examples and let's dive into another kind of event we can listen to. For this, I'll add a form element here below my div with the buttons and in there, I'll add a label for title which says title and an input, type text with ID title let's say, very simple form here. Action can be left empty and with that, all we need to add to finish this form is a button of type submit, that's now important, that you set this type where we for example say submit as a caption. If you now save this and you reload, you'll get this form.

Well the button is pretty big because it gets the same styling as up there but for this example, it doesn't really matter. We have this form here, we can enter something here and I can press submit and now watch closely what happens if I do press submit here, you see the page reloaded which reset my zoom in this case. Now it reloaded because the default behavior for the form element in HTML combined with the submit button is to send this form data to your server, so to the server which serves this page.

In this case we have no web server, we serve this through the file protocol but still it tries to send this to you could say to the source which served this HTML file and this can make sense depending on which kind of application you're building because eventually, you want to get that user input to that server so that there you can work with it, store it in a database, do anything like that. Often however when you use HTML, you also want to prevent this from happening, you don't want to send that data to the server always when this button is pressed, instead you want to step in with Javascript and maybe validate the user input before you then take it and send it with the help of Javascript, something we'll also dive in in a separate module, how to send HTTP requests from inside Javascript. So you might want to prevent the default behavior of the browser, which for a submit button in a form is to submit that form and here again Javascript and the browser got you covered.

So let's say we want to listen to that form submission, for that in events.js we can select our form, maybe down there with document query selector form, I only got one form tag in there so this will select that first and only form. And then on that form, not on the button as you see but on the form, we can add an event listener and there's a special submit event which the browser exposes on form elements and that is one of the rare events which does not exist on all DOM nodes because only form elements can be submitted, only form elements have that submit event, again MDN also tells you that.

So here we can listen to that submit event and then execute some function when it occurs, in this function of course again, we get an event object and we can console log that. Now as a default, you will see that if I try to execute this and I reload this page, if I click submit here, we briefly saw that being logged but since we send that to the server automatically and that server or the file protocol in this case therefore reloaded the page, we lost our output there because the page reloaded and now we can do something which we haven't done before. This event object does not just give us a couple of properties, it also gives us methods to control this event and there, we got a method which we can call right at the start for example which is prevent default.

This exists on any event object in Javascript, not just for the submit event and it does what the name implies, it prevents the default behavior the browser would apply for this event otherwise. Now the default behavior of course depends on the kind of event. For the submit event on a form, the default behavior is to submit that form to a server. For a link for example, the default behavior would be to go to that link and you can always block the browser from doing that and from following its default behavior and then instead implement your own logic.

So now with this added, you will see that if we now reload again and I click submit, now we don't lose this because now the page doesn't reload because now, this default of taking the form data and sending it to a server and hence reloading the page, that is now prevented. Of course this means now you will need to implement it on your own and as I mentioned, we'll have a whole module where I show you how to send HTTP requests on your own from Javascript but it's a powerful feature to be aware of because you'll often need it to build exactly the user experience you want, where you sometimes, especially when working with forms, want to avoid that default behavior and want to override it.

lectures.title: Understanding "Capturing" & "Bubbling" Phases
lectures.text:
So prevent default is a very important method on the event object which you can use to control what the browser does with that event. We also got another important method for which we first of all need to understand how exactly the event behaves. Our events in Javascript, in browser side Javascript have two phases through which they run essentially and where they then trigger your event listeners, a bubbling and a capturing phase. Let's say we have a button in a div which is in a section, this could be the markup we have.

Now we click that button here, now what actually happens is that the browser runs through two phases where it checks for listeners to that event. First, it runs through a phase which is called the capturing phase, second it runs through a phase which is called the bubbling phase. Now the capturing phase goes from outside to inside, now what does this mean? It's important to understand that a click event on such a nested button here cannot just be listened to with event listeners on the button but for example also with an event listener on that section and the browser during the capturing phase checks if you got a capturing event listener on let's say the section registered which would then actually run its function before any event listeners registered on the button because it's from outside to inside in the capturing phase and the section is outside of the button.

The bubbling phase on the other hand does the opposite, it goes from inside to outside. Now all event listeners you add with add event listener are by default registered in that bubbling phase which means if we have an event listener on the button and on the section, the button event listener will run first, the section event listener will run second. We can change this and we can also do interesting things with that bubbling and capturing behavior as I will show you in the next lectures.

lectures.title: Event Propagation & "stopPropagation()"
lectures.text:
Let's first of all make sure we fully understand what's happening and for this, I'll again use my buttons however just the first button here which I find with query selector and then I can add an event listener to it as we did before. So button add event listener, to a click again and then maybe execute this anonymous function where we get the event object and where we then console log the event object. Now I'll not just do it here on the button however, I'll also get access to this div here, the only div I have on the entire screen, so therefore here I'll get my div with document query selector for that div tag and also add an event listener on that and it doesn't matter if you registered that event listener before or after the button event listener.

So here I will also log my event object and now for us to be able to differentiate them, here I'll also log clicked div and then I'll copy that and down there, we can log clicked button. OK now with that set up, if I reload and I click on the button here, you see both execute button and then div. So it executes from inside to outside because as I mentioned, by default all event listeners are registered in the bubbling phase which means that capturing phase which runs first is totally ignored but thereafter when the browser checks from inside to outside for that element on which the event occurred, it first finds that on the element itself, we had a listener, therefore this runs first but then it checks if there was a listener on the surrounding element, which in this case is the div and there we also had a listener so it executes that as well, then the browser by the way also goes onto the body and checks if there we had a click listener but we don't so therefore it doesn't execute any code for that because there is no code to execute but it goes from the element from which the element occurs to all its ancestors and checks for event listeners on them and if they are there, it executes them,

this is what the browser does. Now we could switch to the capturing phase by adding an extra third argument on the event listeners. So here on the div for example, we could add a third parameter and if we set this to true, the default is false and therefore doesn't need to be added but if we set this to true, we're telling the browser this event listener should be part of the capturing phase. Now we don't have to switch all event listeners to the capturing phase, we can just add this one here and now you will see that it will actually run before this button event listener here runs.

So if I reload now and click this button, you'll see the div was clicked first or the event listener ran first and then the button, because this listener here triggered in the capturing phase which comes before the bubbling phase and since we registered this listener for the capturing phase, it executed its code. So this can be useful if you want to switch the order and you have event listeners on the element itself but also on some ancestor and for whatever reason, you want to execute the ancestor listener first, that can be done by passing that extra third argument. Here I'll remove it because I don't want the behavior here but it is something you could do. Now this entire process of having multiple listeners for the same event because the event does not just trigger on the element itself but also on ancestors, that's called propagation, it means that the event propagates up, it bubbles up or in the capture phase, it kind of goes from outside to inside but it basically means the event does not just occur on the element itself but also on all ancestors or at least we can listen on all ancestors, it occurred on this button but it's listenable on all ancestors because it propagates up,

it bubbles up, it can be used anywhere above. Now you can prevent this however. Let's say we do have an event listener on the div here but we really only want to react to clicks on the div here, not to clicks on a button in the div, that could be a requirement you have in an app where you really want to make sure that button clicks don't trigger the div click listener. To make sure that the click event for the button for example doesn't propagate anymore, you can call event.stopPropagation.

That's not the same as prevent default, prevent default stops the default behavior the browser might perform upon such an event, for a click event on a button, we have no default behavior for a click event on a link for example, we would have one, there the browser would leave the page and go to that links destination. Stop propagation does nothing with the default behavior, the default behavior still executes, so for a form for example, the form would still be submitted but it stops the propagation which means any other listeners for the same type of event on some ancestor elements will not trigger their event listeners for this event.

So now you will see that clicked div will not be printed to the console when we click on a button. So if I reload and I click on a button, we only see the clicked button event listener, I have to click somewhere else on the div to trigger that div click listener. So that's what stop propagation does, you also have stop immediate propagation, that is useful if you have multiple event listeners on the same element, so if we had more event listeners on the button, then after the first event listener, the other button listeners, so the other listeners on the same element also wouldn't run anymore. With just stop propagation, all button event listeners would execute and only ancestor element clicked listeners would not execute.

That's the difference here and just as prevent default, this can be a very useful tool to make sure that you can handle the events in exactly the way you want. So you learned about stop propagation, it's important to understand that not all events propagate. Again, common sense is a good starting point to find out whether an event propagates or not, for a click, it makes more sense, when we click something we could also want to listen to a click on a parent element. For a hovering over something, it makes less sense.

If I add mouse enter here to my button and also to my div and I reload, you see now I entered the div, so yes I'm still printing clicked div but it happens because of me hovering over it, now I hover over the button and therefore you see indeed, I only trigger clicked button and not the div as well, that first output here was from when we reach the div for the first time. So mouse, mouse enter, mouse move events typically don't propagate, if you're not sure whether they propagate or not, whether they bubble up, you can always just print the event object and have a look at it because you will find a bubbles property in there and as you see, it says false here which means this does not bubble up and hence you don't have to call stop propagation because it won't propagate anyways and there are a couple of events, drag events for example for drag and drop which don't propagate up because that typically would lead to an undesired behavior.
