lectures.title: Using Event Delegation
lectures.text:
With event propagation, you can do quite interesting things, specifically you can implement a pattern which is also called event delegation, let me show you an example. Let's say in events.html, so in our little demo file here, we have an unordered list here or any kind of list data, that's where this pattern typically shines, with a couple of list elements in there, item one and then we also have more items - two, three, four and five. Now I'll quickly add some style so that we can have some output there or that we see this at least a bit and I'll style each list item to simply have a padding of 1rem and to have a border of one pixel solid and then some other color here and the unordered list will get a list style of none to remove the bullet points.

So some basic styling you can add to events.css and then this basic list here which I added to my HTML file. Now if we reload this, we see this list down there. Now we want to be able to click on these items and color the clicked item red, let's say that's our goal here, if it is red already, we want to remove the color. Well for that, let's go to events.js and now of course we've got two possible approaches. One is that we select all list items and we add multiple listeners, so we could get all list items here with document query selector all, select all li's and then use list items, forEach for example to go through them or use a for/of loop of course and then on each list item, we can add an event listener, for click event and then have a function in there where we get the event object and then in here, we can say event target and then let's a class list because event target is a DOM element, so we have the class list property available even though my IDE doesn't know it and then here we simply toggle the highlight class let's say and now we just have to add this highlight class to events.css, like this and there, let's say we have a background color of red and a text color of white then. So this is something we can

do, define this highlight class, register multiple click listeners on all the elements and now if we save and reload, we should be able to click them and toggle our colors here. Now that is working, however this approach has a couple of disadvantages. For one it's pretty cumbersome to add multiple listeners like this, additionally it can get bad from a performance and memory perspective because we got a lot of event listeners out there. So let's have a look at the alternative which uses this delegate pattern, this delegate approach. There instead of adding multiple listeners on each list item, we take advantage of event propagation, of the event bubbling up and therefore we get access to the entire list with document query selector ul, so with the list that holds the list items.

Now we can register an event listener on that list, so I listen to a click event on the entire list because since events bubble up, we can also listen to a click on the list when we actually clicked on a list item because that's how Javascript events behave, most events at least. So here I can now copy this logic here, this function, copy it in here because I still want to use the event target and toggle highlight and that's now by the way also the advantage of event target.

Even if my listener is registered on the list, event target will refer to the actual target on which we clicked, which in this example is our list item. So now if I save that and I reload, I got the same behavior as before but now with only one event listener instead of multiple event listeners because we're taking advantage of event propagation and then we're adding a listener on the next higher element which in this case is the list instead of every child element itself, this is the event delegation pattern.

Now this event delegation pattern can become problematic if we have a more complex structure. Let's say here for our list items, they are not simple like this, instead inside of li, we got a h2 tag which wraps our item one text here and then next to that or below that, we also got a paragraph with some text. Now let's say we have a couple of those items here, so I'll just quickly copy and paste them and change the numbers here so that we can differentiate them and auto format and now if we reload, we have a problem, if I click on the title, yes now you see this gets the red background, not the entire element.

If I click somewhere else, the entire element might get this or just a paragraph. So now because we were referring to event target, we have a problem, we have a problem because event target is the actual DOM element on which we clicked and that's the lowest possible element, so that's either our h2 tag or if we clicked outside of h2 and outside of paragraph, it's the entire list item or it's just a paragraph or whatever else we might have in there, so just coloring or using event target is not helping us here.

Now we also do have another property available and that is event.currentTarget. This is different from event target, let's see if that helps us. If we reload and I click somewhere on the h2 tag, well event current target is the entire unordered list here because current target, unlike target is not the actual element on which you clicked but the element on which you added the listener. So current target here always refers to the list element because that's where we register our listener.

So that can also be useful sometimes but here it isn't, it's still not the element on which we clicked, it's still not the list item, it's just a list which also is not what you need. Well we can use a combination of event target and DOM traversal which I covered earlier in the course, in the DOM module to get access to the list item. What do we know about event target? Well we know it's inside of our list and if we have a look at our list, we see it's definitely somewhere inside of the list item, right, because we have just the list and the list items.

So we know it's inside of our list item, hence it's either the h2 tag, the paragraph or the list item itself. Now you learned about a specific method that can help us here and that would be on event target which is some DOM object inside of our list, the closest method. Closest exists on all DOM objects and it traverses up in the ancestor tree and there you can select the closest element with a certain CSS selector, you could select by ID, by class or just by tag and in this case I'm looking for the closest li.

The cool thing is closest does include this element on what you call it itself. So if we clicked on the list item itself, this will give us the list item itself, if we clicked on some h2 tag inside of the list item, this will give us the closest li ancestor which is this list item. So it always gives us the closest list item which is exactly what we need here and therefore here, we can now call class list toggle on the closest list item and now this will work because now, no matter where we click, you see I always select the entire list item and color the entire list item.

So this is now the perfect event delegation pattern because now we delegate our event and we still make sure we worked with the right element, with a combination of event target and DOM traversal.

lectures.title: Triggering DOM Elements Programmatically
lectures.text:
With that we learned a lot about events, how to listen to them, how to work with the event object, what we can get out of the event object and also about this event delegation pattern. Now sometimes, you don't want to listen to an event or at least not just listen to an event, you also might want to trigger an event programmatically. I'll show you an example for when you could do that a little bit later in this module, in our project application, let's for now just see how it would work.

Let's say when I click any list item for whatever reason, I also want to trigger a click event on my button. So first of all here, I'll again listen to a click event so that I can see that it worked but now back to the list item from inside this event listener, I want to trigger this event listener. Now of course, we could store this function in a named function and then just call this function from inside here but let's say for whatever reason, that's not really an option, we really want to click that, a better example might be with our form by the way. There we could say we want to submit the form, not just with the submit button in there but also when something else happens on the page, that's probably a better example because it's a bit more realistic.

So let's say when we click any list item for whatever reason, we want to submit this form. Now to do that, we need access to that form element, so we need access to the element for which we want to trigger an event and then here in this case on a list item or when the list is clicked or any item in the list, I want to call form and now you can call click there for example to simulate a mouse click on it or also submit, as a method just like that and this does not just exist for the form but basically for any DOM element, a lot of the events you can listen to can also be triggered programmatically, especially something like clicks or form submissions.

So now with that if you save this and you reload, you will see that if I click any list item here, the page reloaded because the form was submitted. Now you might be wondering why our event listener here for the form submission is not doing its work and preventing the default. Now if you trigger a submit event programmatically, then indeed the submit event listener is skipped, typically event listeners execute. If I for example instead of submitting the form simulate a click on my button and please note that I do have a click listener on the button, you will see that if I do that and I reload, this click listener does execute, though with a dummy mouse event where all coordinates are zero by the way. For form submission, the event listener is not triggered.

So triggering such an event programmatically is not exactly the same as when a user clicks on it, it can bypass certain listeners like a form submission listener. Still from time to time it can be useful and it is good to be aware of it. Now if you still wanted to work around that by the way, you could of course select the submit button here in the form and instead of calling submit on the entire form, you call click on the submit button, then it will basically do the same as if a user click the submit button which will trigger the submit the event listener and allow you to prevent the default, so that would be possible.

So even if you need to submit the form, you can still trigger that programmatically by simulating or by triggering a click on the button instead of the form submission itself.

lectures.title: Drag & Drop - Theory
lectures.text:
So now that we gain some experience with events and saw a lot of examples and how to work with events in Javascript, specifically in the browser, let's have a look at drag and drop and how we can implement such a behavior in a web page. Now we'll do this on this project example we already worked on in the past but before we dive into that, let's go through the steps that you need to go through to make elements draggable on your web page and then also to make sure that they can be dropped somewhere and that something happens if they are dropped somewhere.

So to make elements draggable, you have to mark them as such and you do that by adding the draggable attribute or setting the draggable property on the DOM elements to true, so both needs to be set to true, either the attribute or directly through the property. Once you did that, this element is draggable. The next step then is to listen to a drag start event on the element which is draggable, this will be triggered whenever a user starts dragging the event. In the event listener there, you can also interact with the event object to describe the drag operation if you are copying or if you're moving which will for example also affect how this is displayed to the user, how the cursor changes and so on and you can also append data to the event because a drag and drop operation is actually a combination of different events, on different elements on your page and in order to make sure that they can work together and that you know in the place where you dropped something what you started to drag in another place, you can add data to that drag event which is then invisibly kind of passed around to the other events related to dragging and dropping.

So once we started our drag operation and we configured the drag event, we have to tell Javascript where the item can be dropped. Of course, the user can drop the item anywhere but we typically don't support it everywhere on our page, instead we kind of mark the areas where an item can be dropped by adding an event listener to the element on which the other element can be dropped. We add a listener to the drag enter and the drag over events. You can omit the drag enter event, you definitely need the drag over event.

Both will be triggered whenever an item is dragged onto that element, the difference between the two elements is that drag over basically also triggers for child elements of the element where you added it, drag enter won't trigger there and then here, the trick is that in the event listeners you set to these events here, you have to call prevent default because the default is always that a drop operation is cancelled, so that drag and drop isn't allowed onto an element because as I said for most parts of your page, you don't want allow it and therefore that's the browser default, you have to prevent that default to allow a drop operation, so it's an important step to listen to these events and prevent the default to allow a drop.

Now before we react to a drop, you can also optionally listen to a drag leave event if you want to update the UI for example, updates some styles when the item is dragged away from the element on which it was dragged over. That is optional, not optional at least if you want to do something upon a drop is that you listen to the drop event on the same element where you listened to drag enter and drag over. The drop event will only be triggered if you prevented the default in drag enter and drag over and the item is then dropped onto that same element.

Now in that drop event, you can then do whatever you want to do upon a drop, update some data, update the UI, move the element on the UI, anything like that because that's also important. When you make an element draggable, you'll get some visual feedback that looks like the user is really dragging the element but it's actually not getting moved in the DOM technically, you have to do that programmatically through Javascript if you want to update the DOM after performing such a drag and drop operation.

You also optionally can then listen to a drag end event, not on the place where it was dropped but on the dragged element itself and there you could also then update the UI or some data, whatever you want to do. The drag end event is always fired even if the drop is cancelled, so if the element was dropped in an invalid area but as I will show you, you will get some property on the event object which tells you whether the drop was successful or not.

So that's the theory, let's now go through these steps and implement drag and drop step-by-step in our project.

lectures.title: Pure Functions & Side-Effects
lectures.text:
Let's start with pure functions and side effects, what is that? Well, a pure function is a function which for some given input, so for some given arguments, always produces the same output, so the same arguments, the same values for the given arguments always produce the same output and it also does not trigger any side effects, which means it does not change anything outside of the function. So let's have a look at this in practice. For this again, we get a very basic project, an empty HTML file pretty much with no content and an app.js file which is also empty, you can create it yourself or take the one which you find attached and in there, I want to create a pure function without side effects with you.

And a basic example for this and of course you can create the function in any way you want with the function keyword, as a function expression or as a function expression with the arrow function syntax, here I'll go through the good old function declaration syntax. So I'll create such a function and l name it add and this will take two numbers, num1 and num2 as parameters let's say and then return num1 + num2 , so it's a very basic function which adds two numbers. We can then console log a call to that function with the numbers 1 and 5 for example and another one with the values 12 and 15.

Now if we do that and we execute this function simply by loading our empty HTML file, we see that we get the results 6 and 27 and no matter how often I reload, which I'm doing here, we always get the same result which shouldn't be a surprise because there is no randomness in this function, there is no strange behavior. For the same values as I input, we always will get back the same result, 6 and 27 and therefore this is a perfect example for a pure function. It does not change anything outside of the function and it always produces the same result for the same inputs.

Now what would be an example for an impure function? For example, add random where we always get an input and then we return num1 plus math.random, so we return our input plus a random number. If we then call add random, let's say with a value of 5, then we of course see that if we run this code, we get different results down there every time I reload this page, you see how this changes. Of course we do because we add a random function but because we can't predict the output for a given input, this would be an impure function, so a function that is not pure. A function is also not to be considered pure if it introduces side effects which is a fancy term for saying it changes anything outside of the function, that could be an HTTP request which you are sending or data which is stored in the database but it could also be something more trivial, like let's say changing some variable which is defined outside of the function. Let's say we have our previous result variable which is 0 and then we had a function, add more numbers, where we have num1 and num2 again and I do still sum them up, num1 + num2 but then I also set previous result equal to sum before I return the result.

So this function here would now not be pure because it introduced a side effect, the side effect is not that we calculate the sum here because that is stored in a constant which is part of the function, this would be absolutely fine, the side effect is this line here, we change a variable that is defined outside of the function. So when you call this function and you don't see the function definitions, if you just call it like this, it might not be obvious that besides returning a result, this function changes something and therefore, this might be something you want avoid.

Now I'll talk a bit more about the rules regarding when you should use pure functions and when it's OK to use other functions in the next lecture but for the moment, just be aware that this function would hold a so-called side effect. Another example for a function with a side effect would be a function that changes an object or an array that you pass into it. Let's say we have our hobbies here and there we got an array with sports and cooking and then we have a function, print hobbies and we expect to get our hobbies here as an argument, as a parameter, I'll just name it h here and of course we console log h here but let's say for whatever reason, we also push a new hobby onto that array, new hobby. If we now call print hobbies and we pass in hobbies, we'll see that what actually gets printed is our hobbies array with the new extra hobby here, as you can see here and the reason for that of course is that we change that array but because arrays are objects and objects are reference values, when we change that array here, we change the original array because what we get here in the parameter is not a copy of that array but a copy of the address of the array and therefore, we work with the exact

same object in memory, so when we change it inside of the function, we also change it outside of the function, hence again we have a side effect. So that are pure functions and side effects, is it now a good idea to use pure function? Is it bad? Is it bad to use side effects? How should you work with functions with this extra knowledge gained?

lectures.title: Impure vs Pure Functions
lectures.text:
Typically it's a good idea in programming, not just in Javascript but especially in Javascript, to aim for pure functions without side effects simply because they are predictable and if someone calls them without knowing the function definition, it's always good if you can rely on the fact that this function doesn't do anything strange behind the scenes. Now that being said, when you're building an application, when you're writing code, it will be impossible for you to avoid introducing side effects at some point of time.

A function might need to set up some event listener or might need to send some data to a server and that is absolutely fine. The goal just is to minimize the amount of functions which are impure or which have side effects, just work with your code in a logical way, try to keep your functions predictable and pure and if you then occasionally have some functions that need to perform a side effect or that needs to be impure, that's absolutely fine.

Maybe just try to be clear regarding the function naming that this might be a function that does something as a side effect, for example a function which is named send data to server would be expected to send some data to a server and it wouldn't come as a surprise that this function as a side effect produces an HTTP request. A function which is just called add on the other hand should probably not create some side effect or be impure because a function with this name, well we would expect this to be pure, right?

As always, it comes with experience and now of course it's OK to not be perfect regarding that, you should definitely be aware of this concept of pure functions though and as I said, aim for more pure functions and less impure functions that might introduce side effects.

lectures.title: Factory Functions
lectures.text:
So now that we know what pure functions are, let's dive into factory functions. Pretty unrelated to pure functions but still an important concept. The idea behind factory functions is that you have a function that produces another function, now that might sound strange but it makes more sense once we see an example. Let's say we're building a web application, some accounting software where as part of that software, we need to show various tax amounts and of course as you know, we got different taxes based on which amount we're working with, for our revenue we might need the value added tax, for our profit before tax we might need the income tax or the corporate tax. Now the tax calculation typically always is the same.

If we had a function, calculate tax, then we probably would have a function that receives a tax rate and an amount and then we just return amount times tax, something like that, that could be a function that calculates a tax, of course it's a trivial function but you get the idea. Now the problem is if we have our value added tax amount, we might need to call calculate tax with our amount, 100 and the tax rate of let's say 90%, so 0.9. For our income tax, we might need to call calculate tax with an amount of 100 and 0.25 or whatever.

Now of course it's fine to do it like that and because it's a trivial function, it definitely seems doable to call it like that but what if you needed that amount in different parts of your software? Then you need to call the functions with these tax rates in different parts of the software. Now that's where a factory function can be helpful. You would create another function which you could call create tax calculator, so I try to make it clear by the function name that this function will return something which then does something for us and in this function, we create another function, as you learned you can have functions in functions, so we can move that calculates tax function into the create tax calculator function. So now we have that function in there and now the interesting thing is the create tax calculator function could take our tax parameter and we can therefore actually remove it from that internal function because of that scope thing too which I'll come back in the next lectures as well, a function in a function can access everything which is available outside of that inner function, so that tax parameter which we have in the outer function can be used in the inner function as well

and therefore now here, we have our tax calculator function as part of that outer function. Now here in the outer function, we can return calculate tax and I don't return the result of it, so I don't execute it, instead I just return a pointer at this function. Now what's the benefit of that? Well now we return a function which expects an amount as an input but which doesn't need the tax percentage as an input. So now what we can do is we can create a vat calculator or name it calculate vat amount and that simply is a call to create tax calculator where we pass in the vat percentage and then we might have our income tax amount which we create with create tax calculator, .25 as an argument.

So now what I in the end store here and I should name this calculate income tax amount, so what I store here are in the end two functions, this constant holds a function, it holds this inner function configured for this percentage and this here also holds the inner function but configured with a different percentage because I call the outer function twice, so it runs separately two times, with different arguments for the tax, so different values for the tax argument and therefore this inner function is recreated two times, once for every execution of the outer function and every time it logs in the tax percentage of that outer function which differs for the two executions and therefore the function which we return is this preconfigured inner function with the logged in tax amount and hence now if I console log calculate vat amount for 100 and then again I repeat this for let's say 200, I just need to call this calculate vat amount function like this without passing in the value added tax percentage over and over again because I configured this once here with the help of this factory function and we're good to go thereafter.

So if we save that and we reload, I get my different value added tax amounts. So that's the idea behind factory functions, if you have a certain function which you call multiple times in different parts of your app and it can be preconfigured in a certain way so that calling it is easier and you don't need to repeat yourself as often because our second argument would always be the same here if we would expect two arguments as we did earlier, in such a case, a factory function can be convenient and can save you time and code.

Now here's an important rule which you can memorize for Javascript interviews, every function in Javascript is a closure, so why is every function a closure then? What is that concept of being a closure then? Well this is closely related to the idea of having scopes for our variables. As you learned earlier in the course, you have different scopes - you have block scope when we're working with variables that are created with const or let and that simply means that inside of curly braces like for example here in a function definition, if you create a variable in there or if you get a parameter, it's only usable inside of that function but not outside of it.

On the other hand, global variables or constants which are created outside of functions can be used inside of the functions, that's something you already knew. Now if you have a function in a function, that inner function can use all the variables or parameters of the outer function and all variables that are defined globally, the outer function can not access the inner functions specific constants or variables. So for example here, amount could not be accessed from inside that outer function, only from inside that inner function, so that's what you already knew.

The more technical term for this would be that we have different lexical environments. Each function has its own lexical environment and you have a global environment as well and the variables and constants are registered in these different environments you could say. Now when a function is created as we do it here with the function keyword by using this function declaration, then this function creates a new lexical environment and registers any variables it has access to inside of this environment.

So in this case for the outer function, the create tax calculator function, the tax parameter here for example would be a variable of its lexical environment. The global environment would have the hobbies constant for example. The inner function has its own environment with the amount parameter but it also has access to the outer functions environment. Now when we call create tax calculator, then this inner function is created, not before we do so because it's inside of that creates tax calculator function, so where this function the outer function is created when the script parses this file, the inner function is only created when we call this function, when we call the create tax calculator function.

So when this function then is created in here, something interesting happens, it's in this case here logs in the value for tax when this outer function runs. So if you then call that outer function again with a different value, since we execute a brand new function, since we have a totally different function execution, the inner function receives this brand new tax value and is totally detached from that other function execution. Now on the other hand if we have some other variable, let's say a multiplier for whatever reason we need that, 1.1 and we refer to that inside of that function no matter if it's the outer or the inner one, then this will be updated when it changes outside of this function.

So for example if I multiply this with multiplier here and I then call the create tax calculator function and thereafter change the multiplier, so after calling this outer function but before calling the inner function to 1.2, you will see that a multiplier of 1.2 will be used, to make it easier to see, I'll print the multiplier here. So let's save that and reload and you see 1.2 gets printed here. So what does this tell us? It tells us that we do log in tax here because that's part of this specific environment of the outer function when it runs but we don't log in the concrete value of multiplier because that's part of the global environment and in the end what happens is just each function registers its surrounding environments and the variables that are defined in there and if these variables change and this function uses such a variable, then it takes the latest value.

Now for tax in this case here, that would be the case too but when this inner function is created, it has a look at its surrounding environment which is this functions, the create tax calculator functions environment for example and there we have a tax variable, a tax parameter and if that would change, the inner function would take the new one but this never changes because the only time we pass in a new value is when we execute this function again, this however will be a brand new execution and not change that inner function that was created on the first function execution here, which is why that inner function created by that first function execution still has its old environment with the tax you set up here as an argument. Now why is it called a closure then?

Because every function closes over the surrounding environment which means it registers the surrounding environment and the variables registered there and it memorizes the values of these variables. If you then change a variable, well that is reflected inside of the function but if it does not change, the function still is able to use for example the tax value you passed in when you created the outer function. That is not something you should take for granted because you could also read this code here in a different way.

Now in Javascript, you can indeed take for granted that it will not be missing but I want to emphasize that this is not something you can take for granted in all programming languages.

It is like this in Javascript but it's not necessarily like this in other languages. lectures.title: How Numbers Work & Behave in JavaScript
lectures.text:
Now let's start with numbers. Numbers are of course an important construct in Javascript and it's important to keep in mind that in Javascript, every number is a float, a floating point number which means a number with an integer place and then also with a couple of decimal places. So there is no specific integer type for numbers without decimal places, that does not exist in Javascript. We do have a special integer type in certain other programming languages but Javascript is not one of them, every number instead is a float which means a number with decimal places.

Now internally, numbers are stored as 64 bit floating points, so there are 64 bits available to internally represent a number, bits are these things which can be either 0 or 1. One bit is reserved for the sign, so if it's a positive or negative number and the other bits are basically there to represent the digits of the number and where the dot is, so where the decimal separator sits and the combination of these bits is therefore capable of describing numbers, of course within certain boundaries.

Now before we have a closer look at these boundaries, if you want to learn all the theory about floating point arithmetic and how numbers are represented as bits, not just in Javascript but in any programming language, you can check out some of the attached articles and resources like Wikipedia article or this discussion on stack overflow. There you can dive much deeper into this, something I won't do here simply because it's not really the core of Javascript, it's definitely interesting to notice and to understand this but for your day-to-day work, you typically won't need this which is why I will ignore it here.

The important takeaway from these resources or without them by just listening to what I'm saying here I guess is just that of course, due to the fact that we have 64 bits available to represent a number, there are certain limits in Javascript, there is a maximum and a minimum number and there also is only a certain amount of precision we can get regarding the decimal places of a number, so you can't represent every number in Javascript and there are of course certain ways around that if you really need to, though of course we're talking about very large numbers or numbers with lots of decimal places and the question is how often you really need to work with such large numbers or with such detailed numbers but be aware of the fact that there are certain limits and these limits are actually with what I want to start here.

Attached you again find a very basic starting project, HTML file and an empty script and for now we'll just work in the console here. Now in Javascript, we have a maximum and a minimum number and you can easily find out what the maximum and the minimum is by using the global number object which is built into Javascript and then with a dot, you got a couple of methods and properties available and for example, there is a MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and this gives us just what it sounds like, this is the biggest possible number you can represent with the normal number type in Javascript, that's 9 quadrillion, so a relatively large number and just in case you're interested, it's basically the same as two at the power of 53 - 1 which you can calculate with the math object where you we have a power of function, basically the same function we wrote in the functions module with our recursion built into Javascript on the math object and there, you can enter two at the power of 53 - 1, this is the largest number Javascript can reliably produce.

Now you might wonder why we then can also print this number, the thing simply is whilst Javascript can display this number, calculations with such a number will not really work, for example if we add one here to this limit, you see this number was not changed, we get the same result as when we just output the number. So that proves that this is the highest possible number we really can work with. Of course if you would add anything to that number, we again would enter that range where Javascript is not able of representing it and therefore working with that number is only possible if you deduct something from it basically or if you divide it by some other number, so that's how you can think about this maximum number.

Of course you don't just have a maximum integer, you also have a MIN_SAFE_INTEGER which is essentially the same number with a negative sign in front of it and you also have a max value here, the difference is that this is actually a decimal number, so here we don't have the largest integer but the largest number we can express and in the end, that's 1.79 and so on multiplied with e at the power of 308, so that's the biggest value you can work with in Javascript, not the biggest non-decimal value, so not the biggest integer but the biggest value in general and these biggest and smallest values and integers simply result from the fact how Javascript numbers are represented internally, how they are stored in these 64 bits in the end.

Again, the resources attached to the last lecture are a great way of diving deeper into that if you want to learn all the theory behind that. The core takeaway here is that if you ever should work with such detailed or large numbers or integers, you want to be aware of the fact that there are limits, you want to be aware of the fact that for example you can't deduct anything from that number because it already is the smallest possible integer, you can't deduct any other integer I should say. You can't add anything to that number because it already is the biggest number you can represent in Javascript.

Now if you still do add something to that number or you do deduct an integer from that number, you don't get an error as you see if I deduct 10 here, the thing just is Javascript gives you an imprecise result, for example here you see we exceed that bit range and therefore we simply get the result where Javascript cuts the number after its 64 bits and then converts this back to a decimal number, so in a decimal system I mean, with a base of 10 and that would then be this number. So it can be difficult to wrap your head around that because we're also working with two different number systems here, the decimal system with a base of 10 and the binary system with a base of two which of course gets used when we work with bits where we only have 0 and 1, that is what the binary system is all about and therefore, Javascript internally works with the binary system and then always converts it back to the decimal system when it outputs that number.

This is how is such a strange result happens when we deduct 10 from this number, we exceed that bit range which is available for numbers and then Javascript just cuts off the bits and converts that bit, that binary number back to a decimal number which would be this one. Now again, it can be tricky, you rarely of course work with such large numbers or with numbers with that many decimal places here in the end but it's important to be aware of the limitations you might be facing.

lectures.title: Floating Point (Im)Precision
lectures.text:
Speaking of the binary system and the decimal system, you might remember that sometimes throughout the course, you've got a strange output for a seemingly easy calculations. Let's say we're adding .2 and .4, now what we get as a result is actually this which makes little sense, right, this should be 0.6 and indeed if you would compare the result of that with 0.6, you would get false. Why is 0.2 + 0.4 not equal to 0.6 in Javascript? I mean that's certainly not what we learned in math.

Well it's all coming down to that binary system which Javascript and which actually all programming languages use behind the scenes and the decimal system in which we, the programmer, work. When we say 0.2 and 0.4, we're of course working in the decimal system, so with a base of 10. Now Javascript internally as you learned works with the binary system and as I also just said, pretty much all programming languages do that. Now therefore, Javascript converts this number to the binary system for doing the calculation and then basically converts it back to give us an output that makes sense to us humans because we rather work with the decimal system than with the binary system, right? Now that's exactly the issue, it's important to understand that in the end, numbers like this one here with decimal places are in the end just represented as fractions of integers you could say, so for example 0.2 in the decimal system could be represented by 1/5 and 0.4 could be 2/5 of course, in the decimal system.

So in a decimal system, these calculations are super simple right, we can perform them perfectly. Now in the binary system, that's different, to understand this, let's first of all have a look at a calculation which we can't really solve or where we have no perfect result in the decimal system as well and that would be 1/3. In the decimal system, we get this number when we try to do that calculation because as you are aware in the decimal system, we can't find a perfect solution for this division and in the binary system, similar cases exist, not for 1/3 necessarily but for example, for 1/5.

Now for that, it can be convenient to find out how numbers are represented in the binary system and that can easily be done by entering a number, for example 1 and if it's just an integer, you should wrap it between parentheses to tell Javascript that now with a dot, you're accessing a method on the number and not adding a decimal place to it. So then you can enter to string here and to string actually takes an optional argument where you can define the base to which you want to convert that number, if you enter two here, we're printing the number 1 in the binary system which however still is 1 because in the binary system, we have the numbers or the digits 0 and 1, so 1 is also 1 in the binary system, now that changes if we try 5 here. Remember 0.2 is the same as 1/5, now 5 in the binary system is 101, so in the end you're dividing one by 101 in the binary system when you're trying to express 0.2. You can actually see the exact result of that division if you execute 1/5 and then call to string at a base of two, this number here, that's in the end what we end up with in the binary system if we try to divide 1 by 5 in the decimal system, so this is the result of the to the binary system converted calculation Javascript performed.

So this number, 0.2 in the end is this number here in the binary system you could say, you can of course also see that if you call to string here and add two here as a base on 0.2, here we don't need the parentheses because we already have one dot in there and therefore it's clear to Javascript that this is the number and this is then a method on the number. So this is how this number is represented in the binary system and here it's simply getting cut off but in the end this pattern here would be repeated infinitely in the binary system, just like the three is repeated infinitely in the decimal system if we divide one by three. So there simply are certain fractions where there is no perfect solution in the binary system just as there are certain divisions, like 1/3 where there is no perfect solution in the decimal system and it's because of that why we end up with this strange result here.

In the end both 0.2 and 0.4 don't yield a perfect result, so if we then add these two not perfect results, we get a imperfect result because we add two numbers which can't really be solved in the end. It's the same as if you would say 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3. Now here, we get one because Javascript does some rounding for us to give us a result that makes sense but in the end, you are working here with 0.33333 + 0.33333 + 0.33333 in the decimal system and hence you would end up with something like this in a decimal system, you can't really reach 1 and it's the same for the binary system with 0.2 + 0.4, you can't really reach 0.6 because in the binary system, both these numbers can't really be solved, there isn't a finite amount of decimal places that would be needed to represent each number.

Now often in Javascript, Javascript fixes this for us, it shows us a number that makes sense to us even though in the binary system, it can't really be represented, for example if we just use 0.2. You just learned that there is no perfect representation of that in the binary system. Still if Javascript converts the binary representation, which just to bring it back in memory was this here, when it converts this back to a decimal number to output it to us, it converts it back into a perfect decimal number and not in to something like this but this is just a trick by Javascript and many programming languages do that, they of course don't want to show this to us, instead they want to give us a result that makes sense to us and they're generally pretty smart about rounding the numbers they got in the binary system.

Nonetheless, you can see that there is imprecision if you use another method which is to fixed, to fix does not convert this, instead here you can set a certain amount of digits you want to output and for example if you enter 20 here, you force Javascript to represent this as a number with 20 decimal places and you see, at some point of time, we can see that imprecision here, so Javascript is really just doing some smart rounding for us when it just outputs 0.2, behind the scenes, that number looks like that. Now is that a problem?

No, generally that's not a problem. For most calculations, this automatic rounding works just fine. Now if you want to output a number to the user, you of course want to avoid that 0.2 + 0.4 is printed like this somewhere on your page. To avoid this, you can use that to fixed method you just learned about, there for example you could force Javascript to just display two decimal places and you would end up with a perfectly fine number and of course you can specify any amount of decimal places you want - 2, 1, 0, whatever you want and Javascript will round it and avoid showing this imprecision here.

So for outputting results to your end users, to fixed is a great way of working around that issue here. Now there are certain other calculations however where you don't just worry about the thing or the result you show to the user but about the result itself. Let's say you have an online shop and you're working with prices there. Now if something costs 20.2 euros or dollars and you send that to your server to charge the credit card by that amount, then behind the scenes, you are sending this number to your servers and therefore here in the end, you're charging not enough.

Now of course chances are that when you're charging something like this, the payment service you're using automatically rounds this to fix your error or do anything like that but chances are also that you in the end do introduce some small errors and therefore you sometimes might charge too much or too little and over time, even such small deviations can really add up. Imagine Amazon charging to a little bit too much or a little bit too less on every transaction, well they're handling thousands of transactions every hour of course, so there, that would quickly add up and therefore, there are situations where you need perfect precision.

Now to get perfect precision, one common solution is to simply multiply your number with 100 in the end so that you only work with integers. Now you learned there are no integers in Javascript, everything is a floating point number but of course this integer here whilst it not being an integer would be this floating point number and this can be represented perfectly in binary notation so you won't have any imprecision here. So working with integers only can be one workaround around such imprecision here.

You also can find certain Javascript packages and libraries, by the way libraries are a topic we'll have a closer look in detail later in the course but certain third-party add-ons you can add to your page, to your application so to say which also provides you tools, utility functions to fix such imprecision or of course, you know you are using some service maybe on your server or some third-party service your web app talks to which fixes such issues for you.

Again often, they may not matter especially for outputting something to the user, you can just use to fixed but in some cases where they do matter, you should be aware of that imprecision and that there are workarounds, like for example only working with integers by multiplying with 100 for example.

lectures.title: The BigInt Type
lectures.text:
So that was a lot about precision and numbers but it's important to understand it. In modern versions of Javascript, there actually also is an alternative to the normal number we worked with all the time and that's a big integer. Now the big integer type is a primitive value and its goal is to allow you represent numbers that are above the maximum safe integer we learned about, so a number bigger than that. If you for example wanted to represent a number bigger than that by adding extra nine at the end, you would see what I explained before, we get a totally different number because Javascript only works with 64 bits and we would exceed that and therefore Javascript cuts the number at a certain point and shows a different number.

Now a big int can help us with that, you create a big int by simply adding a n after your number and now you see, this looks a bit different here in the console because it's a different type, this keeps its precision, its value and we can represent arbitrarily big numbers with that because internally, this is managed differently, not as a 64 bit floating point number but instead in the end as a string and Javascript does all the heavy lifting of converting this around when you use it in calculations and so on.

So the big int can be useful if you're working with very large numbers, of course not just positive ones but also negative ones. Now be aware that there is no floating point calculation there, that there are no supported decimal places, you see I'm getting an error if I try to add a decimal place, it's called big int because it's only about integers and it's the perfect type if you are working with very large integers. Of course you can always represent smaller numbers with that, the question is if this makes a lot of sense and then you can also perform typical calculations with it, just important, you can't mix big int and other numbers, for example 10n and -4, where 10n is a big int but 4 is a normal number would yield an error, you see you cannot mix big int and other types, use explicit conversions so you would have to convert this to a big integer or this to a normal number before mixing it. You can convert it to a normal number with parseInt for example, that would work or by converting four to a big integer by wrapping it with that big int function call here, not new big int but just big int like this, this is how you can convert numbers back and forth and this is how you then can work with them and how

you can run various calculations. Of course conversion is only needed if you want to mix types, if you have a big integer and you want to multiply it with another big integer, you don't have to convert anything, you can just run this calculation like that. One important note, if you divide a big int, since decimal places can't be represented there, Javascript will actually omit them and we don't see it here because this can be divided with a perfect result without decimal places but if we have 5n divided by 2n, then you see we're not getting 2.5n because this does not exist as you see, instead we get 2n because Javascript simply cuts off the decimal place that would otherwise be added.

So that's a big integer, not the type you'll use every day but can be useful if you have very large numbers with which you need to work.

lectures.title: The Global "Number" and "Math" Objects
lectures.text:
Now that we learned a lot about numbers and big integer, before we move on to strings, let's have a look at the number and the math global object. We used some of the features of these objects already and now I just want to have a second look and walk you through the important ones, let's start with number. There we saw MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, MAX_VALUE, MIN_SAFE_INTEGER and MIN_VALUE, you also have negative and positive infinity. These are special values in Javascript which you also can just type like this by the way, infinity and -infinity and this is the value you for example get if you divide by zero, you'll not get an error which you might expect, instead you get infinity because it basically approximates the result you could say.

So infinity is a special value you can get and you can also check for infinity in places where you need true or false, for that you've got the isFinite method, also on the number object but also available just on a global object to which you can pass a number to find out if this is finite, like an example of 10 is true or if it's infinite as an example of infinity because that is not finite and therefore, this returns false. So number isFinite can be useful, we also have isNaN there, we saw that earlier already, also exists as a global method.

We got parseFloat and parseInt here which also exists globally though and therefore we don't really need that here and that's therefore basically it for the number object. More interesting than that is the math object, there you get various methods and constants or properties that help you with mathematical operations. You've got the value for the E number, for Pi if you need that in calculations, methods for calculating the square root, for working with the sin for example, also the power of method we saw a second ago in this module already, the abs method to give you an absolute number based on some number you pass in as an input and many more methods, like for example also the random method you already learned about which also can often be very convenient.

I can only recommend that you scroll through the various methods you've got there, as you can see, there are a lot, of course the MDN docs are also a great place to learn all about them and whenever you have a mathematical operation you need to perform in your code, chances are that you don't need to reinvent the wheel and you don't need to write your own logic but that the math object has got you covered and provides the operation you want to perform.

lectures.title: Example: Generate Random Number Between Min/ Max
lectures.text:
Before we move on to strings, here's a little demo with the math object and a little convenience function which you might actually need in many of your programs. We have math random to give us a random number, now what does math random produce though? It produces a random number between 0 and 1. Now that's nice but sometimes you need a random number between 10 and 20, what can you do in such a scenario? Well we can write our own function that builds up on math random and allows us to provide an upper and lower boundary.

Now for that, I'll create a new function and of course you can create it in any way you want, with a function declaration, function expression, arrow function, whatever you need and I'll name it randomIntBetween, now of course the name is totally up to you. Now here I expect two values, a minimum and a maximum value, so my lower and my upper boundary and we want to return a number here. Now it all starts with math random but of course, that is between 0 and 1 as we learned and that's not what we want here.

Now to respect our minimum boundary, we can add the minimum, if we call this function for example with a value of 5 for min, we now get a random number plus our minimum, so we can't get a number lower than min because we add min, so we're already respecting our minimum which sounds quite good. Now we also of course want to respect the max however. Now to respect the max here, we need to multiply our random number here. What happens if we multiply it with our maximum? Let's say our minimum is 5, our maximum is 10, this gives us a random number between 0 and 1, we multiply this with 10, So if we have 0 which is of course very unlikely, then we would stick to 0, we add min, we have our minimum number, sounds about right.

If we have one, then we multiply this by max, so if our max value was 10, now we have 10 and we add 5 to it, so now we would have a value of 15 which is above our maximum. So we actually need to multiply it with max minus min, so only with the range between max and min. Now if max is 10 and I can put this here to make it easier to keep in mind, so these are the values we're working with in our fictional example to verify the function. If min is 5 and max is 10, then this yields 5.

If random, math random gives us 1, then this overall term produces 1 times 5 equals 5, we add 5 to that, we have 10 which is of course our maximum so that is all right. Now theoretically, that would be great but even though it's not saying it here at the tooltip but you could find it on MDN for example, it's important to understand that for the random method here on the math object, 1 is actually not included, so the random number we'll get might be 0.99999 but we'll never get a 1.

So as a result, the biggest number we can get here is max minus min, so that's 5, 5 times 0.99999, so that's almost 5, plus 5 is almost 10. Now if we want to include both the minimum and the maximum here, so we want to make sure that both numbers can occur, then we're not finished yet because right now this can never yield the maximum because random only yields 0.99999 and therefore we can only get close to the maximum. Now to get the maximum, we can add one here to our multiplication term so that this actually is 6 for these values we're providing here and therefore the biggest number we can reach right now is 10.99999, right, because we have six times almost 1, so we have almost 6 as a maximum result here, plus min which is 5, we have almost 11. Now of course we want to stop at max however which is 10 and not at almost 11 and now we can leverage another function on the math object and that's the floor function. Floor rounds this number down to the nearest integer, so we can wrap this entire term with math floor and it will basically just cut the decimal places you could say. So if we had this as a result, then floor will turn this into 10 and now we have a function which yields a number between min and max where both values are included.

Now of course you can deviate that and you can play around with that and if you google for Javascript, random between and so on, you'll find many examples where min is not included, where max is not included and so on but this here is a pretty common scenario which is why I wanted to show it to you. Well and with that if we give it a try and we console log random in between let's say 1 and 10, let's see what that gives us. If we save that and we go back to our page and reload, now we should get a couple of integers randomly but never above 10 or below 1.

So now we can run this as often as we want, we'll never get a number bigger than 10 or smaller than 1.

lectures.title: Tagged Templates
lectures.text:
We worked with template literals already, the idea here is that you could have some variable or some expression that produces a result that can be output in the string and then you might have your template literal where you say my name is and instead of having to concatenate strings with a plus which can be very cumbersome for long strings, you can use the ${} notation here to just inject any valid Javascript expression, so any expression that yields a value which can be output as a string.

Here I'm referring to the name constant but we could also be calling a function, if we had a getName function here that returns something we can output or do whatever you want, only important thing is it has to be an expression, you can't put an if statement in there for example but that's what you already knew, that's the template literal syntax and that can be really useful. Now you can do even more with it than just output simple strings like this, you can create so-called tagged templates. A tag template is in the end a function that works together with a template literal.

It all starts by creating a function, for example product description and this will make more sense in a second, a regular function which expects let's say three arguments and I'll come back to why three and what each argument holds in a second. Of course you can name all these arguments or parameters however you want but let's name the first one strings here, the second one product name and the third one product price. Now in here, I'll just return this is a product, nothing fancy, just a string.

Now we can use that and for example create a constant, product output and there, we add product description but we don't call it like this, instead we do something which looks super strange at first, we add a template literal right after our function name. So there are no parentheses anywhere, we don't pass that as an argument to that function, we have our function name and after that, two back ticks and that's a syntax we haven't seen before. Behind the scenes, Javascript will call this function and kind of pass in this template literal but not just like this as a single string but it will actually split it up into for example three arguments here and send these into the function.

Now the amount of arguments it sends in actually depends on your template literal. So here we could have this product and then for example parentheses which are part of the string, no special syntax, then for example an injected expression here where we have the product name and for that, let's add a new constant here, prod name Javascript course and refer to that here in our template literal interpolation syntax here, is and then for example the price, so here let's have the prod price and have 29.99 here and then insert this here.

So it's a regular template here in the end if we ignore the function name in front of it where we inject or interpolate two pieces of information into our otherwise normal string, the strange thing here is that we have that function name in front of it. Now I said that Javascript would call this function for us and pass this in but not as a single argument but actually as three arguments. Well, that will make more sense if we start outputting this, let's console log product output here, product output and see what this yields us, what this function actually does. If we save that and we reload, we see this is a product.

So what we see here is actually what this function returns, so it looks like this function was called and the result of the function is stored in this constant. OK so let's see what happens inside of the function and what we actually receive as arguments here. For that, we can of course console log strings, console log the product name here, so our second argument and console log the product price, our third argument. All of that gets logged here and with that let's save it and reload and now we see something interesting, now what we see here are these three outputs, these are from the lines 9, 10 and 11 which are just these three lines in the function. Now for strings, we see we're getting an array. We're getting an array which consists of three elements where each element is a string and the interesting thing here is in the end these three elements make up all the text we have down there in this template literal without our dynamic parts, so without the interpolated or the injected segments you could say. This product, blank opening parentheses, this is our first element, then between the first interpolated element and the second one, we have a closing parentheses, whitespace is whitespace and that's exactly our second element here in this array.

And then after our second interpolated value or segment here, we got a dot which is also a regular string and therefore our third element in this array is is just that dot. So in the end, what this function does or what Javascript does with this special syntax here is it calls this function here product description and the first argument of that function always is an array of string segments which are taken from your template literal and which represent the string parts between your dynamic segments.

Now your dynamic segments and of course here I should output this correctly now that I see it, your dynamic segments are passed in as additional arguments into that function in the order they appear in here in the template literal. So that's why, if I reload again, we see Javascript course and the price here. We see that here because these are our arguments, 2 and 3, in this function and Javascript simply goes through your template literal, takes all non-dynamic parts and puts them into this first argument which is an array and then takes the dynamic parts and adds them in the right order as argument values to this function. Now that hopefully makes sense, the obvious question is, why would we use that? Where can this be useful? Tagged templates can be useful if you have a scenario where you conveniently want to create some output, could be a string but could be something totally different as well, based on some string input, for example you could be using that to take some input here, some input text and convert this to a different text where you replace some values, for example here we could check if product price is greater than 20 and if it is, then we set some variable which I introduced in this function, price category maybe, to cheap here

and if the price is greater than 20, we set price category to fair. Now we could output our string down there by constructing a new template literal for example and then by injecting strings, the first segment of our strings here which is the first segment of that template literal string here, thereafter the unchanged product name, thereafter the second segment of our strings which is this segment but then instead of the original price, we insert the price category here and then we insert the last piece of our original string.

So now we're outputting a fully dynamic string, a dynamically generated string where we swap a value with some included logic and especially if you for example have a more complex logic for encoding a numeric price into a category as we're doing it here, then you might be better off using such a tagged template function here instead of using a ternary expression down there for example, which would take up a lot of space and could quickly be unreadable or hard to read at least.

So that would be a scenario where such a tagged template can save you time and lead to a better, more readable output because you can run your more complex logic in there and then just output the updated string down there in the end. So if we for example run this, we get this product is fair, we could of course also say fairly priced here and there, pretty cheap regarding its price, something like that and if we do that, you'll see here we got is fairly priced. So that's how you can work with that and of course there are many things you can do, you're also not forced to return a string here. Whilst that is a possibility, you could also return an object here with the name which is product name and the price which is product price and now you would have a function that simply converts a string into an object. It throws away the string parts you got and then just gives you the data that you dynamically injected there. If you needed that for whatever reason, you could do that and you would be getting an object without any errors because you're not forced to return a string in a tagged template.

lectures.title: Introducing Regular Expressions ("RegEx")
lectures.text:
Now to conclude this module, let's have a look at regular expressions. Regular expressions help us work with strings, consider this example - you're having an input and there, you get some user input and that should be an email address, something like test@test.com, this is what you get from an input you might have on your page. Now of course, users can enter anything in there and by accident, they might enter something which is not a valid email address, let's say for some reason the @ symbol was forgotten.

Now you want to verify whether what the user provided to you in your code, when you work with that value, whether that is an email address or not. Now a trivial test you can make or you can perform is you can use a string method for that, the includes method and check if that string includes an @ symbol and we would get false here and hence you would know that the user input we got is not a valid email address but a valid e-mail address is not just determined by the existence of an @ symbol, instead we also want to have a domain ending at the end, dot something.

So of course we can also check whether it includes a dot but that would also mean that something like tests.t@test would be treated a valid email address because it includes a dot even though it's in the wrong place and that's where regular expressions can help you. Regular expressions don't just exist in Javascript, they exist in most programming languages and they help you search for patterns in strings. Now you create a regular expression in Javascript in one of two ways, you can create it with the new regex constructor and then to this constructor, you pass a string which describes the pattern you want to look for and there is a rich regular expression language and syntax you can use here or you use a literal notation for creating that regex object, just like you can use square brackets to create an array object, you use two forward slashes like this and then in between these slashes, you define your pattern and a simple email validation pattern could look something like this, the carry symbol here, then \S+@\S, capital S, that's important in both places, \.\S+$. Now this looks super weird right now but let's just accept it as it is and make sure you don't mistype.

Now with that, you can use this and as I said, it is an object and call a method on this object and there we could call the test method and to the test method, you can pass a string where you want to validate if it meets this pattern and there we could pass in user input, we would get false. On the other hand, if I test a valid email address, let's say here I test test@test.com, I get true. Now the reason for that is that this in the end describes a regular expression which says we accept any kind of word at the beginning, this symbol means we start from the left so we have to start with any kind of word, like test, then somewhere in the overall string I want to have an @ symbol, thereafter again, any kind of word, so this test here for example, then a dot which we have here and then again, any kind of word with which we end this string.

This is what this expression means in the end and this string here for example fits into this pattern. Now of course, there is a rich regular expression syntax you can learn and it's almost like a programming language on itself. In the next lecture, I'll provide a brief introduction into this syntax but by no means a complete overview of all the things you can do there, however linked to the next lecture, you'll also find an external resource, a little bit of a more detailed introduction I prepared in the past which you can have a look at and also some MDN documentation to learn more and I will also show you how you can find out which pattern is best for your use case.

lectures.title: More on Regular Expressions
lectures.text:
So let's learn a bit more about regular expressions. For that I just reloaded this page here and now again let's create a new regular expression and store it in a regex constant. Again you can create it with new regexp and pass the expression pattern as a string to the constructor or use this literal notation with two forward backslash. Now a regular expression as learned describes a pattern which you try to find in some text in a string. A simple pattern could be hello, so just a couple of characters, normal characters.

This regular expression would yield true if we test any string which includes hello, so if we test just hello, we get true, we also get true if we say hi there, hello or if we have hello anywhere in there. So if hello is part of the string, this yields true because we're just checking if this combination of characters is part of the string we're validating. Now we don't return true if I try to validate hello with a capital H because regular expressions are case sensitive.

So this here does not yield true because we're checking for hello like this, not for a lowercase or uppercase H, however you could do that, you could also create this pattern in a more flexible way. You could say I'm looking for hello but I don't care where we start with an uppercase or a lowercase h. You would express this by wrapping this into parentheses, then adding a pipe symbol and then an uppercase H and this means we want to have a word which ends with ello and starts with either a lowercase or an uppercase H and of course we should store it in a new constant here to not reuse that name and now if I use regex2, I can test hello and you see we get true, also if it's somewhere in that string but I also get true if Hello starts with an uppercase h. We by the way don't get true if we just have ello, so the H really is needed, we just don't care about its casing.

So this would be one example of how we can alter this to be a bit more complex than just a straightforward word. There also are other modifiers, you can also work with wild cards, so after reloading this page here again, I'll create a new regular expression and let's say I want to check for ello but I don't care about the first character. For that you can use a dot here and this signals well you want to end with ello but you don't really care about the starting character of the word, so it has to be a five character word but the starting character is not relevant to you.

So then if I test hello here, I get true, if I on the other hand test just ello, I get false. On the other hand, I can use jello like this and I would also get true or something like this, this also would yield true but I have to have a starting character and this is then a wild card. By the way you can also escape in regular expressions, you might remember our email regular expression, email regex. There I used s+@s+ and then I used backslash dot in here, this is how we say I'm not looking for any character but really for the dot character, since the dot in a regular expression has a special meaning, it's that wild card you just learned about, you escape it with a backward slash, just as you can escape some characters in a normal string. Same by the way here with s+, I escape this s here so that I don't mean the regular uppercase s character but this now basically has a special meaning, in regular expressions, it means any word so to say. Now there is way more you can do there and as I mentioned in the last lecture, attached you find some links that allow you to dive deeper if you want to.

I however also want to be very honest with you, learning regular expressions and writing very complex expressions on your own will take some time to master and you might not need it that often, therefore a lot of people, myself included if I'm honest, often look up certain patterns, especially if I'm not sure if the pattern I came up with is the best one. So for example if you want to validate some email address in Javascript, you can Google for email js regex, something like this or Javascript regex email, anything like that and you'll find some discussions on Stack Overflow typically where you find some ideas.

So here for example, you find very complex patterns that match a lot of different email addresses or you find the more simple pattern I showed you, basically a combination of this one here and this one here and this is of course not just possible for emails, if you want to validate a URL, so if you want to find out if a string holds a URL, you can google for a URL js regex and you would find this discussion with some ideas on how you can validate a URL.

There you see a lot of different rules and syntax features of regular expressions in action and again with the attached resources, you can learn more about that but if you just need to find a certain regular expression to validate a certain pattern, this is how you can find it and how you can work with it. It's also worth noting that you can not just call test there, you also have an exec method on a regular expression. If you pass a string to that and keep in mind stored in regex is this regular expression, so if you pass a string to this, let's say jello which matches my regular expression, then you get back an array with some information about the pattern and where it matched in the string. You get the matching string back but you also see where this pattern started in the string and here since the entire string matches my pattern, we start at index zero.

If I would try to match this on let's say hi jello, then you would see we got index four because the pattern we found in there which was jello that matched our regular expression pattern, that started at index 4, index 0, index 1, index 2, index 3 and then index 4, so the fifth character was the first character of the matching pattern. So you also got exec if you need to find where in a string your pattern is matched. You also can do it the other way around, if you have hi jello here, then you can also call match on this and pass a regular expression to that and you get basically the same output, as you see matching pattern and where it started but you call this on a string instead of on the regular expression, it's of course up to you which one you prefer.

And that's it for now about regular expressions, definitely an interesting and sometimes important topic. You've got the basics here, searching for patterns is a good idea and something you will do in practice a lot and if you want to learn more, check out the attached resources of course.
