lectures.title: Sending Data with a POST Request
lectures.text:
Now let's make sure we can also send a post request, so a request that adds data on the server. For that here, I'll add a new function, async function create post or however you want to name it and there let's say I expect to get a title and the content of the post and then here I'll have the post ID which I'll generate with math random, just a random number and now overall I have the post object here you could say, where we have a title of title, where we have a body because our API here actually wants a body field, it wants that we send it a title, a body field and a userId, so actually this here should be userId, sorry, so userId, then title body should be the content argument we're getting and then userId and make sure you write it exactly as the API expects it, so with a capital I, that can be equal to a hardcoded value or to the userId I set up there.

So this could now be the post data we send to the server, the question just is, how do we now send this? Well we can reuse our sendHttpRequest function which we created up here and now the URL is actually the same as before, the server we're talking to supports this URL, you can see that in the examples here as well, this is a URL we can send a post request to but the method is a different one, the method now is post. By the way, it does not matter if this is all uppercase or if you write it like this, the convention is to use all uppercase but it's not required technically. The URL is the same URL as before and now we will actually need to enhance this method because now, we need to be able to also add a body to the request . For a get request, you don't need that you just want to get data so you don't append any extra data to the outgoing request, for a post request where you want to create data on the server, you need to add the data you want to create to the outgoing request and to do that, we need to tweak our function, the sendHttpRequest function to also expect a data argument or to support it at least. By default this can be null or it actually is undefined by default anyways if we don't pass it so we don't need to set this up and now

we can append this to the outgoing request. To append data to the outgoing request, you go to the send method and pass your data to send, however not just like this but it needs to be JSON data, so we should call JSON.stringify and pass data to JSON.stringify and then pass the result of this stringify call to send, so this will now add this extra data here. With that, we can call create post here after fetching the posts and create a dummy post with a dummy post as content maybe and just dummy as a title and now we just have to make sure that in create post, we use that post object which we created and add that to the request we're sending.

So here as the third argument which we just added to the sendHttpRequest method, we can add post and inside of the sendHttpRequest method, this will be converted to JSON and attached to the outgoing request. With that if we save that and we reload our page here, we don't get an error, let's check the network tab and there we see this extra request down there. Now the status codes here by the way signal whether it worked or not, 200ish status codes mean that the request succeded, 201 means that it succeeded and a resource was created on the server and therefore this is looking good, though keep in mind no actual resources are getting created here, we're talking to a dummy API which just fakes that it does something. Nonetheless if we inspect this, we see a response, this could be an ID which the server automatically generated for our send data and on the headers tab, we see our URL, our HTTP method and if we scroll to the very bottom, we see the request payload and that's the data which was appended and here we see that indeed is the data we generated.

So this is how we can send a request with JSON data to an API, it's as easy as that. Now let's tweak our little project here a little bit and let's make sure we actually send the data which the user entered and we also only send it when we click add or we fetch it when we click fetch.

lectures.text:
We're not restricted to get and post requests, there are more HTTP methods and it just depends on the API you're working, which kind of requests you can send and here this JSONPlaceholder dummy API also supports deleting a resource, again it's just a fake as it says here but we can send a delete request to this URL and now please note that this new URL is a little bit different, here it includes the ID of a concrete post to fake that we delete that post.

Now if we have a look at our list, we do have a delete button on every post, now we just have to make sure that the ID which is part of every response is kind of mapped to its element so that we can then find out on which element we clicked the delete button to send the right delete request. For that in the place where we output all posts, here, when we render the post elements, I actually also want to add an ID property here. For that, I want to go to my post element there and then use query selector li to select the li element itself and set the ID on that to post.id, so that we have that ID assigned to every list item element. If I now reload this page and click fetch posts here and we go to the elements tab, you'll see every list item has its ID as an attribute added.

Now we can use that to then make that delete button work, for that we should add a listener to the delete button and now we could add a listener to each delete button or we use event delegation, which we learned about in the events module, to only use one listener on the list and then find out which list item or which button in which list item was clicked. For that we need access to the overall list here, post list with document query selector unordered list because I only have one unordered list on this page and here on post list, we can add an event listener for a click and then accept the event object and do something.

Now of course, I don't want to delete anything just because a click happened anywhere on that list, instead we now need to find out which item was clicked and if it was the button that was clicked there and not just anything else in the item. To check that, we can reach out to event.target, we can then have a look at the tag name property. Now if that is button, all uppercase, then I know I clicked on a button. Now let's first of all check if that works by logging clicked on button, like this and if I now save that, reload, fetch the post, if I click anywhere nothing happens, if I click on delete, we see clicked on button.

Now we need to find out to which list item this belongs and for that we get the post.id by using event.target.closest to get the closest list item, we know we clicked on a button, now I'm interested in the closest list item and then on this list item, we have the ID. So now this should give us the ID of the post we clicked on or on which posts delete button we clicked on. So if we save that and reload, if I fetch posts and I click on delete, here I print one, here I print three, here I print five, so that seems to work.

Now we can work on the actual delete request. For that, let's again send a HTTP request here, this time of type delete and for the URL, I'll now use back ticks because I want to inject something into the URL so to say. The general URL is the same as before, so we can copy that but then we need to add a new segment to the path, so a new slash and then dynamically injected the post.id so that we add this at the end of the path because that's what the API wants. The API wants that the ID is part of the URL, the ID of the post which should be fake deleted. Well and with that, we should be good, now a delete request should be sent when we click on delete.

So if I click delete here and we check the network tab, we see here this request was sent, it's a delete request to this URL and that's all right. The API doesn't seem to reply back with anything, it doesn't say so on the guide here either and therefore, that's it. Now of course you could delete the element from the UI, that's something you absolutely can implement, it's not related to HttpRequests though and therefore I'll save the time here, not update the UI and instead move onto other nice things you can do with HttpRequests.

lectures.title: Handling Errors
lectures.text:
Thus far we always assumed that everything works but in reality, of course you'll also have HttpRequests that fail and handling such errors is always important. Now HttpRequests can fail for many reasons, because the internet connection is bad, because the server is down, because you send invalid data, there are many ways HttpRequests can fail. Now to be informed about a failing request, we have to add another listener to our XMLHttpRequest object and that's the onError listener or handler. This will trigger whenever we have an error when we send a HttpRequest.

Now let's see what we get here and for that, let's console log xhr.response in the error case and let's also console log something else and that's the xhr.status, this gives us the status code we got back. Now to simulate an error, we can for example go to our get request and send this to an invalid URL by basically cutting off the ts of the path and therefore we have a path which is not supported by the server. If we do so and we now reload, let's open the console here and now click fetch posts and you see, here I'm getting an error, this is getting logged from line 25 of my script, so from the send request in the end, not from line 21 or something like that and here we also got another error from line 37, that's just indicating that we failed to loop through all the posts.

If we have a look at the network tab, we also see there we got a 404 response back, what we don't see is our error handler doing its job here though and that's indeed important to understand. The error handler here does not kick in for HttpRequests that are technically successful where we just have a server side error, so where we just get back a non-200 status code. This error function instead will kick in if you for example have a network error, so if the request fails to be sent or does time out or anything like that.

If you have a request that leaves your page successfully and you get back a response, even if that response indicates that something is wrong on the server side, for example that the path wasn't found there, then you're not making it into onError but instead to onLoad because technically, you have a correct request and response. So what you should do is you should check if xhr.status, if that is let's say greater or equal than 200 and at the same time smaller than 300 which indicates a success case, in this case I want to resolve, else in the other cases, I know something went wrong and then we can reject this and for example reject with a new error object here where we say something went wrong, like that.

Here in the onError handler, I of course also want to do that, I want to reject with a new error, failed to send request but this will simply happen at a different time, this will happen if we technically fail to send a request. Now we have proper handling for server side errors as well, by checking the status code here in onLoad and therefore now if we try this again and we click fetch posts, now you see something went wrong which is my own custom error message and now we can of course use the normal ways of handling this on promises, with catch blocks or when using async await, with the help of try catch to make sure we don't continue if we have a problematic promise here.

So here, we could then wrap this all into try and catch and error here and then maybe show the error message to the user and now with that, we would properly handle that error, if I click fetch posts, now we just get that error message here instead of that broken script. The key takeaway here really is that you don't make it into onError because the server reports back a non-success status code but that you instead stay in onLoad if that happens and you only make it into onError if the request fails for different reasons, if you have no Internet connection for example, then this would trigger, otherwise you reach onLoad and therefore in onLoad, you should also handle non-success status codes as we're doing it here.

lectures.title: Using the fetch() API
lectures.text:
So we got started with HttpRequests, with this XMLHttpRequest object. By the way you might be wondering where the name is coming from, in the parsed, actually quite some time ago, this was basically introduced so we could fetch XML data behind the scenes. Nowadays of course it's more common to use JSON data, the name however still is the same. Now there is more you can do with it, more you can configure and you can dive deeper into XMLHttpRequest as you can actually dive deeper into almost all things you can do work with in Javascript. Attached you therefore find some resources that do allow you to dive deeper in case you're interested, now however I want to have a look at a more modern alternative which was added to browsers a few years ago and which actually is not supported in all browsers, especially older browsers, Internet Explorer don't support that new API which you can use and that new API I'm talking about is the fetch API.

Now to use it, let me comment out all of that here inside of my promise construction function so to say, let's keep the promise itself however, so all the XMLHttpRequests logic in there is commented out and let's instead use the new API which we have for sending HttpRequests. It was invented to be more modern, to be less clunky with these strange event handlers there which is really not modern Javascript at all, that's why this new API was introduced and that new API is commonly called the fetch API.

Now it is called such because it all works around one key function, the fetch function and this is built into browsers, it's exposed in Javascript just like that, you don't have to call it as a method on any object or anything like that, it's a globally available function in modern Javascript, as I said not in old browsers though, more on browser support in the browser support module of this course. So how do you use fetch? In its simplest form, fetch just takes a URL, so we can pass URL which should be a string to fetch, then it will send a get request.

So if you just pass a URL to fetch, it will send a get request to that URL. Now fetch by default is promise based, so that's the first native promise API we see in this course. We don't have to promisify ourselves, it uses promises on its own. That means we can actually remove our promise wrapper here, we don't need to build our own promise, instead we can just return the result of fetch which as I just said is a promise. So we can fetch URL and then return the result which is a promise that helps us work with the response.

Now let's see how that works before we then fine tune it for the different kinds of requests and let's get started with fetching posts where I call send HttpRequest and therefore, we try to send a request to this URL which we should now fix by the way with the help of the fetch API. Now if we try that and we reload and I click fetch posts, you'll see that I actually get an error, I get this alert here. Now this can be a bit deceiving, to see the actual problem, let's temporarily remove try catch here in fetch posts so that we don't try this block and catch any errors, like that and let's try again.

Let's reload and click fetch posts and now we see, I get this strange error, list of posts is not ignorable. OK, so what's going on here? What's failing? Somehow we don't have list of posts, so somehow we don't get the response data when we called sendHttpRequest. Now in send HttpRequest however, in this function, I do return the result of fetch, sending a request to that URL. Well let's check the network tab, there we see posts were indeed fetched, so that seems to work, so what's wrong then? What's happening?

Well the problem is or one difference is unlike our XMLHttpRequest approach here, fetch does not give us the parsed response as we had it available here with xhr.response but instead, it gives us a streamed response, which means basically that the response object we get here does not hold the body, the response body in a way that would be ready to be used, instead what you would have to do and we can do that here inside of the sendHttpRequest function, instead here, you get your response object and there you have access to a response JSON method and you can return the result of this because that actually yields a new promise as you see. Now JSON, when you call it on the response object which the fetch API gives you will parse the body of the response and transform it from JSON to Javascript objects and arrays but it actually does not just parse that, so it's not just a replacement for JSON.parse, it also turns the streamed response body which you have in the response object into a snapshot so to say with which you can work.

So long story short, you need to call response.JSON to convert your response body, the streamed unparsed response body into a snapshot parsed body. So now with that, the overall sendHttpRequest method will yield a promise which will eventually return that parsed response data, response JSON is important for that. Besides response JSON, you also have response text for example to return plain text, so that will then just do the conversion from streamed to snapshot or response blob if you would be downloading a file, that would give you access to the file.

Here however, we got JSON data so we need to return that. So now with that, if we save that and we reload and I click fetch posts, now we render the posts again, so now the other logic works as before and just as before, we get the parsed data, the parsed response but here important we need that extra step because it's not just JSON's data but also streamed data which we need to turn into a snapshot so to say and all of that is done by that JSON method on the response object.

Okay, so we get that, we can get our posts, now let's make sure we can also create a new post.

lectures.title: POSTing Data with the fetch() API
lectures.text:
In order to be able to create a post, we need to make sure that this function can succeed and for that, we need to make sure that we use the HTTP method in the fetch API and also the data, the body that should be appended to the outgoing request. Right now, we always just send a fetch request to a URL and therefore we always send a get request. Now just as with XMLHttpRequest, we can configure the outgoing request, however unlike XMLHttpRequest, you don't pass the request method here directly as an argument to the fetch function here, instead you can pass a second parameter here, a second argument which should be an object where you can configure the request and there you've got a couple of keys you can set as you see, a lot of them are pretty niche and rarely need it but method is one of the more important ones.

Method should be set to a string and by default, it's set to get so you'll never need to set this but you can but you always need to set it to post, put, patch, delete and so on if you plan on sending such a request. So here I'll set it to method pointing at the parameter I'm getting here in send HttpRequest and forwarding my parameter value as a value to this key-value pair here. So that will set the method, now you can also set the body and that has to be set to JSON data.

So not just data like this, data would be my third argument here but instead, to data converted to JSON which we can do with JSON.stringify around data. If we now do that and we reload and try to enter a new post, does this work? Let's see if it works if I now click add. So if I clicked add, we go to the network tab, we see this is the post request we just send, status code 201 and indeed here, that's the body we appended. So here we can see, yes this worked, this request successfully was sent now with help of the fetch API.

Now let's also check if deleting works, if I fetch posts and I click delete, let's say on the second post, then a request is sent here to the post with id 2, the delete request has a 200 code so that seems to work. Now before we have a look at how we handle errors here, let's have a look at how we can add headers to HttpRequests, not just with the fetch API but also with XMLHttpRequest.

lectures.title: Adding Request Headers
lectures.text:
Headers can be important. Now thus far we haven't really needed them but for some APIs, you need to describe which type of data you sending for example or other APIs might need some extra authentication data and headers are basically metadata you can attach to outgoing requests. If you inspect requests, you see there are some default headers added by the browser and the response also has headers set by the server. Now we can add more headers to the outgoing request and we do that here on fetch by adding a new key to that configuration object which is the headers key.

This takes a Javascript object where every header which you want to add is a key-value pair. Now the types of headers you can add are generally standardised, there are some default headers which are typically used but you can also add any arbitrary header you're coming up with, so you're really flexible there. Of course a header makes only sense to be added if the server expects it and does something with it, otherwise you can add it but it won't have much effect.

Now a header which is often added, even though it's technically not required here for this API is the content-type header, typically written like this. lectures.title: fetch() & Error Handling
lectures.text:
So we see that the fetch API thus far is pretty easy to use and it uses promises by default and actually it only works with promises, so it looks a lot better than XMLHttpRequest. Now one downside of it, of the fetch API could be that it doesn't support older browsers but as you will learn in the browser support module, you might be able to work around that. A bigger problem or a bigger annoyance at least can be seen when we have a look at error handling, so let's see what happens there.

Again I'll break my get URL here by simply changing this to a URL which does not exist on the server we're sending the request to and let's see what happens in that case. If I reload, click fetch posts, well at some point we get an error that we can't use the response data. So of course we work with promises there, so since this returns a promise, we could use try catch to wrap this all into our try catch block and do our error handling or if we didn't use aync await, we could use the catch method in our promise chain.

Now the problem with that just is just like with the XMLHttpRequest, that a request that technically succeeded, so where we don't have a technical issue but maybe just a 400 or 500 status code sent back by the server will not trigger a traditional error. So if I would to try to add some first error handling here in my sendHttpRequest function, then I could add a catch method here in my promise chain which I return and keep in mind that this promise chain itself also returns a promise, that's how promises work. So here I could then catch any error we might be getting and we could handle it here, store it in some internal log and then maybe just throw a new error object where I say something went wrong or maybe we also provide more information than that.

The problem is, we'll never make it into this catch block for the error we currently have, if I fetch posts again, you see this is coming from a different place, we got no log coming from line 44, we got the line 56 here. So we don't make it into the catch block and the reason is the same as with XMLHttpRequest, only technical issues like network connectivity issues would lead us to go into that catch block, instead we're here in the then block.

Good thing is just as with XMLHttpRequest, we can check the response status and find out if we have an error here. So if response status is greater or equal than 200 and response status is smaller than 300, then we have a success case and then I want to return response JSON, else I know we have an error, so else I can throw a new error here, something went wrong server side, anything like that. So if I save that and I now reload, if I fetch my posts, now we get that correct output but still we have a problem here.

What if we want to look into the body of our response because often for server side errors, the server might attach extra information to the response body. So it's not just about the status code, even in the error case, we get back a valid response with a response body and we might want to parse that response body to get the data that the server might have added. Now in the XMLHttpRequest world, that would have been easy, here in this else case if we got an error, we could still access xhr.response, that would be possible here in the XMLHttpRequest world.

Unfortunately that's not the case in the fetch API world. Remember, the body is streamed, so at this point of time we have no direct access to the body, we first of all need to call response.json in the error case as well. So we always need to call that in order to get our data. Now of course, you could think then I just add an extra step here, return response.json here no matter if it's an error or not and then I check my response status code in the next then block where I have access to the body data.

The problem just is here we get the data but we don't have access to the response object anymore, we only have access to that here. So the place where we need the status code is a different place than where we get access to the body and that's the problem we face here. Essentially we need to write some wrapping code here to make all of that work. We can say if we have an error, then I want to parse my body with JSON, that yields a new promise and now we have a promise chain in a promise chain which is never such a great idea but then here I have access to my error data and now here, I could throw my error and maybe utilize this extra error data we might be getting by the server. So let's now give that a try if I reload and click fetch posts again and now you'll see a different problem, now we throw the error basically in that nested promise chain, so the outer promise chain doesn't have an error and hence we again think everything is fine and we try to list our posts and that of course breaks.

So throwing the error here in the nested promise chain is also not an option, we need to throw it outside of there but there, we don't have access to the error data so how can we solve that. Well we can move that back in there and simply return that inner promise chain so that it is basically merged into the outer promise chain or now connected to the outer promise chain and now with that, if I reload and I click fetch posts, now we have the proper error propagation and we have access to the error data. So it's possible we can solve this but of course that's not the most beautiful error handling code you ever saw.

It is what it is however with the fetch API and this is how you can use the fetch API and implement proper error handling, with access to the response body at the same time. Now with that if I go down here and I re-add try catch here, let's see if that all works, if we add this block again, reload, click fetch posts, now I get something went wrong here as an error alert and we don't try to use the invalid data. If I on the other hand fix this link again and then I reload, then fetching works again.

So that's the fetch API and how we can handle errors there.

lectures.title: XMLHttpRequest vs fetch()
lectures.text:
So now we had a look at XMLHttpRequest and the fetch API, both allow us to send requests, the fetch APIs more modern and not supported in older browsers. A big plus is that it's generally easy to use and uses promises out of the box, a minus is that error handling can be clunky. Of course not the end of the world but not the most beautiful approach. Now arguably, that's also not that beautiful but if you hide it behind some custom function, it might be fine and might be a bit more straightforward to understand, in the end however you can also hide this behind a custom function and you're probably fine again.

It's up to you which approach you use, both are fine to be used and actually another alternative which you have is that you use a third-party library, something we haven't really touched on yet which might wrap this, so the XMLHttpRequest or this fetch API approach and gives you a nicer API to work with, where you don't have to care about how it's implemented internally and that's actually something we'll have a look at in the third-party libraries module which comes right after this one.

But it's important to understand how to implement this natively and often, the fetch API is great because it's easy to use, quick to get started and uses promises out of the box but also be aware that XMLHttpRequest has better support for older browsers out of the box and in some places, regarding error handling specifically, might be more straightforward.

lectures.title: Working with FormData
lectures.text:
Now besides different ways of sending HttpRequests, we also can send different data, in theory at least, it always depends on the server and the URL you're sending this to, which kind of data the server accepts, for example our dummy server here really only works with JSON data. When we for example send the data to fake create a post, then we have to add JSON data there, it does not accept any other data but of course you might be working with different APIs in your project and there, different data might be accepted as well.

Now you can send files, you can send binary data and add this as a body here, so you could add a pointer at a file which a user picked in a file picker for example or another very popular data format, you could add FormData Now let's see what FormData is and for that let's go to create post, here I create my post object, add this to send HttpRequest and in there, we basically convert this to JSON and add it to the request. Now we can also add FormData instead.

Now again, this API does not support it but other APIs might and hence I want to show to you how that would work. For that, here in create post, let's say we can create FormData by creating a new constant, fd for FormData, name is up to you, by calling new FormData. That's a constructor function built into Javascript or built into the browser, provided in Javascript. Now FormData builds a new object to which you can add key-value pairs, so a bit like a Javascript object like this but internally or when it's sent over the wire, it will be sent in a different way than JSON data, it's not JSON format, it has a different format as you will see. Now to FormData, you can append new entries with the append method and there, every entry has a key and a value, so for example we could add a title and then pass on the title we're getting here as a value for this key, same is true for the body, here we could pass in our content value and also our userId, append userId, userId, now we would have prepared such a FormData object.

Now let's add fd here, FormData to this request, so let's pass in this as a third argument and inside of sendHttpRequest, we now have to change the request a little bit, I'll comment out the headers because I no longer want to tell the server that I'm sending JSON data because I'm not and instead, set body not equal to the stringified data version but just to data which should already be FormData and for FormData, the fetch API will automatically see that it's form data and automatically send the right headers.

So if we set this and we reload, let's try it out. Let's create a new post with FormData and click add. Now if we inspect the network tab, we see the API is quite forgiving, it still reports a success because it really doesn't care about the data we send in the end because it's a fake API but if we scroll down in the headers, we see we add a different data, it's indeed FormData and that's a special type of data which is added to the outgoing request. If we have a look at the other headers, we see that there content type was automatically set to this value which was automatically derived by the browser in the end.

Now the advantage of FormData is that for one, you might find it more structured to build your data like this, b) a second great thing about it is that you can easily add files, if you append some file, you can have any identifier you want here, you could point at a file here, for example picked in a file input and then as a third argument, even provide a file name like photo.png which the server can use. So you can easily send a mixture of text, content text, key-value pairs and files to the server which can be really convenient depending on what you build and a third advantage is you can also use this to automatically parse a form and that's actually what I also want to show you here.

Let's say we don't manually add title and body but instead we want to utilize the form fields which we already have here. Essentially what we want to do here is we want to replicate the default behavior the browser would have if we wouldn't call prevent default upon a submission. When we call that, we make sure the browser doesn't collect the FormData and send it to a server. Now we still want to make sure that the browser doesn't collect and send but we then manually want to collect it in the same way the browser would and for that, you just have to pass a pointer to your form element, to FormData, so to the constructor and form here really is just this pointer I select up there, it points at the form element in the document and if we pass that to FormData, Javascript will try to automatically collect all the data from the form.

Now for it to succeed though, you need to make sure that your inputs have a name attribute, title and here, may be content or actually body because the API wants a field named body. The name attribute is important otherwise FormData is not able to identify these inputs and get the data out of there and store it correctly in the FormData. Now you can then still append extra data which might not be included in the form, like the userId here and with all of that, let's give it a try.

Let's reload a new post, does this work and let's click add here and if we now inspect this outgoing request and we scroll down, we see this was still populated but now automatically from the form. Now again, it's important to realize that not all APIs support FormData, if an API wants JSON data, you can't use this no matter how convenient you find it to be but if you have an API, an API endpoint, so a specific URL HTTP method combination that does support FormData you can use this approach and therefore form data besides JSON is also an important data structure you should be aware of when we're talking about sending data with HttpRequests from client side Javascript to a server.

lectures.title: Example: jQuery
lectures.text:
Now Lodash is just one library, a very popular one but absolutely not the only one, there are thousands of available Javascript utility libraries, for Javascript in the browser but also for Javascript on Node.js and as I said this concept exists not just for Javascript but for all programming languages you could say. In addition, the complexity of the library differs, it can be something like Lodash which offers a bunch of utility functions, it can be something else which allows you to write Javascript in a brand new way.

There also are Javascript frameworks which are basically very large libraries, like Vue.js React or Angular, due to their complexity we'll have a look at those in a separate module though but we'll also cover this, these would be very big libraries. Typically when you say library, you mean something a bit smaller which focuses on one core task, in the case of Lodash it focuses on giving you a bunch of utility features and it is really good at that typically.

Another popular Javascript library for example would be JQuery. It was very popular around 2010, 11, 12 and it still is heavily used but it was more important in the past because JQuery actually made working with the DOM, adding elements, querying elements way easier. Now since then, since the early days of JQuery, Javascript has come a long way and nowadays it's really easy to work with the DOM, traverse the DOM, work with CSS classes there and so on with native DOM APIs which is why you don't really need JQuery as often these days but you still might encounter it in a lot of tutorials and threads on the Internet you find and therefore you should be aware of it.

It's a Javascript library which you add to your project basically as you added Lodash by downloading it or by using a CDN, as you see down there and then JQuery is not about giving you utility functions like getting the difference of two arrays but it gives you a lot of functions that help you work with the DOM and that can also be interesting but again as I said, basically all of that can nowadays also be done with the core Javascript APIs you learned about in this course.

So you might not need that but you should be aware of it.

lectures.title: Third-Party Library Considerations
lectures.text:
So libraries can be really useful, axios was really useful, Lodash also is really useful here. Now still there are a couple of things you should keep in mind when working with libraries, for one keep in mind that for example Lodash here, if you add it like this, includes a lot of functionality which you never use. We only use the difference method here and yet we still import all the other features as well, that means that users of our application will download all that code even if we just use one feature.

We can see the effect if we reload our page, you see the Lodash package here has 24kb. Now obviously that's not that big but it's way bigger than the rest of our application, so that can be a downside, you're downloading way more than you might need and that could slow down the initial loading time of your application which matters a lot if your application primarily targets people in areas of the world with poor internet connection. So that's one thing to keep in mind, you might include a lot of overhead.

That being said however, it is worth pointing out that many libraries allow you to import them in different ways, for example Lodash gives you a core build which only comes with some of the features, which is way smaller or in more advanced project setups which we'll also cover later in the course, you even have other capabilities of basically just importing parts of a library and then stripping out the parts which you don't need. This project setup is not capable of doing that but we'll have a look at our project setups later in the tooling section. So you can mitigate this problem but still, it is something to keep in mind, also because not all libraries allow you to be as selective as I just described.

In addition to that, you also want to make sure you are working with libraries which are secure and well maintained, let's use axios here. It's open source which means everyone can view the source and everyone can collaborate. Now typically when you want to work on the code and share your edited code, of course it's validated before it's merged into this codebase, so you can't easily hack this library, instead open source typically actually improves code quality and security because more people are looking over it and working on it.

So having open source is generally good but you want to make sure that the library you're using is also actively maintained, so that if there are bugs, bugs that break your application or security issues which of course also are very important, that they are fixed in time. Now an indicator for that for example is to view the last commit, this basically means when the code was edited the last time. If this is two years old, then it looks like it's not actively maintained anymore, two days, a week, a month, that is pretty active.

You can also check the releases page on Github to find out how often new versions are released and if that is fairly regular, let's say once a year, twice a year, then this also seems to be actively maintained, for example axios here had its last release on June 1st at the point of time I'm recording this, which is not too far in the past. You can also check out the issues here and it's quite normal that every package which is popular has a lot of issues to get an overview if there are any big problems, though the sheer number here shouldn't be an indicator, as I said the more popular packages, the more issues it will have, not all issues here have to be real issues let alone big issues.

So these are some of the things you want to watch out for. You can also judge the popularity of a package by looking at the Github stars, axios has a lot of them. if you also have a look at some other packages, some other projects in Github, you will see that they typically have way less stars than that. So these are some of the things you want to consider when choosing a package, why are these things important? Because for one you of course don't want to add a package which might open up a security hole, that's very important that you don't do that and in addition even if it's not insecure, if it has bugs which are not getting fixed because it's not maintained anymore, then your application might break and all of a sudden, the package you're depending on is not getting updated anymore, so your application is broken and now you have to find an alternative or write the logic which you previously used from the package on your own to make your application work again.

So these are some considerations you should keep in mind and with all of that in mind though, there is nothing that speaks against using third-party libraries, they can really make your life easier and in modern development, it's normal to use typically a couple of external libraries in every project you're working on.

lectures.text:
If you have programming experience with some other programming languages, then you might notice approach of specifying import statements or references to other files directly in a file. So you could say my tooltip here actually extends the component, so this tooltip.js file definitely needs access to the component.js file, this is a dependency we have. Now we fix or we implement this dependency currently by ensuring the order, for example if I would switch tooltip and component, this would break because tooltip would try to use component before component is defined.

So we have a dependency here, project item for example uses the tooltip class, though only at runtime when this code executes, so we might be able to mess up the order here and still get away with it, nonetheless here, we also have a dependency. So it would be nice if we could say, at the top of the tooltip.js file for example, this file depends on component and then we could remove this component import here and tooltip would automatically import component when it needs it, so when tooltip.js runs basically and that can be done with Javascript modules. So to show that, let me comment out this component import and therefore of course the tooltip.js file breaks as you learned.

So now let's see how Javascript modules help us with that. We can go to the component and there, we can add a special keyword that makes it clear that we're exporting this so that this class should be available outside of this file because by default and that's an important rule, as soon as we switch to modules which we haven't done yet but as soon as we do so, we will have locked files. Currently where we import everything with normal import statements here, when I assign a class like this, when I declare it here, it gets added to the global object.

So it's globally available and every other file can use it, as soon as we switch to modules, this will change and then every file will be locked down, its content will not be added to this global object, it will not be globally available, every file will get its own scope instead. So how do we switch to modules then and which keyword do we have to add here? The keyword is the export keyword. This is a keyword built into Javascript which signals to Javascript that inside of a module, I want to make this class here available to other files as well. As I just said, normally that's not the case, with export we can make it available.

Now we need to switch to modules and for this, we go to our script here, to our root script which we always will need to import here because there is at least one script which we have to import into HTML file because whilst scripts will be able to point at each other, we need one starting point and to that starting point script, to the script tag we add type and set this to module, so type module needs to be added here. This is understood by the browser and tells the browser that now this script and all scripts referenced by this script, currently there are none, soon there will be more, will use modules. So now if save this, this alone won't do much, if I now reload, we got even more errors and this is actually an important error which we'll need to fix.

lectures.title: We Need a Development Server!
lectures.text:
Where is this error coming from? What does this error even mean? Modules are a relatively new feature and as you might imagine, since scripts can point at other scripts that should be imported, we have to be strict regarding security, we need to make sure that a script can't import a script from another page which might be malicious. You might think why would I add such code to my own scripts. Well if you're using third-party libraries, then such a library might be compromised and might try to download files from other malicious files, this is why we have a cross origin request policy which basically means cross origin, so cross domain requests are not allowed, you're only allowed to download scripts from the same domain your page is running on.

Now the problem we're facing here is that we're serving this app with the file protocol. Remember, what we always did thus far is we double clicked index.html in the Windows Explorer or in the MAC finder and this opens it up in the browser but actually does not open it up as it would be opened if it is served by a web server, it just opens it with this file protocol, which simply just means it displays the content of the file and is able to execute Javascript conveniently. Thus far, this wasn't a problem because a lot of features worked just fine with the file protocol but web server dependent features, like using this cross origin policy don't work there, this policy requires the page to be served from a real web server in order to be validated and therefore we now need to serve our app here, our page through a web server and not through the file protocol.

Now that sounds difficult, it sounds like we need to setup our own server, host it somewhere, maybe pay for it, the good thing is you don't. if you google for servejs, you should find this serve package here on npmjs.com, we had a look at npmjs.com in the third-party library module and here, you get a basic web server which you can install on your system and run on your system, you don't need to deploy your page anywhere, don't need to rent any servers, it spins up a little server on your machine, works on Windows and macOS and this server will serve your application. Now to install it, we need to install Node.js though, we haven't used Node.js in this course, I will have a Node.js section later in the course but we also don't need to write any Node.js code right now. We just need to install the Node.js runtime on our machine because this serve package requires Node.js because that little server which it spins up is written in Node.js.

In addition, Node.js will also give us a tool which we can use to install this tool here, this serve tool on our machine, so we get two benefits at the same time. So visit nodejs.org and download the latest version of Node.js, at the point of time I'm recording this, it's 12 but it doesn't really matter, simply pick the latest one. It should automatically preselect your operating system, it is available for all operating systems, if it doesn't, simply go to other downloads and manually pick your system there.

So once you downloaded it and walked through the installer, it's a normal installer, nothing fancy about that, you can run a special command to install this serve tool, not this command but a slightly different one. For that, open up your terminal or command prompt which you have on your system, the path where you navigate to does not matter and run npm install -g which stands for global serve. On Linux and Mac, you might need to add as sudo in front of this to get the right permissions, on Windows this is not required.

Hit enter thereafter and you might be prompted for a password, if you are simply, enter it and now what this will do is it will install this serve tool globally, Node.js ships with its own package management system which we'll have a close look at in the tooling module and this manages packages on a per project basis but also on a global basis and here we installed a global package which is now available on our entire machine. So with that installed, back in our project you can open up a terminal which is navigated into this project, so you can either navigate into your project with the cd command here or in Visual Studio Code, if you go to view, you can also click on terminal here and this opens up a terminal, your default system terminal or command prompt but built into Visual Studio Code and already navigated into your project folder which is very convenient of course and now here with serve installed, you can simply type serve and it will automatically search for the index.html file and serve that through this dummy web server.

So now this gives you the address you have to enter in the browser to view your project, in my case it's localhost:5000 and if I do enter this here, I load the same page as before and we get some errors because we haven't fixed all errors but we're not getting this course error anymore because now, we can use modules and this course setting which they managed for us behind the scenes. You can ignore that favicon error here, we don't have a favicon hence we can't load it, we now just need to fix our modules and make sure we utilize this exported component.

Important note, you should keep this serve process running, you can always quit it with control C or control D but if you quit it, you can't visit your page here anymore, so you will always need to restart it with the serve command whenever you want to continue working on the project. You can only visit this page here on this localhost:5000 address as long as this process is running.

lectures.title: First import / export Work
lectures.text:
So now let's fix this or let's work on that. We have our server, we change this app.js file to be of type module, so now let's make sure we use this exported component and we use it by importing it somewhere. Exporting it is one part but that still does not make it globally available, it just means that we can now import the exported thing and you can not just export classes by the way, you can also export functions, variables, constants and so on so that you can use the exported thing in another file, here the tooltip.js file is that other file and to import something exported, we indeed use the import command.

So we start with import and we also need to tell Javascript from where, so we add the from keyword and then as a string, semicolon thereafter, a path, a relative path to that file. A relative path starts with a dot and then dot slash means you want to look in the same folder, dot dot means you want to go up one folder which we could use to then navigate into utility or just a slash could also be used to have an absolute path from your root on but that's a bit more typical to resolve in our heads at least, so therefore you typically work with relative paths and here I want to import from component.

Now you see I still got an error here, the problem is I am exporting something in component, in that component.js file but you can export more than one thing in your files, here I have only one thing but that's not a technical limitation. So we have to tell Javascript what we want to import from that file and for that, we go to that place where we import it from and here, you add curly braces, now the error is gone at least. Now between the curly braces, you write the name, the exact name of what you want to import and typically you should get autocompletion here, if you hit control space, it should suggest you this component in my case, this component class. So if I hit enter, this is added here, of course you could have also just written this manually and now we're importing component into this file.

Now this is good but what's not so good is that our application will still not work if I reload. The reason for that is that we still load the tooltip file with such a traditional import. We need to add type module there, to make sure that it can utilize module features which is the export keyword but also the import keyword. If we do so and we reload, this error is gone but we get an error that component is not found. The reason for that is that in this path here, you need to add the extension at all times and regarding the extension, some people like to name the files which are only imported mjs at the end, this is totally optional though, you can go with .js, .mjs, the M would stand for module but technically here, it makes no difference so I'll stick to js. The extension is important to be specified though, whatever it is.

So now if I reload, this works and our application works again but now we're using modules to express this relation between tooltip and component and this improves our application because now, it's also super easy to see which dependencies we have in this file and in addition to that, we also don't have to worry about correctly ordering the imports here because the import is right in our Javascript file.

lectures.text:

So I'll comment out all these imports here, also the DOM helper and I'll only leave the app.js import here as our root entry point.

Now that of course breaks everything and now we therefore have to switch to modules entirely. So let's start our way from the bottom up, let's start in app.js because that's our entry file, this will be the file that is loaded first. What do we have in there? lectures.title: More Named Export Syntax Variations
lectures.text:
Now regarding modules, there are a couple of alternative syntaxes and I want to show you which syntaxes exist. Let's say we have more than one thing which we want to export, here in the DOM helper, I only have the DOM helper class, now let's say we would not have that class as a wrapper but we would export two individual functions. We could just copy these functions, remove static here and instead add the function keyword for example and we'd be good, these are two functions and we could have created them as function expressions with for example arrow functions stored in a constant as well.

Now these functions can also be exported by adding an export keyword, you can export everything; functions, classes, constants, variables, everything which you use in your code like this. So now we export these functions, both of them and still also the class and that's absolutely fine, you can export as much as you want. Now in project list where we need the DOM helper, down there I'm using move element. Now we also now export a move element function, this one here so I could also just use that.

So in project list, we could remove DOMhelper. and just access move element but of course this would fail because we're not importing it, we're referencing this function but it's not getting imported anywhere. Now you might say I am importing from DOM helper but imports don't work file wide, instead you really have to specify what you import and here, we're importing the DOM help helper class, not the move element function. So therefore if we save this, our code would fail, as soon as I drag and drop, we get an error that move element is not defined.

So just importing from a file is not enough, you need to be specific what you import, you don't import the entire file content. So here the solution of course would be to switch DOM helper, which I'm not using in this file anymore, to move element and now I'm importing that function which I'm referencing further down below and with that import added, if we now reload, this works again. So this is important to know, that you have to be really specific regarding what you import and that you can export more than one thing.

You also therefore of course can import more than one thing, if we would still need the DOM helper class in here, we could simply separate it with a comma and then import it as well and now we're importing DOM helper and move element from the DOMhelper.js file, we're not importing the clear event listener function for example though, that's not happening. So we're very specific about what we need and we specify it in a comma separated list here in our import statement. Sometimes you do want to import everything that's in a file, let's say here in project list, for some reason we want to import this clear event listeners function as well. Obviously we can do it like this and there would be nothing wrong with that, for a lot of reasons you might want to do it like this but maybe you want to bundle all these things which are getting exported by this file in one object which you then have available in the projectlist.js file on which you can access these different exported features through the dot notation and that is possible with a special syntax. If you have named exports like we do have it here, so where you have multiple export statements in front of something, then you can go to the file where you import

that and remove this curly brace list here and instead add a star and then you also add as and then any name of your choice, like domh or DOMhelper or Domhelp or whatever you want, any name of your choice here, doesn't have to be the file name and what this tells Javascript is that you want to bundle together all the exports of that file into this object and now in this file, in the projectlist.js file in this case here, you can and you have to access this bundled object with the dot notation to then access the DOM helper class for example or the two functions.

So now this looks like you're using an object with a move element method, instead we just bundled all exports of the DOM helper file together into one helper object which exists in the projectlist.js file so to say. So this is an alternative which you can use if you prefer that for whatever reason, this is how you can bundle multiple exports together and then access them through this helper object in the importing file. This as notation can also be used in general to assign new names. Let's say, still here in project list, for some reason I'm not happy with project item here. In projectitem.js, I named it project item but I don't want to use that name in project list, maybe because I would have a name clash, maybe we have some other element, some other constant or class named project item in this file which we don't want to rename for whatever reason, so this would result in a clash for example. Whenever you have something like this, you can also assign an alias to this imported thing. You can use the as keyword here inside of that curly brace list and assign a new name to that exported and here, imported element which will only be relevant in this file here.

So here, we could name this to projitem for example and now inside of this project list file here, we have to use this imported project item under this alias. So now in all the places where I create a new project item, where this is the only place, I have to use projitem instead, my alias. Now of course, this does not change the name in the original file, it really just is an alias in this file. So with that if I save that and I reload, we should still have the same behavior as before because we haven't changed anything about that logic here, it's really just an alias which we assigned here.

lectures.title: Working With Default Exports
lectures.text:
Now one last important feature regarding the export import syntax we saw here, if you have one core element which is exported in a file or maybe the only element which is exported, like here component is the only exported thing in component.js, then you can absolutely export it like this but you can also name it the default export of this file by adding default here, this keyword. You can then even omit the name here because you'll now not import it by name but by just pointing at that file and then automatically the default export will be picked and I'll show you how that pointing works in a second.

Now you can still have named exports along that, so here if I had the doSomething function here, so export function doSomething which actually does nothing here, then I could do that, we could import this by name and this as a default which now just leaves the question, how do we import something as a default? We'll, we're using component in tooltip after all and this import would now fail. If I save everything and I reload, we would get an error because as the error message says, component.js does not have an export named component because I removed that name and even if I would add it by the way and I reload, it would still fail because we export this as a default in which case Javascript will ignore the name.

So how do we now tell tooltip that we're interested in the default export of components.js? Very simple, you just use a syntax you already saw before, you just say import anything, any name of your choice like cmp for of course also component but doesn't have to be the exported name or the file name, can be any name from file and then here we could use cmp instead of component. This tells Javascript that since you don't wrap this in curly braces, this should be the default export of that file and of course therefore this syntax only works if a file has a default export, otherwise it will fail.

So now with this line, we import the default export of this file, which in this case is this class, under that name which is totally up to you. You can use this feature, it has the tiny disadvantage that since you have to rename it when you import it, if you're working in a team, every team member might have his or her own naming convention and you might end up with code which uses different naming conventions and therefore, using named exports where you're all forced to settle on some name might be better.

Nonetheless it is a feature which you can use and if you now would want to import that named doSomething export, you would do that by simply combining this with a comma, with a curly brace list of named imports, so here I could import doSomething. So you can have a default and non-default, also called named export side-by-side and therefore of course you can also have them imported at the same time. This is the default export and here you list all named exports, so all the things where you just added export in front of them without the default keyword.

Also of course important, should be self-explanatory though, you can only have one default export per file, you can't have more than one.

lectures.title: Dynamic Imports & Code Splitting
lectures.text:
So that's the Javascript module import export syntax. Now if we have a look at our project, we can see something interesting if we go to the network tab. If I open that and we have a look at the HttpRequests here, if I reload this page, you see we got a bunch of requests here because we're using a bunch of files and they are getting imported when our app starts because what happens? Well the HTML file gets loaded and there, we request the app.css file and the app.js file. Therefore logically first, the HTML file is loaded, that's basically what's hidden under localhost here, then the CSS file, then the Javascript file. In the app.js file, we refer to project list, therefore it makes sense that the next item in the list here is project list which is getting imported and so on, so this is how all these things are getting imported. Now obviously we're sending a lot of HttpRequests here and for a small project like this, this is no problem, for a large project, this is not that great because even though the files are all small, sending a request, getting the response and parsing the response always has a bit of that's time which is always there, which you can't get rid of, network latency, the browser getting started, it's time which you can't get rid of.

So the more requests you send, the more of that time you accumulate and therefore having hundreds of modules would not be a great idea because you would import hundreds of files and you would send hundreds of HttpRequests. This is a problem we'll get rid of in the next course module and in the next course section when we have a look at tooling and in a concept called bundling. One other improvement which we could add here is also that some features are not always needed, for example the tooltip. The tooltip here, this Javascript file is loaded because we might eventually show a tooltip but unless we click this button, we don't really need the file and of course it's a small file but in bigger applications where you have more logic in your files, that can add up.

In addition, the tooltip file is the only file that needs the component, so actually we have to add the two together. So if you would only load these files when we need them, we would speed up the initial page load because we would request less files to be downloaded and parsed and that's also something we can do and something we can do in this module already. So to load modules conditionally, we can use an alternative import syntax. The import syntax you solve thus far at the beginning of the page is the static import syntax, it statically defines the dependency of a file. As an alternative to that, you have the dynamic import syntax and for some scenarios like the tooltip where you know that the code will not always be needed, it makes sense, if you know something always needs to run, like for example project list which is imported in app.js and which we need right at the start to construct our lists, there it makes no sense to load that dynamically because you'll always need it but for the tooltip, it can make sense. In project item, I need the tooltip here if we click on this show more info button. So therefore instead of importing tooltip up there statically, which means it will be

downloaded when the project item file executes, I can also just download it here and request it here. How? With a special syntax. We can call import as a function and then pass a string with a path to the file I want to import, in this case tooltip. Now this import function is built into the browser and exposed in Javascript and it gives you a promise, so you can add a then block here or use async await of course. Now here, you get your module in the end and now in there, we can run code that requires the module, so in this case this code which wants to attach our tooltip and create it and so on, so cut it and move it into this then block. Here we can now access module.tooltip, I know that we'll have a tooltip in this file so I can access it on module, it is simply a property of this module object so to say and now this will only reach out to this file, we should add the extension though, it will only reach out to this file here when this code here runs and not at an earlier point of time.

So now if we save that and we reload, you'll see we get no error but in the network tab, you see the tooltip and component.js files are not getting downloaded initially. If I click on more info though, then you will see these two requests are being added and are being sent but that happens at a later point of time, not when our app loads but only when we need the code. This can be a huge improvement, of course you don't really feel it for such small files but for larger files, not having to download them initially but only downloading them when you need them can really speed up your startup time which makes your app faster and more responsive when it first loads up.

lectures.title: Module Scope & globalThis
lectures.text:
Now before we quit, one additional word about scope. Now you learned that you can only use in other files what you export in the files you want to use the features from. So if you want to use that tooltip class, because we're using modules now, we can only use it in files that import tooltip, which is why we export it here, if you wouldn't export it, you also couldn't import it. Now the global object which we abused sometimes earlier in the course therefore doesn't exist like this anymore.

If we define something global here, in app.js let's say which is the first file that runs, default value Max, something like this, if we want to use that in another file, it's not that easy. If in project list I want to output this, well let's try, if I console log default value here, make sure I don't have a typo, let's copy this here, use it here, if we try that, you'll see that if we reload this, we get an error that default value is not defined, so it's not exposed on this global object anymore.

Now we do have access to window though, if I console log window here in project list and comment out default value and save that and reload, you see this window object is still output. Now that's quite important because what we saw earlier in the course is that window is kind of a global object where some of our variables end up on when we define them globally. We could also access window with this in the past by just logging this here outside of a function, however here in modules, this gives us undefined, so modules also run in strict mode out of the box.

So in strict mode, you learned this gives you undefined and not the window and that's the same here. Now why am I showing all of that? Because it's important to know that and because in the past when you define a global variable like this, it would invisibly automatically be added to the window object which acted as a global object that spans across your entire app so to say. This was Javascript's way of sharing data across files you could say, by having that global object which every file can automatically use.

Now this window object is available if we target it with window but not with this. So modules have their own scope, something defined in a module is not shared with others unless you export it and this does not point at window. Now what you can do is you can add something to the window object, like this as a property which is added dynamically and then use it. Now if we try to access window.defaultValue here however, it will not work because this code will actually be executed before this code runs because here I am importing project list, this is the point of time where the code in project list runs and therefore this code where I want to read from window runs before I set default value.

Now switching the order is not an option, this is not allowed, if we tried to do that, we still get undefined because imports are automatically sorted to the top, so this will not work. To still simulate that sharing data across window works, we can just move this into for example connect droppable which will be called at a later point of time because this executes when the constructor of project list runs which happens when we create a project list here in app.js which is the case after we store default value in the window.

So now if I reload, we see Max being output here, we see that twice because I'm creating two project lists. So the window object can be used to still share some data globally on your app, you need to explicitly add something to window but then this is an option, a hack around the otherwise scoped data so to say and hence, you should really just use it as a last resort if you really need to share some global data and for some reason, exporting and importing is not an option, otherwise don't do this.

Now besides window however, you also now have another identifier and that's global this. We haven't seen that before, as the name suggests, it's basically an alternative to this which points at some globally available object, the idea is also that this is available both in browser side Javascript and Node.js side Javascript, the window object is not available in both. Now global this can be used to store data and in project list of course then also to read data, so here I can also reach out to global this.

Now if we save that and reload, we get the same output as before, the more interesting part therefore is what's inside global this besides our custom value? So if I just output global this in project list and I reload, you see it's the window object again. So in the end, global this in modules replaces this as your pointer at the window object because this inside of modules is not defined, it's just what it is, they run in strict mode and there this does not point at window but we got global this as an alternative and an extra benefit is that global this will also work in Node.js.

So you can always use global this everywhere and you're guaranteed to not get undefined and point either at the window in the browser context or add another global object created by Node.js in the Node.js context. So it's a little bit of extra information, often that will not be too important because you should really use exports and imports to share data. The key takeaway is that data that's not exported and that's not shared like this with this hack is not available outside of this file because you've got a special module scope which ensures that anything that is defined on the top level of such a module file stays in that file.

lectures.title: Wrap Up
lectures.text:
And this is it for modules, an extremely important feature for serious Javascript projects. Having all your code in one file quickly makes it hard to maintain and read, having manual imports in the index.html file on the other hand means a lot of micromanagement and it can easily become an error source. With modules which you unlock by adding type module and by using a web server, even if it's just a dummy one for development, with modules you get rid of that because there every Javascript file states its dependencies and has its own import so to say. Now you can only import what you export with the export keyword, either with such a named export where you're just throw export in front of your class, function, constant or variable or with a default export, something you can also do and which we did in the component.js file for example.

You can have both named and default exports in the same file and when it comes to importing, you also got a lot of flexibility. You can import named exports without or with an alias, you can bundle all exports together or of course, you can also import default exports and named exports at the same time. Last but not least, we also had a look at the dynamic import which can help you split your code and download things only when you need them instead of in advance and that's it for modules.

Modules are a core feature and in the next course section, we'll build upon this knowledge and see how we can improve them even more.

Therefore in this module here, we'll have a look at Javascript tooling which essentially is all about managing our project with certain tools that automatically optimize our code, combine our code and get out of our way when we are writing our code so that we can write our code in the best possible way and still get an optimized and better output than we're currently doing it. With that development server, we have that. So this is already one example of an extra tool we can use to have a more realistic development environment and to fully use all the things we can use with Javascript, it's of course not the only tool though.
