lectures.title: Determining Required Support
lectures.text:
So now we know how we can check browser support, now with that, the naive thought might be that you simply check all these resources and then you need to find a way to make the feature you want to use work in all possible browsers across all browser versions and here, the clear answer is don't do this. For one, this will never be entirely possible, there are super older versions of Internet Explorer that don't support anything, you will never be able to make your application with all its features work there.

You would just cut so many features that just to support a small fraction of the user base, you pass on some awesome features and awesome improvements you could offer to the vast majority of the user base. So you definitely have a tradeoff there and you want to be careful regarding your decision. Don't build an application for the smallest possible denominator, instead analyze your market, get an idea of who your users will be and then build your application for those users and use the features or make the features you plan on using work for these users and their browsers, not for the global user base.

Here are some ideas, let's say you're building some internal tool or application, so something that runs in the internal company network and only employees of the company will be able to use that. It's a common use case, all companies have their own internal systems which often also are just web applications. Now there, the company browser might be clearly defined, maybe as a policy in your company, everyone has to use Chrome or Chrome or Firefox or everyone has to use Internet Explorer 11, then you know exactly what your user base is, you know exactly for which browser you need to build and you certainly don't need to support any other browser or let's say you are building some web page that targets tech savvy users, some blog about technology, some online learning site, anything like that.

Well there, it's very likely that you have users who are using cutting edge or modern browsers and versions of these browsers by default because they're interested in technology, they keep their system up-to-date and of course they're using the latest browsers because they want to use all these rich web applications, then you might not need to support very old legacy browsers because only a very small fraction of your users visits your site with these browsers and it might be fine to pass up on these users, you can't satisfy everyone, maybe you want to show some message to these users who won't be able to use your site but that's all.

Or you're building a site that targets older people or is simply a non-tech savvy audience, so then of course these people might be more likely to use slightly older browsers and therefore you want to make sure that you support these people and their browsers. You might not be able to rely on your audience to use cutting edge browsers and maybe therefore you need to be more cautious regarding which features you use and how you test your code on older browsers and that's one other thing by the way.

You of course also want to test your application in a broad variety of browsers, reflecting the browsers you would expect your users to have.

lectures.title: Solution: Feature Detection + Fallback Code
lectures.text:
So now with all these things we learned about browser support and how to determine the correct support level, let's learn about some strategies on how you can build a web application that works in a broad variety of browsers and there, one thing we could do is we could use feature detection and provide fallbacks if a certain feature is not available or not supported by a browser. Let's say we want to use the clipboard API, that's a relatively modern browser API that allows us to interact with the user's clipboard, so the thing you use with copy and pasting. If we search for clipboard API and we check the MDN article and we scroll down, we see browser support is not looking that great.

It works on FIrefox and Chrome, we don't know whether it works in Safari, it does not work in Edge and not in Internet Explorer. Now let's also check caniuse.com, let's search for a clipboard there and there if we scroll down a bit, here to the clipboard API, we see the same picture. For Safari it's simply not clear whether it's supported but we definitely know it's not supported in Edge or Internet Explorer, now in Chrome and FIrefox however it does work.

Now how can it be not clear for Safari? Well it's not about people not testing it there, it is about how the browser vendors, so the people working on Safari, how they communicate features they want to support and if they haven't communicated any information regarding their plans on whether they want to support the clipboard API or not, then this is treated as unknown, we don't know what their plans are we don't know if they're about to implement it, if it should be working and it's not working due to a bug or anything like that.

So this could be a reason for this feature being unknown rather than being marked as not supported. Now this also is a feature that might be nice to have in an application to simplify some process for the user for example but that's not a must-have, so therefore here we could use feature detection and then simply provide two routes. We can check if the feature is available and I will of course show you how that works and if it is available, we execute the code that relies on this feature to exist, otherwise if it's not available, we execute some fallback code or we show an error message to the user, we give the user another way of letting him use our application.

So basically what we try to do is we want avoid that the application crashes and instead just provide two different code branches that can execute based on the existence of this feature or not and for that I got a simple application which you find attached, it has a button, do something, it's this project setup. It uses some tooling as you learned it in the tooling section, you need to run npm run build: dev to spin up that development server which uses webpack dev server behind the scenes.

We will work in app.js here and our code will be output in the assets folder thereafter from which we also import it and then in the end, we'll get this button here and our working code. Now let's say we want to use the clipboard API and therefore temporarily, I'll add a paragraph here, some text you could copy and we want to make sure that when this button is pressed, copy, we put this text into the clipboard, so the same thing should happen as if you manually mark this and press control c, that's what we want to replicate here.

Now to make it work, let's go to app.js and you've got some starting code here which selects a button, let's also select the text paragraph here with document query selector and then just the first paragraph we find because that's the only paragraph we have and now we can get our text here by accessing text paragraph.text content, this is the text which is written in there. Now we want to use the clipboard API and place that in the clipboard of the user.

Now for that, we can use navigator.clipboard, use the right text method there and then this needs a data piece here, here I'll just put in my text because it wants a string and thereafter, this will give us a promise. lectures.title: Solution: Using Polyfills
lectures.text:
Another strategy for making code work in more browsers is to use polyfills. A polyfill is a third-party package that adds a functionality which otherwise might be missing in a browser, let's say you want to use promises. Promises might not be available in all browsers, for example Internet Explorer does not support promises and therefore to still make it work there, you can add such a polyfill which again is just a third-party package that actually teaches the browser how to use that feature.

Now obviously, this is not possible for all features, some features rely on some core mechanics which can't be worked around with Javascript, some features however can be replicated with other Javascript features and therefore an older browser which might not support let's say promises but supports other features with which you can rebuild the idea behind promises might be able to utilize such a promise polyfill. So it's a third-party Javascript feature that simply adds something to a browser which otherwise is missing there.

So for some features and functionalities, this might be very interesting to have. Now how do you find such a polyfill? For example if you search for fetch here on caniuse and you want to use fetch and you know you also need to target older versions of Edge and let's say Internet Explorer. Well then here under resources, you would find a link to a polyfill, of course you can also just try your luck and search for fetch polyfill. In both scenarios here with that link or with our first search result, you actually would end up on this GitHub page here and there, you learned about this fetch polyfill and here you learn what it does, what it is able to do and what it is not able to do and how you can add it and how you can use it.

You also learned that for this polyfill to work, you also need to add another polyfill to make promises work and there, you could for example dive into this recommendation and make this promise polyfill work, then you would also have to follow the installation instructions there, here you can simply use the CDN link for example and throw that into your index.html file and with that you would be able to use promises and with this polyfill, you would also be able to use the fetch API because what the polyfill does behind the scenes is it basically adds this fetch function, fetch method to the global window object you could say and it does so by rebuilding the fetch API with features that are available in older browsers as well.

And if you're interested in seeing what happens under the hood, you can simply dive into that open source code here and learn how they rebuild the fetch API with other tools, to be precise with XMLHttpRequest here. So polyfills can also be a very nice feature to making features work in browsers that would normally not support it. Of course not magically, you're not touching the browser source code after all but by simply working around the features with features the browser does support.

Therefore this is not available for all features you might want to use but for some, especially promises and the fetch API are prominent examples which you can make work in older browsers even though they normally would not work there.

lectures.title: Solution: Transpiling Code
lectures.text:
For some features, you can't use feature detection, you can't use fallback codes you can't use polyfills and you can't ignore them, typically that's the case for core Javascript syntax features like let, const, async await, arrow functions, all of that. These are features you as a developer might want to use because they allow you to write cleaner code, work around certain issues you have with older Javascript code and so on, so you want to use this modern code but you also need to support browsers that might not support these Javascript syntax features.

Let's take let or const as an example here, if we search for it on caniuse, we see const has decent browser support, even Internet Explorer partially supports it but older versions of Internet Explorer don't for example and that might be an issue if you need to target these top 0.3% of users. If you search for arrow functions here, you see there it's even a bit worse, Internet Explorer for example doesn't support this at all, not even in version 11.

Now what do you do if you still want to write modern code with all these features and you still want to support let's say Internet Explorer in this example or these older FIrefox or Chrome versions, what can you do in that case? You can't use a polyfill because it's a core language feature and if the let keyword is not recognized there is no way of making it work, unlike promises and fetch, these are not functions you call after all, instead const really is just a keyword that tells the engine what the code after it is all about, that it creates a variable that does not change and in the example of const for example and therefore this is a functionality that can't be rebuilt with other tools, it's just missing the const keyword, it's not recognized and therefore browsers that don't know it, that use a Javascript engine that doesn't know it I should say will just crash when they detect this keyword.

Now to still make that code work or to still ship, so deploy code that does work, you can use transpilation. The idea behind transpilation is that you transpile, transform your code, your modern code into older code and this of course is not done manually because if it would be done manually, you could just write older code right from the start, instead you have tools for that, most prominently Babel is a tool that does that for you, it can even be integrated into your webpack workflow so that that all happens in one step.

This allows you to write modern code, use cutting Edge Javascript language features and still ship, so deploy, cross browser code that for example still uses var instead of const and let or that uses normal functions instead of arrow functions. So how would that look like? Well for that, we need to quit our development server and now install that transpiler, you do that with npm install --save-dev and now let's see which transpiler we need. For that, you can just google for Babel and you should find babeljs.io, now actually let's search for Babel loader, this is the webpack integration and go to that GitHub repository we find there, on babeljs.io however, you can learn more about the Babel project and all its rich configuration options and so on, so definitely also check this out. Now here on Babel loader, you learned how you can install it and you will actually need to install Babel loader, @babel/core, @babel/preset-env, and webpack we don't need that, we already got this in our project setup but we need the other three packages, so you can just copy that and add this here after --save-dev, by the way --save-dev is just a longer form of just -d here.

So now hit enter and this will now install these three packages into your project and we can then tweak the webpack configuration to use them. In the end what we got here is Babel loader, which is the integration into webpack which basically does the connection of webpack and the Babel tool, we got Babel core which is that Babel tool, so the tool that actually knows how to translate modern code to older code and Babel preset env is a preset that controls which features are compiled in which way, so actually this is the package with the concrete translation rules you could say. So now we have these three packages, now how can we use them?

Well just as explained here, you have to add this entry here to your webpack configuration, so let's copy that actually and then go to webpack.config.js and there let's say above the plugins, though the exact position does not matter, you paste this in and add a comma after it. This adds a module entry which basically gives instructions to webpack how to transform your different modules and a module in webpack world is just a file, so it basically tells webpage what to do with the files it's managing, then you can add a rules entry here and that takes multiple rules because you can control different kinds of files with different so-called loaders.

A rule is a Javascript object where you have a test property, there you define how the file you want to translate should be identified. This is a regular expression, you learned about these briefly in the strings and numbers section of this course and here we're basically saying any file ending with .js or mjs, so with an extension of js or mjs, should be treated or should be handled by this rule, other files ending with a different extension of which we have none but if we had them would be ignored. Now we also want to exclude any files that are in those modules or power components which is another package manager which we don't have here, so we can actually remove that, will be ignored so that we don't start transpiling code which is part of third-party packages, these should be ready to use out of the box and then we have the concrete action that should be taken with the use key here.

It's again an object where we configure the loader that should be applied, so that Babel loader should take care about such Javascript files and that as an option, it should use that preset-env ruleset. This is now what we're doing here and we also should do that by copying that in the webpack config profile. Arguably there it's even more important because this is the code we ultimately want to ship to our users. So here under testing, we might test this in modern browsers anyways, though you should still compile it there so that you have the same experience as the users who use your actual code but it's the users who get your production ready code that actually needs that code that works in older browsers as well.

So now that's a first step, now we're not entirely done though, we need to configure which browsers we want to support because that's the cool thing about @babel/preset-env, I said it's a set of rules that controls which features are translated to which older code, for example that let and const are translated to var. Now of course the exact translation you want depends on which browsers you're targeting, this is where we come back to our market analysis because keep in mind if you revisit this compat table that the different features modern Javascript offers have different browser support, for example const and let have quite decent browser support so we might not even need to compile them if all we want to target is Internet Explorer 11 and higher and these partial features which are missing are not a problem to us. On the other hand, there might be other features which are also important to us which are not supported in the browser we want to target and therefore they should be compiled.

So we want to tell Babel and this preset-env package for which browser is the compilation should be fine tuned and thankfully, Babel works exactly like that, it wants this information and then it really gives you code that is fine tuned to the browsers you want to support. Now how do we pass that information to Babel however? We can do that with the package.json, there simply add a new entry, let's say here which you name browser list, like this. The value it holds is also a string with double quotes and now in here, you can specify a browser list configuration string, browser list is a separate package and tool that is used under the hood by @babel/preset-env and attached, you find a detailed description of which options you can set there.

You can do stuff like set > 2% which means you want to output code that works in browsers that have a market share of greater than 2% and of course every time you build, this is checked and this under the hood taps into a source which is always kept up-to-date so that you build code that works in browsers with greater than 2% market share. Now with that, that should be browsers list by the way with an s after browser, now with that we can run npm run build prod or just build to get the unoptimized output and now in scripts here we see an app.js file with our code and yet now the interesting thing is of course this is the webpack world so it has all this webpack extra code but what we can see if we scroll down a bit is for example here, we see const button equals document query selector.

Now if I change this to let's say we want to support browsers with a market share greater than 0.2 which of course includes way older and smaller browsers and I now rebuild this, let's check the output again. If we now go down there, we see we get a var in there. So now our code really was translated to code that would work in older browsers as well and this all happens magically with the help of webpack Babel loader and the browsers list and again, attached you find the link to the documentation of which options you can set there because you can not just target market shares, you can also be specific about different browser versions, so you could say Chrome version 58, Internet Explorer version 11 or higher and so on, so you can also set stuff like that.

You can also combine multiple queries or multiple instructions, for example you can add not dead here, this means only browsers that still have official support, for example Internet Explorer 10 at the point of time recording this would be considered dead because it's not receiving any official support anymore, Internet Explorer 11 is at least receiving some support still. So these are some things you can set up there and this will influence how your code is transpiled and how you can make your modern code which does use constant arrow functions also work in older browsers because const and let is translated to var and an arrow function for example is translated into a normal function.

Now one problem we still might have in this example here for example is that we still use then, so we still use promises and now we have code that works in older browsers from a Javascript syntax perspective but it still might not really work there because whilst we transpiled core syntax features like let and const, other features like promises might still not be working in these older browsers. So we might want to combine this approach with a polyfill and as it turns out, this is also rather simple.

lectures.title: Improvement: Automatically Detect + Add Polyfills
lectures.text:
We have this great tool, Babel loader combined with Babel preset-env which takes our browser instructions here and then gives us code that just the works in these old browsers or almost, together with feature detection it might work there because we're not even trying to get the clipboard API and therefore execute this promise if the browser doesn't support it but if we had other code that also relies on promises that can't be compiled to older code by Babel, we would have code that works in older browsers from the core syntax perspective but doesn't really work because we still use other features like promises that aren't supported in the older browsers, so we might need to add a polyfill here into our code so that we have the best of both worlds, feature detection, transpiled code and polyfills for features that we need.

Now of course if we know we worked with promises, we can search for promise polyfill, follow the installation instructions here and add it to our project and that would be absolutely fine but if we have a project that's getting bigger and bigger, it can be cumbersome to manually manage all these polyfills, to find out which polyfills we need, you have to check everything, that's annoying because after all the advantage with Babel is that we don't have to think about modern Javascript syntax, we can just write it and rely on Babel to compile it, would be nice if the same would happen for polyfills.

If Babel sees that we use a promise, it would be nice if it would just include a polyfill for that so that we don't have to do it and the good thing is Babel is capable of doing that. Under the hood, it relies on a package named core-js, if you google for that, you will find that github library and in the end core-js is like a collection of polyfills you could say, it's a huge package with a bunch of built-in polyfills. If you dive into the repository there, you see you've got a bunch of subpackages there, bunch of code in there.

Now that's nice, you can import core-js and suddenly you have access to all the Javascript features of the world in all browsers so to say. The problem is you could do that, you could import or install core-js with npm for example and just import it at the top of your file but then you would really add everything, even features you don't need. So let's do that first and see how we can then improve that, let's install it with npm install --save, now not save-dev but save because it will be a third party library that's part of our final code and not just some development tool, core-js, that's the name of the library.

Let's install that and now let's add it at top of our app.js file simply by writing import core-js like this. This will work, webpack will be able to handle this but we'll have a problem there. Let's run npm run build: dev to start our development server again. If we do that and we reload our page, it works but if we go to the network tab, we will see that we have a huge app.js file, it has 2.4mb. Now it's also that big because it's not optimized at all and it has a lot of debugging instructions but still that is huge.

Let's see how big it is if we remove this import, so let's come in and out, save that, it automatically rebuilds and now you see it's just 900kb. It is still pretty big for this small of an app but again that is because of all the development mode overhead code, in production it will be way smaller. So already here we see it's only a third of the size as it is when we add core-js, so simply throwing in core-js like this might not be that nice because we bloat our application just to make promises work because it adds so many other features which we aren't even using here, so we want to be a bit more careful.

Well we can use core-js also in a different way and import just what we need, for example core-js features promise. If we tweak our import to just use the features part and there the promise part of the package and we save that, we see if we go back to our application, now it's still bigger than before, bigger than the 900kb without the import but only a bit. So really not that much and far away from the 2.4mb we saw before, so this is better but we still have to manually manage what we use and that's ultimately not what I want to do, Babel should do that for me and therefore, I'll actually comment this out and with core-js installed and you need to install it manually, that's important but with it installed, we can now go back to the webpack config here and tell Babel to actually use that polyfill or do that auto polyfilling for us. For that here in presets, we need to tweak this and actually wrap this preset in a nested array here, so an array in an array because that allows us to add a second element to that inner array which is a configuration object for this preset.

Now in this object here, we can configure this preset-env there, there is a use built-ins option. Now this option is the option that allows us to control polyfilling behavior, the default is false here which means no polyfills are added automatically. Now we can set that to usage or to entry, with entry you manually need to add polyfill imports, very generic imports like this general core-js import we had there earlier and Babel will then replace it with the actual polyfills you need or you just use usage here and then Babel will add polyfill entries as it detects it, so it basically checks which features your code is using and then it will add imports for these feature polyfills automatically.

So let's try usage here. Now one note, you need one other package which you can install with npm install --save and that's the regenerator runtime package here. So you can simply copy that name and then here, install this as well. This is simply another polyfill package handling some other features which core-js does not handle which Babel also will try to utilize if it sees that it needs it. Now with that, we're not entirely there though, at the moment you also need to add a core-js option here, might not be required in the future but right now it is and that in turn takes an object as well where you set the version to three.

This basically tells Babel loader which version or Babel preset-env I should say, which version of core-js you're using because there was a bigger change between version two and three and we're using version three here, the latest version which is better and we need to tell Babel preset-env that we're doing that so that it uses this package correctly. Now with that, let's run npm run build: dev and see what we get. This now starts the webpack dev server, seems to compile without errors and on my page I get this app.js file.

Now as you see, the size hasn't changed, the reason for that is that Babel checks my app.js file and it doesn't really see that I use a promise here or to be precise, it sees no need to add a polyfill for this promise here and correctly so because the clipboard API won't be available in browsers that don't support promises anyways, so we don't really need to polyfill for promises if the only place where we need a promise is an API that won't work in these old browsers anyways.

So having a promise polyfill would not help us. So to still show you that it works however, let's create our new own promise here, simply a dummy promise with which I do nothing else but output it but that it's enough to show Babel and Babel preset-env that I do have a promise it should polyfill. If I now save, indeed you see app.js grows to 1.1mb. So it's bigger because this now includes some core-js polyfill, we can also check this response here and search for core, core-js and you will see there is some core-js content in there.

So now this is getting included here and we therefore take advantage of Babel and its auto polyfilling feature. Now an alternative configuration you can set here is that you change this to entry, if you change this to entry here, then you need to add imports and app.js at the top of the file, you need to import core-js/stable and import regenerator runtime/runtime. Now these imports will now actually be replaced by Babel with polyfill imports that make more sense for your project.

If I now save this here and restart the build process to take the new config into account, you'll see if I reload, we now have a far bigger file because now we include almost all polyfills. The reason for that is that in the end, Babel of course analyzes your code but it does not load polyfills based on the features you're using but actually based on the browsers list you specified. So it loads all polyfills you would need to support browsers that meet this specification.

Now why would you do that? Well this is a good option if you don't know which exact features you want to use and if your code is not all the code that should be taken into account. If you're using a bunch of third-party packages which might be using features older browsers don't support, Babel does not check these third-party packages, so then your browser list might be the best indicator to show which browsers you want to support so that you are better safe than sorry and load all polyfills these third-party packages might need and that's why you might want to go for this entry configuration instead of usage.

Here however I want to use usage because for our project where we use no third-party packages, this makes more sense. With that of course we can comment out these imports, save that and restart our build process so we're back to the smaller package here. So now to conclude this, let's now also copy this setup for the presets here that utilizes our core-js polyfilling into our production code and let's replace this preset here in the array, not the entire array, just the preset with that array so that we have an array in an array to make sure that we now also apply this automatic polyfilling to our production code.

So now if you run npm run build: prod, we basically do the same as in development mode but now we get our production ready code which also uses polyfills our code might require.

imagine rich web applications like Google Docs and so on,

lectures.title: Getting the User Location
lectures.text:
Now how do we get the user location? You learned that for that you can use navigator geolocation, geolocation is a browser API that is provided in Javascript that allows us to get the user's location. If we search for MDN geolocation, we find the official MDN documentation on this API and what you'll see here if you scroll down is that this has quite decent browser support. The geolocation API here has really good support, Internet Explorer 9 and higher supports it, Safari supports it, so this should really work in all the browsers we're targeting.

Nonetheless if you want to be super safe, you can add an if check here and check if navigator.geolocation is a thing or to be precise, if it's not a thing by adding an exclamation mark in front of that and if we make it into this if block, we know that we don't have access to the geolocation API and in that case, we might want to return and not continue here with this function and simply throw an alert or show an alert to the user where we say location feature is not available in your browser, please use a more modern browser or manually enter an address.

So here, my fallback code is that I tell the user who might be using my web page here that we can't auto locate him because it's just not supported by the browser and that therefore the fix for the user is to either use a more modern browser or use that alternative of entering an address here and with that, I think we're really doing our best here to make sure that we support this feature and give a helpful feedback if it's not available. Now after this if check, so if we don't make it in there and if we would make it in here we would return, so if we make it past this if check, we know that geolocation is available, well then I indeed want to get the current location of the user.

So for that, we can use navigator.geolocation here and then call get current position, this will get the current position of the user and it takes two callback arguments here which we can pass in which will be the two functions in the end which will be triggered when we either succeed getting the position or when we fail. So here we either get a success result in the first callback function and I'm just passing in an anonymous arrow function here, this will be the argument automatically given to us by this browser API if we succeed or we make it into this second callback, the second argument here which I pass in, this would be my anonymous function that gets triggered if we fail to get the user location. Now let's start with the failed case, if we do fail to get the location here, well then I want to show an alert where I just say could not locate you unfortunately, please enter an address manually.

So again even if we fail to automatically get the location here, we do offer an alternative to our users that tell them what they can do to still use our application and of course that is something you want to do in your applications so that you provide a good user experience. In the success result on the other hand, we know or we will get the user location data and we know that it succeeded, so that is where we will later then display the map in the end.

So here for the moment, I just want to get my coordinates and I can get them out of my success result argument here and my coordinates should be a new object here where I have a latitude, so a lat key and where I have a lng, a long key and by the way of course you could create a new class for this which you then just create with the new keyword to make sure that you always have the correctly named properties in there, here I'll do it on the fly with this object literal notation.

So my latitude can be received from success result.coords.latitude, I also get autocompletion here, if you want to see what else is in success result, you can of course always console log success result, that would be possible but here I know that my latitude will be stored here and here for successful result I got my longitude. Now one thing I will do here which you of course don't need for the application in general but which I want to have here is I'll add math random * 50 and I'll add this to both and I'm just doing this so that I can show you the result without you being able to locate me here, sorry about that but I don't want to expose my address here so that's what I'm doing here, of course you would omit this, this is not needed for the app, this will actually ensure that we're not getting the correct position, you of course want to get the correct position, I'm just doing this here to kind of not show my exact location here.

So with that, we got the coordinates and for the moment, we can just console log them to see that it worked and of course later, we'll change this and make sure that we don't just log them but that we use them to show this on a map. Now with that, we need to make sure that we of course trigger our constructor here for the place finder and we do that by instantiating place finder. So here below my class, I will call new place finder and actually that's all I got to do here, we don't even need to store the instance in any constant because I'm not doing anything with the instance, I just want it to exist, of course you could nonetheless store it in a constant if you wanted to. With that if you save that and you then click on get current location, you should be asked by your browser whether you want to allow this and yes I do want to allow this and thereafter, we'll need to wait, we probably should add some kind of feedback here and then we get back a location here.

lectures.text:
So let's make sure that finding a user address works or an entered address and we'll do that in the find address handler here of course. For that we need to do a couple of things, we need to get access to what the user entered here, we need to prevent the default so that submitting a form doesn't actually submit it, it doesn't try to send the request to the server, we then need to reach out to Google's servers and translate a user entered address into coordinates, latitude and longitude, this is how you express places, coordinates on the map or on in a geographic way in general.

So let's start simple, we will get the event argument here and we can call prevent default on that to prevent the submission of the form. Next I want to get the address the user entered and we can get this by using event target which will be our form, that's the target which triggered the event in the end and there we can use query selector to get the input in the form and I only have one input in there, so we'll get that input then. Now I'm not interested in the entire input, I'm just interested in the value the user entered, so we can access .value here to get that value.

Now we can do a little bit of validation here and check if we don't have an address somehow or if we do have an address but after trimming it, the length is zero which means the user didn't enter something and then I just show an alert where I say invalid address entered, please try again and I return. If we make it past this if check, we know we have a valid address or at least we have some text and we can try to look it up. So here, I will again show my loading spinner then, create a new modal and point at the same content I have up there, loading modal content, we can actually take both arguments we have up there and we could therefore also refactor this into its own method but I'll just do it like this and I will call show here to show that spinner. Next, we need to make sure that we reach out to Google's servers because they do have an API for us which we can use to translate the entered address which could be something like a street name into coordinates and I don't want to do this here in this class, this class should be focused on working with the inputs and so on, instead I'll create a new folder, utility and you can name this however you want and in there I'll create a location.js file and this should be a file which holds utility methods for getting

coordinates for an address for example. So in here, in the location.js file, we can add a new method or a new function now just like this, doesn't have to be in a class, get coords from address would be a fitting name where we get an address as an argument and this should be a function and we then make a HttpRequest in here and return the coordinates. Now I want to export this function so that we can use it from outside this file as well and I will add the async keyword inside of it because we will use a promise in here, we will send a HttpRequest and I want to use that async await syntax you learned about in the course to have this more readable promise syntax instead of using then and catch but of course you could use then and catch as you learned it in the async code section.

Now in here, we need to send a request and we need to send this to Google's servers, to be precise we'll need the geocoding API Google offers and if you google for Google geocoding API, you should find the official docs here. Now as always here you can learn all about that and you will need an API key and a working project for all that but with that, we can just copy this example URL here by clicking this copy button and send a request to this with our real address for what you want to get coordinates. So we can use the fetch API here which of course not all browsers support, so we might want to use a library like axios instead but here to also practice fetching again, I'll go with that and send a request to this URL, enter it as a string here. Now actually, I'll not enter it as a string but as a template literal so that we can inject content into the string easily because there are a couple of parts that we'll need to replace, for example the address. This is a dummy address which is getting looked up here, Google headquarters and we can replace this entire part here with our actual address, so here I'll inject some content, same for the API key, we need to replace that and I want to inject it because I will set up a global

constant here, Google API key where I want to store that key and that can be the same key as you're using in your index.html file, so here you can grab this key which we added there earlier and add this here in this constant in the location.js file as a string and then we can use the Google API key here as a key which is injected into this dynamically generated string. Now for the address, I want to use the address we're getting here but one important note, since it will be part of a URL, we have to make sure it's converted such that whitespace or special characters are translated into a URL-friendly encoding and for that we got a helpful utility function built into Javascript or exposed by the browser in Javascript I should say and that's the encodeURI function. It's globally available, made available by the browser, we can pass in a string and we get a URL-friendly string back.

So here I got my URL address which we can now inject into our string here and with that, we should send a request to a URL that works there. It should be a get request so we don't need to configure it in any other way and instead we can just await it because I'm using async here and store the response in a constant, of course as I mentioned, you could use then and catch as well. Now if the response is not okay, then we know we have an error, so I want to throw a new error here where I say failed to fetch coordinates, please try again. If that's not the case, I want to extract the response data by awaiting response.json and now that should be our coordinates data but and that's a Google specific thing, it could also fail without using an error status code, so without making it into this if block and we can tell if it failed if we have an error message property in the response body. So it will have a 200 status code and still it might have such an error message which signals that it failed.

If we make it past all these if checks, we know we have a successful response and we get the response data which should hold the coordinates. Now we can console log the data here to get a feeling for its structure, of course this is also something you find in the official docs though, it will look something like this and in there what you'll have is a results key which is an array and the first element of the array is itself an object which will have a geometry property which will be an object with a location property, which will be an object with latitude and longitude and that's the thing I'm interested in. So to extract this here, we can get our coordinates by accessing data results and there, the first array element as I just explained, there the geometry key and there, the location key and that will then be an object with the lat and long keys and I want to return these coordinates, these coordinates object as part of this get coords from address

function and now, we can use this in share place.

lectures.title: Copying the Link to the Clipboard
lectures.text:
So let's copy the link into the clipboard and for that of course, we can use the clipboard API. I briefly touched on this already in earlier modules, If you search for MDN clipboard API, you can learn more about it and most importantly, you'll learn that browser support is mixed. So we should definitely check whether it is supported by the browser we're running our code in before we just blindly use it. So first of all, I'll comment in this add event listener code here in the constructor and point at a let's say share place handler method, this share place handler.

Now we have to add such a method here, maybe directly below the constructor for that to work and in there, I now want to use the clipboard API of course. So I'll first of all check if navigator clipboard is not a thing, which means the browser does not support it in which case I want to return and not continue and instead as a fallback, just select the text, so that at least the user just has to press control c and doesn't have to select the full URL. Now to select the URL, I need access to the input, for that we can copy that code here where we get access to that input element, of course we could have also therefore initialized it here in the constructor and stored it in a property if you wanted to, here I'll just copy it and then in here in the if statement, set or call shared link input element select. We trigger the select event here which the end selects the entire content in there and marks it. Just to prove that it works, let's do it outside of this if check and let's then get the current location so that such a link gets generated and now if I click share place, you see this is selected. So now I just have to press control c which is better than nothing but of course if the browser supports it, I want to take

that one step further and not just do this as a fallback in this if check but if we make it past this if check, we know we have support for the clipboard API, then I want to use navigator clipboard and call write text, this write text method on the clipboard object and write my text which is in that input into the clipboard of the user, so shared link input element.value, that's the link we generated and that's now stored in a clipboard of the user.

Now this returns a promise and we could use async await, just to mix it up here, I will use then and catch and in the then block, we know that this succeeded, so here I'll just throw an alert, copied into clipboard so that we get some feedback and here we might get an error which I will just log here to the console, we could then as a fallback since it failed at least mark it again. So now with that, if we save all of that and I clear my clipboard by copying something else, you see now I got enabled in my clipboard, now if I click get current location, still got enabled there, if I now click share place, it's copied into clipboard and indeed, here it is.

So now this worked, now I got this in my clipboard and now the only missing thing is that if I visit this page here, we load a new page as you can tell, we load that other index.html file in the my-place folder, here I want to show the address here in the header and render the map here, share a new place always takes us back to this page so I just want to make these two things work now and we'll be done for this little demo application here.

lectures.title: Rendering the "Shared Place" Screen
lectures.text:
So let's make sure that when we visit this my-place index.html file, we do actually render the address here in the header, in the h1 tag and we do render the map. For that, we can use the my-place Javascript file which is the file loaded in that index.html file and in here, I will create a new class, place or maybe loaded place or how you want to name it and there in the constructor, I expect to get the coordinates and the address, so the two pieces of information we can get from the URL in the end because keep in mind that this link which is generated has the address encoded in the URL and it has these coordinates encoded in the URL. Now in there, I then want to build a new map, so we can import map from the UI folder from the map file there and build a new map here by forwarding coordinates.

I also want to output the address in my header, so for that we can access the header title and store it in a constant with document query selector header h1, this is a CSS selector which selects the first h1 element in the first header element on the page and here I got exactly one header element with one h1 element so of course we'll select this one. And now here in the header title element if you want to call it like this, header title el, I'll set text content, so I'll set the text node in there equal to the address we're getting. Now after this, we can instantiate this and we have to parse some data from the URL, so we'll call new place, new loaded place and I'll need to forward coordinates an address and that is part of the URL and needs to be parsed. For that again, Javascript and the browser got us covered, we haven't used it before but we'll use it now.

There is a built-in URL constructor function or class, however you want to call it, so you can create a new object with new. To that, you can pass a URL and I want to pass the current URL which as you learned earlier is stored in location.ref, this is the current location, the current URL which is loaded in the browser and pass this to this built-in URL constructor function and it creates an object with options for us to get information out of that URL, that's what this URL utility class provided by the browser does.

So I'll store it in a constant here and now we can get our query parameters as it's called, stored in a query params constant maybe by accessing url.searchParams, this is simply provided by this built-in object here, by this built-in class. So this will be our dynamic options here, so the thing after the question mark basically, stored as key-value pairs in query params now, thanks to search params, so stored as key-value pairs in search params so to say. And then we can get our coords here, create a new object where we have a lat key which is query params and there we have a get method and then get the lat argument, so with that we're saying hey, I want to get the value which is stored for this lat identifier in my URL which is this number here in the end and of course I'll repeat the same for the longitude. So I'll add a longitude here and get it from query params, get lng. Now important, what's retrieved here will always be a string, however I need a number here and we can convert it to a number by adding a plus or by using parse float of course, that also works, you can do both, so I'll do both here to show you both.

So we get the coordinates, for the address, I will store that in a constant and get it from query params and there, get address and what you get here of course have to be the keys you find in your URL, so here I am getting the value for the address key, so the value after this equal sign which is this address here in the end and this is then retrieved and automatically parsed to a human readable format, so from that URI optimized format to a human readable one and then we can forward both here to loaded place to this constructor. With that if we now save that and we reload this page, I get an error that Google is not defined which makes sense because I'm using the map in here and for that of course, I use the Google Maps API, now that's imported in our root index.html file with this script import but not imported in our my-place index.html file so of course we should add that import before we add our own script here too.

So let's add the Google Maps Javascript SDK import with our API key entered here in the index.html file in my place folder so that we do have access to the Google Maps API in all the scripts that belong to this file as well. With that if we now reload this, this still fails. Reason for that is here, we've got async on the Google Maps import and we actually should remove that. It can result to the Google Maps script loading too late and then our script might execute before Google Maps was loaded, so let's remove that so that we only have defer and they are executed in order and therefore now this works and here you see that location which is shared is loaded here and if I share the 6th Avenue, find that place, click on share place here, got the link, enter that link here, we got that here.

So this is now working and I mistyped here but this is now working and this is our finished application here with Google Maps being used, with a couple of browser APIs being used, with browser support ensured by us with certain if checks where we check if the clipboard API is available and so on and with async await used with promises with a lot of async code in general, with the fetch API, so with a lot of features you'll learned about earlier in this course all coming together in this little demo application which hopefully therefore is a good practice and shows you how tthe different pieces work together.

lectures.title: What and Why?
lectures.text:
So let's start with what exactly a framework is. Now I'll be very honest here, you can fight a religious war over this and there are people out there to whom it's very important to differentiate what a library is and what a framework is, I'm not one of them. Still I'll give you the common differentiation and explain why we differentiate it or why that is so important to some people. So we get Javascript libraries and frameworks and a Javascript library in the end is a third-party package, doesn't have to be, you could also write it yourself and and just share it across multiple projects but in the end it's a package which you bring into your project that adds certain functionalities. JQuery helps us with querying the DOM, Lodash added a couple of utility functions and axios helps us with sending HttpRequests.

So libraries typically are focused on one or a few core tasks and they help you with that, so I already named these examples. Now frameworks on the other hand also are third-party packages, they also add functionalities but typically they add more functionalities, also from different areas and they typically also give you certain rules or certain structure on how you should build your Javascript driven application and therefore they force you into a certain rule set but at the same time by doing that, they often make it easier for you to build an application and make it easier for you to focus on your core business logic and spend less time on all the nitty-gritty details.

So they typically provide a complete structure for building Javascript applications and the big examples we got there, not the only ones but the big examples we got are Angular, Vue.js and React.js, though as I mentioned React.js is kind of an edge case, it's actually a library but a pretty big one with a bunch of different features built in and it spawned a huge ecosystem that effectively together forms a framework you could say. So let's have a look at these three here.

We got Angular, we got React and got Vue.js, all these libraries here or all these things here are Javascript libraries or frameworks, React is called a library and Vue.js and Angular would be called frameworks and as I mentioned, to some people that's really important, that help us with building Javascript projects. Now it's important to realize that you will still be working with Javascript and you can do the things with Javascript that you learned about in this course but these frameworks and libraries will help you do that, will allow you to focus on your business logic and spend less time on the details, for example when you typically need to select a button and add an event listener and so on, these frameworks take such work away from you by giving you a totally different way of thinking about your project.

Now these are not the only Javascript frameworks we have, they are particularly useful for building powerful user interfaces but we've also got other frameworks that would help us with building online shops and so on and we also got not just frameworks for the frontend, so for the code that runs in the browser, we also got frameworks that run on the server side if we use Javascript there, for example for Node.js which we'll have a look at later in a separate module, there would be a framework called Express.js but we'll focus on that later when we talk about Node.js, for now let's stick to these client side, browser side frameworks here.

Now if we quickly have a look at them, then Angular for example introduces a new language or uses a new language, Typescript, which actually builds up on Javascript and which as part of your development build process is compiled to Javascript. It's a bit like using next generation Javascript with Babel, just with even more features which don't even exist in the next Javascript generation. Now Typescript is a standalone project detached from Angular but Angular heavily uses it, if you want to learn more about Angular and Typescript, I got dedicated courses on that.

Angular is extremely popular and it's a huge framework, it contains a lots of features, it contains features for rendering beautiful user interfaces, for animating stuff, for validating user input, it contains everything built into the framework for sending HttpRequests so that you don't need axios and much more. Now React is also a framework or a pretty rich library if you want to call it like this and it uses enhanced Javascript syntax as I like to call it here.

It uses a feature which is called jsx and this allows you to add a certain syntax to your Javascript files which is not supported in vanilla Javascript, which you wouldn't run like this in the browser but which, just like Typescript, is compiled to regular Javascript instructions as part of your development process and you'll see that jsx thing in action later in the React example, it in the end helps us with building rich user interfaces with the help of React without having to write all the create element and append and remove child instructions on our own and that's by the way a general idea of all these frameworks, they take away the need for us to manually add elements to the DOM and remove them and so on and instead all these frameworks give us a way of defining the result we want to have, defining certain conditions when that result should change and then the frameworks will take care that changes are applied to the page the user sees when our conditions change but again you will see that in practice at the example of React a little bit later in this module.

Now React itself is a library but it spawned a huge ecosystem which adds certain features around React so that even though React in its core is much leaner than Angular, it has no built in validation, no HTTP support, even without that we get a couple of other packages that we typically combine with React so that we can add such functionality and just like Angular, it's extremely popular. Well and the third big framework you have in Javascript land is Vue.js. It uses regular Javascript, you can use it with Typescript but you don't have to, for Angular you basically have to use Typescript and the good thing about Vue.js is of the three frameworks, it's the easiest to learn I'd argue. It's also popular, not quite as popular as the other two but still very popular and it, just like Angular, contains all important features. Angular ships even more than Vue.js, Angular has even more built-in features than Vue.js but Vue.js has more built-in features than React. So unlike React, you don't need to combine it with other libraries to get everything you need to build powerful applications, Vue.js got all that built in.

Now that's the rough comparison, all three are great, I got courses on each of them so if you want to learn more about React, want to learn more about Vue or Angular, take my dedicated courses of course, I'd be more than happy to welcome you there and in addition, I also attached a link to a more detailed comparison which I created in case you want to find out which one is best for you. Now with that however, let's take a closer look at React and understand what that does for us.

lectures.title: The Idea Behind React.js
lectures.text:
So what's React? It's a Javascript library for building user interfaces in the end. Now as I mentioned, library because technically it focuses on that user interface building part but enriched by everything else the ecosystem that it spawned offers, it's basically like a framework you could say. Now the user interface part is important though, React's all about building user interfaces that look good but more importantly than that, that update reactively, so that you for example can define if this button is pressed, this data should change and if that data changed, instead of outputting this text down there, I want to output that text.

So you basically define different kind of scenarios and results you could say and React will then do the heavy lifting of reaching out to the DOM, adding elements, removing elements, adding CSS classes, removing CSS classes so that you don't have to manually write all these instructions, instead you just manage the state as it's called of your application and React will then update the UI based on what changed. This is called a declarative approach because you declare the goal, you declare what you want to see on the screen in different scenarios and React will then handle the way of getting there. The opposite of that would be an imperative approach and that's basically what we did thus far in the course where we manually had to say now add this button, add this element, add this event listener. Now doing that in bigger projects quickly can become cumbersome and difficult to manage and such a declarative approach definitely has certain advantages over this because it allows you to focus on the result and the state instead of the way of getting there and this is less error prone and gives you more power. In React and also in Angular and Vue, you do that by defining so-called components which are reusable UI elements, now not HTML elements,

these are not elements the browser would understand, in the end these are just components, basically Javascript classes you could say which you define in your code which then at runtime when your code and React's code executes on the page are interpreted by React so that React then knows what to touch in the DOM and what to render where. So you don't render real HTML elements, in the end you just use something which React then understands and which then in the end tells React what it should render on the screen under which circumstances.

So let's have a look at that, this should make it clearer.

So that were symbols, now let's move on to iterations and generators and let's start with iterators. An iterator is simply an object in the end which has a next method, which then in turn returns a result of a certain structure. For that let's say we have another constant, company and that holds an object where we have employees and there I got Max and I got Manu and I got Anna in there. Now this is a regular object, we make it iterable or we turn it into an iterator or you could say by adding a next method here which we can add like this, now the name has to be exactly next. Now in this next method here, we then should return an object where we have a value property, this could be employees this, employees zero so the first element in the employees array and a done property which simply signals with a boolean whether we got more values we can output or not.

Well then we should probably also have another property here, current employee which initially is zero which we use to track which employee we already output so that here we can access this current employee and store that in a returned value variable or constant, I'm not going to change this and thereafter we can set this current employee to current employee plus one by incrementing it and then we return our value here. To be precise, we also want to check if we still have employees left through which we can loop by checking if this current employee is greater or equal than this employees length.

We know if this is the case, then we're out of employees because we then have no more employees left, so here we could return a value of this current employee to return the number for which we failed and set done to true to signal that we are done looping through that. Now what's the idea behind this next method though? Well now we can console log company next and execute this a couple of times down there. If we save that and we reload, you see we print all different employees until we're done.

So what we do here in the end is we create our own method that allows us to loop through a specific field of this object and we could have any looping logic we want in here. So this in the end kind of makes this a loopable object, right now we can't use it with for/of but we soon will be able to do so but we have an object where we have a method which we can call multiple times to go through any logic of our choice, in this case to go through all employees but of course it's totally up to you through which field or whatever you want to loop through here.

So we have a method which we can call multiple times and every time it will return something different and not just that, it will actually go through some list of data, it will exhaust some list of data and when we exhausted that list, we'll not get an error, we'll simply get a response, we'll get back a value where we see that we're done because of this uniform return value where we always have a done property which is true or false, we also know if we can call next again and have more values left or if that's not the case.

Now this alone as I said might not be totally helpful yet but this already is a logic you could use in some applications where you have an object which you use as a data storage and you want to go through some custom logic there to output some data which is stored in there, you don't want to use a for/in loop because you're maybe not interested in all the properties of this object but just in some of the values in one specific property of this object and then such a custom looping logic could be quite interesting here because what you could of course do with that is you could create a while loop and have a result here or let's say an employee and for that you call company next, then you have a while loop and as long as employee is not done, you continue looping and then you can console log employee value here or do whatever you want to do with it in the while loop and thereafter, set employee equal to company next again and now we have a dynamic loop, not a for/of loop but still a loop which will in the end go through all employees with our own iterator logic.

So if we save that and we reload, it outputs the three employees we have and then it stops because then done is true and therefore this exit condition kicks in or this running condition is no longer true and therefore we make it out of that loop. So this would be one example how you can use your own iterator, company, which has this next method which then in turn allows you to have your own looping logic for whichever field or whichever logic related to this company object you might have.

lectures.title: The Reflect API
lectures.text:
With that let's move on to the reflect API, now what is the reflect API all about? It is totally not related to iterators and generators and symbols, it is related to objects though. It is an API that allows us to control objects, to do things with Javascript objects and in the end it's just an object itself, reflect is an object in Javascript which groups, with a bunch of static methods on this class so to say, which groups a lot of functionalities that help us work with objects.

It has standardized and grouped together methods and the reflect API, just like all these features, can be used to control how our code is used, how our code behaves and so on. Now let's see an example and let's see what the reflect API offers us. For this here, in our dummy app.js file, I'll go down a bit further and here I want to start working with the reflect API. So let's say we have a new object here, to mix things up, I'll name this object not person and so on, I'll just name it course. Now a course might have a title, Javascript - The Complete Guide.

Now it's a very simple object of course and we worked with objects so much, shouldn't need much explanation. Now we got this reflect API which we can access on this global reflect object by adding a dot thereafter because this has a bunch of static methods we can use, for example it has a define property method, it has a delete property method, it has a getPrototypeOf method and it has a setPrototypeOf method and for example we can use setPrototypeOf to set the prototype of our course object to an object where I have a to string method, my own to string method where I return this.title and the consequence of that would be that if I now console log course to string here, we no longer use the default to string method but my own one here and hence if I save that and reload, I print the course title in this case. So the reflect API helps us work with objects, with set prototype of we can set the prototype of an object, with define property we could add a new property and not just like this but also with such an object descriptor, this extra argument you might remember where we can set whether this is writable, so whether we can write to this property or if it's locked and so on, I covered this earlier in a lecture where I talk about object descriptors.

So in the end, the takeaway is that the reflect API gives us a bunch of methods that help us change objects, work with objects on a meta level because what we do here is typically something we do to prepare our object to be consumed by some other part in our code. Again, consider that you are the author of a third-party library and you expose certain objects as part of this library and you want to make sure that certain properties can't be changed by the developers using your library, that could be one scenario.

Well then you can use the reflect API to for example set a property and set it to be non-writable. The obvious question that just could arise at this point is why would we use reflect for this? If we used a global object, object with a capital O, we also have a setPrototypeOf method, we also have a define property method and it generally works the same way as the reflect API methods. So why do we have the reflect API if we can already do these things with the existing object API? The reflect API is newer, it was added recently with ES6 to Javascript, the object API is way older.

Now that alone of course is no reason for using it, instead the reflect API has two advantages over the object API - for one there are subtle differences regarding the behavior of some methods, for example if a method fails to do its job, on the object API it might return undefined or fail silently, on the reflect API you might get a better error or it just returns True or False for a given method to tell you if something works or not and attached you find a link with a comparison of the object API and the reflect API that allows you to understand these subtle differences.

Additionally, the reflect API bundles all features that you need to work with objects, for example it also has a delete property method which we don't find on the object API, there this is not a thing, if I try to call delete property here on course and pass in the title with the object API, then you will see that if I print my course down there and I reload, this does not work because object delete property is not a function. The object API has no delete property, instead previously in older Javascript, if you wanted to delete a property in an object, you would have to use the delete keyword and then target the property you want to get rid of.

Now you can do that but it's a bit of a strange code, having this special operator here, I think it's a bit cleaner to have a method you can call on an object if you want to get rid of a property because on the other hand we also do have a method for defining a property, so why not have one for deleting it? Well that's for example one thing the reflect API added, there you now have a proper delete property method and that simply is cleaner than using this delete operator.

Here you can pass the object where you want to delete a property and then the property name and then this will return true or false depending on whether it is operation succeeded or not. So this is simply cleaner and more straightforward than using this delete operator, technically is of course doing the same but that's why we have the reflect API, it's there to group all the methods you need to configure your objects, to work with your objects and you don't have to fall back to different approaches where some things are defined on object and other things are not defined there and you suddenly need a special operator.

Now the reflect API gives you everything you need to work with objects all bundled in this global reflect object here and that's basically the idea behind the reflect API. Whenever you need to do such meta work on your objects - delete a property, define a new one, change the prototype after the object has been created, then you should consider using the reflect API over the other scattered methods or operators you might be able to use for that, that's the primary reason for the existence of the reflect API.

lectures.text:
And that leaves us with the proxy API, just like the other features here it's basically a meta feature which allows us to tweak our objects or add some extra functionality to our code that kicks in when our people work with our code, which is why it's called meta programming. We configure our code to behave in a certain way when other people use it, which is this extra level of thinking we added here. Now the proxy API is all about creating so-called traps for certain object operations and you can almost take the words trap here literally. With the proxy API, you can step it up on certain operations and execute your own code, for example if someone wants to retrieve a property, so the value for a property of an object, with the proxy API you can set up some logic that runs in that case which allows you to either change what is returned or do some additional task, again for this meta level where you might want to track property access or make sure the objects your library exposes are used properly.

So again, it's an API that allows you to control how your code is used and which impact it has, now let's see it in action. lectures.title: Working with Proxy Traps
lectures.text:
The get trap is a very useful trap but you also get other traps for other operations people might perform on objects and again, attached to the last lecture, you find a link to MDN where you find all available traps. Now one other trap that can often be useful is the set trap, the set trap allows to step in when users try to set a value for a given property. So here again we could register a method or we would have to write this as a method and we get the object for which this was tried, so the wrapped object in the end, the property name users try to set and the new value users try to assign to that property and then you could use this to validate all incoming values, to lock down access entirely by not doing anything in here or just simply forward that and you do indeed set the property name on the object to add a new value, this would be a set trap which basically does the same thing you would do by default.

Now if I try to set a rating here for example to 5, this would just work, if I save and I reload, you see I print 5 here for my rating because I just forward the set request. On the other hand I could check that for example if people try to set the rating, so if the property that the user tries to set here is rating, I just return and I don't do anything and I only proceed and do set the value for other property names. So now for example when I tried to set rating to 5 here, you will see that when I print it down there, it is actually not found because it was not set because in my set trap, I actually block access and I return so that this line does not execute if the property name which users try to set was rating. So you can use this to block access, to do any other logic, you could also send data to your own analytics server, sending data to register any settings to any properties in your object, you're totally free to execute whatever you want in these traps.

Now also be aware of the difference to getters and setters, you learned about getters and setters earlier. Getters and setters were always focused on one specific property, you added a getter with a certain name and a setter with a certain name. These traps however are flexible, they're not bound to a specific property name, they kick in whenever you set a value to any property or whenever you try to get the value of any property. So they're way more generic and flexible and you as a programmer therefore have full control over how you want to allow access to properties of the object you might be exposing to your colleagues, to yourself or to consumers of your library.
