lectures.title: JavaScript is a Hosted Language
lectures.text:
As you learned, Javascript is a hosted language, that means Javascript itself, the definition of the language can be implemented in different environments. All you need in the end is a Javascript engine that parses the code and executes it in the end and one very common environment of course is the browser. Browsers have their own Javascript engines, like the V8 engine in the case of Chrome and this in the end hosts and executes the Javascript code therefore. Now togetger with the browser APIs you learned about, like the DOM or the browser storage or the fetch API and so on, you got tools to build rich client-side applications where you utilize the language and all its key features and keywords and so on combined with the browser APIs to provide the user experience you want to provide, all of that then runs in the browser, so directly where your users are but of course nothing speaks against taking Javascript and executing it somewhere else.

We can do that, we can execute Javascript anywhere else we want by simply taking the Javascript engine and taking it out of the browser basically and that's it. We can then add our own APIs if we want to, so not APIs to work with the DOM for example because if the Javascript engine, if the environment is detached from the web page, there is no DOM right, there is no HTML code which we could parse if we run Javascript somewhere else but instead we might want to add new APIs, APIs which don't exist in the browser, for example to work with the local file system which is not possible in the browser due to security reasons and that's exactly what Node.js does. Node.js is essentially the extracted V8 engine Chrome offers enriched by extra APIs, so its that engine you know from the browser but basically instead of the browser APIs, it has access to other APIs and it runs outside of the browser, this is Node.js and of course this also implies that what you learned about Javascript still is relevant, just the browser specific parts like the DOM or the browser storage of course are not important when we work with Javascript outside of the browser.

So let's now have a look at Node.js.

incoming requests.

lectures.title: Understanding Modules & File Access
lectures.text:
So in this basic script here, just output something in the console. Now how about writing this data to a file and then reading the data in from a file? For that, we need a couple of packages which are available when you install Node.js. Node.js works such that certain, very important features are available globally, for example setTimeout. This is a browser API that was also implemented in Node.js and you can just use it like this in any Node.js file but other functionalities which you don't need that often need to be imported explicitly, for example functionalities for working with the filesystem, for that Node.js works with so-called modules and on nodejs.org, you can learn more about that. In the docs there, if you click on API reference, you'll find all the packages, all the core modules Node.js is made up of and for example here under f you find the filesystem module and you find the complete documentation for this module.

Now as you can tell, there's a lot in there and of course we'll just briefly dive into this but we will use it a bit at least. So there for example we see how we can make this module and its features available in a Node.js script and that's one important difference to browser side scripts, the Node.js import export syntax looks a bit different, instead of using the import and export keywords, in Node.js you use require to require a module, be that a module provided by Node.js like in this example or be that your own file and then you store the required data in your own constant which you can then use in your script and I will later also show you how you export something.

So with that, let's copy that and add this here in our app.js file and this pulls in the filesystem module which again was already installed as part of Node.js, so we don't need to install it separately but we still need to add it to this file with this line and now we can use the filesystem object here to work with the filesystem, for example to call the write file method here which takes a path to a file and then the data we want to write to that file and there we could, as a simple starting point, just provide a file name and then this will be written in the same path as the script sits in, for example we could write this to user-data.txt let's say, to write a text file and then as a data, we could have some text here, user name equals Max for example. You can also defined some write options here as a third argument where you can set things like the encoding and so on but we don't need this here, we can just execute this file like this.

Now write file then takes a callback as a third argument which potentially holds an error if it failed and we can then check if we do have an error, in which case we could console log it for example and otherwise we know we succeeded and we could console log wrote to file and now with that if we now execute our app.js file, you see wrote to file here and you should have a new file being added here to your system where our data was written to and this is how easy you can write a file with Node.js.

Of course you can also read in a file, so parse a file, you do this with the filesystem here with read file and then the path to the file, for example with user-data.txt, then again you can set some arguments or just provide your callback here, this is a callback function that takes two arguments, first argument is a potential error object which will be undefined if we have no error, second argument is the data we hopefully get and then here we can check if we do have an error and if we do have one, we can console log the error and then maybe return to not continue with the execution and otherwise, we'll get our data.

So let's see what we get there if we print this and now if we save that and we run this script again, we see wrote to file but we also see this buffer output here which is coming from parsing the file. Now of course that buffer is not that useful, if we call to string on that, it gets more useful though, now this is converted to a string and we got the content of the file being output there. So this is a very simple Node.js application of course if you want to call it like this but we see some Node.js APIs in action here and at the same time we see regular Javascript syntax, like the if statement which we use here or the const keyword which you of course learned about throughout this course.

lectures.title: Working with Incoming Http Requests
lectures.text:
So we played around with Node.js a bit and we saw one of its built-in core modules which you can pull in to add certain functionalities which are not available in the browser but which are available in Node.js. One important difference compared to the browser of course is that some modules need to be imported with this syntax in order to use them whilst others are available globally and most modules actually need to be imported by the way, in the browser all the things by default are available globally, you can just access documents like this, you can just access local storage like this.

That's one difference, in Node.js, it's more of you have to tell me what you need approach, other than that however, it's highly comparable, we have the same base language and then some specific APIs. Now let's move away from this dummy script here, I'll name it files.js and add a new app.js which is empty and let's see what we can do in Node.js when it comes to working with HttpRequests because that arguably is an important scenario where you would look to Node.js running a web server with it.

So let's see how that would work. It all starts with a specific module you can require and that's the HTTP module, it's a module that allows you to work with HttpRequests This by the way does not just mean that you can listen to them, you can also create a request and send it to a server but more commonly, you use Node.js to set up a server that listens to incoming requests so that you can have your own web server and in the end by the way, that's also what the webpack dev server and all these other development servers do, they use Node.js to set up a basic web server which runs locally on your system to host your HTML files, your simple local web application.

Now we'll basically do the same here but we'll not just build our own development server but instead we'll build a server which also runs some server-side logic, something development servers of course don't do, they just serve our local files. Now to get started with that, we need to create a server and for that on the HTTP method, we can call create server. The create server method does just what it sounds like and it requires one important argument for that, a request listener, this is a function which in the end triggers for every incoming request.

This request listener function takes two arguments which are passed in automatically by Node.js and that's a request object and a response object. So this will basically be passed in by Node.js and will reflect the request which was coming in, so the headers which are part of the request, the data which might be part of the request and so on and this response object is also given to you by Node.js, it's an object which you can then use to configure the response you want to send back and to then ultimately send it back.

So inside here of create server, we can now work with these two pieces to read data from the incoming request and to send back a response and to start very simple, let's start with the response object to right now do nothing with the incoming request but to just send back a response and there we can call write, to write some data to the response, for example a simple string where we say hello there and then we can call end which will send the response, so end basically tells Node.js we're done adding data to the response, you can now close it and send it back and this is a very simple web server we could build with Node.js.

Now with the server created, we need to do one more thing though, we need to call listen on it, so we either chain this here or we take the extra step of storing this in a separate constant and then we call listen on this constant, so on the object, on the server object stored in the constant. Listen is required to then actually start the server, you can think of create server as a method to build the server but then listen starts it up and listens to incoming requests.

Listen also takes the port on which you want to listen and here I'll go for 3000 for my local development only to use this special port locally here. With that if we now save this, we can again run our app.js file which now holds the server and you will notice something interesting. If I do that, we don't get an error but we also don't complete this process, my cursor here in the terminal is stuck. Now you can always quit this by hitting control c but it is stuck for a good reason, it is stuck because this is an ongoing process, this script now doesn't finish once all the lines have been parsed, instead listen in the end sets up an ongoing event listener you could say behind the scenes which waits for incoming requests and as long as Node.js notices ongoing event listeners, it does not shut down script execution which is why this script execution is still going on, because we have ongoing event listeners and that's of course what you want, you want your server to keep on running and not to quit after it was configured, right?

So now we get this ongoing server and to see it in action, all we have to do is we have to visit localhost:3000 and there, you should see hello there on this page. You see hello there there because that's of course the data we are sending back in the simple response. It's not HTML data or anything like that, IT's a simple text but we see it here on our own Node.js server and now we're back in the browser but this is now not browser side Javascript, in the end this is the result of server side Javascript which spins up a server and sends back a response.

lectures.title: Sending Responses (HTML Data)
lectures.text:
Now of course we might be interested in sending back some HTML data, right, that would be great. Now of course we can do that, here when we write our response, we can use HTML, for example we can write Hello there like this and have our HTML tags there. Now if we do so, there are two things - one, we must now quit the server and restart it because we change the file, the ongoing process of course still is based on the old file when we executed the process.

So when we changed the file, we have to quit the server and restarted during development and of course also after you deployed your server, if you change something in code and you want that code to have an effect, you upload it onto your server and restart the server, so onto your cloud machine and restart that server that runs there. Now with that, that is done but now you'll notice something else, if we reload you see Hello there there actually is displayed correctly but if we open the developer tools and go to the network tab and you reload the page so that you see your request there and you access this, you will notice that under headers here, if you have a look at the response headers, so the headers that were part of the response sent back by the server, we say nothing about the kind of data that this actually is.

Now the browser here actually renders this correctly as HTML in the DOM but this is not something we should take for granted, This is a smart guess by the browser here because it sees that our content seems to contain some HTML content, not all browsers necessarily do that. Instead it is a good practice and really important to set an extra header, so to add extra metadata to the response header when sending back the response that explains to the browser which kind of data is attached because this then tells the browser what to do with that data and we're not relying on these smart guesses.

Now we worked with headers before but there, we worked with headers on the requests we sent from client site Javascript to a backend, so we set headers on the outgoing requests, something like the content type of the data we attach there. Now we need to do the same but the other way around, we need to set headers not in the client side Javascript but in the server side Javascript and we can do that, on the response object, we got a set header method.

This takes two arguments where the first argument is the header identifier and the second argument is the value for that header and there for example, we can set the content type. We worked with that before on client side Javascript, it also is a header we can set on the server side though and set this to text/html. This is the standardised identifier for saying hey we got HTML text data attached to the outgoing response, so it's a text, it's a string but it is HTML which is in the text. An alternative by the way would be text/plain and let me do that first to show you the difference. With text/plain we're saying this is normal text, don't parse it as HTML. If we do that and we restart the server and we reload this page, you see now the tags here are output as text because the browser is not guessing, because we're telling it that the data we're getting here is of text/plain and therefore the browser is not guessing whether it should render it, instead it knows I should not render it as HTML because you were telling me it's plain text and therefore it displays it just as a text node. We can of course now change this to HTML, restart the server and now reload and we're back to what we had before but now in a cleaner way because now we explicitly

set this response header and tell the browser hey this is HTML content, please render it as such and all browsers will then do that. So this is actually how we should send back our HTML code here.

lectures.title: Parsing Incoming Data
lectures.text:
Now sending back data is one thing, typically you also want to be able to receive data. Now for that we need to send back different HTML code, we need to send back HTML code which includes something that allows the user to send us a request. Now with that I'm not talking about a script where we used the fetch API, we could do that but would be a lot of code we have to write here, we can instead start simple and sent back a form. You might remember that a form had this default behavior that when a button was pressed, we actually had the browser default of a request being sent to the server that served the page and we had to prevent this with Javascript.

Now here, I don't want to prevent it, I want to have this default behavior so that the request is sent to the server because that's simply another way of building web applications. Instead of having client side Javascript do more of the work, we could take the more traditional approach with less client side Javascript because we maybe don't need it here, we don't want to validate the user input here on the client side and instead we let the browser do its default thing and send the request to the server so that on the server we then validate the input and so on, both is possible and of course both can also be connected as you will see later. So here we could render a simple form with an input of type text, like this and with a button in there and make sure you get these opening and closing tags right. Now in this button here, we could have a send text and the type of the button, and that's important, should be of type submit.

So now here I have a form element, then we have an input element, then we have a button and then we have the closing form tag of course. If we save that and we reload, now you see that here. Now if we enter something here and we hit send, you see the page reloads right, you'll see that here in the network tab, tis flickers because the page reloads and you briefly see a second request, that's the outgoing request before the page reloads. Now the outgoing request by default is a get request, on form we can set a method attribute and set this to post to send a post request instead and we can set an action attribute and point at slash nothing to tell the browser to which URL to send this HttpRequest and then to encode the data of the form properly, we should add a name attribute to the input and for example give this the user name identifier, this is totally up to you though. With that the browser is able to parse that form, have a look at all inputs that have a name and basically create a data object behind the scenes where it stores the data entered here under a user name key and then sends a post request with that data object to this URL, that's what the browser now does and that's a default browser behavior, has nothing

to do with Node.js, has nothing to do with Javascript in general. We could just prevent this with client side Javascript where we listen to the form submission and prevent the default but I don't want to do that here, I want to use that default behavior instead. So now we'll send this request to the server, if I now reload here and I enter something here and I hit send, well we get the same behavior as before but actually we will get a request here, we just have to parse it now and for that here, let's work with that request object which we haven't used thus far.

Parsing the body of an incoming requests can be a bit tricky or strange at first but we'll later learn how we can do it in an easier way. We first of all start by creating a variable, body and that should be an array actually because the body is received as chunks of data for efficiency reasons and we have to basically store all these chunks and then convert them to text thereafter. So here we get our chunks of data, now we need to extract the data from the request body actually. Now before we do that, let's see what's in the request.

We could log the entire request object but this will be a huge object, so instead I want to start by logging the method which is one property we can read and the URL and then we at least see which requests reach this listener here, for which methods and which URLs. If we now save that and we restart this and we reload here without sending that, we already see some output here, get and /?, the question mark was added earlier to my URL when I hit send here before configuring the form, if I remove that and hit enter here, we see just get/. So we see by default when we visit the page, the browser sends a get request to ourdomain.com/, that's what we get here.

The rest of URL simply is omitted here, on the URL property we just get the path on our server here. Now if I entered something here however, for example Anna and I hit send, you see now we also got a post request to slash nothing which makes sense because that is what we configured here in the end. So this is now some data we can get there but of course we want to get the body and to parse that, we need to add a listener on request which we do with the on method, not with add event listener but with on, there is an add listener method but that's not the right one here, we just want on.

Now that's a difference to the browser because we're not working with a browser side API here and of course generally, every API can implement this the way it wants. Node.js typically works with on or with once if we only want to listen once instead of with add event listener but that's just something we have to get used to. So with on, we set up a listener here and I want to set up a listener first of all to the data event here. This is one event Node.js knows, just as the browser knows click on a button for example, Node.js knows the data event on the request and here we need to provide a second argument which is a function that should execute when this event occurs. There, we will get our chunk of data, will be passed in by Node.js and we can then add this to our array by pushing it into it. It's a normal Javascript array with the normal Javascript methods. By the way, on Node.js, you also have all these special methods like filter, map and so on you learned about in the arrays module, this is supported in Node.js as well.

So now on every data piece we read in, so every data piece that's coming in on the request, we add it to this body array. Now we're interested in the point of time when we're done receiving data and for that we can add another listener to the end event. This will be fired when we're done reading in the request, so when it has been fully parsed, there we also have a function that should execute in this case and now we know the body array will be fully occupied now with our chunks of data, we will have all the chunks of data we got in this array.

Now we just need to convert this body from an array of data chunks into some string data we can work with and for that, we can set b ody equal to buffer which is a global object available in Node.js, .concat body, so body before we stored it here is an array of chunks, to string. This is the end just one way of converting this array of encoded chunks into a normal string and store that back in the body variable here, this is also why I use the variable here and not a constant.

lectures.title: Introducing & Installing Express.js
lectures.text:
Doing all of this data parsing and response generation code on our own is quite cumbersome and hard to scale, this already is quite unreadable here and of course we could optimized this in certain ways but it's certainly not how you would want to build bigger applications. Now similar issues exist on client side Javascript though, there also if you have very complex apps with a lot of access to your documents, where you create elements and insert elements, this can get cumbersome. Therefore there we also learned about React.js or other frameworks that help us with that and we also learned that there are in general libraries that can make certain tasks easier, the same exists for Node.js.

You can google for Express.js to find one of the most popular Node.js libraries you can use, you can visit its page, expressjs.com to learn more about it and in the end this is just a framework for Node.js which makes building web applications, web servers with Node.js easier. We install it with npm and in order to do that, we first of all need to turn this into an npm project here, so we can do that by running npm init here, npm is available since we installed Node.js and you can just confirm all the defaults here.

Once you did that, you have a package.json file and now you can install new dependencies in this project, it's the same approach and idea as we had it on the client side when we managed our project there and enriched it by npm packages. The only difference is that now we will not need webpack or any other tool to use that because Node.js natively support these packages in Node modules which is also why the folder is called Node modules as you will see and we don't need webpack or anything like that to combine all these files.

That's one difference, we need it on the client side, we don't need it on the server side. So let's now install Express.js with npm install express --save which will install it as a production dependency and you see this new dependency entry here in package.json and you see the node modules folder and as I said, Node.js is natively capable of working with node modules, you don't need any extra tools to combine all these different files. With that, I will rename the file here to pure Node.js and add a new empty app.js file where we now can get started with Express.js and learn how we set up a web server with that and how that makes it much easier to work with incoming data and also to send back responses, how to outsource our HTML code into separate files and not have it inline here and how we can then build web applications with that.

lectures.title: Express.js: The Basics
lectures.text:
So let's get started with Express.js now that we installed it and to get started in the app.js file we simply start by importing it with that Node.js import syntax where we require Express and then store the imported package or the content of the package, the objects and functions exposed by the package in this constant here which you can of course name however you want. Now Express or what you actually get in there is is a function, so what you can actually do here is you can simply create an app by calling Express like that, like a function.

This gives you such an app object which in the end is an object with a lot of features and functions provided by Express, so you set up Express by calling it like this and then it gives you access to all its cool features on this app object you could say and one thing you can do on this app object is you can call listen again and this of course might look familiar because we called listen on our pure Node implementation as well on the server. Now Express and the app object therefore sets up the server for us behind the scenes and that's really important, Express is simply a Node.js framework, it does kind of the same thing we did here, it calls create server for us but it does so behind the scenes and then exposes this server on this app object together with a couple of other functionalities.

So with that alone, we would have a running Node.js server powered by Node and Express but this alone wouldn't do much. Now what we also typically want to do is we want to act on certain incoming requests and for that, it's important to understand how Express.js works. It's a middleware-driven framework, now that sounds very fancy, what does it mean? It means that in the end Express is all about funneling the incoming request through a bunch of different functions which all received the request and all can do something with it and each function can either stop the request and send back a response, at which point the request will not reach any other function thereafter, any other middleware or a function forwards the request to the next function, to the next middleware in line. So a middleware is really just a function that gets the request and then can do something with it.

Now let me show you what I mean, we can register such a middleware by using the user method on the app object and the use method takes a function as an argument. This is a function which Express will execute for us and it is a function which will get the request object and the response object and also an additional next thing, a next argument to which I'll come back in a second. Now what we got here is basically the same request or a similar request as we got it here in the function we passed to create server but enriched with some extra functionality, the same for the response. We get this response object so that we can work on the response we want to send back and also that when we're done, we can send back a response.

So what we could do here is for example we could set a header on the response, let's say we want to set the content type and we can do that in the same way we did it before in the pure Node.js example and we set this to text.html. Now that might be all we want to do in this middleware for whatever reason, then we can add a new middleware simply thereafter and the order does matter, this will execute first, then the request will reach this middleware, so here we again pass in a function where we get the request, the response and this next thing and in here we could then decide that we're done setting up the response and getting data out of the request maybe and we want to send the response to the client, we can do this with a special send method which is new which was added by Express.js which does not exist in pure Node.js and there we could send our h1 tag where we say hello world, just like this for example to have a very simple response.

So we'll send back this string as our response data, we set the header on the response before and this will be carried over into this function, so the different middlewares all work with the same request and the same response object so to say, so what you set up here on the response also is applied to this response but then here I send the response. Now with that we get two middleware so now the only missing piece is we need to tell Express.js that from this middleware, we don't want to stop the request, we also don't want to send a response yet, instead we want to forward the request after working on its response to the next middleware in line and that's what we do with this next argument.

This actually is a function we can execute like this and all next does is it tells Express.js that we're not done yet, that instead it should move on to the next middleware in line and call that with the request, with the response and also again with next which we don't call in the second middleware though because we're done with the response and the request here. We send back a response so we don't want to handle the request in any other middleware thereafter because we already send the response, what else would we do with the request, right and that would be a very basic setup which should render this to the screen.

So if we now save this and we execute app.js again, you'll see again we've got an ongoing process which we can quit with control c but which of course shouldn't do as long as you're working with that server, as long as the server should be up and running and now if we go back to our page and we reload this page, we see Hello World and if we inspect our request, we see on the response headers we have the content type. You also see there are more headers than before, simply because Express.js also adds a bunch of default headers anyway, so it automatically adds a bunch of headers which we don't have to add on our own.

So here we also see that Express.js is doing a little bit of extra work besides this basic node work we did manually before. And now we already have a bit of a more convenient way of handling incoming requests and sending back responses but we're not extracting any data at this point, so that's something we might also want to do and turns out this is also relatively easy with Express.js

lectures.title: Extracting Data
lectures.text:
To parse incoming data, again we need some data and I'll get it from the pure Node.js file, I will simply copy this response here with the back ticks and replace my response here, this string with that copied string, so that again I try to output a user name and I have a form here. Now the user name is not always set, so here I want to have a default user name and then also get a body though which allows me to get the user name from that, like this.

However actually we can remove the if block because we'll get the user name out of the request body a bit differently. Instead of manually parsing the body like that, with Express.js we can use a middleware that does this body parsing for us. So before we do anything with the response, we could have another middleware where in the function we execute there, we have all the body parsing logic so that in the subsequent middlewares, we get the parsed body available. We could write our own function for that but thankfully, there are third-party packages which can be integrated into this Express middleware flow that do that for us and the very popular package for parsing the request body and adding it to the request object, so adding the parsed body to the request object is the body-parser package.

You can install this with npm install body-parser --save to add an entry to package.json and by hitting enter this will now be installed and is made available in your project. Now we just have to import it here, body parser by requiring body-parser and now body parser and that's the convenient thing can simply be added here as a middleware, we just have to pick one of the parsing methods, for example JSON if we had JSON data or in our case here, URL encoded which is essentially the form data we will receive and if we do that, this package will add a default middleware, so it adds a function like this basically to the Express middleware flow where it parses and extracts the incoming body, the request body and adds the parsed body back into that body field on the request object, so that now here we could say we want to set the user name, which now can be a constant, equal to request.body.username because we gave our input here a name of user name, so this will be the key by which we can access the field value or unknown user, if that should be undefined for whatever reason.

lectures.title: Rendering Server-side HTML with Templates & EJS
lectures.text:
So we want to create a full HTML page to the user. Now we can do that by creating a new folder maybe, views as a typical name but you can name it however you want where you store all your HTML files you want to send back, though we'll not actually create a HTML file in there but instead a template which contains HTML content but where we can also inject dynamic content so that we can have a mixture of HTML static content and dynamic content, this will be all then merged together into HTML file on the server side and sent back to the client, so on the client we will receive an HTML file but it allows us to enrich this HTML file with dynamic content and for that, we need a package, a library that allows us to define such a template which then parses the template file and finds a special syntax in there which we can use to output dynamic content and that makes working with such a template easier and for that I'll install such a package and that's the ejs package.

Now there are alternatives to that and in my Node.js course for example, I dive way deeper into that but here we can use this ejs package which is quite popular and quite straightforward to use. So here we can just npm install this package as an extra library and now we need to tell Express.js, which supports such templating engines as they are called, that we want to use this templating engine and we do tell Express us if we want to do that by calling the set method on the app object which allows us to set up some global options and there we want to set the view engine option with a whitespace between the two words to ejs, which tells Express that the engine for parssing our views, our template should be ejs, the package we just installed and then we also tell Express.js where it finds our views and for that we add a views setting and point at the folder that holds our view files and in my case, that's views but if you named that folder differently, you would have to change it here. Now with that, we can add such a template here and I'll add an index file in here with the extension ejs.

This means that ejs, this package we just installed will be able to detect this file and parse it. Now in there you generally just write HTML code as you're used to it but you can add a special syntax which the ejs package understands to inject dynamic content. So let's generate a HTML file in here and in vs code, you can just type HTML and pick this HTML5 option and hit enter and it gives you a basic skeleton. Now here I'll just use Node.js demo as a title and then here in the body, we can output the content we want to show and it could be a h1 tag where I say hello and then here I want to have something dynamic, I'll come back to that and below that I want to have my form. So I'll grab this code here from app.js and output that below the h1 tag and autoformat it, so now we have does in a way more readable way.

Now I want to output the user name here dynamically and for that, we can use a special syntax which ejs, this package, understands and you can of course learn all about the supported syntax features either in my Node.js course where I cover this as well or in the ejs documentation, here I just want to use one of the most basic features with an angle bracket and then a percentage sign and then an equal sign and a closing angle bracket and now between that, you can refer to any variable name which you plan on providing to this view and I'll come back to how we provide that in a second. So here I'll point at user, you could use user name here, it doesn't matter, I'll take user here and now we have this special syntax in here. This is of course not regular HTML but instead this is simply a syntax understood by the ejs package when it later parses this file. Now to tell ejs to parse this file, we need to make sure that we don't set back a response like this but instead here, I want to render a view as a response and for that, the response object has a render method, also added by Express.js, this does not exist in pure Node.js.

The render method takes a couple of arguments and the first argument is the name of the view you want to render and in my case, that's index because I have the index.ejs file in the views folder. You don't need to specify the path because we set the views folder to be the folder that holds our views up there. So now here, index also no extensions required because we told Express that we use ejs and that will automatically look for a .ejs extension and therefore we can continue with the second argument and that would be an object full of properties or full of data we want to provide to this template and here we should provide a user property because that will be the data ejs then can use when it parses this template.

So here I will set a user key and set this to user name, so to this value and with that, we got a setup where now we should render this file and have our dynamic content in there. So if we now save this and we restart our server and we go into our URL and hit enter here, I get an error, could not find matching closing tag, Yes because here a little mistake, the closing tag also should start with a percentage sign, so it's closing tag percentage angled bracket, so just like the opening tag but without the equal sign.

So now with that if we restart the server and we now hit enter here again, this looks good and now if we enter something here, click send, we see that. So now this is working with the help of our template. Now of course you can render way more than just this single output there, you could have multiple such dynamic pieces as long as you provide all the data to the view here and you can also do more complex tasks, like loop through a list of data or render content conditionally, I covered that in my Node.js course and the official ejs docs which you find attached of course also are a great place to dive deeper.

Important to understand is that if you inspect this in the browser, you of course get normal HTML code which is rendered here, also in the response if we have a look at that in the preview, in the response here I mean sorry, you'll see you get a normal HTML code. We have no dynamic part here because this dynamic segment is filled on the server, on the server we on the fly generate a HTML document which is then appended to the outgoing response. That's what the view engine does here.

lectures.title: Enhancing Our Project
lectures.text:
Now this is a very basic Express.js application, arguably not a very beautiful one either but it shows us the basic idea behind Express.js and Node.js and it gives you an idea of how you work with that and that it is just Javascript with new packages you can use which you can't use in the browser and with some new built-in modules like this filesystem module used earlier but in the end it's just Javascript, just running in a different environment and therefore with a different purpose.

Now here we're building a traditional web page I'd say, where we render all the HTML pages on the server and we return them and there is nothing wrong with that. Again I can only point that my complete Node.js guide if you want to learn all about Node.js because well that's over 30-hour course, there are a lot of topics to cover when it comes to Node.js, so here we can of course only scratch the surface. Nonetheless I want to dive into one other way of web application, of backend, of server side you could build with Node.js.

Here we got a web application that renders HTML files on the server and sends them back to the client. Now if you remember our practice app from earlier, what we did there for example is we got the location or the address or the coordinates for certain places on a map from Google's servers, we send the request to Google's servers. Now clearly what these servers sent us back was not HTML data, it was JSON data which we parsed with this JSON method if you remembered and indeed when sending requests from client side Javascript to some server, you typically exchange JSON data because on the client side Javascript, you might then have logic that edits the existing HTML page you're on but you don't want to replace it entirely with some HTML code sent back by the server, you don't want to reload the entire page, you might want to tweak some parts of the page to give the user that highly reactive feeling. So therefore this is a server which does not return HTML as our server currently does here but instead it returns JSON data and we can of course build such a server too. Why don't we do that and connect it here with this little practice application by ensuring that when we create a place there,

so when we create this share place link, we don't encode all that information here into the link but instead we generate an ID for that place on the server side, store that in a database on the server side and send that link back to the client side code, so to this code and then when a user visits this link which includes that ID thereafter and therefore the user ends up on this other index.html file and and so up in the my-place.js file, we parse that ID from the URL and again reach out to this backend server here to get the data, the address and the coordinates for that ID from our database and then send this data back via JSON or as JSON to this client side application so that there we can then render this. Why don't we do it like this, this would be a nice practice and that's therefore exactly what we'll do next so that we also explore this other way of or this other kind of backend service we could build, also often known as an API or specifically, a REST API, an interface we can talk to from any client we want as long as we send the correct data to the correct URL.

lectures.title: Adding Basic REST Routes
lectures.text:
To implement this new approach, we could delete the view folder but we can also just ignore it. I will comment out these two lines because we won't send back any HTML rendered templates anymore, instead now I want to exchange JSON data. So for that, we can also comment out these middlewares here and when we parse incoming data for our API which we're now building, I also don't expect form data anymore but I expect JSON data, so I will try to parse incoming JSON data here.

Now I want to set up two routes, two URLs which I handle here on this backend Node.js server, one URL which can be triggered from share place, basically when we select a place here, I want to send the request to this backend server with the chosen address and the chosen coordinates, so that on the backend we can store that in a database and create a unique ID for that which we then send back to the frontend and the second URL I want is reached from my-place.js where we extract an ID from the URL and then request the data for that place here from our server as well.

Now to split our code a bit more and have a clearer structure, I'll create a new folder, routes which should hold these routes so that in app.js, we just have the general setup like this body parsing which I set up and then we have our routes, so the specific different paths which we want to support and the logic for that in a separate file. So for that, let's go into the routes folder and here, I will add my-location.js file, you can name this however you want of course and there we also need to import Express by requiring Expressy You need to import this in any file where you want to use it.

Here I won't create a new Express app, so we'll not execute it like this, instead we can use another feature which is part of the Express package and that's the Express router. We can execute this as a as a function here and store it in a constant, the router makes it easy for us to register different routes. You can simply specify the kind of HTTP method you want to support, for example a post method and then any incoming post request to the path which you specify as the first argument, for example slash nothing or /add-location, whatever you want, will then be handled by the function you specify as a second argument which receives a request, a response and the next function here.

So it's like a middleware but filtered for a path and a specific HTTP method and only incoming post requests to this address here will make it into this function. Now that's one of the two routes we need, the other route will be a get route because we want to get data, we want to get let's say a specific location for a specific ID and I'll come back to how that works later, for now let's focus on the post route. So here on the post route, the idea now is that we get some data and keep in mind that we parsed data here, so we got it already extracted and stored in this body property of the request object and the data we get there are the coordinates and the address and then we want to store that in a database.

Now let's add the database later, for now here I'll just use an in-memory storage which will basically live as long as our server lives but whenever we shut down the server, it will be lost, so it's not a great permanent storage but here to get started it's fine and there I'll have my location storage which simply is let's say a Javascript object and there I have my locations which is an array and now here when we got an incoming request, I'll reach out to location storage.locations and I push a new location in there and this new location will receive an ID which I want to generate on the fly.

For that, we can for example use math random which is not perfectly unique but for now it will do, later we'll have a better ID and then I will have my address which we get from the request body, request body.address let's say, we expect an address field on the incoming request body and the coords, the coordinates which could be a nested object with a lat key which we get from request.body.lat let's say and a lng key which we get from request.body.lng.

Of course it will be our duty to make sure that when we sent this request, we do provide this address field on the body of the request and this lat and lng fields on the request body and with that we should add this to our location storage. Now sending back a response would also be nice so that we basically provide some answer to the client who sent us this data and here we can use the JSON method to send back a JSON response. It's like using send and setting the content type to JSON manually, here we can simply abbreviate this and just send back JSON data, we can send back an object which will be converted to JSON automatically by Express.js and there we could have a message maybe where we say stored location or whatever you want to send back. You could always add an extra validation where you first of all check whether you got valid coordinates and you may be send back an error if that's not the case but to not dive too deeply into that right now, let's ignore that and let's just assume we get valid data here. With all of that, we got our first routes set up but it lives in the location.js file. Right now nowhere in this application we tell Javascript or Node or Express that we're interested in this file.

So back to app.js which is the file we actually will execute with Node with this command here in the terminal, here we should import this location.js file or the routes set up there to be precise and we should then also tell Express.js that it should consider these routes when it funnels the request through all the middlewares. Now to import something from that file, we first of all need to export something here and here Node.js has its own export syntax, you don't have an export keyword as you have it in client side Javascript, instead you export with module.exports. This by the way might look familiar to you, it is what we had here in the webpack config earlier because I mentioned that this would be handled by Node.js, well here is how we export something in a Node.js file. We then point at the something which should be exported and here, that's the router with these registered routes that are added to it.

So here we export this configured Express router and now we can import it into another file and we do import with the syntax you see up there. We can import our routes here, however you want to name it, by requiring this file where we store them, so ./routes to go to the routes folder and then location, maybe name it location routes therefore but the name is up to you. Here we have a relative path, before we just had the package names but now we're not working with a package but with one of our own files and therefore we have to specify a relative path here and also important, you can and should omit the file extension here, Node.js will add it for you automatically when it looks up this file, it will look for a Javascript file in there after all.

Now we just have to tell Express.js that it should consider these location routes and for that, after parsing the body but before you listen, you want to register a new middleware here and that should just be the location routes here because it turns out the Express router is actually a middleware you can register in your Express application and now Express knows that it should funnel incoming requests through these routes as well and there, we have our filtering logic by HTTP method and by path to then execute these functions which in the end are also just like middleware functions you could say. So that was a lot of talking, now if we start our server, let's see if it works. Server is running, now we need to work on the client side and make sure that in share place, once we got coordinates and address, we send a request to our backend. Now the backend is running on port 3000, the frontend by default has port 8080, the webpack dev server takes this. So we have no clash here, we have to use different ports because these are two totally different servers as if they were running on different domains and therefore now here, we can use fetch for example to send the request to HTTP localhost:3000 for now because we're running this locally

but again this is like a separate server, it is technically a separate server and then here, we want to send the request to /add-location because that's the path we're filtering out with a post request here. So send this to /add-location and now configure this request because as I just said it should be a post request, so we want to add the method here and set this to post and add a body to this request and this body should be the coordinates and the address.

lectures.title: Understanding CORS (Cross Origin Resource Sharing)
lectures.text:
CORS stands for a cross origin resource sharing. Now the idea beyond CORS is simple, you have some applications, some web site running on yourpage.com, for example our find a place application where we see something on the screen and pick a location and then we have another server, for example our backend with these two routes we added, othersite.com which you want to talk to from your first page. So we get these two applications, maybe we build both of them but they're running on different servers as it is the case for us, one is running on localhost:3000, the other on localhost:8080 and these are technically two different servers.

Now we might want to exchange some resources, that could be a script which we want to fetch from the other side, we can send a request and get it but it could also be a request which we want to send to the other side. And now by default, browsers block such cross origin requests, only requests to the same origin, so to the same domain, are allowed, so on yourpage.com, we could only communicate with any routes that are registered on the same server, not on a different server.

Now this exists for a good reason because by default, you of course want to protect resources, you shouldn't be able to fetch any data from any server but in the modern web, where this setup of having standalone API servers is quite common, you of course want to be able to eject from this default, you want to tell the browser that this access is OK. So in our example here, on the backend, so on the Node.js server and always on the backend when you have CORS issues, we have to set some extra headers that signal to the browser that this is fine, that this access is fine, that we're allowing this access from this other page, so we want to grant access to our post route and our get route for example and we do so by going to app.js and by adding some extra headers. We can add these headers here before we reach our routes where we do send the response, simply with a middleware function here where we get the request, get the response and get this next function and there on the response, we want to add a couple of headers. The headers we need to add there are access-control-allow-origin, the value for that can be a star or the URL from what you want to allow access, so we could also specify localhost:3000 there but I'll add a star which means any other server

can send me a request. We also should add another header here, allow methods, here we can restrict the HTTP methods we want to support and since I only have post and get routes which I want to expose to the public, we can write post, get here, so if you send me a put request you would still not be allowed access but these two methods are allowed and you can also add other headers to restrict the usage of your API, of your backend server here. Attached you find a link where you can learn more about CORS and which headers you can set there, these two are all the headers we need however. We thereafter should call next here so that the request is able to continue to our routes and with that we can save this and restart our backend server.

Now back to the application, let's try this again. You don't even need to reload this page, we can just clear the error here to see if we get a new one, click find place again and still fail. The reason for that can be really tricky to understand but for post requests, browsers actually also send another request first where they try to find out whether the post request is allowed. You can see this in the network tab actually, here this add location request has a method of options.

We never send an options request here in our code but the browser does this automatically for some HTTP methods, for example for post requests. So on the server side, we need to allow options requests as well by simply adding this to the allowed methods and now actually one more thing we should also do is add one extra header here and that's the access-control-allow-headers option where we defined which headers the client might send to us, which special headers and there I want to allow the content type header because we're setting this in the client side code as well.

And now with that, we can restart the server, clear our errors here on the client, click find place again and now it works and we get back our success response there. So this is now how we can send a post request from a different server, from our client side server which has this static application, which has some client side Javascript running on it to our Node.js backend application which also uses Javascript but in the Node.js context and which now communicates as REST API with this client side project and that's quite a typical setup actually.

lectures.title: Wrap Up
lectures.text:
So this is it with this module. We learned a lot about Node.js, that it uses regular Javascript syntax but adds its own APIs, like the filesystem, its own packages we can use and does of course not support the browser default APIs like the DOM or browser storage because it doesn't run in the browser but that instead we run Javascript in a different environment, on our machine or on any machine where Node.js is installed. We can also not just use Node.js to run utility scripts like this one, we can use it to set up a HTTP server, either by doing everything on our own or by tapping into the rich ecosystem that exists around Node.js, where we have packages and frameworks like Express and other packages together with Express.js, that allow us to focus on our core business logic and where we don't have to worry about parsing data and so on.

And there you learned how you can set up a server which returns some server side rendered HTML files or how you can create a so-called REST API, where you have various endpoints, various URLs you support on that server that do different tasks depending on the HTTP method path combination that reaches your server. You even learned how to store data in a database and get it from there and with that you should have a good idea of which problem Node.js solves, how it generally works, that it's just Javascript in the end but with a totally different purpose or giving you totally different options of what you can do with it and therefore now you really have a broad overview of Javascript and what you can do with it and where you can run it and what that means for your applications.

lectures.text:
So what could go wrong when we write Javascript code or when we expose our Javascript code? For that, we also have to differ between writing code that runs in the browser and writing code that runs on the server and I will start with something that is only relevant if you're writing browser side Javascript code and that would be security details in your code or private information in your Javascript code. We'll also have a look at cross site scripting attacks though which is also relevant for browser side Javascript code.

I'll briefly touch on cross site request forgery or CSRF attacks which is related to both frontend backend code but which only works or only is a thing if you have some backend you're sending data to and therefore I'll briefly talk about that as well and I'll revisit this concept of cross origin resource sharing we already talked about earlier. So let's start with the security details in your code, what do I mean with that? The important thing to understand about Javascript in the browser is that your Javascript code is part of what the browser downloads and runs in the browser, so all your code runs on the machine of your page visitors and it's important to understand that your Javascript code can be read by them, anyone who is visiting your page can read your Javascript code that runs on this page, it's not hidden, it's not compiled to some unreadable machine code, it's totally available to anyone visiting your page and that is super important.

Therefore any security relevant details you have in there, any confidential data you have in there is exposed to your users and therefore it should not be in there, you should not have security relevant information or confident data in your client side, in your browser side Javascript code because attackers may be able to abuse that exposed data, for example if you have your database credentials in there, attackers could read them and could connect to your database to then read your data, change your data or do whatever they want to do or if you're storing some client related data, so about all your users, not just this user who's visiting your page but all users of your page, if you have something like this in your browser side Javascript code, well then anyone can read it and you might expose information about other people to all users.

So therefore because of this database example or any other data that might be confidential, you should ensure that such does not end up in there and let me show you what I mean. I'm back in our practice application we wrote, so this application and you might remember that in the debugging section, we had a look at the sources tab and there we actually could read the source code of this page, here in the assets scripts folder, there it is. Now of course here, we're seeing the code after webpack worked on it.

This is the code in development mode and therefore if you scroll enough at some point, you will find your actual code and it will be quite readable because it's not minified because it's not optimized at all. So all of this actually will be quite accessible and quite readable if you scroll down far enough and therefore anything you have in there is exposed, for example if I scroll also the bottom where our script code should actually be found, we see here it's hinting at location.js and if we scroll to the right, we actually find our code in here, this all inline code, that's our code, it's of course a bit hard to read but it is readable and it's not just us who can read that, anyone visiting our page can read that.

Now once you build for production, this will be optimized and it will be more unreadable Bbut there are tools to make it a bit more readable, actually built here in the dev tools if you click on pretty print, this code is formatted such that it's a bit easier to read if it were minified and besides that if someone is really interested in getting your data, there are certain pieces of data, like your database connection string and your password which is just a string which of course will always be the same string, no matter if the other code is minified or not, so such data can be found and can be used.

So any data which could be abused by other people should not go in there, should not go into your client side Javascript code. Now in this project specifically, you might be wondering about things like our Google API key, isn't that for example a security relevant detail? Well it could be but in Google's case or in the Google API key case here, you can actually restrict the usage of that key in your Google developer console, there you could restrict that only certain IP addresses can use that key so that only the IP address where you are hosting your application can really send requests with that help of that key and if anyone steals that key and tries to use it, Google will block requests by that person's IP address.

So this is some security mechanism which a lot of APIs offer if you use their API keys and therefore this is not a security relevant detail. That would be a different thing though if we would expose data from our backend, from this Node.js application. Now keep in mind here, I loaded a different project, this is the Node.js application we wrote and there for example in the location.js file, we are connecting to the MongoDB database, here I got my password and my user name I use there.

Now this is data which is not exposed to our users because this is now actually only running on the server through Node.js, this runs on a machine and the user will never be able to see that code because this Javascript code is never sent to the user, it's never attached to the outgoing HTML page, it's not loaded by any outgoing HTML page. So this code here is secure, it runs on a server and unless users can access our server, which of course requires them to effectively hack our server, they can't read that code, so this code is secure but if this code here were in our client side Javascript code, so in the code which is loaded by the browser and which the user can see, then users could see that data and abuse it.

So long story short, don't put any important, confident information into your client side code, users can read it and there is absolutely no way for you to avoid that. You can make that code harder to read, you can minify it and so on but it will always be readable and people can therefore read it.

Still having a green zero here is nice to have but even more important is that any packages you use that end up in your code, like the Google Maps package here, that these packages are also trustworthy and secure.

lectures.title: CSRF Attacks (Cross Site Request Forgery)
lectures.text:
So that were cross site scripting attacks, the most dangerous attack pattern when we talk about Javascript code. They only affect browser side Javascript code but since this is the part where you typically run a lot of Javascript code, it is a thing you definitely have to watch out for it and you have to be aware of. Now with that however, let's move on to cross site request forgery. What is this attack? It can be related to cross site scripting attacks but it doesn't have to be. The idea behind cross site request forgery is that people trick you into clicking on a link that leads to a prepared page where they abuse your local cookies to then send a request to the page you would normally talk to as well, let's say your online banking backend but since you are coming from a prepared page, you then do something there automatically without you recognizing that you don't want to do, for example send money to someone you don't want to send, maybe that even as possible to happen behind the scenes without you noticing.

So this attack pattern also depends on injected content, so injected Javascript code but it can also be just HTML content which submits a form to the trusted server, the problem is that the form is part of an untrusted page which you might not recognize if the URL look similar and then requests on your behalf with your cookies can be made to the trustworthy server, so the only danger and the only problem is that this is all happening from a malicious site.

So actions might be executed on the trustworthy page with your data without you knowing that it happens and therefore you might want to protect against that. Let's have a closer look at this pattern, though I do talk about it in more detail and also how to prevent it in my Node.js course because this is more a server side issue. You need to protect against CSRF attacks on the server side by using a mechanism which is a CSRF token and again I do discuss this in my Node.js course where we work on the server side on the backend all the time.

So CSRF stands for cross site request forgery and the idea is that if you're the user of a web app and you have some backend, let's say the online banking site which uses Node.js or any other programming language, this is not exclusive to Javascript, uses any programming language and it talks to database, the server. Now you are visiting the frontend of this page, let's say that the user interface of your online banking site and now when you have such a setup, typically the server-side application identifies you with a so-called session, so you logged in and then the server side generates this session object, stores session data on the server and sends you the session ID which is stored in a cookie, that's a typical authentication setup you have in web pages where frontend and backend work together.

Now then you might be sending an intended request, for example to send money to be and all is good. The problem is that if you now visit a fake site because someone sends you a link to it, which looks like the trustworthy site but which isn't, then you visit this page and there, people send a request to the trustworthy backend, therefore the browser attaches cookies that belong to this trustworthy backend which is your session ID for example and everything works.

The problem just is since you're on a fake site, the request might be one that is intended by the fake site but not by you, for example to send money to C and this request will succeed because you sent the right cookie, the right session ID and you sent it through the right backend. So again more details can be found in a Node.js course but this is also a potential tech pattern but not directly linked to Javascript. It can be implemented with cross site scripting attacks but it can also be implemented by using such a fake site which does not require cross site scripting attacks.

So therefore this is not really a Javascript security thing, it's more a server side or general web application security thing and therefore I do discuss it in more detail in my Node.js course where we write a lot of server side code.

lectures.title: CORS (Cross Origin Resource Sharing)
lectures.text:
The last security hole you should be aware of or the last security relevant concept you should be aware of to be precise is cross origin resource sharing and I did talk about this earlier already. It's not really an attack pattern but a security concept. The idea here is that requests from your browser side application can only be made to a backend, so to a server side that runs on the same server, so that the HTML page and the script that executes there was served by the same server you're trying to send the request to, that's how browsers by default work with your pages, this is what they allow by default.

Now in modern web applications, you often need to send requests to other servers though, so a server which did not serve the running HTML and Javascript code but which only provides some API endpoints, some URLs to which you can send data, to store data or to fetch data, this is something we had to look at in the Node.js module. Then you can control via server side headers and only via server side response headers whether this request, this incoming request is allowed and you send back a valid response or not.

So this is a concept where by default browsers would not allow you to reach out to some other server but with the right server side headers, you can override this. So it's a concept which in the end should secure servers so that not everyone can access their resources, not every page can access their resources at least but with the right headers on the server side, you can allow this and an example for that actually would be Javascript modules. This built-in Javascript concept also required a development server if you remember and it required a development server because Javascript modules, so Javascript files you import into another file are only allowed if they're from the same server.

So I'm only used to importing another Javascript file which sits on the same server which is served by the same server and here we have no real way of changing this because that's a built-in security mechanism by browsers specifically for this Javascript feature. Another example though would be the Node.js application we worked on. There, we have our different routes which we handle on the backend, like add location and the request which is sent there is not sent from some page that is served by the same server, it's sent by a page that runs on a different domain, on a different server and still it works because here, I set these right CORS headers which tell the browser that's okay, this page which sends the request is allowed to get the data and therefore the browser won't block it.

So it's a security mechanism which you can use or disable or configure to your needs based on your requirements. That's the idea behind CORS, this cross origin resource sharing concept.

So let's dive into this deployment process, starting with a web application, a web site which has no server side code which is only powered by HTML, Javascript and CSS and which therefore needs a static host. Now we clearly wrote our code, we tested it throughout this course and if you're working on your own application, you of course also at some point tested it, now we need to optimize it and build it for production and then we can deploy the output.

Here's this practice app we worked on and we wrote the code, we tested that, now regarding the optimization and producing the deployment output and so on, for that we've got webpack, we got our webpack configuration, both a production configuration and a development configuration for testing this, for bundling this and for production, for also optimizing this which webpack will do automatically if the mode is production. So here in package.json, we got this build prod script and now we can simply run this, we can run npm run build: prod and what this will give us is an output which we can ship to a web server to then host it there, to a static web server to be precise.

So here, we got our dist folder and in the end we just need to take that entire dist folder content and deploy that. Now the only adjustment we specifically need to do here is our output, our Javascript files of course have this random hash in there and we should respect this in our imports. So on these Javascript files in the end, you can copy that file name and take the my-place file and replace this import here in assets index.html with this name here and do the same for share place.

Now you can also set up more elaborate build workflows, where the HTML file is automatically adjusted but this requires advanced webpack knowledge and so on and therefore we'll take this manual approach here. Now once you did that, once you prepared these script imports in the two HTML files and you have your optimized script outputs here, you're ready to go and you're ready to upload it to a web server. We can ignore this warning here by the way, it basically warns us that our my-place output is pretty big, well that's the case because I'm importing the sanitize-HTML library there which is rather big, another reason for why you should do this on the server side and not on the client side by the way but we have it here for a good reason because in this app, we have no server side code, so we have to live with that.

Now once we adjusted everything, we built everything, we're ready to ship this onto a static host. Now as I mentioned you could set up your own computer, connect it to the Internet, allow incoming requests as well and configure everything on your own, well this however is not easy to do. It's easy to do in a wrong and an insecure way so that your server could easily get compromised and even in that way, it still requires some network knowledge to set up such a computer and connect it to the Internet, therefore what you would typically do is you would go for paid hosting.

You can search for a static web hosting for example and you'll find a couple of services, both in the advertisements as well as in the real search results which help you host a static web site, for example AWS, the Amazon Web Services have a service that makes that easy, the S3 service. There are other services as well and one service I like because it's really easy to get started with is Firebase hosting. Firebase is a Google service which offers more than just the hosting but here we just need the hosting so we can use that. You can click on that Firebase hosting search result here and it takes you to the Firebase documentation where you can learn more about Firebase, Firebase hosting and how to use it and of course here you can also learn more about the other Firebase services in case you should be interested.

Now here, what we can do is we can simply click on get started here and we'll learn how we can get started with Firebase hosting and it all starts with installing the Firebase CLI for which you can click on this link here to be taken to a page where the installation is explained and you can simply download an installer here, an alternative to downloading an installer here is that you simply use npm for the installation and you run this command here on your machine anywhere.
