Once you run init here, you might be prompted to log in first, so simply go back to Firebase and create an account there, you don't need to pay anything, it's free, just create an account or log in with your Google account and once you do have an account, log in here in the console by entering your email address and thereafter your password when you're being prompted for it.

Once you did log in, you should see this menu here where you can choose from a variety of Firebase services and we need the hosting service, so navigate there and press space to select it and thereafter press enter. Now you can choose your option here and here I want to create a new project, this talks about Firebase projects which are created on Firebase servers and we don't have one yet and you can enter any name here, I'll name it js-static-hosting, you can choose any name you want here.

Now this actually was the project ID, now you can choose a project name which can be the same though so I'll go with the default and just hit enter and not provide a different name and now this will set up this Google Cloud Platform, which behind the scenes powers Firebase project and make sure that this is all configured on Firebase servers. So let's wait for that to finish and once this finished, you're prompted to tell Firebase what your public directory is which in the end means which is the directory where your deployable files is seated and in my case that's not the default, a folder named public but instead it's this dist folder.

So we should write this here to make it clear that the dist folder is the folder we wanted deploy. Now once you hit enter, you're asked if you want to configure this as a single page app, which means that anything the user enters in the URL is redirected to the root index.html file and here I don't want to do that, so I'll enter no here, an n because we have different folders with different HTML files, I don't want to redirect all requests to this top level index.html file.

So enter n here and hit enter, you will also get a 404.html file now which is a default error page which you of course can customize in case the user enters an invalid URL and when you're asked if you want to override this index.html, you should choose no of course because we want to keep the existing index.html file in there and with that, we're done. Now you can run Firebase deploy here and it will go ahead and deploy this project which was just configured to Firebase servers, which means it uploads your files in the dist folder to Firebase servers and configures everything you need there and once this is done, it gives you the URL where where you can find your application.

So now here if we enter a new tab, we can visit our application here, also check the console, the only error I'm getting there is the favicon which is not found and that's OK and now in here if I try to get my current location, I can allow this and check whether that works, whether I am being located here, yes that works. I can click share place and enter my shared place URL here to see this page. So this all works, this is our deployed project, our deployed static project I should say which only consists of HTML, Javascript and CSS files which we now deployed to Firebase and of course the exact deployment steps, for example the command line tool which we used here will differ from host to host, the general idea regarding the fact that you deploy everything in this dist folder and so on will always be the same though, so that's something which does not change.

Also worth noting, in Firebase case you get a firebaserc and a firebase.json file which allows you to configure the exact hosting setup and you learned more about the available options there, of course in the official documentation in case you're interested. So check this documentation out if you plan on using Firebase, if you plan on using a different service which of course is fine too, there are many great services, check out this services documentation to learn about the exact steps you need to execute to get your code onto this services servers.

lectures.title: Injecting Script Imports Into HTML Automatically
Example: Dynamic Page Deployment (with Server-side Code)
lectures.text:
So we deployed our static page with HTML, Javascript and CSS, what about our Node.js application now? Here we have code that needs to execute on the server, not in the client, therefore this is not a static application, it's a dynamic application because we have code that needs to execute directly on the server and by the way, it does not matter if you have an application which produces HTML files and returns those as we set it up at the beginning of the Node.js module or if you have an application which just has a couple of routes and exchanges JSON data, that does not matter, you need to execute Node.js code on the server, That is what matters.

So now we need a host that supports this and Firebase is not such a host. Well they do have some cloud function service which actually allows you to execute code on the server but it's a little bit different, it's not really meant for this kind of deployment, even though technically there are ways of making it work. However it's not what we will use here, instead if you for example Google for Node.js hosting, then you will find a couple of advertisements and of course also real results that guide you towards Node.js hosting services and of course you can perform a similar research for other languages like PHP as well.

Now one popular service for hosting Node.js applications is actually Heroku. It's of course again not the only one, AWS also has services for example but Heroku allows you to get started for free without a credit card just like Firebase and that of course is very convenient. So you learned a lot about the Javascript syntax and how to write Javascript code and obviously that's what this course is about. Now in this module, we'll also dive in an important related topic and that would be performance optimizations because of course it's nice that we're able to write Javascript code but we want to write good Javascript code and most importantly, you should be able to find out whether you wrote code that offers a good performance to your end users or whether there are things you can improve or you might need to fix to avoid a bad user experience.

Specifically in this module, we'll have a look at what exactly performance is because it turns out that is rather a broad term and it can be a lot of different things. We'll also have a look at some tools or approaches of measuring and analyzing performance and finding out how our application behaves. So in this module, I want to get you started, we'll dive deeply into all the important concepts but thereafter I'll also give you the tools so that you can build up on this and analyze and optimize any part of your web site, of your web application. So let's dive right in.

lectures.title: What is "Performance Optimization" About?
lectures.text:
So what is performance? Now when we think about performance in the context of a web site we're visiting, performance can be a lot of different things but I think there are two main categories into which we can split this term performance. We can have a look at the startup time of a web site, of a web application and we can have a look at the runtime performance because these are really two different things that of course in the end work together end and which both matter. Startup time is all about the question how long does it take to see something on the screen and how quickly is a user able to interact with the page, we all know how it feels like when we visit a page which is slow, which takes forever to load or which at some point seems like it loaded but when we try to click something, nothing happens, so we all know that and therefore this is of course one important part. But then once a page did load, of course it should also offer a great performance and also avoid certain bugs.

Here the question is how is smooth the application runs in general, does it occasionally freeze or lag? We of course don't like visiting pages where we for example try to enter some text into a text box and it takes us forever to do so because our input is only picked up with a lag, especially web sites or web applications, I use these terms interchangeably as you can tell, with a lot of animations could end up in a state where we have a lot of visual lag, a lot of visual change where the animations don't play smoothly or anything like that or where a running animation prevents us from doing anything else or of course we could have a web site with certain memory leaks which add up over time, so where some part of the code is buggy and actually occupies more and more memory the more often it runs and depending on the device you're running this website on, eventually the device or the page might run out of memory and the browser might shut it down therefore, so that of course is also something we want avoid but it's also important to understand that performance is not just about Javascript but about everything that's involved when it comes to visiting and using a web page.

It's influenced by a lot of factors, the CSS code and HTML code also play a role. If you have very complex CSS selectors, that takes the browser longer to apply styling. If you have a lot of unnecessary HTML code, that is more code which needs to be downloaded initially hence slowing down the startup time but of course Javascript is a major factor because that influences a lot of the parts related to runtime performance and if you're downloading a lot of Javascript code, it of course also influences the startup time negatively.

Also of course the speed of the server you're hosting your web site on, as well as the configuration of the server can have a negative impact on your users. If you have a server that resides in the US and you have a lot of users from let's say India, well it simply takes you a bit longer to get your data from the server. Now of course we're talking about milliseconds here and it might not really have an impact but the bigger your application is, the more users you're reaching, the more you want to think about all the factors that influence performance or that could potentially influence performance and optimize them.

In this module however, I will focus on the Javascript performance part but I want to put that out there that there are other factors which also play a role. Now when we talk about Javascript performance, what influences our performance there? When we think about our Javascript execution, of course here again we have two different areas, we have the startup time, the question here is how fast the script loads and is able to execute and we have the runtime performance and here it's all about the work the script has to do and how efficiently it does that work and it's not just about the work the script does on its own but also about the interactions with our other web page, when you work with the DOM for example, when you add and remove HTML elements via Javascript, that can have a negative impact on the overall web application performance if you doing this in a poor way and I'll come back to that in this module and of course we have this memory thing. You want to avoid memory leaks to make sure that you're not slowing down the application over time or that you even have the worst case scenario of the browser shutting down your application.

Now also it's important to understand that I talked about the browser here, I talked about the DOM but of course Javascript as you'll learned does not just run in the browser. Now the startup time, that's really a thing that is primarily related to the browser side because when we're talking about server side Javascript with Node.js, then there is no download delay or anything like that, The code already is on the server where it will get executed, so that whole startup time thing is less of an issue on the server side because all the code is already there so therefore it can be executed very efficiently and quickly by default.

But when we talk about runtime performance, that affects all Javascript environments, all places where we can execute Javascript. Of course there are certain problems which can only occur in the browser, for example when we talk about DOM interaction but there also are other parts, other things about Javascript which apply to both browser side and server side Javascript. In this modular, I will focus on the browser side because there we actually have more pitfalls but we'll also have a look at certain things which you will see really affect any Javascript code no matter where it runs.

lectures.title: Optimization Potentials
lectures.text:
So we have these different layers of performance optimization we could say, we have the startup time and the runtime and now let's have a look at the different things which affect performance there. Now of course there are a lot of tiny factors which influence it but there are a couple of bigger categories and potential improvements I'd like to think about when we have a look at these different layers. For the startup time, an important factor is the size of our scripts, so simply the question how big is our Javascript file we're forcing the user to download before anything is able to happen on the page?

Remember when I said a couple of minutes ago that we have two parts when we think about startup time - the time it takes to display something on the screen and the time it takes until the user is able to do something with that screen, well the script size can affect both. If your script renders a lot of visual parts on the screen, then of course it affects how quickly the user is able to see something on the screen but it most certainly will impact how quickly the user is able to interact because if your script is needed to add event listeners to a button and so on, then of course even if the button is visible the user will not be able to do anything with it if your script hasn't finished downloading yet and isn't available yet.

So therefore the script size, the size of the script file really plays an important role here, the bigger it is the longer it takes users to download them and the longer it will take users to work with your page and keep in mind that not every user is visiting your page from a great Internet connection. Users might be using slow devices in slow network areas and therefore even a script file which is only 100kb big can take a couple of seconds to download and that could lead to a bad user experience.

Now besides the script size, it's also the amount of HTTP round trips and I covered this earlier when we talked about Javascript modules and when we introduced webpack to bundle them into a single or a few bundles and the reason for a that is that if we're working with a lot of script files and of course the same is true for a lot of CSS files by the way, then the browser has to download all these files to make your page work and every HttpRequest that needs to be sent to download something has a certain base cost it takes to set up that request and send it, no matter how big the file is which you're downloading.

So the more HTTP round trips it takes to finally have the final state of your page, the longer it will take until your page is ready to run and therefore this is definitely a part you want to optimize and of course we already started optimizing both the size and the number of HTTP round trips by adding webpack which does minify and optimize our code and which also bundles our code together. So now what about the runtime performance? There, it's of course all about optimizing our code execution. If we're working in the browser environment, that also includes one important aspect and that is DOM access, so when we work with the DOM, when we add elements, when we remove elements, we want to avoid unnecessary code execution, we want to write code which is efficient to execute and we definitely want to avoid unnecessary DOM operations because if we unnecessarily for example re-render too many elements on the screen even though maybe just one element needs to change, then we affect performance because it turns out working with the DOM is really expensive from a performance perspective because Javascript has to talk to the browser, the browser has to go through the DOM and find the place you want to change, it then has to create a new element, it has to add the

element or remove one, whatever you're doing and that all are a lot of steps. Now of course we're still talking about milliseconds here but they can really add up, so being efficient here is super important as you will see in this module. The other big factor are memory leaks, it's easy to introduce leaks and not all leaks are horrible, you might not even recognize them and I can tell you a lot of web pages out there do have tiny memory leaks but if you have bigger ones, they can really add up and can lead to your page becoming slower or to actually even crash in the worst case scenario. Now it's also interesting to think about different ways of solving one and the same problem in Javascript, so to find code alternatives with better performance. I will show an example for this throughout this module. In the end here this is related to the first box here in the runtime performance part, the code execution which we want to optimize. When you for example loop through an array, it turns out you have a couple of different ways of doing so and they don't all have the same performance, so that's also a thing you could think about and you could try to optimize. Related to that is another approach which is called micro optimizations,

you can optimize certain parts of your code and actually looping through an array with a quicker alternative would be one example for such a micro optimization, you can optimize parts of your code for specific use cases. You could opt to use a certain data structure because it's a bit quicker than that other approach you used before. Now generally, you want to shy away from such micro optimizations though and I will come back to those throughout the module and explain why you should be really careful when you try to optimize everything but it is a thing which can matter in niche scenarios and very large applications, the most important parts you want to care about are the first two boxes here in the runtime performance part and of course all the boxes in the startup time performance part. And of course as mentioned, always keep in mind that Javascript is just one part, when we talk about optimizing our web page, it also includes things like writing efficient CSS and so on but that's simply not the focus of this course and Javascript typically is the most important thing to optimize.

So with that we're almost done with the theory, let's now find out how we can approach this whole performance optimization thing.

lectures.title: Measuring Performance
lectures.text:
Now when you want to optimize your page, it's actually wrong to just go into the code and start changing anything, instead you want to measure and audit your page and find performance bottlenecks. Don't guess, it's that measure. You want to find out how many round trips you have, how big your script is which needs to be downloaded. You maybe want to set certain budgets so that you know okay, my script has to be below 100kb and if it is above it, I will do everything I can to shrink it.

So that's of course one important thing and you want to find out how big it is and how long it takes before you start optimizing it. You also want to measure the runtime performance with the help of browser dev tools. There are a lot of useful features in modern browser dev tools which you can use to find out how long certain parts of your script take and then you can find out if that seems too long to you, you can try out an alternative and find out if that is actually better.

You can also explore best practices and patterns and benchmarks you find on the Internet, you will find a lot of blog posts and discussions when you Google Javascript performance or even more specific performance questions and you can then have a look at how other people are solving certain problems or how they are approaching certain things, so this can also be a useful thing to find out what you could look into and also important because that is a common mistake, when you do measure performance, measure your production ready code.

Don't do this in development mode because in development mode, your code is not optimal at all, build tools like webpack where you use the webpack dev server inject a lot of extra code into your code to enhance the debugging experience. Now that's great for finding ordinary issues and problems but it's not great for measuring performance because the performance during development will not be that great because it's simply not what matters during development but if you want to of course have great performance in production, so it's the production ready code you should test.

Now when we talk about measuring performance, there are a couple of different ways of measuring it. Now I mentioned the browser dev tools, you also can add certain code snippets to your code, to be precise you can use performance now which is available in the browser to get a time snapshot and you can take that before and after your running operation you're not sure about and this allows you to find out how long an operation takes. Then of course outside of your code, you do have the browser dev tools as I mentioned, where you have many features that allow you to detect all kinds of different problems and bottlenecks you might have in your code and you also have certain web sites like jsperf.com which allow you to benchmark certain code alternatives against each other and find out which one is quicker.

You also have webpagetest.com, which is a site you can use to test a hosted web site, so not your locally running one but a hosted web site and which then we'll give you a rich report on how that site performed and what you could look into there. Now these are just some tools and I can only recommend that you also Google web site performance, Javascript performance to find more approaches and more tools that might work well for you.

So in product management, in delete product, I don't want to call a render products in the end but instead update products. Now we can optimize this code later, for now I'll add a variable, deleted product and here in this loop where I go over all my products, I'll check if the product I'm looking at does not have the ID of the deleted one which means I want to keep it which is why I add it to updated products which I then set as my new products array, so else if the IDs do match, I know this is the product which was deleted, so I'll set deleted product equal to prod in that case. And then down there, deleted product is what I want to forward here, prodId which is the argument I get here is the ID I want to forward, here I point at the function itself for this argument which the delete part of the update products function won't even use though and important, for is adding, we set false because we're not adding, we're deleting.

Now definitely, use this now as a chance to pause and try coming up with an approach of implementing adding in a way that doesn't affect everything or doesn't re-render everything, of course in the next lecture, we'll also do it together.

lectures.title: Micro-Optimizations (Think Twice!)
lectures.text:
Now one thing which also costs performance but it just is what it is in this app is the fact that we unshift the array because as you learned in the Arrays and Iterables section, this simply means that Javascript has to revisit all array elements and push them all to the end of the array because we add a new element at the very beginning, so all elements have to be moved but it is just what it is, if that is what we want to do in this app, well it is what we want to do and that's the part where you should be careful when you try to optimize everything.

It's easy to think in a super complex way and try to optimize things which really don't need optimization. Sure, using unshift is slower than using push but unless you're doing this every second on an array with thousands of items, you probably won't notice a difference because when we talk about performance, sure we might have a difference of let's say 10 milliseconds but will this matter? No, this will not matter. So you should be careful when you try to optimize everything, it's often not worth it and you might even break your app or come up with some strange workaround which offers a bad user experience or which in the worst case is even slower just because you try to avoid a certain way of doing something which just turns to be out the right way even though it technically is slower than some other way.

Let's dive a bit deeper into these micro optimizations though, i told you that you should measure before you optimize. Now thus far we haven't done too much measurement because the optimizations we did, mostly those regarding the DOM are no-brainers, they are better, they're also not micro optimizations, these are really optimizations which can matter. Now here's an example for a micro optimization where we want to check if it's better. In rendering.js, in render products here, I'm using for each.

Now this is not the only way of going through all items in an array as you know, so let's find out if it's the best one. For that, let's log a start time with performance.now which is a function that helps you measure performance, it gives you a timestamp in the end. Then here we have the end time which is also performance.now which executes after for each and then we can console log end time minus start time to get the time difference. Now let's save that and let's see what the time difference is.

Open the console here and you see here it logs around .33 and if we reload here multiple times, we see there are quite some differences which already shows you that you have to be careful regarding such optimizations, you would want to run this a couple of thousand times by writing some extra script which just refreshes this or executes your script to find out what is better. So here we see we have a couple of different numbers but we're somewhere around 30-ish but really there is a lot of deviation. Now let's try a different approach, let's comment out this approach and instead let's use a regular for loop, not even a for/of loop, a very traditional for loop where we have i which starts at zero, where we then loop as long as i is smaller as products.length, where then increment i by 1.

And now let's grab this code here, put it in here and here of course, we have to access products for index i and here, it's also products i and yes that should be it. Now let's save this. Now when you execute this a couple of times, you most likely will not see a significant difference, you might see some results which are faster, you might see less results which are on the higher end as we saw it before but there really is also a lot of randomness involved, as I said you would need to run this tens of thousands of times.

Well turns out there are pages which do this for you, jsperf.com is such a site. Now you need to log in with a github account here to create your own test cases which in the end are comparisons of different approaches but you can also go to the popular test cases down here to find comparisons other people ran and here I'm talking about Javascript code comparisons. For example here we have a comparison of for and for each and you see a lot of other comparisons down there as well.

Now this here is in the end of benchmark which in the end has an array with bunch of numbers as you can tell and then these different tests are being run, it tests going through all these items with a for loop, with a for/of loop, with the for each function and also with the reduce function. Now let's click on run tests and now it runs these tests for a couple of times and then it gives you an average, So let's wait for this to finish and what you should see and the exact results will differ, you can also run this for multiple times but what you should see is that the traditional for loop actually is fastest and if you google that, if you google for versus for/of Javascript and so on, you will find a lot of discussions where this is also discussed.

Indeed right now at least, the traditional for loop is faster than the for/of loop is faster than for each and so on. Now does this mean you should switch and replace all for/of loops with this loop? Why did I even teach you for/of if it's slower? Because when we talk about it being slow here, we have to be really careful. When we talk about a difference, like here in my browser of 11%, that's not a lot, you might not be running across an array with that thousands of items multiple times every second, if you do that, the difference might matter. Most of the time, 99% of all applications, you're not going to do that because if you would do that, even with the fastest approach, it would probably be slow at some point.

So when we talk about differences here, we really have to be careful that we don't go for the fastest result just because it shows it here and totally forget that this doesn't matter in most cases. So when you're comparing results, if you're benchmarking and you're checking whether approach A is faster than approach B, for example with benchmarking web sites like jsperf.com, you have to interpret the results with caution because of what I just said that you might not be running thousands of operations and the performance difference therefore really will not make a difference and then you should go for the code which is more readable and shorter and not for the most complex code which theoretically might run a bit faster and in addition, keep in mind that performance is not a fixed thing.

It might differ from browser to browser, thus far we only tested in Chrome, in Firefox it might be a bit different and it will change over time. Of course if approach A is slower than B at the moment, this does not mean it's slower in a year or in six months especially the newer Javascript engine features which were added one or two years ago will most likely become faster over time and they might overtake the existing, the older approaches then.

So of course you can then always go back to your code and reimplement it with the then best approach or you keep in mind that you're not running this operation thousands of times and therefore this micro optimization really doesn't matter. lectures.title: Wrap Up
lectures.text:
And with that we're done, now let me briefly sum up what we learned We had a look at runtime performance and potential improvements we can implement there. You should avoid unnecessary code executions, batch operations together and avoid unnecessary DOM access as you learned. You should of course also find and fix memory leaks, even small ones because they can add up and make your page slower or make it crash. For high frequency operations, you can compare different approaches, like the two for loop alternatives we had a look at and use the faster one and in general you might consider micro optimizations but you should also be careful about them because performance isn't a fixed thing, it can change in the future and you might be optimizing for something which really doesn't matter. When we have a look at startup performance, then we want to eliminate unnecessary or unused code, to download as small of a code package initially as possible.

You also want to avoid using too many third-party libraries for that reason because every third-party library you add is extra code which needs to be downloaded and parsed, so the more third-party libraries you load, the more code you have to download. If you use third-party libraries, you also want to consider importing them into your script files and then using webpack for bundling and code splitting instead of using CDN links because if you use CDN links, you can't use code splitting.

So bundling code and using lazy loading here really is a great idea for ensuring that your code starts fast and is able to execute as early as possible. Of course you should also minify code and webpack does this automatically to ensure that you ship as little code as possible to your end users and this is really it. You saw a lot of examples throughout this module, i hopefully could introduce you to how you should think about performance optimizations.

You also got some useful external resources where you can dive deeper and in general, performance optimization is a topic which you can't really master, it's an ongoing journey, there are always new things to explore and it's also very specific to your exact use case. It's always very specific to that regarding what you want to look into and what you might want to consider optimizing. You can also google for Javascript performance optimizations and you will find many examples, some which you already saw here, some which you didn't.

This can also be interesting to learn more about this topic but always also keep in mind that you shouldn't overdo it, you want to improve your application, you want to fix bugs and leaks but you don't want optimize every tiny bit because you could end up with code which is actually longer than before and therefore adds to the bundle size or you implemented an optimization which isn't optimal anymore in the future. Still, this hopefully got you started and i showed you some of the most important and critical aspects when it comes to performance optimizations and what you should keep in mind there.

lectures.title: Module Introduction
lectures.text: In this course we wrote a lot of code and we tested a lot of code of course. We always tested it manually by simply clicking around in our web application. In this module here, we'll dive into automated testing, that means we'll write code which will actually test our code, so code that runs to run other code and evaluate the results. This is indeed what this module will be about, we'll dive into what exactly testing is and why we use it, we'll have a look at different kinds of tests namely unit tests, integration tests and end-to-end tests and we'll also explore how we can test both synchronous and asynchronous code and in general, get a thorough introduction into the world of testing.

lectures.title: What Is Testing? Why Does It Matter?
lectures.text:
Now what is testing and why would we want to test ? Now testing, when you hear it for the first time, sounds pretty obvious, pretty straightforward. We are writing an app, we're creating an application and we simply test it, right, we had a feature, we opened the browser and we test our application and that is indeed how you will continue to work even if you do add this kind of testing I'll dive in in this video. So testing manually still is something that makes sense, you want to see your application run.

So in the end, the idea always is that we have our code and we have some expected result, so if we write some code and then we go into the browser and test this code we have some idea of what should happen, we want to open that modal, we want to add that user when we click that button, something like this. So we have our expected results in mind and then we simply test our application and if we are successful, we are fine with that, we can continue with writing the next piece of code and if we're not happy with the result, well then we can modify our code and fix the issue or adjust it such that it works in the way we want.

Now the idea of Javascript testing or code testing when you read it like this is that we automate this testing part, so that we automate it so that we don't have to manually test everything in our application. Now we will probably still test everything manually but automated tests can be run whenever we change something in code to see if that affects any part of our application without us having to test everything manually again, that's the idea behind automated testing, that we can see breaking changes or issues in our code, maybe introduced by a change in place A in a totally different place of our app, that we can see this instantly, That is one of the major benefits of writing tests.

So that is also one answer to the question, why would we want to test? We want to get an error and see the error if we break our code, we want to see that immediately without us testing everything manually, we might still do manual testing but it's still worth a lot to have a suite of predefined automated tests that we can run to quickly see did this change break anything, well with well written tests, we'll get the answer right away. We'll also save time if we don't have to test everything manually over and over again and we are also forced to think about possible issues or bugs when writing our tests.

We have to think about what do we want to test, how do we write a test that makes sense and I'll dive into that and this video already. We also can integrate it into our build workflow, this is something more advanced but there I mean that you could have a build workflow where you push a commit, so a git commit to your code repository like Github and then you have a workflow that automatically is triggered where this code is then tested in the cloud on some server and if the test succeeds, it's maybe deployed automatically. So you can build a very complex deployment chain there and tests are then an integral part of ensuring that no breaking or invalid code is deployed, so that is always an advantage of tests or something you can use tests for. We can also break up complex dependencies and that is also something I'll show in this video, we have to make sure we write code that can be split up, that is modular because this will make testing easier and ultimately it will make working with our code easier and it improves our code therefore since we are forced to follow certain patterns or to write code in a certain way or at least that will make testing easier, we will write better code all together.

So these are a lot of great advantages but they might still be a bit abstract when you have not written any tests, so let's dive into testing soon but not before I try to answer one other question and that is, which types of tests do we have? I'm talking about automated tests, so some code we write that tests our code, so code that tests code, that is a good description of what testing is or what automated testing is I guess and there we have different kinds of tests.

We have some tests that test a fully isolated piece of code, let's say a function that takes some input and returns some output. We can test such a function with a test because it has a clearly defined structure and we can say for input x and y, we expect to get output z and that would be a so-called unit test because we test a single, isolated unit of our application. We also have some tests that test units with some dependencies, so we have no isolated piece of code anymore but we might have a function that calls another function let's say and therefore the function we're testing depends on the result of another function and that is called an integration test because there, we're testing more than just a single unit, we test the integration of a feature into another features so to say. We also have the full flow which we can test or the user interface, so the full application or a part of the full application and this is so-called end-to-end or also user interface test.

The idea here is really that we do what we could do manually as well in the browser but that we write kind of an automated script that executes a certain series of steps for us and then we can check if the result is the result we expected to get. Now these kinds of tests have a different complexity, units tests are relatively easy to write because you have a small unit and you know it is easy to infer what you want to get as a result. The more dependencies you add, the more complex it becomes because it gets harder to differentiate between what exactly is causing an error, is it a dependency or the function that uses the dependencies.

Also you might have some dependencies that reach out to a server and fetch data, that is also complexity you have to handle and I will show you how to handle this in a separate video. And the full user interface test is the most complex one because there, you have to define every step that should be executed and cleverly think about what you want to test and what you want to expect there. Now also due to this complexity, we write tests in a different frequency.

We typically have a lot of unit tests because if you test every unit of your application and it works correctly, you can kind of infer that the overall application will also work correctly, so we will have a lot of unit tests. We then have some integration tests to rule out that two individually working units don't work anymore if you combine them and we have a few UI or end-to-end tests, to test some steps or some flows in our application in the browser, in an automated way.

So these are the kinds of tests and in this video I will show you all three already and with that I'd say it's enough of the theory, let's start writing some tests.

I got util.js which holds the functions and importing into app.js I'm using Node.js modules syntax here simply because that's a bit easier to test and doesn't require a complex build workflow setup, on which I simply didn't want to focus on this video but I use webpack to then bundle this all up and get a main.js file which is the file we then use.

Now what you can do is you can simply double click index.html, I got no dev server in place here or anything like that, simply to not focus too much on the frontend workflow and if you did double click on that file, this is what you'll get, you can enter some data and add a user and that is all we can do here. So it's a relatively simple app but that is great for starting with testing because we can easily confirm if our tests make sense, if they do test something we would test manually as well.

So this is the application and now let's write some tests. Now for writing tests, we need some tools to help us with creating these tests. What do we need? We typically need three kinds of tools - we need a test runner which is simply a tool that executes our tests and summarizes the results and gives us some output on the results, we can use something like mocha there, that is a popular test runner. lectures.title: Writing & Running Integration Tests
lectures.text:
So let's now write an integration test and for integration testing, if we have a look at all our code, which function could we use there? Well we got, in the app.js file, we got add user which uses a lot of other functions which has a lot of dependencies. So testing this function would be an integration test but this is a function that does neither take an input nor return an output, instead it's a function that really added something, that DOM, so this is something which you might want to test in an end-to-end testing scenario or in a user interface test but an integration test would be kind of hard here, we would have to do a lot of manual DOM interaction inside of our test which you can do but which you might not want to do.

Instead there is something else I can test and that is basically a part of that function you could say. In the end what I'm doing in add user is I do select a couple of elements, then I do validate the input and then I generate a text based on the input. Now we could outsource this into a separate function and that is a part of writing modular code that I mentioned earlier, you are forced to write modular code which also makes your code easier to manage and reuse though.

So in util.js, I can export a new function and let's name it check and generate or whatever you want to do. Now check and generate will get a name and an age as an input and then I will go to my app.js file and I will grab that validation code and move it into check and generate to validate input for and now that's important, for the name here and then there, for the age like this and then if we make it past this if block, I will return a call to generate text where I pass a name and age because that is what I then return here, I return the checked text.

So in app.js where I'm using this, output text in the end just the result of my call to check and generate, I don't need validate input here anymore, I don't generate text anymore, I'll just import check and generate, this new function, I'll import that in app.js and down there, output text is the result of check and generate and I can move that up here and here I can now simply check if not output text, so if we did return let's say false here, we return false if validation fails, so if this is returned and therefore if this is not true-ish, if it is false for example, then it will return an add user too and it will not continue creating that element.

So now this is the tweak add user function and this gives us the check and generate function which is great to use in an integration test. So let's write the test for it and I want to test if my validity works correctly and I then get the expected text back, so I should generate a valid text output, something like this and then here in this function, I will test my check and generate function which I therefore have to import and I can simply create my text with check and generate and I pass Max and 29 here and I would expect this text to be equal to Max 29 years old.

So my expectation actually is the same as in this unit test but it's not a simple unit test because the function we're testing has more to it. We could fail because validation fails or because generate text fails, however generate text is kind of ruled out because we have a separate unit test for this and this is also how you want to write your test by the way. You want to ensure that you drill down like to the smallest possible level and write unit tests for all your units, so write a test for generate text would also be worth writing one for validate input and then your integration tests really just rely on the units being tested and ensure that the units also work together well, so this is then the idea behind an integration test.

So here I have this test and if I now save this, it actually fails. Now I get an error that validate input is not defined here and that's true because I do export validate input, I don't need to do that anymore, I should instead create it or define it as a constant, the same is true for generate text so that I can use these functions directly in the util.js file and then at the bottom, I should also export generate text and assign the generate text constant here and also export validate input maybe and assign that constant, so that I could use it in other files too and now you see my tests passed, both tests passed.

Now the idea about the integration test is that if I do change something in my check and generate function, for example here I use my validate input function incorrectly, so the result of that is used incorrectly, now it fails and now this is a great example of why I have an integration test. I could have a separate test in validate input and validate input does work correctly, I can tell you that but my error is directly here in check and generate, I'm using the result of validate input incorrectly by not checking for it being false but for it being true and this means if my name is valid, then I actually return false which is of course the wrong logic in check and generate.

So even though my units work correctly, the combination of the units fails because I have an error here and this again shows you the power of tests and why integration tests makes sense too and unit tests alone could not be enough because all units could be working, if you are combining them incorrectly, you still have a problem, so now it's working again though.

lectures.title: Writing & Running e2e Tests
lectures.text:
Now that we had a look at unit tests, what they are, why we use them and integration tests, let's have a look at end-to-end tests or user interface tests. For this, I'll need to install another tool. So I'll quit my jest process here and I will install, with save dev, puppeteer, which is a headless version of Chrome, of the Chrome browser. So it basically is a browser we can use to interact with the DOM and so on, we can even run in a version with the head, so where we see the browser and we can basically define steps that should be executed in that browser so that we can automate certain processes on our web page and then of course test the result of these processes as well.

Now this download will take a while because in the end it downloads the entire Chrome codebase because it needs that to be able to simulate that browser ANd once it's done, I'll be back. So I'm done installing it, LEt's start using puppeteer now and for that, I'll go to my utiltest.js file and I will import puppeteer. So I'll import puppeteer by requiring it from puppeteer like this and I will write a new test now and there, I will just write should click around for now, we'll fix this later or change this later and in this function which should be executed here, I want to use puppeteer.

Now how can I use it? First of all I set up a browser by using puppeteer launch. Now this will launch a browser with some options which I can define here, for example I can set headless to false to actually run a browser with a user interface as well, you can set a bunch of stuff here and you can find it all in the official docs of puppeteer of course. I will also set slomo here, that will basically slow down the automated operations so that we have a chance of seeing what's happening and I'll set it to a value of 80 and we can also set some args here which is an array where I can pass dash dash in and for example window size to launch this browser with these arguments and window size allows me to set a width height pair, so I can set this to 1920 and 1080 for example, like this, this should launch a browser with this size and that of course can be great to also test if certain responsive features are working the way you want.

So now this will create a browser. Now actually, this will return a promise, so we can use async await here if we want to by placing async in front of this pair of arguments here or this empty argument list and now we can await this to launch. The alternative would be to just use then and catch, async await in the end does this for you. So here I'm awaiting this and storing the result in browser you could say, as a next step, I can now create a page object by awaiting the browser to create a new page, like this.

Now I'll also need to tell the browser which page to load and I'll grab my URL here and then we can say page, go to and then you enter your URL which should be loaded and you also should await this because all these browser related things are promises that simply take some time to execute so you have to await each step. So now this should open a browser and load this page. Let's try this by running npm test and it should indeed open up a brand new window in Chromium which is basically like a Chrome or the core functionality of Chrome and you also see that this is being tested or controlled by automated test software.

So this was opened automatically, now let's go back and let's add some logic here. We don't just want to go to that page, let's say we also want to enter something. For that I want to enter something into my input with the ID name and age, so in my test I will await a step or I use that page where I navigate into my app where I will then click into the field with that selector, so click takes the selector of the item it should click on. Once I click there, I will type and again you can find all commands in the official puppeteer docs, so you can really like instruct the browser, the headless browser, what to do. So I want to type and I want to type into the same input and we wouldn't have to click on it first but I want to simulate all the steps a user would do and I want to insert let's say Anna here to mix it up, not always Max.

So now I type in there, I will repeat these steps once I type the name for the age, so for the age field I will enter 28 let's say. And if you save that, it will open up a new window where you can see that it enters these things. Now we can now also add another step and click on this button at the bottom of our page, so in app.js, in the end it's this button we're listening on for an event here with ID button add user. We can grab that selector and make sure we click on that in our setup and now we get a full flow setup where you see that this gets entered and then we click this button here at the end. You also saw that it didn't add an item and this already shows us that writing this text was not the worst idea because it looks like something was broken and indeed here in our automated test, if we open the developer tools, we see that it didn't find the validate input function here. So since that was missing or is missing, we have to check our util.js file and see what's wrong with validate input in here I'm using validate input here and I'm defining it as a function here but one thing I never did is I never recompiled my code, that's something we have to do because the code that gets imported in the browser is packed with webpack

and I never recompiled it after changing my code. So in a separate terminal window, I'll quickly run npm start to get webpack to run my code and It'll now also watch my code and recompile if I change something and with that, it should have executed your test automatically, in case it didn't, simply add a blank and reopen your browser and enter and it will reopen the browser and execute this and now you see this works and this puppeteer being used for automated testing with a graphical user interface.

Now obviously, we can automate this a bit more and check the result programmatically now to see if we got to the expected outcome because what I can now do is I can also await and now that everything executed I can check if something is the case, for example I can check for the existence of this list item with a class of user item being added to it. So in my test, I can await my page and there, I can use $eval to get access to an element and I will look for the first element with a class of user item and I pass a function as a second argument to eval where I then define what I want to do with the element I selected there and here I will get an element as an input and I will for example return the text content and this means that now the result of this function will be returned by this overall promise, so I can store it here.

Final text for example will be the text that I fetch from this element that was created and now I can expect final text to be Anna, 28 years old. Now it's again checking for that text but it's now using the full flow in the browser, it's not just a unit or integration test as we have it up there, it's really going through all the steps we would execute manually as well and then of course we should have that text but we could check anything here.

We could also check for the existence of this class and we implicitly do so because if that class would not be there, we couldn't select the element by it and therefore for final text would certainly not be that text but now if I save this, it executes all our steps here and it actually fails here because it basically timed out and that's just a limit set up by jest to ensure that our tests don't take too long. What we can do for that is the test function actually takes a third argument and that is the maximum timeout and we can set this to 10 seconds to 10000 to increase the time we give our browser to complete its operation so that it doesn't timeout and now you see it finishes successfully because should click around, to which we should assign a better name, does give us the result we want and here I will now say should create an element with text and correct class, something like this.

By the way we can of course now also set headless to true, disable the slow motion and not set these arguments and this will now speed up the testing because now it doesn't have to go through that step in a real browser, it does so behind the scenes and that's one of the advantages of having a headless browser, that you don't have to watch it execute the steps but it can be nice to see the steps, you can do both and now we got a full e-to-e test or a user interface test in place too.

lectures.title: Dealing with Async Code
lectures.text:
Now we had a basic introduction to testing now, to the core types of tests but thus far we always tested relatively simple code, synchronous code where nothing special was happening, where no side effects were involved like a HttpRequest going out when a function is called. Now things like that can cause problems when you're trying to run tests because your tests will also trigger that code which might send a HttpRequest or which might do something which makes the test take longer, might hit a backend API or might towards results.

So now we'll have a look at what we can do to make our test simpler and focus on the core things and really only test what matters to us. So for this, again I prepared a starting project which you find attached to this lecture here so that you can follow along and if you start the project by double clicking the index.html file, you'll see a button there, if you click that button, you will eventually see an all uppercase text being printed here. Now responsible for that output is this code here, I got a very simple setup here using webpack and here I'm getting access to a button in my DOM, I'm adding a listener to print the title. In print title, I call load title which is this function here, in that function I reach out to fetch data which is provided in a different file also created by me.

There, I seem to get some data object of which I extract the title, I then transform this title to be all uppercase and I return that hence I can print it here. Now if we have a look in this HTTP file, into this http.js file, here I'm using a third-party package, axios, so this is not written by me, this is another third-party package and here in fetch data, I make a get request to a dummy API, so this is a real API in the web, a real request is made here, this API is not maintained by me, it's just an API we can use for playing around, for testing and there, I get back a response object, axios gives me such a response object which happens to have a couple of properties, like the status code for example but also the data property which I'm extracting here.

This is essentially what I do, now let's write some tests. I already installed the jest package here and I also already configured my test command here to use jest, I also have a project where I use Node.js import export syntax because jest uses that by default and just as with my other testing video where I gave you an introduction to testing with jest, there I explained that jest uses that syntax, that setting it up to understand a different syntax would be more complex and I still don't want to do that here because here, I want to focus on testing async code.

So we got everything set up to write some tests, so let's do that. You learned in that last video that you can create a new file with .test.js at the end to have Jest.js pick it up and execute it automatically. So this will be the testing file for app.js and let's say we want a test print title. Conveniently I'm already exporting it here at the bottom, so what can we do? Well in app-test.js, we can use the test function which is globally available when we run that file with jest, there we give it a description, some text, yes some description of what should be tested here and there I have should print an uppercase text for example. I have my arrow function then that should execute or that contains the testing logic and in there we define our expectations.

Now we could expect uppercase text with the help of some regex magic or anything like that but here because we'll change that anyways, I just want to expect this text because right now I will always get the text for the API endpoint I'm hitting. So I expect and now I need to import that function which I want to test, so that will be print title, I am pulling that out of my exported object in the app.js file, so I expect a print title, the result of that function call to be equal to my all uppercase text here, this is my expectation.

We can now run that test by running npm test and this executes all test.js files and this actually fails because it fails to execute add event listener null. Now the reason for that actually is that app.js contains some code that will always run when this file gets executed and it does get executed when I import from that file and it tries to access the DOM here which just doesn't work in this environment here, the real DOM is not loaded here, so an easy way around that is to take that function and export it into a separate file, maybe a util.js file, this is also something we did in the last video already, export print title here and what this allows us to do is it allows us to import something from that file only without executing app.js and therefore without hitting the real DOM. So we can rename that testing file here to utiltest.js and we import print title from ./util and in app.js since I removed print title from there, we also need to import print title by requiring it from the ./util file here and now for that to work, I'll also have to move load title over to util.js because print title depends on that, so let's move load title into that file as well.

That means that fetch data also needs to move in there, so from app.js let's grab the fetch data import and move that to the util.js file and now with that setup, if we rerun npm test here, now it should be able to run our test here and it does but I get an error that essentially it expected a string but it received undefined and now this already shows us a problem we have with asynchronous code testing. Well actually in print title, I am indeed returning nothing, so getting undefined as a result makes perfect sense but even if I would return something, like for example in here, if I not only log the title but I also returned the title here, if I do that and I rerun, I will still get that error, I can already say that. The reason for that is that and that has nothing to do with testing, that's normal Javascript behavior, return statements inside of callbacks or inside of promise then calls are not executed or are executed but Javascript does not wait for them, it does not return this value as a return value for this overall function, instead this is the return value of that inner function here and we're not testing this inner function, we're testing that overall function.

So in our case here, one simple solution would be to test load title. Here we return something in the inner function and we also return something in the main function, we returned the whole promise. So chances are that we get back a promise here to which we then can listen and that might allow us to expect something helpful. So let's change something, let's export load title here so that we can test it, let's go to utiltest.js and there, I will not expect something like that but I'll get my title but instead, I will import load title here and I will execute load title and this gives us a promise so I will add then here and in there, I know I'll get my title because that's exactly the way I use it in print title right, I have load title and then I get my title.

So now I have the exact same usage here in utiltest.js and now here I want to expect something, that my title should be equal to that uppercase title I got here. So we can grab that title here, copy it and that is what I expect as a value. Now if I rerun npm test, it actually passes because now this test succeeds. So this is better, this is how we could test our asynchronous code but we still have a problem here, the problem is we're still hitting our API.

So here in util.js, I'm using fetch data and if you remember, we're defining that in the HTTP file, so here and there we're making a real API request. We typically don't want to do that in testing, we might exceed certain API quotas if we do that, if we're testing post requests, we might even edit something on the API which we certainly don't want to do as part of testing, certainly not with our production API at least. So hitting the API is typically not something we want to do, there also are other reasons against it, what would we achieve by really making that HttpRequest? Do you want to test if your API works correctly?

If you're building that API, you should do these tests during the API development, not when working on your frontend, these two should be separated, so that is certainly not something you want to test. If the API works or not is not something you test in your frontend code, you might test error fallbacks or anything like that but not if the API works correctly. You also don't want to test if the get method exposed by axios works correctly. That is a method provided by a third-party package and we rely on that package doing its job, so we also don't test third-party package functionalities.

We want to test our own code and our own code here for example is that we extract data and that here, that we transform this to uppercase and that we pull out the title.

lectures.title: Working with Mocks
lectures.text:
Now to focus on that, we do something which is called mocking, we mock features which means we replace features we don't want a test with some dummy implementations and how could this look here? Well in utiltest.js, we got load title and we want to test if that successfully transforms our title to be all uppercase, to be this text. Now to test this, what we need to do is we need to replace fetch data with a mock. Now jest gives us a great way of preventing us from using that fetch data method.

We can create a new folder called __mocks, all lowercase, __ next to the files that contain our raw source code, so in this case in our root folder. Now here, we can add a http.js file, so the same file name as the file that has the function we want to replace and now in http.js, we can now do some magic to set up some functions that will replace our real functions when running the tests. For that, I'll copy my code from http.js, I'll get rid of axios though because I'll not use that here, I'll still export fetch data though but in fetch data, I'll simply return a promise which I instantly resolve with promise resolve to an object that has a title property with the text I want to test which I'll now convert to all lowercase though, so delectus aut autem and now that I'm exporting this here, something interesting will happen. In http.js, I added a console log statement to fetch data to see when we're hitting this API and when we're not.

If I now run npm test, we are hitting the API as you can see here, we have that console log statement from the HTTP file in there. Now we can go to utiltest.js and in there, we want to add jest mock at the beginning and mock the http.js file like this, you can omit .js though. Now if I run npm test, you see it also took close to a second because it had to do some magic behind the scenes but you don't see that console log statement because what now happens is when this test gets executed, when this testing file gets executed, jest goes ahead and replaces the HTTP file with our mocked file, so all the functions that are export that here are then replacing the functions we are normally exporting in the real HTTP file for our tests only. So for the tests only, we use our mocked functions here, so this dummy fetch data which gives us back an object that allow us the other functions to work fine but which does not hit the API because we don't want to test the API response and we don't want to test the access get method, so we can rely on the API returning as an object that has a title property and we can rely on the access get method giving us an object and a response which has a data property, so

we don't need to test that. We want to test whether our code in the util.js file correctly extracts the title and transforms it and that is the case otherwise this test would not have succeeded for our mocked implementation of fetch data where we return an object with a title that is all lowercase, so not what we test for lowercase this text and therefore since our test succeeds, we know that our transformation here does work. So this is how we can test async code or how we can replace code, how we can replace functionalities if we don't want to in this case hit the API, the same would be the case for let's say code that accesses the filesystem, you don't want to do that, instead you want to mock such functionalities. You can by the way also mock global packages, like axios itself. Instead of mocking our fetch data function, you could create an axios.js file here and there, we could export our own get function here which we of course have to define because remember in my https file, I am using the get method of the axios object.

So here I want to export a get method and that would be a function that takes a URL as an argument but we don't care about that URL here, what we want to do here is we can return an object which in this case, since this is faking the response from axios, so we want to fake whatever get gives us back and that should be a response object which at least has a data key because we're extracting that, so here in the axios mock, we want to have a data object which should in turn be an object with the title we want to test, so that lowercase title we defined here.

So basically we're now mocking a functionality which is one level above the last functionality, where we mocked our own function, now we're using we're mocking the function, this raw function so this function depends on. So now in the axios.js mock file I'm returning an object which has a data key which has an object as a value, which has a title key which is the lowercase version of our text and with that being mocked, we can go to our utiltest.js file, we can comment out this mocking of our HTTP implementation, so we'll now not use this HTTP file we created a second ago, Jest.js will automatically use mocks of global node modules though, so axios.js this module should be used automatically, we don't have to instruct jest to do that and now we can simply run npm test and here it fails because what I return here is not a promise and this already proves that this mocked file is being used, otherwise it would not have failed. I'm returning an object there and therefore calling then fails, I of course have to return a promise here by using promise resolve, so a promise that eventually yields this object and once I do that and therefore my mocked get method provides a promise as the real axios implementation does, once I do that, it passes again. We see fetching

data here because we are now using my original fetch data implementation but the get method we're using here is not the real one, it's our mocked one, so this one here. Now this is how you can mock certain functionalities to test async code or code in general which might depend on third-party packages. Now there are other strategies as well, you'll also find the term spies or stops when you went deeper into testing and you can definitely also check out these alternative approaches to learn about alternative strategies for working with async code and third-party libraries. Attached to this lecture, you also find additional resources that allow you to dive deeper into these topics and into jest in general and learn more about testing and build up on the knowledge you gain here.

sections.title: Bonus: Programming Paradigms (Procedural vs Object Oriented vs Functional)

lectures.title: Module Introduction
lectures.text:
In this module we'll have a look at programming paradigms, what this means and most importantly, three important programming paradigms you could use when writing Javascript code. We'll have a look at procedural, functional and object oriented programming and what that means for you and how code would look like if you followed one of these paradigms. Specifically as I said, we'll first clarify what exactly programming paradigms are before we then have a closer look at procedural, functional and last but not least, object oriented programming.

You already learned the basics you need for all these paradigms throughout this course, now we'll have a look at what exactly such a paradigm is and when you use which.

lectures.title: What are Programming Paradigms?
lectures.text:
So what are programming paradigms? That's of course important to understand. In the end you could say it's just a way of writing code, it's about how you write and organize your code. It's not a syntax feature, it's not a special feature exposed by the browser or anything like this, it's really just how you structure your code and how you reason about your program you're writing, so how your code is organized and in the end there are three paradigms you could follow.

You have object oriented programming, you have procedural programming and you have functional programming. Now what does this mean? If you're writing your code in an object oriented style, it means that you organize your data and logic in objects or in classes and then in objects based on those classes, which means you store your data in properties of objects, you store your logic in methods of objects, that's how you typically think about your code here, everything in your application, in your project gets represented as a class and then in the end, as an object.

So you organize who code in logical entities you could say, you kind of try to translate the application you're writing into the real world and you think about your application and the things that make up your application in real world terms. If you're building a shop application, you think about products and a shopping cart and so on, that's how you think about your code and how you organize it. Now when you're following a procedural style and that's probably the style with which you got started when work with Javascript, you simply write a sequential series of execution steps and tasks, so you have a top to bottom code execution you could say. Now you always have that in every style but here you simply list these different steps the engine in the end should execute and should perform, you don't organize your code in logical groups or in logical pieces of data, you don't use objects and entities to structure your code, in the end you just execute step after step.

And then we have functional programming and there, we organize our code in, if possible, pure functions with clearly defined tasks. You get all the data a function needs as parameters and then this function often also return something new, so you pass data around with parameters and your functions are your way of organizing your code. You have many functions, probably more than you have in the other styles and your functions hold your logic, every function if possible works on its own and this is how you structure your code.

Now that's the theory, it of course becomes way clearer if we see that on a real example.
