lectures.title: Procedural Programming in Practice
lectures.text:
So let's work on a very simple example application and this indeed will be a very trivial application here. It's an application where I in the end have a HTML file which renders a form, a form with two inputs and then with a button and I got some styling so that this doesn't look super ugly. Now we can simply open this by in the end double clicking that index.html file in the finder or Windows Explorer and what we get is something that looks like this.

Now here nothing happens, if you enter something here and click the button, you'll just submit the form and therefore reload the page, besides that nothing will happen. We will now write code that changes this and we will write this application code three times in the three different programming styles and we'll start with procedural because as I mentioned, this might be the style you used when you started with Javascript because I would argue it is the style that's the most obvious to use if you're getting started with programming. So let's add a new script here here, procedural.js, you can of course name it however you want and in the index.html file, below that link here, I'll add a script import and point at procedural.js, add the defer attribute to make sure that this script only runs after the entire file has been parsed and of course closed the script tag as well and now we are importing this and we're ready to write some code and now we can really think about the different steps we want to execute because that's what procedural programming is all about.

So if we have a look at our HTML file, what do we want to do? Well we want to listen to a click on this button of course or to be precise, we want to listen for the submission of the form, we want to get the values the user entered for the username and for the password and we might want to validate those values, so at least make sure both fields are not empty, show an error message if they are empty and then in the end if everything has been valid, do something with the data, let's say create a new object, a new user object and then log that to the console or something like this.

So something fairly trivial, that is what we could do here. So for that, back to the procedural.js file, what do we need to do here? Well we need to get access to the form and to the two inputs so that we can work with the data there and then we can add a listener to the form and so on. So getting access to those things is easy, we have IDs, we have the user input ID on the form, we have the username ID on this input and the password ID on this input, so we can use these three inputs to gain access. So I'll store the form in a form constant or I'll store a reference to the form in the form constant and we can get access with get element by ID and then here it was user-input and then the second const that I want to create here is the username input, we can get access with document get element by ID username and last but not least, the password, so the passwordInput, that can be fetched with document get element by ID password like this.

Okay, so we get this access, let's now add an event listener. So on the form I'll add an event listener to the submit event because that is the event we want to listen to, right and then we want to trigger a function when that executes, we could use an anonymous function here but I will create a named function, the signup handler let's say. It will get an event object automatically and I will point at this function when this event is triggered, when this event is fired.

Now this is vanilla Javascript and of course even though we're using the procedural style, we are allowed to work with functions as well, this is not forbidden, we just don't organize our code around the idea of using functions all the time. So we point at this function here when this event is triggered and now in this function, we write all the logic, again step-by-step which you want to execute. So thus far our logic is get access to the different elements step-by-step and then define this function and then set up this listener.

Now when this function runs, we need to get the inputs here, the values the user entered, we need to validate them and then create a dummy user object with that data and actually first of all, I want to call event prevent default to prevent that browser default of sending the form to a backend server which in the end leads to a page refresh which I don't want here, so let's call this as well and now we can get started. Let's get the concrete values the user entered.

So we got the entered username and we can get this out of usernameInput.value, we can access .value here because we know that the element we're selecting here is an input element which will have a value property. Side note, you could actually also only get access to the usernameInput in here if you wanted to because we really only need the two inputs here inside of this function, so you don't have to do it globally here, in this function it would also suffice, so maybe let's reorganize our code to do that inside of this function, maybe even after preventing the default, really right before we need a value, that's not required but it is a possibility.

So we get the entered username, we can also get the entered password and we get that from the passwordInput.value of course, just like this. Now with the two values, we can validate them, we could do this with an if check where we check if the entered username, if we trim it to remove excess whitespace at the beginning and end, if the length is equal to zero which means this is an invalid input, it's empty. In this case, we could show an alert to the user and say invalid input, username must not be empty, that's something we could do here and we also return here which means we cancel this function execution so that we don't continue in the code. If we make it past this if check, we might still have an invalid input because our password, our entered password, with a double s here, entered password, that might also be wrong, so we trim this and check if the length is zero or maybe if it's smaller or equal than five because let's say we want the password which has at least five characters, if it is too short, we can say invalid input, password must be six characters or longer and again we thereafter return so that we don't continue with the function execution.

If we do continue, we made it past both if checks and we now know we have a valid input and that's where we now could create a new user object, simply with an object literal. Again just like functions are not forbidden here, objects are not forbidden here, it's not like you're only allowed to use objects when you're writing object oriented code, it's more about how you organize code and here it's really a step-by-step execution and we're using a very simple literal object here to store some data, to group some data.

So here we then have let's say the username which is our entered username, we have the password which is our entered password, entered password and with that we're good and now we can console log the user and maybe also send a greeting with Hi I am plus user.username, like this. With that, we had a very basic procedural program. If we now save this's and we go back to the browser and reload this page, if I enter Maximilian here and then any password of my choice which is let's say too short actually, I get this error, invalid input password must be six characters or longer. If I don't enter Maximilian here but I leave this empty, I get this error regarding my username and if I do have valid inputs in both fields here, you see we're logging the user, we're logging Hi I am Maximilian.

Now as I mentioned, this code here should look fairly straightforward to you, there also is nothing wrong with it but this would be the simple procedural way of writing your code, you think about the different steps you need to execute and you then just write them down and don't get me wrong, code will always be executed from top to bottom but you could also organize this differently. So let's have a look at the object oriented programming style next.

lectures.text:
So we wrote this code here in the procedural style you could say. Now let's create a new Javascript file, oop.js where we will write basically the same logic but now using an object oriented style. So for that in index.html, I'll swap the import for the oop.js file here. Now how would this look like if we think about this in an object oriented way? Now there are certainly different ways of approaching this but I would like to think about the different entities, the different types of objects we could work with here.

We could say our form for example is one object, it's one object which in the end will have two inputs which has this button and which will have a method which is triggered when the button is fired. The validation could be organized in its own object as well, in a helper object which holds validation logic that we could reuse in different parts of the application if we had multiple forms and the user we create in the end, we could create a blueprint for this user as well, a class or constructor function which allows us to create user objects which has a built-in greet method to show this greeting for example.

So here in the object oriented Javascript file, I will work with classes, if you were working with an older version of Javascript, you could of course also work with constructor functions instead. Classes in the end are just syntactic sugar with some extras and you'll learn all about that of course in my complete guide in the object oriented and classes course section. So which classes do we need here? Well we have our form right, so I'll a user input form class here and this should hold everything that is related to my form.

I also want to have another class and the order does not really matter here, I'll just have the form at the bottom because it is the thing I will actually start with and it will use all the other classes which I'm about to define, so I want to define them first, though technically as I said, you could also organize this differently but here, another class we'll need later is the user itself, so not the input form but for the concrete user object we work with and then maybe also our validator class here which holds our validation logic.

Now let's start with the user input form though, what could be in there? Well I want to define my constructor function which allows us to do some initialization work whenever we create an instance based on this class. Now my goal is to create an instance based on this class when the app starts in the end. So therefore here, I want to get access to the different inputs in the HTML file and to the form itself so that we can add a listener. So here I will add some properties to the instance created based on the class with the this keyword, for example a form property and the name is up to you and here I get access to get element by ID, user-input, so here I store access to this user input form.

I also want to get access to the different input fields in the form, so I have my usernameInput field, document get element by ID username and of course one for the password, so passwordInput with document get element by ID password. So basically what we stored in constants before, here this constant, this constant and this constant is now getting stored in properties of this class or to be precise, in properties of the concrete objects created based on this class. I also of course will reach out to my form and add an event listener here for the submit event and when this is triggered, I of course want to trigger a function.

Now we could work with an anonymous function here but since we're in the class and we want to write object oriented code, it makes much more sense to create a method, so a function inside of an object, inside of a class here. So for that, I'll add the signupHandler method here which gets the event object and now I can point at it here, this signupHandler. This ensures that this function which is registered on this class and which therefore is called a method is fired whenever the submit event occurs and in here, we can now do stuff, we can call even prevent default but we can now also get the concrete entered values and validate them and so on.

Now one important word, if I want to get the let's say entered username here, then I of course can reach out to this usernameInput, so to this pointer at this input element in the HTML code we stored here and access .value but this won't work, why won't it work? Because the this keyword inside of this method will not refer to this class in this case here, why? Because this method gets fired upon this event and when you point at a function or a method based on an event that gets triggered, so here on such a event listener, the this keyword will be bound to the event target, that's a default behavior. To override this, we have to call bind this here.

This ensures that the this keyword inside of signupHandler will point to the exact same thing this would point to in the constructor and that will be the instance created based on the class. So now this will work correctly and we can therefore also get the entered password here with this passwordInput.value. So now we get the two values, now it would make sense to validate them and here again thinking in an object oriented way, we could outsource this validation logic into a validator class.

We don't have to do that, we could write it inline here, we could just copy over this logic here from procedural but that means that whenever we have some other form in our application, we can only reuse our code by copying it again and copy and pasting is not something we want to do too often because that is a bad programming style, you're repeating yourself and you shouldn't do that. So instead, I'll add something here in the validator class, I'll add a static method validate, this means we can call it without instantiating this class and there, I expect to get a value and then let's say a flag and a validator value if you want to, so I'm writing a little bit of a more complex validator here.

What does this mean? Well. value should be the value I want to check, so the entered username and enter password. Flag should then allow us to identify which kind of validation we want to perform and then validator value is basically optional allowing us to configure the validation. Now for this to work, I'll add two new static properties here - required and I'm writing in all caps to make it clear that this is basically a globally unique value you could say and min length here and these are just identifiers which we can then use because my idea now is that I can check if in here in the validate function, if the flag argument I'm getting, if this is equal to this required, so if we're running some required validation and if it is, I want to return true or false, I want to return true if the entered value is not empty and false if it is empty.

So I will return value trim length greater zero, if it's not an empty input, this will return true, otherwise this will return false. If the flag is let's say this min length, then I will return value trim length greater validator value, so this extra argument with which we can configure validation. Why am I doing it like this? Well simply just to show that now we would have a reusable validate function because in the user input form here, in the signupHandler, we can now use this.

We can now simply check if validator, so this class I just worked in, .validate which we can call like this because it's a static method hence we don't need to instantiate the class, if this yields true for the entered username which is the value and validator.required as a flag. So i want to validate this here with the required validator and check if it's not empty. If this returns true, I'm fine, if it does not return true indicated by this exclamation mark here, I want to show an error but this is not the only validation of course, I also want to check one other validation logic here, one other expression, if not validator validate for the entered password, for the min length flag and a value of five as a minimum length, if this returns not true or this first one returns not true, in any of these cases I want to make it into this if block and here we can now show an alert and say invalid input, username or password is wrong, password should be at least six characters. This is the alert we could show here and then we want to return here to not continue with this method execution.

So the error message, the error handling still happens in this class here which makes sense because this is the place where I do work with my concrete values but the logic for checking the input is outsourced in a separate class. Now this is not a must do but it ensures that we could now reuse this validator in other forms of this application as well and we might of course have more complex validation logic in there than we currently do. So now with this, we know that after this if check, we have valid inputs and hence we could now create our new user.

So for this, let's go to this user class and work on this, here I want to define how a user should look like and attach any logic to it which it should have, so for example here let's add a constructor to define some values with which we create a user, specifically the username and the user password let's say and then in here, we have this user name, set it equal to uName and this password set it equal to upassword here, this would allow us to create a new object with these two properties but I also want to add some logic, I'll add a greet method here to this user object where I just say console log Hi I am plus this username.

And with that, we can create a new user based on this class down there, our new user with new user, here we need the new keyword to construct a new instance of the user class and we forward our entered user name and our entered password here and thereafter we can not only log the new user but also call new user.greet to execute that greet logic and with all that done, there's just one remaining thing now. Thus far all the logic lives in the user input form but this is just a class, right, we need to instantiate it to bring this code to life.

So below this here, we can call new user input form like this to create a new instance. We could store it in a constant but if we don't work with this constant, we also don't have to do that, so here I'm just creating a new instance and with that, this class here now comes to life, we run this constructor, we set up this event listener and we're therefore good to go. So now if we go back and we reload this page, if we submit an empty form, we should get an error and indeed we do.

If I enter a valid password here but I have an empty username, it still gets this error and if I enter a valid username here but my password is too short, we still get an error here. If I enter a different password which is long enough, we do log our user object here and this greeting. So this now works and it's essentially the same logic as before in the procedural style, the difference is now that we think about our code as different objects working together and we split our code logically into entities which can make it easier to reason about your code.

It can also help with reusing code as I mentioned at the example of the validator because we can use this anywhere in the application, in the procedural style, in the way we're doing it at the moment here, we would have to copy this around to share it and again copy and pasting is bad because you need to change your logic in one place, you then need to change it in 10 places or how often you're using it. So that's the object oriented style, let's explore the functional programming style now.

lectures.title: Functional Programming in Practice
lectures.text:
So last but not least, let's explore the functional programming style. For this, I'll create a new file here, functional.js and of course import this here in the index.html file, functional. The idea behind functional programming now is that we organize our code around functions, so we can still then reuse and share logic by simply sharing a function, by exporting it and importing it in another file and so on. So how could we split this application here into a functionally written application?

It can be hard to think about this if you're relatively new in programming. My personal experience shows that object oriented programming is relatively easy to pick up because it's close to the real world so to say, we think in objects and that's how we think about the real world as well. The procedural style also is not too hard because we execute code step-by-steps and therefore all we have to do is that we have to think about what we want to do in our application step-by-step, so what should happen when and then this code is basically writing itself. Now in the functional world, it's a bit like in the object oriented world, we think about the different things that make up our application but the things are now not objects but instead of different logical blocks, something like a validate function, a function to get access to a DOM element, a function to extract user input, a function to create a new user, a function to greet a user.

So basically we try to split our code into the different logical blocks we have here. So in functional.js, how could we get started because maybe that helps us understand how it works? It still starts with us getting access to the form right, we need access to the form so that we can listen to the form submission. To get access here, we could write a new function, connect form, name is up to you and by the way you can write this function in any way you want, in this function declaration style here, you could also write it as a function expression or of course, you could use an arrow function here if you wanted to, that all works, here I'll just write it like this. So connect form, just like this without any parameters for now and in there I want to get access to my form and I do so by calling document get element by ID user-input and thereafter I will reach out to my form and add a submit event listener here and then, then what? Then I want to point at a function that should execute when the form is submitted.

So maybe let's add a new function here, the signupHandler which gets this event object which calls event prevent default, it will also do more than that but this is something we definitely need to do and then I point at it here. This is something we could do but it's not the perfect way of setting this up. Instead the idea or the core philosophy you really should embrace when writing functional code is that your functions should be pure and all the data they work with is received as parameters, so that your functions are as predictable and reusable as possible.

So for this connect form function, this means that we would probably get the form ID as a parameter and also the form submit handler function as a parameter and then here instead of pointing at user input here, we would point at form ID and here we would just say form submit handler and now this function has code which is totally reusable, which makes no assumptions about what's in your HTML file, it makes no assumption about this ID and about the name of the function that should handle the submission.

Instead we would call connect form here when our app is initialized, so when this Javascript file is passed and executed for the first time and here I would feed in the concrete values, so user input and a pointer at signupHandler. Now of course in this simple app we don't gain much by this but now we really have a function which is pretty focused, pretty straightforward, pretty easy to understand and which is also pretty reusable because it's not tied to a specific form in the HTML code.

If we had multiple forms which we wanted to connect with submit handlers, we could reuse this function and we could just call it with different arguments, that already is how you should think about code when thinking in a functional programming style. So now we connect this form, we point at the signupHandler when the form gets submitted. In the sign up handler, we now want to get our user input and we now also of course then want to validate it and create a new user.

Now again we could copy our logic from procedural right, we could copy this logic here for getting the user input for the moment and paste it in here and this would work but we're not really thinking in a functional way. What did I just say about functions? Well they should be pure and should receive all the inputs they need as parameters and here again I'm hardcoding IDs which are IDs for my HTML document into the function. Now we could do this but is this good?

Well it's certainly not bad. Now you might argue that hardcoding these IDs into the function is not something you want to do because we got rid of it here but I would argue that the signupHandler is of course a very specific function which indeed can be tied to the HTML file because it really is about this sign up form. It's not a general function here, like connect form was which should work with any form, this way you should only work with the signing up logic so that is fine but we're basically having some code repetition here.

Why don't we create a new function here which we name get user input and here I expect to get my input element ID and in this function we then return document get element by ID to which I forward the input element ID parameter and then I access .value here. Now of course, this only works with the input elements but that's the idea behind this function, so we could add an extra check which checks if this is an HTML input element but here I just assume that it always will be one and now we can rewrite this.

We can get rid of this line here and entered username now simply is get user input for the username ID and we can get rid of this line and the entered password now just is get user input for password and again we have a reusable function here and this is now leaner and more focused. So now we get the input, of course we want to validate it. So unsurprisingly we create a new function for this, the validate function and here we could again follow the logic we set up into object oriented part.

We can expect a value, a flag and a validator value here and then basically copy over to logic from oop because object oriented programming and functional program is not that far apart. It's a bit more than just translating classes to functions but the idea of organizing logic in methods and in classes is not that far away from the idea of organizing logic and functions. So unsurprisingly, we can copy the logic from the validate method here and add it in the validate function here.

Now we just need to replace this required and this min length with just required and min length and add some global constants here and yes this is also possible, not everything has to be inside of a function. Here we want some global flags, some global identifiers and therefore we can define them just like this in our script here. So now we have that, we have our validate function and we can now use this validate function here in the signupHandler.

So here we could now call validate and forward the entered username and so on and that again would not be wrong but I want to create yet another new function, maybe here which I'll name create user and this is a function that takes the username and the user password and this should now run the validation and that's just of course one way of doing it, not the only correct one, just one way of doing it. So I want to run validation here and then if it succeeds, also create my user. So in here, I will now check if not validate for username and the required flag, so if this yields false or if validate for the user password and the min length flag and a min length of five, if either of the two yields false, we could throw an alert but this would be a side effect.

Now what's the side effect? lectures.title: Wrap Up
lectures.text:
So we saw three different styles and of course, you can also mix these styles, you could have a procedural style where you also work with classes and where you have multiple functions. You can have a functional style where you somehow also sneak in some classes, though then technically it wouldn't be a pure functional style anymore. Which style is the best though? Well the best style is the style which best works for you, that really is the truth. Now, there will be people who strongly disagree because like a couple of other things in programming, this really is something where you can have religious debates.

You can really discuss this and for a lot of people, it seems to be the most important thing in life, not to me though. You can write code, you can write apps with either style and you should find the style that best suits your needs. Now the more experienced you get as a developer, the more you will see that for a certain application types, some styles tend to work better than other styles and again you can find discussions about this on the Internet, some of them are even kind of friendly, which will show different applications and different examples for when to use which style. You'll also sometimes have programming languages which strongly favor one style over another, for example C# is a programming language which is heavily object oriented, Javascript on the other hand is pretty versatile, there you can follow any style and therefore sometimes you also are forced into a certain style and sometimes you are not.

It's important to be aware of all these styles and nowadays at this point of time, the functional style is really having a strong comeback and is super popular and it does have great advantages. It's quite readable, your code is really nicely organized, it's very straightforward, functions tend to be relatively small if you're using this style correctly and it also produces highly reusable code. Object oriented programming was extremely popular a couple of years ago and it's still far from being not popular, don't get me wrong and it does have advantages.

It's also producing reusable code and it splits your code into logical pieces. Now with the classes, you sometimes have a little bit of overhead which you don't really want though and sometimes it's easier to split it when following the functional style. The procedural style is not bad at all and great for some simpler scripts, the more complex your application gets, the more complex it might get to work with this style though because you will naturally end up with at least using some classes or some other functions to make it more readable at some point because if you only use this style and you write your code step-by-step your code can get harder to organize and to reason about but again here also, you can mix in more functions and so on and therefore also write great applications with the procedural style.

I hope that this overview was helpful and that it helps you make decisions about which styles you want and most importantly, that it helps you understand styles being used in different projects or in different frameworks you work with in your future as a Javascript developer.

When we have multiple available solutions for a given problem, we of course want to find the best one and for this, we need to compare the solutions but how do we compare different algorithms? Now the problem just is, of course we could use a stopwatch and measure how long our different algorithms take for different inputs but this would not really be a good idea, it depends way too much on the hardware we're running on, which other processes might be running in the background and for small data sets, for small amounts of data, there might be a lot of variation. So indeed we try to measure and express this in a generalized form and not in time units, not in seconds and so on because that would be really hard to measure, instead we use something which is called time complexity and there, you could simply imagine a chart where you have two axis and one is the time axis and one is the number of items or the size of the input you're feeding into your algorithm and then you have a certain relation between the number of items

you're passing into your algorithm and the time it takes to execute and this is expressed with something which is called the Big O notation, which we write like this. lectures.title: Diving into Data Structures & Time Complexities
lectures.text:
So what's up with data structures? For this I'll add a new file, data-structures.js and in there I want to get started with data structures. So let's import them and for data structures, it's important to understand that data structure is anything that stores data, so a string like this is a data structure but of course a fairly trivial one where we can't do much with and which is also already built into Javascript. An array is a more interesting data structure, also already built into Javascript but very important and of course one we use a lot, the same for an object or maps or sets, these would all be data structures, data structures built into Javascript.

Now maybe let's start with the array and let's say we have an array of ages 30, 29, 54, something like this. With this array, we can of course do things, we can sum it up as we did before here with the sum up algorithm or we can find the minimum value, something like this. Now it's important to understand that certain operations with data structures also have certain time complexities, for example if I push a new age onto this array, what would be the time complexity of this action?

Now of course push is not an algorithm, not a function we created on our own but still it is a function that does something and if you want to learn what it does, you can check out MDN or other resources that explains such built-in functions like this one. Well it's important to understand how push works. When you push something, you have an array like this one here and then push adds a new element in this array and it adds it at the end, so here where I added this blank space, that is where push inserts an item.

Now it's also important to understand and you learned this, that in an array, the elements are ordered and every element has an index that identifies the element, so here we have an index of 0, here we have an index of 1 and here we have an index of 2, right? Now when we push here, we of course create a new index for that newly added item, the index three in this case. So what happens when we push? We add a new item at the end and this item gets a new index.

Does this affect the other items? No, not at all. So adding an item at the end of an array with push has actually a constant time complexity, O(1) because the other items are not affected, we add an item, we don't affect the other items, we have a constant time complexity. Now that changes if we use unshift, unshift adds an item at the beginning of an array. So if we take a closer look at this and I copy that here, then we see that what unshift will do is that it adds the item here at the beginning.

Now the problem with that is that means all items effectively have to be moved you could say, they get a new index. So here this new item receives an index of zero, the item which previously had 0, 30 had 0 now receives a new index one, the item which previously had the index one which was the item 29 receives a new index 2 and so on. So here for unshift, all existing elements are touched, so this actually has a linear time complexity O(n), for every new item we add we have to touch and move all existing items, we have to reassign indexes, so that is of course way worse than pushing.

It's also something I mentioned earlier in the course already in the arrays section. So unshifting sometimes of course is what you want to do and then you should do it but you should be aware that it's way more expensive from a performance perspective than pushing an item to the end of the list. What's also important to know and to understand is that of course it also costs you something, it takes some time to find an element, for example if I want to get my age and let's say I am 30, then of course if I know that my age is stored in position 1 or here after unshifting actually at position 2, I can get it by its index, index 1 here, index 1 gives me 30. So if I know that I want my age and my age is the second item in the array, so it has an index of 1, then I can access it like this and this actually accesses it at constant time complexity, O(1).

Why is this constant? Because every item has an index, so Javascript can immediately go to that place in memory and give me that item, it doesn't need to look at all the other items. Now of course, this changes if we work with a different data structure, so here's a new example. Let's say we actually have an array, name popularity. Now what's in there is a bunch of objects, so we have objects which is another data structure in an array and there we have an ID or a username, whatever you want to call it, like let's say Max and we have a number of usages, let's say five times and then here we have the username, Manu and that's getting used six times and of course we could have more and more items.

So effectively, we have identifiers and then we have values for these identifiers and now we want to get the usages of Manu, so we want to get the number of times the name, Manu, gets used. So Manu usages could then be name popularity where we use the built-in find method which executes a function on every element in the array, looking at that person or whatever we want to name it and we have to return true if it's the item we're interested in and false if it's not.

So here I look for Manu, so I check if person username is equal to Manu, if that's the case we return true, we stop searching for more and then this object will be returned by find, so what I get back is an object which has this usages key and this gives me the usages of the name, Manu. So what I'm doing here is I'm looking for the item with a username of Manu and then I get the usages for this item, that's what I do with this line here. Now in the best case, Manu is the first item here, so we execute this function which we pass to find exactly once because we find Manu right away for the very first item we're looking at, so we have executed this function once, we get the usages and we basically, in the best case, have constant time complexity, right?

The very first item was the one we were looking for but that's of course not always the case. The worst case is that we have linear time complexity, O(n) because Manu is the last item and the average case of course is somewhere in between but for a large number of items, this in the end also ends up to be linear time complexity you could say. So on average, we'll have to walk through all the items or close to all the items to find what we get because the elements are randomly distributed let's say, we don't know at which position Manu is and therefore we have linear time complexity because find executes this function on all items in the array.

Now this is a scenario where another data structure might be a better choice, instead of using an array like this, why don't we use an object or a map? Let's rebuild this in this better way. We have our name, map let's say and we can use a normal Javascript object for this and now the keys here are the usernames and the values for the keys are the usages, like this and now when we want to get Manu's usages and I'll just name it Manu usages2 to not clash with this name, then we can simply reach out to the name map and access the key, Manu, like this and then this gives us the usages for Manu. Now this is way better because this will be constant time complexity, O(1) because the way Javascript stores objects internally, they are just key-value pairs and for a given key, Javascript can instantly give us back the value that's stored for the key, so it doesn't have to go through all the key-value pairs, just as an array can instantly give you the value for a specific index, an object can instantly give you the value for a specific key.

So if we have a scenario like this, using an object might be better than using an array of objects as we have it here because we go from linear time complexity in the worst case or in the average case to constant time complexity. Now if we had a key which is not a string but let's say some other object or anything like this, then of course we could use a real map and you learned about that in the data structure section earlier in the course, we can create a new map like this and then simply add our items to this real map which is capable of using anything as a key, not just strings or numbers but also other objects and so on.

So a real map is already built into Javascript and if you had a scenario where you need uniqueness, you could use a set. So you have these different built-in data structures and for different operations, they offer different performance or different time complexities. You should be aware of that so that you can use the right data structure for the task you are trying to solve. Now just as before, here I also got an article I can strongly recommend about built-in data structures and also other data structures you could build on your own, where you also see time complexities for different operations, some comments and then also some examples for these data structures and how to use them with certain operations. Now important, this article does not just include built-in data structures like the array, it also shows you how to build brand new data structures with the built-in ones, so building up on the built-in ones of course.

that can be better suited for certain operations or certain tasks. This is a bit more advanced and I will say right away that in many scenarios, you will not need these custom built data structures but for highly sophisticated or advanced applications, you might need to build your own data structures which is then optimized for certain tasks to be faster than what you got built-in but that's a next step after you master the basics, for now it is important to understand different time complexities of different operations and that therefore it is important to think about what you plan on doing and coming up with the right or with the best solution for the task at hand to have a well performing solution.

lectures.text:
So now in this module, you had an introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, to time complexities and also saw some example algorithms in action. lectures.text:
In this course, you learned a lot about Javascript. Now what if I were to tell you that there is another programming language, closely related to Javascript, which is also worth knowing and that is Typescript. Now don't worry it's not a brand new language you have to learn, instead Typescript is a language which does not run in browsers, which does not run in Node.js, so it's not like Javascript when it comes to that but instead it's a language which builds up on Javascript, which has to be compiled down to Javascript with help of a tool which we're going to install and which adds new features to Javascript to make Javascript development easier, maybe more fun but definitely also cleaner and helps you write cleaner code.

So in this module, we'll have a look at what exactly Typescript is and how it works, how you can use it and how it looks like and you will then also see why you might want to use it, how to write Typescript code, that it's not that different compared to Javascript and how you can utilize it for your projects.

lectures.title: What is TypeScript and Why would you use it?
lectures.text:
So what exactly is Typescript, that's important to understand right because without knowing that, it will be hard to learn it and to use it. Now it's important to understand and I really want to stress this, that Typescript is not a brand new language with a totally different syntax, no, it builds up on Javascript, it is a so-called superset to Javascript which in the end means it is Javascript but it adds more features, more syntax features you can use.

Now it is worth noting, as I mentioned, that Typescript does not run in browsers, browsers don't know how to execute Typescript, they know how to execute Javascript. So whilst you will learn how to write Typescript in this module here, it's not a language you can use like this in browsers, instead and that's of course also something you learn in this module, we need an extra tool which compiles Typescript code to Javascript code, so which converts the code to Javascript so that we have the Javascript code we learned about but during development when we write Typescript code, we have a better experience because of all these extra features.

Now speaking of that, which features does Typescript add? Well most importantly the thing that gives Typescript its name, it adds types and with that, I mean data types. Now of course in Javascript, we also know types, you learned about the core types Javascript has - strings, numbers, boolean, objects and so on. Now it is important to understand that Javascript is a dynamic, weakly typed language which means that types are evaluated during runtime, so when your script executes but they're not something you define when you write your code, of course you might know that here you're working with a string and in another place you're working with a number but you're not putting that into your code and let me give you an example where this might matter. Consider this simple add function which adds two numbers, presumably at least but now let's say you're calling this function with two strings which you're passing in, please notice the quotes around the numbers.

Now of course you might wonder why you would do that but consider that this is coming from an input field in your DOM, in your web page, what you get from there will always be a string so even if the user enters a number there, it's technically will be a string. Now if you add these two strings here, you will actually find a bug in your application. It will not crash or show an error but what you will get is basically the concatenated strings and I can quickly show this to you here in the normal Javascript console in a browser, if I add five plus three, we get 53 as a string because it simply concatenates those instead of adding them.

Now that's probably undesired and in Typescript, you can avoid this because in Typescript, you can add types and this is now a syntax feature which is added by Typescript, which does not exist in Javascript. Notice the colons after a and b in the parameter list of the function and after the colon you see the word number. This is Typescript syntax which in the end tells Typescript that both a and b in this case here should be of type number, so we must only call this function with two numbers being fed in, not with two strings.

So here in Typescript, when we compile this to Javascript, I mentioned that it needs to be compiled, we will get a compile time error, giving us as a developer a chance of fixing this before we even test it in the browser so we can catch errors or bugs like this way earlier and that's the huge thing about Typescript or one of the huge things. Now besides adding types, Typescript also adds some other nice features which don't exist like this in Javascript, of course these features since Typescript doesn't run in browsers are always compiled down to Javascript workarounds to make the same feature work there as well but in Typescript, it's often easier to implement certain things thanks to these extra features and in addition, Typescript also compilers next generation Javascript code to old generation Javascript code you could say.

So the thing Babel does, the tool we learned about in the browser support module, Typescript actually has this built in. Typescript also allows you to write modern Javascript Typescript code in the Typescript files and as a result, get Javascript files which will run in older browsers as well. So Typescript sounds pretty interesting to me, let's take a closer look at it, let's see how we install that compiler and let's write some Typescript code.

lectures.title: Working with Types
lectures.text:
So in order to get started with Typescript, we have to install this Typescript compiler because I explained that Typescript doesn't run like this as a language in a browser, instead the browser understands Javascript, so we need this compiler, this tool which takes our Typescript code and converts it to Javascript code. Now for that you can visit typescriptlang.org and on this page, you'll find a download link, this is the official page of the Typescript project by the way, so there you also find the official docs if you want to dive into those but for the moment we can click on download here to learn how to install this compiler and here we actually don't have a download link, instead we install this Typescript tool with npm, so with the Node Package Manager.

Now we already used this before in the course but in case you somehow skip those sections, you get this tool as a command you can use in your terminal or command prompt once you install Node.js. So for that, you can visit nodejs.org and there simply download and install that latest version, with this button you downloaded you get an installer, you can walk through the installer and you can install Node.js on your system. Now Node.js is runtime for Javascript and this gets used by the compiler behind the scenes but most importantly if you install Node.js, you also install the Node Package Manager. a tool which actually allows you to install packages, for example global packages global tools like this Typescript tool.

So with Node.js installed, you can open up your system command prompt or terminal and there, simply run npm install -g for global Typescript, this will installed this tool globally, now on Mac and Linux you might need to add a sudo in front of this to get the right permissions. Once this installation finishes, you got Typescript, this compiler installed and you're ready to write some Typescript code. Now to do that, let's head over to a new project and here, I essentially got an empty folder opened up in Visual Studio Code which is the IDE I'm using here, the two files and folders you see here are only configuration files which you can ignore and which you don't need and in there, we can now add our first Typescript file, for example app.ts, the name is totally up to you.

Now .ts is important, this stands for Typescript and this simply is the extension we use here to make it clear that we write some Typescript code in there. Now in this Typescript file here, you can write Typescript code and it's important to understand here that Typescript, as I mentioned, builds up on Javascript, so generally you can write normal Javascript code in here and indeed, any Javascript code works in a Typescript file but you can then also add certain features which only work in Typescript, so it's Javascript++ so to say. Now what can we do in here?

Well we can for example add a function, add, where we get two parameters, A and B and where we return a + b, that's the example from the slide I showed earlier. Now let's create a result constant here and call add and pass in 5 and let's say 3 as strings, this was the example where we might get an unexpected result. We can console log result here and now we can execute this. Now to execute this, one way is to simply add index.html file and if you are using Visual Studio Code, you can then just type HTML here, you get these auto suggestions and if you hit tab here, you get this HTML5 skeleton where l'll just set a title of Typescript and where I will now add a script import. Now important, here we don't import app.ts but app.js because as I mentioned, the browser won't be able to run our Typescript code anyways.

Now of course we have no app.js file right now but that will soon change. Now I will add defer here to make sure that the script gets downloaded early but only executes once the entire DOM has been rendered and with that, that's it. For the moment, I need no content in here because in the script we got some code which runs automatically anyways and which simply prints this result. Now the app.js file is missing as I mentioned, right? Now with the help of the Typescript compiler, we can get this. All we need is a new terminal and here I will use the built-in one, so your normal command prompt or terminal, simply navigate it into this project folder and there since we installed Typescript with this command, we can now run tsc, this is a command which is now available thanks to the globally installed Typescript compiler, app.ts and what this command does is it takes this app.ts file and converts it into a Javascript file, converting any Typescript specific code into Javascript code and of course running all that Typescript logic, checking for all these types and so on and right now please note that in here we have absolutely no Typescript specific logic, this is all regular Javascript code but as I mentioned, we can write this in Typescript files and therefore,

this will also compile. So if I hit enter here, you'll see this completes and now we get this app.js file and if we have a look at this file, we see it's generally the same content, whitespace was removed and you also see that const was translated to var because and I did mention this, Typescript also converts code to code that runs in older browsers as well, this is an extra benefit we get, so this is actually Javascript code which also runs in older browsers.

Later I will show you how you can tweak the configuration to make sure that it works according to your plans and you for example keep const here if you want to but for the moment, this is fine. As long as I have this file open, I also get some errors here in app.ts because my IDE thinks that all these functions and constants are now declared twice, to get rid of this, we simply close app.js and the errors are gone, these are not real errors. So we get the app.js file, now let's simply open index.html and for that we can simply open it up in the MAC finder or Windows Explorer and click twice on it.

Now that's of course not the result of five plus three but please note that I passed in two strings and therefore if you add two strings, Javascript concatenates them, it does not add the mathematically, it concatenates them and that's the bug I mentioned on the slide.

Now how can Typescript help us with that? Well in Typescript, so in the ts file, we shouldn't work in the js file because this is generated automatically when we compile, so in the ts file, we can now add some Typescript features, the reason why we use Typescript - we can add a type assignment here, for example on the parameters. We can make it clear to the Typescript compiler that A should be a number and B should be a number, we do that by adding a colon after the parameter where we want to assign a type and then we write the type name and there for example, number is one of the types Typescript supports, we do this after both A and B.

So now what we're telling to Typescript and to the Typescript compiler is that both A and B should be of type number and you see in my IDE, I now automatically get an error here because Visual Studio Code, the IDE I'm using here is actually an IDE with built-in Typescript support and therefore it automatically parses my code and detects that I'm violating my type rules here, so it gives me an error here. Now even if you're not getting this in the IDE, you you'll see we now get an error if I try to compile this file again by again running tsc app.ts. You see now down there, we actually get an error that the argument of type 5 which is wrapped in quotes, so which is of type string, is not a sizable to a parameter of type number and it also shows us which line violates our rule.

This is Typescript in action, this is one of the main reasons why we use Typescript. Now I am very specific about the types of data I want to work with here and I avoid mistakes like this one here where I pass the wrong type of data into this function. Now of course since we call the function here on our own, it might be unlikely that we pass in string data like this but imagine we're actually gathering input from a user input field in the DOM, values we get from there would always be a string by default and we might have forgotten to convert them, in that case Typescript can help us tremendously because it shows us such an error before we even run our code and we have to find the bug there, now we get an error during compilation.

Now it still compiles the code, it still generates the app.js file but it warns us here, it gives us this error and now we can go ahead and fix this error by passing in values of the correct type and now if I try to compile this again, it compiles without errors and in the running application if we reload, we got rid of this bug. So this is how Typescript can help us write cleaner code and avoid unnecessary mistakes, simply by adding some types here.

Now that's not all you can do in Typescript and not the only way of working with types but it is an important start, now let's see how else we can work with types in Typescript.

lectures.title: Core Types & Diving Deeper
lectures.text:
So we got our hands dirty with Typescript and we see why Typescript might be helpful. We also already learned about the first type Typescript supports and that's the number type and how we can assign this type to, in this case, a parameter. Now before we dive into other types, let me also make it clear how else you can work with types in Typescript, here we are assigning a type, we are actively telling Typescript hey this parameter is of type number.

Now actually, in the snippet here, types are also getting used in other places, for example in this line here, which type does result have? We don't assign a type here right, we have no colon after this. Well, turns out that we don't need to, we can actually add one and make it clear that result will also hold a number, of course it will because we return the addition of two numbers here but we don't have to do that. We can do that but it's not necessary because Typescript has a built-in feature which is called type inference, which means Typescript is really doing its best, and it is really smart, about inferring types you're working with and in this case if I hover over result here in Visual Studio Code, I see that Typescript inferred that this is of type number.

Now how did it do that? Well it actually also inferred the return type of the add function. If I hover over add here, you see this is basically the type of this function, you see the two parameter types here and then after the function as a whole, you also see a colon and then here also the type number. Now that basically is what Typescript inferred to be the return type of this function, so Typescript correctly infers that since we add A and B in here and return the result and A and B a numbers, we have a return type of type number.

Well and since we store the return value of the add function in result, Typescript also infers that result holds a number. So type inference is really a key feature of Typescript as well and it is a good practice to not unnecessarily reassign a type, Typescript could infer anyways, it's also not a bad mistake but it's simply not required, Typescript already knows which type we have here and side note, if I now were to assign another type, for example string which Typescript also supports, I of course get an error because I'm actually storing a number in constant which I defined to hold a string. So if I wanted to store a string in here, then indeed I now need to fix something about it my code, I either need to return a string here, for example by wrapping this into parentheses and calling to string here or instead of doing that, of course we also could call to string here, so that is something we can do but here I will get rid of it and I will use this type inference because I'm fine with using a number here.

Now speaking of numbers, which other types do we have? We just saw the string right, I assigned the type string here, so string is another core type Typescript supports and in general, it supports all the core types Javascript knows as well - numbers, strings, booleans, objects and so on. So this is the string, if we wanted to work the boolean, like isDone, well then here Typescript would infer that is done holds a boolean, actually it infers here that it holds exactly false and I'll come back to these exact types later but we can also accept any boolean here and if I would turn this into a variable here where we can assign a new value, then Typescript also infers that this is a boolean and it would allow us to assign true as a value as well, just for a constant, it inferred the concrete type, false, because constants can't get new values, so there Typescript knows that it's not even a boolean, it's really just false, for a variable it is a boolean. So booleans, strings, numbers - we have all these types, makes sense I guess.

Which other types do we have? Well, we also have function types and with that I don't mean the types of the parameters, I really mean the type of the function as a whole, so a type that describes the entire function. What do I mean by that? Well if we hover over add, we see the function type, this is how the function type in the end is inferred, the function type includes both the parameters as well as the return value and we can of course also set our own return value here by adding a colon after the parameter list and then defining our return type and here again if I set this to type string, then of course my current logic and a function is not correct because this will return just the result of two numbers being added together which is a number, so I would not meet my function type here.

So we might want to get rid of that and use type inference or change our logic. So the function is made up of the parameter types and the return type. Now when it comes to the return type, you can also of course have functions that don't return anything, for example print result. Let's say this is a function which takes a result and there, I console log the result like this. Now if I use this function down there to print the result I got here, you see this will work but now of course this function doesn't return anything.

We can make clear that this function won't return anything by adding a return type of void here, now that's a type added by Typescript and this basically means this function has no return statement. We could also go with undefined here, undefined is also valid type in Typescript but as you see I'm now getting an error. Why? Well technically a function that doesn't return anything returns undefined in Javascript but in Typescript, there is a slight differentiation between these cases.

If I set the return type of a function to undefined, Typescript expect that I have a return value which simply is undefined. If I don't intend on returning anything, then technically still if I would use the return value I would have undefined but then in Typescript, I should set this to void to make my intention clear, my intention is to not even have a return statement and we do make this clear by setting this to void here. If I now would return undefined here, I also could do that but the better practice is to now not return anything.

Now just as before however, Typescript infers that I don't return anything, so we don't need to add to return type of void here, if we don't add it, then Typescript correctly infers that the return type is void and you'll always see one other important type here, the any type. You see that for result, I didn't assign my own type. Now of course, Typescript can't infer the type of result because we just defined a function here, it is as if we would create a variable A here, how would Typescript know what we plan on storing in there?

How does Typescript know what we plan on receiving here? It's not inferring the type by how we call the function later, so it can't infer the type here. In such a case, the type by default is any and of course we can also explicitly set the type to any here if we want to. Now you should use the any type carefully though, it's kind of the last resort type you have in Typescript. This is basically the default for all values if you don't work with types at all and therefore, you give up all the advantages Typescript offers because any really works with any value. So the advantage you get by being explicit about your types and the advantage of being able to catch errors early, that is all lost if you work with the any type because of course with that, Typescript accepts any values.

If on the other hand I make it clear that I want a number here, then I really only can pass a number into print result and if I would pass in anything else - a string, a boolean, whatever, then it would fail. So sometimes it's fine to use the any type but you should be careful about that, here I will leave it like this for the moment. Now before we move on, let me also show you another way of working with types and how you can override type inference by Typescript. To give you an example, let's say in the index.html file, we actually have two input fields, an input field with an ID of let's say num1 and then one with num2 and then we also have a button and when we click this button I want to trigger my add function here.

So now we got these two inputs and the button, now of course we need to get access to those inputs and the button in order to work with them and in order to read the values from there and add an event listener. So at the very top of the file, we could add a constant here, num1Input and use document get element by ID and use the ID num1 here to get access to this element in the DOM. Now num1 simply is the ID I assigned here, the other input has the ID, num2. Hhence we can duplicate this to get the num2Input by that ID and also get access to the button element with document query selector button, we only have one button on the page so we can select it with this query selector. Now with all that, I will actually comment out this code here at the bottom because we don't need it right now and instead I'll use the button element to add an event listener for the click event and upon a click, I want to call add and I want to use my two inputs here.

So we'll actually use an anonymous function here, a little arrow function here simply and in there, I will get the two concrete values the user entered into these inputs and then call add with those values. So num1 here simply is num1Input.value and you already see I didn't get autocompletion here and I do get an error here in my ID, even though this should work right, we are selecting an input element here. So I'm not sure where this is coming from, we'll fix it later, for now let's live with the error and let's also extract num2 from num2Input, then we can calculate the result by calling add by passing in num1 and num2 and then last but not least, we can call print result and pass in the result.

Now we have errors here but let's try running this code. So I will compile app.ts and of course we get errors here because we get the same errors my IDE already detected but as I mentioned earlier, the file, the .js file is still generated, so we do get this file here. Hence if we go to the running application and I reload, I got these two inputs and I can enter my two values and click add and it does something. Now we are looking at an old bug again though, the two values got concatenated instead of added.

Now this is not really what we wanted right and why do we get this? I think we got rid of that when we introduced types, so why do we have that error again? Well keep in mind that types can help us but only if we really use them and here we clearly have an error, so Typescript doesn't really understand that we have a value property on num1Input and if we take a closer look, it therefore of course also doesn't know what's inside of value. So num1 effectively is of type any and we pass that into add and indeed add expects two numbers but it turns out since num1 is any, Typescript trusts us, maybe that is a number so it doesn't complain here, also because we already got an error here so Typescript kind of gives up and allows us to pass in values which seem to be strings, okay. Well maybe let's resolve this error first, why does Typescript not understand that there is a value property on num1Input? We are selecting elements in the DOM here and we know these will be input elements and of course they therefore have a value property and indeed this part is not failing, our code is working here.

So why does Typescript not understand that these are inputs? Well how would it? We only tell Typescript that we select an element in the DOM by ID but this could be any element, you can have any ID on any element, it could be a paragraph, it could be a button, it could be a list item, it doesn't have to be an input element and therefore if we hover over get element by ID, we indeed see the Typescript only infers that this is of type HTML element and that's of course very unspecific, it just means any HTML element, not specifically an input element.

Now we of course know as a developer that we will get an input element here and by the way, Typescript doesn't scan our index.html file to check what we're selecting there, so we can't rely on type inference here, instead we can do something which is known as type casting. We can override the inference made by Typescript, we can tell Typescript that this will be of a different type. Now you could think we'll do this by adding a type here and here we could use the HTML input element type. You might not notice type, it's one of the built-in types for working with the DOM and this basically says what I store in here has to be not any HTML element but a HTML input element. Now of course you see we get an error here and we get an error here because just because we want to store such an element here doesn't change the way get element by ID works, Typescript still doesn't know what we get here.

So instead we'll use this type casting thing I mentioned, you do that by adding the as keyword after the thing where Typescript infers some type which you want to change and then you set the type you want to use instead of the type Typescript inferred, so in this case HTML input element. Now this is pure Typescript syntax, this will all be lost once we convert it to Javascript but this now overrides what Typescript uses or infers here, if we now hover over num1Input, we see what's stored in there is a HTML input element and if we scroll down, we see that therefore for num1Input, we don't get this error anymore, we now know okay yes, this is now clearly available, this property exists. We get a new error which I'll come back later but this error is gone. So this is type casting in action, there also is another syntax you can use, you can use angle brackets in front of the thing you want to cast instead of after it as we do it with as and then use the type here. Both works, this syntax is a bit more common now but both does the same thing in the end. With that we're simply overriding the type Typescript inferred and I'll leave both syntaxes here to show you both, of course in your apps you should be consistent and typically use either of the two. So now the errors down there are gone

but we've got a new error here and that error now makes sense. It's important to understand that the value property on an input element always returns a string, no matter which type this input is of, so even if you set this to type number here, this doesn't change the type of value you get from the value prop and it also does not change with the value the user entered. If a user enters the number 10 into an input, it's still a string, it's wrapped into quotes so to say, value always gives you a string.

So num1 and num2 are strings and therefore we are now calling add with two strings and that's what Typescript is not liking here. If we would compile this file, we would get errors where we clearly learn that type string is not allowed here but that we want the type number instead. So to change this, we now need to parse these strings to numbers, so we can add a plus in front of both value it retrieves here to cast the string into a number. Now that of course means that if anything which can't be cast is entered, this will be converted into not a number but that's fine for now.

And with that, we again see the power of Typescript in action, by being clear about the types we're working with, we can catch this nasty bug we introduced where we forgot to cast the values and where we hence concatenated the two values instead of adding them mathematically. So now with that if we save this and we compile this, we can reload this page and now if I enter the two numbers here, we get the additions in a mathematical sense instead of the concatenated strings.

So this is how we work with types and some of the core types we can work with. Now of course you can learn about all types in the official docs here, in the handbook but we will also have a look at some other core types and features throughout this module, so let's continue.

lectures.title: Object Types, Array Types & Function Types
lectures.text:
So we saw some core types in action - we saw type casting in action, now let's dive into a bit more advanced types - objects and arrays for example. Now thus far, I only work with strings of numbers and yes actually HTML input element is an object in the end, just a specific type of object but let's have a look at objects in general. Let's say for whatever reason, when we calculate our result here, we don't want to store that in a constant result like this or not just in that constant but instead we also want to create a result container and that should be a Javascript object where we have the res property and that holds our result. Now of course, it's a bit redundant to have this extra container but for demo purposes, it's fine.

Now clearly we have an object here, now in this object we have one property - the res property, now which type is result container now? Well it is of type object, if I add object here, this works, I can explicitly set this to type object and Typescript won't complain. Now one problem with this approach is that we don't get the best possible auto completion and type support. If I access .res here, I get an error and if I access anything else here, I also get an error.

Now for age, that makes sense but res should definitely work, right, because we have a res property here. Now in Javascript, we can work with classes to define blueprints for objects, right? And of course we can use classes in Typescript as well, it supports this feature as well and since it compiles code to code that works in older browsers as well, it even compiles class code down to Javascript code that does not use classes but constructor functions and runs in older browsers as well. In Javascript, the field syntax is pretty new and experimental and not supported by all browsers but since Typescript gets compiled down to Javascript code which will work in all browsers, Typescript can enforce certain features which wouldn't work in browsers otherwise and here we have to simply add name and age as fields up there so that we can work with them in here in the constructor.

This is just how Typescript works, it forces us to use this setup because this in the end just leads to cleaner code, other developers reading our code can quickly see which fields, which properties this user class will have and of course for this simple class, it wouldn't have been too hard by just looking at the constructor but if this is a bigger class with a lot of properties that get added everywhere throughout the class, having a list of properties right at the top can be very greetable and very helpful.

There are certain values in Javascript as well as in Typescript therefore that simply work together with other value types and other values and the array is such a value, the array itself is a value, any array is an object but an array of course only really works because it stores other values, so we get two types work together, the array and the data in the array and therefore, we want to be clear that results holds an array but we also want to be clear about which array.
