lectures.text:
So what are web components? Web components really are just your own custom HTML elements, HTML elements that are not built into the browser but that are created by you as a developer or by some other developer and you are now using them in your project and what could be easier to dive into them than to just use such a custom web component, so let's have a quick look. Here I have a simple index.html file and I opened it in Visual Studio Code, the IDE I'm using in this course, you can do this in your normal system text editor, that really does not matter, it's a normal HTML5 skeleton we have here, you'll find this exact file attached to this video in case you want to start with that too but there is nothing special about this file.

Now in that file, let's say we're creating an application where we want to show a modal so that info box pop over overlay thing you see on many pages. Now obviously, we can create one from scratch, we can add a div here, add some styling to the div and then write some Javascript to conditionally show and hide that div and also add another div that can act as a backdrop, so this gray area behind the modal that blocks access to the rest of the page, we can write all of that but we can also create our own web component for that or use a web component someone else created and here I created one for you and you also find that attached to this video.

There you will find this modal.js file which you can just download and drag and drop into the same folder as the HTML file you created or you downloaded. Now you can go through this file, in the end, here we create or I created a so-called web component, a custom HTML element and we will do this together in this course, this is taken directly from the course, we will build this component later in the course. So I won't go through that right now, there is a lot of stuff in there we don't know yet and this video is not about understanding all of that, this video is about seeing what custom elements do or what such custom web components do.

This web component in the modal here is in the end registered as a custom element with the uc-modal tag, that is what I can tell you right now about this code. This creates a new HTML tag that we can use in any file that imports this modal.js file, so let's do that. Let's add a script import, here in the head section so that it gets loaded early and let's point at that modal.js file and for that, it needs to be in the same folder as I just mentioned. Now with that imported, we can use the uc-modal element as if it were a normal HTML element and of course this is not a built-in element, normally using this tag would do absolutely nothing because the browser doesn't recognize that but it now does as my Javascript file, it registers a custom element under this tag.

Now this modal happens to work in a way where we need to pass in some information between the opening and closing tag, for example a h1 tag, the modal title where we set the title of the modal and there we use a feature called slots which you'll learn in detail throughout the course which tells that web component where to position that content inside of the component. So here I can say slot equals title because this is one of the reserved slots I have in this component and now we also need some content that is shown below the title and there I'll add a paragraph, this is our first web component. With this added, if we now double click this index.html file, you will not see anything because the modal isn't opened right now.

You can open it by adding a special attribute to this uc-modal tag and that's all logic we added or we will add in this modal.js file, so that is why this will work, you can add the opened attribute, make sure to spell it right. After you did this, if you reload, hey here is a modal and you can even close that by clicking one of the buttons or clicking the backdrop and you see we have a nice animation there too and this again is all stuff we will build throughout this course.

Now of course, we can also open this programmatically if we wanted to. So instead of hardcoding opened in there, we could add other scripts, so another Javascript code which is not related to the web component which could be our normal application code for this web app we're creating and there the cool thing is we can interact with our own custom elements, just as with native HTML elements. So here I'm getting access to my modal and I'll store that in a constant named modal, by the way I will have a Javascript refresher where I explain what const is in case you don't know that and now I can use the normal DOM operations like document query selector to get access to an element with a CSS selector and here I will use uc-modal, my own tag as a selector. And with that, let's say we add a timeout here and after three seconds, I want to open the modal. For that, I'll add an anonymous function here, an arrow function in this case and there I can access my modal and call an open method and this open method also exists because I added the logic for this method in this web component and we will do this together later in the course.

So now with that, if we reload, there is nothing there but after three seconds, you will see that modal opening and you can still close it with the buttons and so on. So this is how a web component works and what a web component is, it is your own HTML element which you can configure in the way you want. Behind the scenes, such a web component also just uses native elements like divs or a header as you can see and we will learn all of that step-by-step in the course but we can group that together, add additional logic like here the open method, the opened attribute and so on, add special styling and add for example an animation and hide that all under an HTML tag that we can dump into any project which imports this web component.

That is what web components are in a nutshell and that is what makes them awesome but now let's have a closer look at what makes up the web components specification and why we might want to use them.

lectures.title: What are Web Components?
lectures.text:
So being able to write custom HTML elements is pretty cool, I did mention though that web components is actually a broad term for a couple of specifications that are built into modern browsers that make up that web components term. Custom HTML elements is just one part of that set of specifications, it's one specification, it's arguably the most important one because this defines a couple of features modern browsers exposed to you and you can use these features in Javascript then and you will also learn how to make it work in older browsers in this course. So you get this set of features that allows you to register your own HTML tags and define some basic logic behind that.

However this alone will not give you great web components, another important specification that makes up the web components turn is the shadow DOM specification. The shadow DOM is all about having a separate DOM, a tree of DOM nodes behind your custom element that is separated from the normal DOM, this helps you for example with scoping your styles to your custom element, so that styling you set up for your custom element doesn't interfere with other parts of your application, really useful. Templates and slots is another important part of the specification.

Your custom element will in the end just be a combination of default HTML elements because in the end, the browser only knows how to handle these but you can compose them and add styling and add Javascript logic to create more powerful widgets, like the modal you saw and you will learn how that works throughout the course. Templates and slots are another important specification here because here, you define this core structure behind your element, so you basically define the template which is then rendered as a shadow DOM and slots are helpful for exposing certain entry points, like that title we used in the last lecture, this h1 tag we passed to slot title that allows us to pass dynamic content into our web component so that developers using our web components can use them and the set of features that are baked in and still if our components wants that, pass extra content into the component and you will learn all about that throughout the course as well.

Now last but not least, there's another specification you sometimes hear about when hearing about web components and that is the HTML imports specification. That was meant to be a feature which allows you to import HTML files into HTML files so that you can define these templates for your components in HTML files that are then imported dynamically. Now this is not continued anymore because the industry moved in a direction where we use Javascript for all of that and where we use modern build tools and Javascript modules to import and export inside of our Javascript files and import the HTML templates as strings there as well and this is also the approach you will see in this course and I will explain and show it there.

So it's just important to be aware of these three core features - custom elements, shadow DOM, templates and slots and we will dive deeply into them and learn all about them and how we use them throughout the course of course.

lectures.title: Why Web Components?
lectures.text:
Now that we have a rough idea of what web components are and you will hear me use the term web components and custom elements interchangeably in this course by the way, now that we know that, the question is, why would we use web components? Well one great advantage is that a web component, like this modal component you saw, allows us to encapsulate logic and a user interface in one custom HTML tag which we then, another advantage, can also reuse across our page or even reuse across multiple projects.

We can just take that Javascript file and drop it into any other project, just as you did it with my modal.js file. So encapsulated logic and an encapsulated user interface is of course great because it's easier to understand, we have connected code in one element and another element cares about something totally different so we have separated code which is always great, it's therefore also easy to maintain and we have a separation of concerns. Every element takes care about one tag, the modal takes care about displaying itself and showing some content in this pop-up window style, it does not care about the side drawer or sending HttpRequests or anything like that.

The reusability across the page means that we only have to write a certain logic once and then we can use it multiple times, that modal might be something we show when the user orders an item but also when the user login fails. So we can write this logic one and then just pass different dynamic content into it in the different parts of our page where we use it. So we don't have to worry about overlapping logic and we also don't have to write logic in the user interface more than once, which is great and the same advantages are true when we share our component across multiple projects.

We still use it like a normal HTML element, we don't have to worry about setting up a complex development environment there or using a special framework, we can even have projects written in different frameworks, let's say in Angular and in React and we can use one and the same web component in both. So that is a great advantage, we wouldn't be able to share React Components with an Angular project for example. We also of course can reuse core UI elements across multiple projects, so you could create a set of core UI elements that have your corporate identity baked in, like a toolbar, the modal, the side drawer which you use in all your projects then, so that can be really helpful and save you a lot of time and we again also don't have to repeat ourselves when it comes to writing all the logic and the user interface.

lectures.title: Getting Started!
lectures.text:
So let's dive into the basics about web components then, how they generally work, how we create our own web components and for this, we will use vanilla Javascript. This means no third-party libraries, no other packages, just Javascript as it natively runs in the browser but first of all, let me come back to the question, what web components are? Obviously we already learned that web components are basically our own HTML tags, like my tooltip here, which is not a tag built into the web or were built into the browser and that these are basically HTML tags which we define in Javascript code and which we then can use on our page. So web components are really as we use them, custom HTML elements but they are made up of three, theoretically four, but three important parts.

The first and the core part that makes up web components, the web components specification set is the custom HTML element specification and since we in the end built custom HTML elements, this is the core part, this is essentially a bunch of Javascript functionalities that allow us to define our own HTML tags and the logic behind them, so this is a crucial part. Now you might wonder, okay what else could be important if we are talking about creating our own custom HTML elements?

Well there are two other pieces which are also very important and which are used in that Javascript logic we write behind our custom HTML element and the first additional set of functions or of features offered in Javascript that is important related to creating custom elements is the shadow DOM specification. The shadow DOM specification is all about giving us some features to create our own DOM tree, our own elements behind that elements you could say that are hidden away from the main DOM and I will come back to that in more detail later where this will become clearer, so which is in the end just allowing us to define our own HTML tags which are then grouped together behind our custom HTML tag and which are separated from our main, our normal DOM and this is especially helpful when we talk about CSS styling because the shadow DOM will allow us to define CSS styles that only affect our custom element and even if we style a h1 tag in our custom element, we would not affect other h1 tags on the page and this will become all clearer once we actually use it and dive deeper into it, so it's another crucial part when it comes to separating our logic from the rest of the page you could

say. The third important specification is about templates and slots and this is also something we will use in great detail, which in the end allows us to define our own HTML structure which is hidden behind our custom element and which allows us to add some flexible entry points, these so-called slots, that we can then actually populate with information from outside when we use our custom element and again, this is something which will become clearer later.

So I know that this is all very confusing right now because I'm throwing a lot of interesting words around, a lot of specifications without explaining in detail what they do because it makes more sense to gradually build up the knowledge and we will actually start with custom HTML elements before we add these other features, before we add the shadow DOM and the templates. Now I also mentioned that there are four specifications that make up the web components spec and the last specification is about HTML imports, the idea here was that we can actually import HTML files into HTML files, just as we can import CSS and script files but this is actually not a continued specification because as you will learn in this course, there is a more elegant way of importing your components and of importing the HTML inside of your components.

So we will not need this and indeed, it's not continued, it's not added to all browsers and there are no plans to do so.

lectures.title: A First Custom Element
lectures.text:
So with all the base setup out of the way, let's now finally create our first web component, our first custom element and for that, in the tooltip.js file, I will create a new class and classes allow us to build blueprints for Javascript objects and it's such a blueprint that we will in the end wire up with our own custom HTML tag. Now you can give that class any name you want and I'll name it tooltip and now here's one important part, to be usable as a custom element, you need to extend something with extends keyword, which means you have to build your class based on some other base class and here we will use a base class that's built into the browser, we'll use the HTML element class here.

Now this is a class, an object built into the browser, not defined by us and we extend that and every custom element has to extend that. It's still an independent and autonomous custom element though, I will show you extended built-in elements later, there you will not extend the HTML element but more specific versions of it. If you extend this, you have a basic vanilla green field HTML element you build on your own which does not depend on any built-in element, This is simply a base element you always need to extend and now in here, you will put all the logic that makes up your custom element.

The question just is, what does this mean, put all the logic in there? Well let's say this tooltip component should in the end show us a tooltip button, a tooltip icon and when we hover over that icon, we want to present a tooltip to the user and for this, we can define a couple of things in this custom element to make this work and the first thing we can add is a constructor. A constructor is also a default method name which is detected by Javascript and Javascript will automatically execute this method, so this function inside of a class, whenever this class is instantiated, which means whenever a new object based on that class is created and later these new objects will be our own custom HTML tags in the index.html file.

We haven't added them yet, we'll do so later. For now let's start simple and let's simply add a console log statement here, it is working and this should theoretically be output in the console whenever a new tooltip class is created or a new object. Now this is just a Javascript class, HOw can we now create our own HTML tag? For that we use another object that is built into Javascript and that's the custom elements object. This is an object which allows us to register our own custom elements and we do this by using the define method here, so this is a function on this object which you can execute, all built into Javascript. This define method takes at least two arguments - the first one is a string and there, you define your own HTML tag.

Now there are some rules for that tag name, for example it has to be a single word which has to consist of at least two parts separated by a dash, so my-tooltip is a valid name, just tooltip alone is not. The reason for that rule is that all built-in HTML elements, like button or p or h1's are single words and by forcing you to have double words so to say, you are forced to not accidentally override one of the built-in elements, also possibly future added elements, So therefore you have to have a dash in that name and it has to be a dash, an underscore is not allowed for example, so it has to be a dash and therefore here we could have my-tooltip.

Now the prefix here at the beginning is totally up to you, it can be my-tooltip, it could be tooltip-tooltip but in reality, you want to choose a prefix here which kind of guarantees that your web component, your custom element has a unique tag, so that if the users using your custom elements in their app because maybe you share them with the web, so that users using your custom elements have a very low chance of having clashing custom elements from different libraries.

Therefore actually my-tooltip is not that great, often you use your company name there or a shortcut for your company name, like acad for academind in my case, in your case it should be your company or your initials, like ms for Maximillian Schwarzmuller in my case. So I will go with uc for Udemy course but in the end, choose a prefix here which, combined with the part after it, kind of guarantees that this is a unique name. So this is the HTML tag chosen now, by the way you can also have multiple dashes in multiple parts, at least one dash needs to be included, the second argument you pass to define then is your Javascript class that holds the logic for this custom element, so in our case this is the tooltip class here.

So this class we defined up here, we pass this as a second argument and with that we're telling Javascript, hey whenever you detect this HTML tag in an HTML file, you want to instantiate this class, you want to create a new object based on that class and you want to use that object for all the logic behind that custom element and now with that and this tooltip.js file being imported here, we can actually add the uc-tooltip element here in the body of our index.html file and it will not do much, it should print this though.

So now let's save both files, make sure you don't forget that and then let me simply run this by double clicking the index.html file. Now we'll not see anything on the page because we haven't added any visuals but if you open your developer tools under view, developer, developer tools or with the shortcut you find there, then you should be able to open the console part there and you can ignore the error you'll be getting, you should see it is working though.

This shows, this proves that this code here runs and it can only run when an object is created based on this class, we never do that but we define our own element and therefore this element has to be responsible for this code running and indeed it is. Now to get rid of this error, there is one rule we have to follow when creating our own elements and adding a constructor, you always have to call super first in there. This is a built-in method you can call inside of a class which will execute the constructor of the base class you're extending and this is required.

So if you add super here and you then reload this page, you will not see this error again, clear your console before reloading to make sure that you clear all past errors. So this is our first custom element added, obviously it's not doing anything useful but we have our own working HTML tag. Now we can start adding more logic to it.

used and here we can use all the features we can use on normal HTML elements when we select them in Javascript too, for example we can append a child node, so we can append another HTML element inside of our custom element and that sounds promising because there, I actually want to append my own icon let's say, my own icon above which we later can hover and for that, I can simply call document create element here and I will create a span here, a span element and that of course is not a custom web component, it is an element built into the browser because in the end, all your components you're building will be made up of these core primitives, of these built-in elements, you just compose them differently, style them differently and add your own event listeners, your own logic to do something when a certain button gets clicked and so on.

So all this composition, all this logic will in the end make up your own element. Now to find the right place, we need to learn how the browser or Javascript, the Javascript engine, actually goes about creating our own custom elements because it follows a specific lifecycle for that.

lectures.title: Understanding the Custom Element Lifecycle
lectures.text:
So I mentioned that there is a specific web component lifecycle which the browser follows when instantiating our own custom element objects in the DOM so to say. The first thing that gets executed is the constructor because this always gets executed when an object gets created based on your class and then the class's constructor gets executed, so this is essentially called when the element is created. Now it's important to highlight here that the moment where the element is created is not the moment where the element is then also attached into the real DOM by the browser, instead it's created in memory first and it's not part of the DOM at the beginning.

So the constructor is great for some basic initializations, some basic values for the different properties and variables you might be using in your class, in your component but it's the wrong place for accessing the DOM because your custom element has not been added to the DOM yet. For this, there is another method you can add in your class which will be executed by the browser once this element, once this custom component has been mounted onto the browser's DOM and that is the connected callback method. This is called when your element has been attached to the DOM and therefore this is the place for DOM initializations, so where you can now start adding content or where you can start accessing the DOM.

We're making progress and we're now able to render some text through our web component. Now still a lot of the logic is missing, for example where we hover over this, we get no event listeners that would do anything but we're getting there step-by-step. Let's now add such event listeners to see how we can quickly add more logic to this component which we then can easily reuse by reusing our custom selector, our custom HTML tag, we want to listen to when we hover over that tooltip icon and then we want to show a tooltip. For this, I will simply add an event listener.

This is a normal DOM element and therefore we can call add event listener and we can listen to the built-in mouse enter event which is fired when the mouse enters this span in this case because I'm attaching it to that tooltip icon span. Then I want to execute a function and for this, I will create a new method which is simply a function inside of a class and I will add this to this class, now I will name this method show tooltip. Now I added this underscore here to kind of make it clear that I only intend on calling this method from inside this class, as you learned earlier in the course Javascript in the past didn't really have private methods and it doesn't even have them right now in all browsers, there is is extra syntax with the hash in front of properties and methods to signal that they should be private but it's in the early stages, it's not supported everywhere, so I'm using this convention which you find in a couple of programs out there where you add an underscore in front of properties or methods which you want to mark as pseudo private so that you only intend on calling these methods from inside the class and therefore even if you name it like this, you can call it from outside too. Now by the way if you're wondering

what I mean with from outside, well since this is now a normal HTML element, you can of course also select it with document query selector and then you can access its properties and call its methods, just like you can do it on any other HTML element. So with an underscore in front of this name though, I'm indicating that this is a method you should not call. You can still do it and we can't stop that but at least we're clear regarding our intention of how this component should be used and if other developers are then using it or we are using it some time in the future after we don't exactly remember how we created it, then we know okay this is a method which should only get called internally which we don't have to care about when we work with our component from outside.

So this show tooltip method is what I want to call, so here I will call this show tooltip and important, I don't add parentheses because I don't want to execute this method here, I only saved a pointer to this method and set this up as my event listener so that when the mouse enter event occurs, then the browser can automatically execute show tooltip. Now inside of show tooltip, I then want to create a tooltip element which I can display. For this I'll create a new constant and I'll name it tooltip container and with documents create element, I'll create a new element of type div, again using one of the built-in HTML elements.

If you have multiple custom elements, you can of course also create those but here I will build an element that only uses primitives, so only use this built-in elements. So I create a div here and in that tooltip container, I can then set a text content of this is the tooltip text which we'll make more generic and settable by the user later and now of course it's all about attaching this container to the DOM and showing it there. So for that, again I will access this, this referring to the tooltip element and now there's just one thing to watch out for, due to the way that this keyword works in Javascript, we need to call bind this here when we point at show tooltip.

This ensures that the this keyword inside of show tooltip always refers to this class. Now here, I can append this child, I can append my tooltip container, the styling will be awful but it should work. If we now save that and we reload the browser, if I now hover over this question mark, indeed we see this is the tooltip text. Now it's not getting removed when I hover away though, you see that when I leave with the mouse it's still there and if I hover over it again, it adds more and more of these texts and that makes a lot of sense because we never remove that when we leave with the mouse.

So I will duplicate my event listener up there and besides mouse enter, I will also add mouse leave here and I will add a new private method, hide tooltip which should in the end remove this tooltip container. Now to access the tooltip container which I create in show tooltip and which therefore is not accessible from inside hide tooltip, I'll turn this from a constant in show tooltip into a property of the whole class. For this in the constructor which is a great place for basic initializations, I'll add a new property by using this keyword and then dot and then the name of the property and that property is basically just like a classwide available variable and I will name that underscore. to also mark that this is only used from inside the class, _tooltipContainer and I will not set an initial value, so it's basically undefined initially but then here in show tooltip, I will store this created div, not in this constant but in this _tooltipContainer and that of course means that the places where I used tooltip container like this also now have to become this _tooltipContainer.

The advantage of this approach is that the newly created div is now stored in a class property and unlike the constant, this property is not just accessible from inside this method but from all the methods in a class. So now in hide tooltip, i can also access this tooltip container and remove that note and for that I will actually access this remove child and I will remove that tooltip container child. Now when we leave this with the mouse, if we don't hover over the question mark anymore, this tooltip container which was added should be removed.

However of course that means that I now also need to hook hide tooltip up as a method that should be executed for mouse leave. Now with that if I save that and we reload this page, now when I hover over the question mark, the tooltip still gets added but if I now leave with the mouse, it's gone and now we have a tooltip that only shows up whilst we hover over the question mark. Now obviously styling is missing and the question mark is still positioned incorrectly but this is another great step forward and we can already see some custom logic doing its job in our web component because you must never forget that this whole hovering logic and so on all happens inside of our web component and that already means that if we copy that and we add another tooltip, so another instance of this element somewhere else, here we go, then there we'll also have this question mark over which we can hover, so we can easily reuse this functionality already.

Now of course it would be nice if we had more styling, more flexibility regarding our tooltip text and so on, so let's work on that tooltip text next because having this generic dummy text here, this is the tooltip text, does not make a lot of sense, the text here should be settable from outside instead. So let's take care about that in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Using Attributes on Custom Elements
lectures.text:
So let's make sure that the text that shows up on our tooltip can be set from outside and for that, we will use an attribute. Now attributes are not something that is exclusive to your web components or your custom elements, attributes exist on a lot of built-in HTML elements, take a link for example, here the ref thing here, that is an attribute and it allows you to configure this element, so the link here, in a declarative way which means you don't have to write any code, no Javascript code to set the target of this link and we want to use the same approach for our own tooltip, for example it would make sense that on our uc-tooltip tag here, we can use a text attribute or a tooltip text attribute or whatever you want to name it, I will name it just text and here, web components is a set of standards for example. This could be the text I want to display when I hover over this uc-tooltip element, now for the second one, I won't set a text attribute, so here we maybe want to have a default value.

How do we now use that attribute from inside our tooltip? Well it's actually pretty simple, inside of our constructor, we can initialize a new private variable and I will name it tooltip text. Now there, I will call get attribute and now enter the name of the attribute for which I want to extract the value and in my case that is text because I chose text as the attribute name here. So now we save whatever we stored as text or as the text attribute value, we save that in tooltip text and we can now use that down there where we save or we set up some text to be displayed.

So here instead of this hardcoded text, I will set this tooltip text as a value. Now with that if we save this, we can go back and reload this page and now if we hover over that, we don't see anything there right. Well the reason for that is that here, we're initializing it in the constructor but as you learned, the custom element has been created at this point but it has not been mounted to the DOM yet, this will only have happened inside of the connected callback.

So we should move this line into our connected callback so that we can safely access this DOM nodes attributes because at this point of time, it will have been rendered into the DOM and now if we save that and we reload this page, we see web components as a set of standard. Now for the second question mark, we don't see anything because we have no default value there. Now to make sure we have a solution for both cases, I will actually go back into the constructor and set the tooltip text here to some dummy tooltip text, maybe something that makes a little bit more sense than that and here I only want to override it when we have that attribute. For this, I'll add an if check where I see if this has attribute text, so only if we have that attribute being set, I will extract that attribute and store its text in a tooltip text, otherwise this will not be overriden and we'll be using our dummy text.

So now we have the basic initialization which does not access the DOM in the constructor and then we do access the DOM and override the default value with a more specific value if we have the text attribute being set in the connected callback and now we can reload this page once again, we see web components is a set of standards for the first tooltip, for the second, we see our dummy tooltip text. lectures.title: Styling our Elements
lectures.text:
It's all nice that we have some functionality in our web component but it would now be nice to work on the styling, for example that this tooltip does not kind of split our line here but it should be like an overlay being positioned next or near to our question mark here. So how can we achieve this? Well since we are creating our tooltip container here, we can of course also style that and there are a couple of ways of styling that, since it's a div, we could set up some general styling for divs of course, alternatively we access the style attribute and we add styles step-by-step, for example on the tooltip container here, we can access the style property which every DOM node has in Javascript and we could give this a background color of black and then we duplicate this to set a text color of white maybe. Now with that if we save that and we reload, we have this style, a bit better but of course the positioning is still off.

Now we might want to make sure that this has an absolute position, so that our tooltip container style, the position is absolute. That means that when it should be positioned relative to our entire custom element, we should give our custom element a style of relative. So in the connected callback where our custom element has been rendered to the DOM, there we can access our style, so the style of the custom element itself, the style of the uc-tooltip and there, we set the position equal to relative. If we now save that and we reload, now this looks a bit better, doesn't split our line any more.

Now maybe we also should set a z-index here so that it is above all other elements, z-index and set this to a value of 10 maybe. Now if you reload this, this looks better, it now really is an overlay near to our question mark, I'm liking this. So this already is a nice way but we also have a problem here. If I, for some reason, have a general style in my page with style tags or a CSS file which I import where I let's say style all my divs to have the border of two pixels solid and orange and obviously this is a bit of a made up example but you could certainly have some global styles affecting all divs or all h1 tags and maybe in your custom web component, you are using a h1 tag or as we are doing it, you are using a div and now what you will see is that if I save that and I reload this page, I have that orange border on that div in my web component too and you typically don't want that, you typically don't want to have global styles affecting your web components and you also don't want to have styles you defined inside of your web components affect outside elements.

In addition, it would be nice if we don't have to create everything programmatically like this with one line of code after the other and if we could define some HTML template instead of adding or creating HTML elements with create element all the time and for that, we have a solution, the shadow DOM and the templates. Both these techniques will help us with ensuring that we write a nice, reusable and encapsulated custom web component.

In addition, it would be nice if we don't have to create everything programmatically like this with one
line of code after the other and
if we could define some HTML template instead of adding or creating HTML elements with
create element all the time and for that, we have a solution,
the shadow DOM and the templates. Both these techniques will help us with ensuring that we write a nice, reusable
and encapsulated custom web component.

lectures.title: Working with the "Shadow DOM"
lectures.text:
To understand the shadow DOM, let's understand how the normal DOM, also sometimes called the light DOM, works and for that in your developer tools, you can click on the elements tab. This is your DOM tree essentially, you see that paragraph and in there you also see your custom component. Now when you expand your custom component, you also see that span that was added and when you hover over the question mark, you see that this div gets added here too.

Now there is one important thing to note here, the span with the question mark and that overlay div are all added to the normal, to the light DOM here. We are not using anything special here, we're not using the shadow DOM, so our custom component here in the end has a child which is this span with the question mark. Now what would be nice is if in a normal, in the light DOM, we had our custom component and the span or anything else like this overlay div which gets added is kind of hidden away behind that and is not added to the normal DOM because that would then mean that any styles we set up in a normal DOM would not affect our nested custom component DOM.

So basically our custom component here should have its own DOM tree which is not mixed or which is not kind of affected by the normal DOM tree and that would be the definition of the shadow DOM, our element should have its own DOM behind it which kind of makes up what we see on the page but which is not directly connected to the real DOM, which is not affected by global styles and the other way around. Now we have a specification in the browser that allows us to add such a functionality and we can unlock it in a very easy way, in the constructor we simply call this attach shadow and there, we pass a Javascript object where we simply set the mode to open. Now you can set it to closed and this simply defines whether you can access your shadow DOM tree from outside this component or not.

Now closing is something you'll typically not do because even if it is closed, there are ways to still access it and it's simply not worth the effort, after all you are the developer and if you don't want to access it from outside, you simply don't do it. So we'll set it to open throughout the rest of this course. Now this element has its own shadow DOM tree attached to it, we now just have to make sure that whenever we add new DOM elements with append child, we don't append them to our HTML element which is still part of the light DOM but to the shadow DOM of that HTML element and for that, when I call append child, I will first of all access the shadow root and that is now set since we set up a shadow DOM here in the constructor, so this will now access the shadow DOM tree and append the child to it. Visually this will not change much but you will see that this will have a great impact and I do the same here where I append this tooltip container, I access my shadow root and also of course when I remove it, I access my shadow root, so I access the shadow DOM. With that you can now save that and if you now reload the page, you will notice one important thing right away, the text which was written between our opening and closing tags here, so web components

and here we go, that text is gone now and the reason for it it can be seen when we inspect our custom element here, you see it now all of a sudden has a shadow root element which it didn't have before and there we see the shadow DOM. Now conveniently, we can see it here in the developer tools but thanks to that shadow root this is now detached from the main DOM and we can prove that by hovering over the question mark, you see the orange border of the div is now gone, even though we still have that rule here, we still have that styling rule but now with that shadow root being set up, this is gone. Now obviously as I just mentioned, our text between the opening and closing tag is also gone, so we have to bring that back and to bring it back, we'll use the other feature I mentioned, templates.

Now what's up with templates?

lectures.title: Adding an HTML Template
lectures.text:
We added our shadow DOM and this changed things by a lot, it is the right way to go but we're now missing our text we had there initially and we'll now dive into a feature called templates to define our base HTML structure of this HTML element, of our custom element and to later also bring back that text we passed between the opening and closing tags of our custom element. Now for templates, we got two alternatives, the first alternative for adding a template to our custom element is to go into our HTML document and there, we can add a new element, the template element.

This is a HTML element built into the browser, understood by the browser and the important thing here is that this element is not rendered automatically. Now here we can take our question mark and add it in there like this, we had it in the span so let's wrap it in a span here too, select that, now we have a template which in the end is just that span with the question mark inside of it. So this is now our template and now we want to use that template as a blueprint for the HTML content that makes up our custom element.

So previously, we simply created that HTML content in the connected callback and we happen to have a very simple HTML template for our tooltip, we only have this span with the question mark being added but it's easy to imagine more complex custom elements like a video player which has a dozens of buttons and so on. Now to use that content of the template in our web component now, I'll first of all give this template an ID of tooltip template for example and now in the tooltip.js file in the constructor where we can access the normal DOM, just not the DOM of this tooltip but we don't need that there, there I will now get my template and I'll store it in a constant by using the document query selector, again accessing the normal page DOM, not the DOM of this custom component and there I will use the ID selector to select the tooltip template, so I'm using that ID which I just added to my template. Now I get access to this template and now I want to basically copy the code I set up in that template, so this span in this case here and use it as a template for my custom component and for that I will simply access my shadow root which is available because I attached the shadow DOM and there, I will call append child.

I can do that here because I can already access the shadow DOM even before the element has been rendered to the real DOM because the shadow DOM remember is kind of abstracted away from the real DOM anyways so this is available in the constructor and now I will append a child here and the child is my template and there, we can access a content property to access basically the content inside of the template and on the content, we can call clone node and there you have to pass a boolean indicating whether you want to do a deep clone or a shallow clone, a deep clone means that you would clone any nested elements in there too, so if you had like a h1 tag inside of that span, you would clone that too if you set the argument to true, if you set it to false, you would only clone the top level of elements.

Now I will perform a deep clone here by setting this to true and with that, if I now save that and we reload that page, we see double quotation marks here actually, the reason for that being that we still have our code in there to add another question mark, so we should remove that and in addition, I will just change this a little bit down there, here I will set my tooltip icon equal to this shadow root and now here I want to find that span by simply adding a query selector because we can query the shadow DOM just as we can query the normal DOM and I will find that span there and with that if I save that and we reload this page, we have one question mark only but I can still hover over that.

So now we are using our template, our HTML template here. Now this is one way of doing it but of course this has a couple of drawbacks, now for example this web component now requires some content to be added to our HTML file where we in the end just want to use that web component and of course we're still losing that text here. Now we can fix that text even with this approach but I will also show you an alternative to this approach because it would be nice to have all the web component being composed in our Javascript file here so that we don't have to add a template to the HTML code and I will show you both this solution and a solution for our lost text here over the next lectures.

lectures.title: Using Slots
lectures.text:
Let's start with our lost text. It's easy to bring back because the template solution here has a tool for us to enable us to pass some content between our opening and closing tags of the web component and this feature is called slots. We can define a slot in the template which basically means hey you can insert the content which is between the opening and closing tag of our element in that place. You do that by simply adding a slot element, opening and closing, nothing in between, like this inside our our template. If you do that with just that addition, if you now reload the page, you'll see our text is back and now the question mark is correctly added after it because essentially, it's now taking this as a template and this template says here is the place for whatever you pass between the opening and closing tag and thereafter we have our own DOM, our own template whenever we want to have.

So this works now as before but now we're taking advantage of that slotting mechanism. Now slots also can have a default value, some default and this will kick in if you don't pass anything between the opening and closing tags. So if I delete my text down there for the second usage of this custom component and I then go back to the page and reload, we see some default here because the text I passed between my slots tags then is used as a default unless we override it with our own text as we do up there.

lectures.title: Defining the Template in JavaScript
lectures.text:
Now that is all nice but we also had the thing that I wanted to get this template out of this DOM, now how does that work? First of all, let me say that having a template in our normal HTML file is of course fine, as you see, it works but if we want to create a fully reusable web component, it would be nice to define the template in the Javascript file too so that in the end, we just have to dump this Javascript file into any project, any web project and we can start using our own component and for this I'll go back to the tooltip.js file and I will define a template in there which is really easy. Instead of appending our template content, so I can get rid of these two files here, I will access my shadow root and there we can set the innerHTML code, innerHTML is a default property you can set on your HTML elements, on the built-in ones too and there you can write any HTML code you want.

So now we can grab this content we had in the template and remove the template thereafter and add this here, like this. If you save that and you then reload this page, you have the same as before, the same behavior as before but now, you have your template as part of your Javascript file. Now I know that it can look strange to start writing HTML inside of your Javascript file, keep in mind that this in the end is just a normal string and it can look strange but it is a nice way of creating a reusable HTML element.

Now we can also use a next gen Javascript feature called template literals where we use back ticks instead of single quotation marks, so this is not a single quotation mark, this is a back tick, opening and closing and this will still create a string but now we can write a multiline string here so that we can format this in a nicer way. If we now save this, you will see it still works as before. So it's just a bit strange to get used to that, in some IDEs, you get really great auto completion support here though, mine doesn't pick it up here but still I will go with this approach because whilst it is strange to look at, we now have all the logic in the Javascript file, making this a really simple reusable web component.

Now one important thing, you might wonder how can I set the HTML content here inside my constructor? The reason is simple, innerHTML is just a property of our element here, of our object and this is just setting up some HTML code that will be rendered to to DOM once this element is mounted to the DOM. So unlike append child, this does not try to access the DOM at this point, it just prepares some content for the DOM once it later is available and the browser will take care about rendering this when it is able to.

lectures.title: Using Style Tags in the Shadow DOM
lectures.text:
Now with our own template being defined here, we can now also define some styles here and by the way this would have been possible with the template in the HTML file too because in here, we can now of course also add style tags as we can do in any Javascript file as we can do in normal HTML too, and the styles here and that is the interesting thing, since we do that on innerHTML of the shadow root, the styles here will only apply to the HTML code in our template, so to this span here or to the div we add dynamically and this means that we can now add all these styles down there in our style tag here.

So I add a div selector and now I want to set the background color with normal CSS because this is now a normal CSS written in a string, so the background color is black let's say, the color, so the text color is white, the position is absolute, the z-index is 10 and now I can't go down there and remove all these manual style assignments and still if we save that and we reload, we have the same styling as before but now we can write all styles conveniently as you are used to in HTML or in CSS syntax and it is scoped to this component only.

Please note that I'm using a general div selector and yet if I go to index.html and I would add a div here, this does not get the web component styles because of the shadow DOM. So if I now reload, you see the orange border which makes sense because we set this up here but you don't see the black background, this does also not have the absolute position because we really have scoped styles, thanks to the shadow DOM and our styles being set up as the innerHTML of that shadow DOM for our custom web component.

And this gives you a lot of flexibility regarding how you style your components, regarding the template you set up for them, regarding the elements you add to them and all of them is part of your custom element and does not spill over to your normal DOM.

lectures.title: Extending Built-in Elements
lectures.text:
So now that we had a detailed look at how we can create autonomous web components by extending HTML element, let me also show you that alternative way which I mentioned where you can create web components by basing them on specific built-in components or HTML elements I should say and for that, I will create a new component, I'll create it in a new Javascript file which I'll name confirm-link.js. Now in there, I will create a new class and I'll name this ConfirmLink as well and here I want to extend the HTML anchor tag element.

Now the HTML anchor tag element belongs to the a HTML element, so to this a href here. Now here we could be forwarding the user to google.com, Google and obviously if we we reload this and we click this link, we are forwarded to that page. Now the idea is that we wrap this in our own web component or that we create a web component based on that anchor tag which still has all the functionalities of the built-in anchor tag, so which still takes the ref attribute and forwards us but which in addition asks us if we really want to go there before redirecting us and this is a use case you could certainly have on a web page where you want to have links leading to external resources, where you want to ask the user before really forwarding the user.

Now for that here in ConfirmLink, I'll add the connected callback right away, don't need to constructor really right now, just want to have the callback and there I want to register a click listener on this element, so on the anchor tag which I am in the end extending here. We could set up a shadow DOM here and that is really important. I'm not doing it here because I don't need it but when extending a specific element, you can use all the same features we used here in the tooltip, so you can attach a shadow root, you can add your own template, you can do all these things here too. Here, I just happen to not need anything of that, I want to keep all the default look and behavior and all of that, I just want to add an extra click listener and I do that here in the connected callback by adding an event listener and by adding it directly to the this keyword, I add it to my custom element which extends this built-in element and I add my click listener here and when this click happens, then I will execute a function and here I will use an ES6 arrow function which takes an argument, the default event object which will be created by the Javascript engine, by the browser so to say and then here I have that function body which gets executed.

Now we could also assign some method of this class which we create here but here I want to keep it really simple, I just have this function which gets executed upon a click and what I want to do here is, I want to check if confirm, confirm is a method or a function built into Javascript, it's a globally available function where I ask, do you really want to leave? And if this is yes, then confirm or if the user clicks yes, then this will return true. If this is not the case and hence I add exclamation mark, so if the user clicks cancel or doesn't confirm this, then I want to stop the default behavior, I don't want to forward the user and therefore on the incoming event object, I can call prevent default to suppress the default behavior which would be to basically redirect the user to the target of the link which would be the default behavior of an anchor tag. Now with that created, we just need to define it, so again we'll use custom elements and there the define method and just as before, we now choose our own selector, our own tag for that element and just as for the tooltip, we still should use a name which has a dash in it and which also has some unique prefix.

So here, I'll again use uc and then confirmlink for example. The second argument then is our ConfirmLink class here which extends the HTML anchor element, so just as before but now since we don't extend HTML element but this specific HTML element, the anchor element and that would be the case no matter if we extend the anchor or a paragraph or an image or whatever this, whenever we extend a specific element and not the generic HTML element, so whenever we have such a specific element, we need to pass a third argument here which is an object, where I set extends to the tag of the element we extend, in this case it's an anchor element, so we have to use the a tag here.

So our custom element extends the built-in anchor tag, the a element and now with that, we can go to the index.html file and in there, I first of all want to import this, so I will copy that import and add an import to confirm-link.js and now at the bottom here, instead of my anchor tag like this, I want to use my custom element. lectures.title: Styling "slot" Content Inside of the Shadow DOM
lectures.text:
Well if you want to style slotted content, there is a special selector you can use inside your web component, so inside your shadow DOM styling and that is a special pseudo selector, ::slotted. This will select all slotted content and the way it works is that you call this like a function here is CSS and to it, you pass the selector of the slotted content, so now you could say I want to select all slotted content that has the highlight class or all slotted content that is a span or an anchor tag, so anything like that.

Important though, you can only select the slotted content itself, so if for example in my slotted content here in this span, I also had an anchor tag in there, then what you could not do, you could not select slotted and then the span, this would still work because the slotted content is the span but you can select a child element in the top level slotted content. So this would not style the anchor tag in your slotted span because you can only select the topmost element for styling, this is an important restriction you have here.

So if you have nested content, you can't select this but you can select a span or since this is also directly on the slotted content in our case here, the highlight class and then here, what we could do is we could give us a border bottom of one pixel dotted and red for example, save that and go back and reload this page and you will see this slight red border here and if I inspect this again, you see here is our styling getting applied, the border bottom is having an effect here.

Still important to highlight the order of the styles here, the styling you set up in the light DOM will override your slotted styling you set up in the shadow DOM and the idea here simply is that you always want to give the user the final say on how things should look like but you can set up some default styling you want to have as we do it here but if we were to set a border bottom in the light DOM too, so in our case for the highlight class, if I had a border bottom of let's say two pixels solid and blue here, then you would see that if we reload this page, we see that border instead of our red dotted border because whilst this rule still gets applied, it gets overriden here.

So the specificity in CSS is such that light DOM styling overrides shadow DOM styling for projected or slotted content. This is just one thing to be aware of, I will comment this out here in the light DOM because I don't want to override this, I want to have my red dotted border but it is something you definitely have to be aware of, this can be overriden from inside the light DOM.

lectures.title: Conditional Host Styling
lectures.text:
Now let's take what we learned in the last lectures one step further. What if we want to apply a default style from inside our component but only if some condition is true on our custom element? Let me give you an example. Let's say on this first tooltip here, we added a class, we might have done this right from the start when we wrote our HTML document or maybe we did this programmatically when our app runs, a user clicks a button and we add a class to this element, as we can do it with any HTML element.

The class here is maybe important, the name does not matter, let's say we added the important CSS class to our custom element. Now we only want to set a background color on our custom element if that important class was set. Now what you can't do is you can't say :host.important, this might be something you would think that works because that is how you'd normally combine multiple selectors together in one rule if they all have to match simultaneously but here if we reload, this actually has no effect as you can see, on our custom element, we now don't have any styling from inside our web component.

So this does not work, instead :host is also used as a function if you have some condition for it. So you then simply wrap your condition, so the other CSS selectors that should be matching on your host element, so on your custom tag and you add all these required selectors, the required conditions in parentheses here and you can have anything in there, you can have an attribute selector in there, a class selector as we have it here, an ID selector, any kind of combinations.

Now with this syntax, with host with the condition of also having the important class, now with that, we get back this gray-ish background but only on the first web component here, not on our second one because we now require the presence of this important class and this is simply not the case on this second component. lectures.title: Smart Dynamic Styling with CSS Variables
lectures.text:
Now there's one thing I want to do to conclude the styling part and there we'll use a relatively modern CSS feature, CSS variables. If you ever worked with Sass, you'll quickly know what CSS variables are, just that they're built into the core CSS functionality and don't require a development environment compiler as Sass does. So what's the idea behind CSS variables? Well we have all our nice stylings in our tooltip here, for example the background color when we have the important class on the host element.

Now sometimes, you want to take advantage of the default styling your elements set up but you still want to customize it a bit, let's say the background color here, when we have that important flag, should depend on a certain theme we have in our application. Now obviously what we always can do is we can go into the style definitions of our light DOM and we could of course also say any tooltip, so we use our tooltip selector, with the important class receives a background of green.

Okay we can always do that and if we go back and reload, we have that green color here. Now this does work, the problem with that just is we have to be totally aware of all the styles we set when the important class is added if we then want to override it as we do it here. Now here we know that the only thing we do with important inside of our custom element is that we set the background but we could be doing all kinds of things there and it would be very inconvenient if we as a developer had to drill into all the web components we're using to find out what they're doing when we add a certain CSS class and we might know that they do something when we add a class in general because we can find that in the documentation for the component let's say but we don't know all the styles this component is applying. What we do know, also because of the documentation for a component let's say, is that we can set a primary color and that the component will then use that primary color besides all other styles it might be setting which we don't want to touch and that is exactly where CSS variables or CSS properties can help us. We can go to our light DOM and instead of manually overriding our style here like this, we can add a CSS variable, typically you

do that inside of these special root selector which simply is like the root of your document, alternatively you could select HTML here in the HTML document and in there, you can add your own custom variable with two dashes at the beginning and then any name you want, something like color-primary and there let's give this a light blue maybe, let's see, let's pick this one and now we just need to make sure that we use that in a component and in reality it probably is the other way around, you are using a web component in your application and in the documentation of that web component, you find the information that this component is able to read the color-primary CSS variable let's say and therefore when you set it in your light DOM, the tooltip can pick it up because in there, we just happen to use that.

So instead of hardcoding the light gray here, we can use that variable and we do this with the special var function which CSS understands and there we now just have to use the same name, so --color-primary. If we do that and we save this, we can go back and reload and we now see this light blue style here as a background but now this is fully customizable from inside the light DOM without us being required to dig into the internals of our component and manually override that, instead we can simply change the color into light DOM, in this variable and it will be picked up by the styling inside of our component due to the way we use this CSS variable.

And if you want to learn more about CSS variables and CSS in general, don't hesitate to take my CSS - The Complete Guide course of course, this is a really neat feature when you want to implement something like theming or dynamic colors which you can set from outside. You are not restricted to colors by the way, you can pass anything, you could also have variables where you set some font sizes or padding dimensions, so pixels, rems, this is all possible and you can find an article with more information on CSS properties or variables as I called them here attached to this lecture by the way in case you want to dive deeper, learn more about them and learn more about the browser support for this feature and so on. This now gives us full functionality though and is an awesome way of enhancing our component.

There's just one other thing we can do here to make it even better, in cases where a color-primary is not set, let's say I'm not setting it here, I'm commenting it out in the light DOM, in such cases we of course have no background color because we're trying to apply this variable here but this variable does not exist, so we can't extract the value from it. To handle such cases, we can set up a default value in the place where we try to access the variable, so in our custom component. We simply add a comma after the variable name we're looking for and then we provide a fallback value, like this light gray and if we do that like this, now if I reload we have that light gray but if I were to override this in the light DOM by defining that variable the component is looking for, if we do that, then this of course gets picked up.

So now we have the highest amount of flexibility we could possibly have for this styling thing.

lectures.title: Observing Attribute Changes
lectures.text:
So with the styling cleaned up a little bit, let's come back to some key functionalities we can add inside of our web components and there is one thing which we haven't done at all thus far. Thus far, the text for our tooltip always was set statically, which means we assigned it through this attribute here but there was no way of changing that at runtime, now I do want to change it and for that, I of course need some logic that allows me to change it.

I'll simply do it in the developer tools for now because there, you have to keep in mind that I can of course click into that text here, double click on it and I can set this to some new text but if I do so and I hover over this, we still see the old text because changes to attributes are not picked up inside of the web component and I want to highlight here that when I change this manually in the developer tools, this is no different to this being changed through some Javascript code for example and that of course would be the more realistic use case for your application where you for example listen to some user input and the text entered by the user should end up here in the attribute and I'm just not doing that here because it requires some extra boilerplate code that has nothing to do with web components, so we'll just do that through manual editing here in the developer tools.

The problem is that right now our changes don't get picked up and that is what I want to change. For changing this, I'll have to go back to my tooltip.js file and there, I can add a new lifecycle hook which I did mentioned earlier in this course. Do you remember which one that was? It was the attribute change callback, this executes when an observed attribute is updated and that observed part is going to become important by the way. So let's add it here, let's add the attribute changed callback method here and this method actually receives three arguments, the name of the attribute which changed, the old value of that attribute and now, the new value. Now in there, for now to keep it simple, let's simply output this. So I'll console log the name, the old value and the new value and if I do that, the expectation would be that when I reload this page and I come in here and change that text to something new, if we then go to our console, we see an output there but this is actually empty and the reason for that is that on the slide I deliberately wrote observed attributes trigger this and we're not observing any attributes right now.

This is simply a performance optimization Javascript forces us to implement, it does not by default watch all the attributes of this element because there might be a lot of elements which can change which you don't care about in your component, let's say you're changing a class which you only use in the light DOM, you're not interested in that class inside of the component then so why would you watch for changes or maybe you are interested in the class inside of the component but only because you use it the styles here, well that will be picked up automatically then but if you don't want to run any logic in Javascript, there's no need to trigger this.

So to get something into this callback or to trigger this callback for a specific attribute, you have to tell Javascript that you're watching it and you do inform Javascript that you do care about a certain attribute by adding a special property to your class here. You do this by adding the static keyword, static simply means that it is a property or in this case, it will be a getter function that can be called from outside without creating this class or an object based on that class first, you don't have to care about that though because you will not be creating it, then you add the get keyword which simply means this is now a function that will return you a value but you can't reassign a value to the property of this class which is hidden behind that getter and then the name has to be observed attributes and this is now written as a normal function or method here.

Now again, might look a bit strange if you've never heard about getters and setters and if you're brand new to object oriented programming in general, the idea here is that this is like a property of this class, so like something we initialized with this in here but it's not. It is accessible from outside and more importantly, it's not settable from outside, you can only get the value here, so this is like a locked down property and in there, you return an array with all the attribute names you want to listen to changes.

So here, I simply add text and I add text here as a string because I have my text attribute here. It could of course also add class if I wanted to listen to changes to the class attribute or whichever other attributes you might have but you should only add here what you really care about. And now with this added, I can save this and go back to my application and if I reload now and edit this text again to something new and I go to the console, now we see output here, we actually see two because when I first clicked into it and deleted the content it registered this as a change too.

This is the change we just applied and there we see the name of the attribute because remember, I am simply logging the name and then the old value and then the new value, so here we see the name of the attribute that changed, that was the text attribute, we see the old value that was this text and we see the new value which I entered, this one and now with that, we finally have a way of adjusting the code or the text we see here when we hover over this and we'll do that in the next lecture.

lectures.text:
So now that we're able to listen to changes in the attributes, we of course can also adjust the content we display in our tooltip text.
