lectures.title: Using "disconnectedCallback"
lectures.text:
So now that we learned more about attributes and how we can listen to changes, let me come back to our general logic here in the web component. For one I noticed we still have a little redundant code in there, here where I append this tooltip icon to my shadow root, this is simply not required anymore, we have it here in the template so it is rendered by default so I can remove that and still have it there but this was not the main part I wanted to focus on.

Instead what we also can do, we can clean up our event listeners we got here, right now we add these event listeners but we never clean them up. Now it's always a good idea to clean up your stuff when this component should ever be removed from the DOM and I can show you how it can be removed in a second and for this we have another lifecycle I hope you learned about earlier, we got the disconnected callback and this will be executed when the element is removed from the DOM.

Now let me simply output disconnected here for now before we add any other logic and let's go back to our page and reload and of course we again could have some Javascript code which simply selects this element and removes it, just as we by the way also remove our tooltip container here. You can remove any node with remove child, you just have to select the parent of it and then get rid of it. So we could get access to the paragraph and remove this child from it or here to simulate it in an even easier way, in the dev tools I can simply select it and hit the delete or backspace key and it's gone and in the console, we see disconnected because this gets executed when this component gets removed from the DOM and of course for every component separately.

So that second tooltip, if I remove that, we see disconnected again, now it was called twice or printed twice because it was printed for the two separate elements, because they are treated totally independent from each other. Now the disconnected callback is a great place for cleanup work, cancel any HttpRequests you might be doing, maybe send a log message to your own statistics server or in our case, clean up the event listeners, the mouse enter and mouse leave listeners.

Now we can clean up these listeners by first of all storing the tooltip icon reference here, not in a constant because constants like variables are only accessible in the scope, so in the function in this case, in the method where you defined them, I want to access it from down there though so I have to turn it into a class property and we do that by simply storing it in one and for that simply to make it clear that we have such a class property, I'll define one here, _tooltipIcon, to make sure it is seen as a private property of this class.

It's uninitialized here and we wouldn't have to define it here first by the way, I just want to have a definition here so that when we look at this component, we quickly see the properties we're using but with it defined, I can now use it and it can use it down there and store my span in the tooltip icon property we just initialized and replace all tooltip icon references here with references to my tooltip icon property, class property and now we can go to the disconnected callback and there, I can add remove listener, remove event listener, call this method and I want to remove my mouse enter listener, so let's add this here and the way remove event listener works is that we then also have to define the method which was connected, so for mouse enter, this was show tooltip like this, so we want to remove that and we want to do the same for mouse leave and hide tooltip, so I will just duplicate this mouse leave, this hide tooltip and with that, if I save all that and I go back and reload, if I select my component and remove it, well we don't see anything here but now we do our cleanup work, we take advantage of the disconnected callback to clean up our event listeners here.

Always a good idea but again you could do any cleanup work or any work in general you have in that method here, in that lifecycle hook. One important note here at this point though, if you watched closely you see what I'm removing here are the event listeners for mouse enter and mouse leave but I'm pointing at my show tooltip and hide tooltip methods like this. Now when we add the event listeners, I actually use bind with this to make sure that the this keyword inside of these methods, well it works correctly basically.

Now when you use bind on a method or on a function, it generates a new function or method, so actually the method I'm removing here as an event listener is not exactly the same function object as I used to attach it. So technically, these remove event listeners have no effect here, well they do have an effect but they try to remove a method as a listener which like this was never attached. Now the good thing is when you remove an element from the DOM and that is true for custom elements as well, any event listeners are automatically removed by the browser, so we won't introduce a memory leak here, that is something you also learned earlier in the course.

That is why I will leave this code here simply to show you that you could use disconnected callback for cleanup work but this specific cleanup work here is redundant and actually won't have the intended effect but if you had other cleanup work here, like cancelling HttpRequest or anything like that, then this would be your method and that's why I will leave the code here.

lectures.title: Adding a render() Method
lectures.text:
Now last but not least, let me show one totally optional optimization or restructuring in the code. Right now I access the DOM here in show tooltip when I append my tooltip container and in hide tooltip when I remove it and there is nothing wrong with it and for a web component as simple as this one, this might actually be the best way of doing it but it's also worth looking at a pattern which you see from time to time and which I at least want to get you thinking about, you can add a method in your class as we did it before, let's say we call it _render, the name is totally up to you though. It's not a reserved name, I just want to make sure it's private to really make clear that we only call it from inside this class and I name it render because this should be a method which is responsible for updating the DOM.

So what I now will do is I will go up to my constructor and add a new property, this _tooltipVisible and I'll set it to false initially, so initially this should not be visible. Now of course we're not using this property yet, I want to use that in the render method now. Here I'll check if this tooltip visible is true and if it is true, then I want to create and append this element. So here I'll go there, copy that code and append this child, else I will execute the code for removing the child, let me grab that and paste it in there. This also means that the tooltip container now can be converted back to a constant that only exists in the render method because I don't access it anywhere else.

So I can go up there, remove the tooltip container in my constructor and in the render method, I'll simply add a new variable with let tooltip container and I'll then simply initialize it here, set its text content here and add it here in the end or remove it here. For this I'll just check if tooltip container is defined and I'll only try to remove it if it is defined, otherwise if this was undefined still and we somehow would end up here, we would face a problem.

Now with the render method defined in show tooltip, all I have to do is I have to switch to tooltip visible property to true, excuse me and then execute the render method again because in there, I will then have all the logic for checking tooltip visible and adding the container and in hide tooltip, I'll do the opposite, I'll set tooltip visible to false and then execute the render method. Now what's the idea behind this approach? Well the more and more logic you add, maybe you also render other things in your component at some point of time, the more sense it makes to do all that rendering in a central place, so that you quickly can have a look at all your rendering related code in one place instead of having different parts of rendering different parts of your DOM distributed throughout your component, instead now we know in the render method, we have all the logic for accessing our shadow DOM and for adding our tooltip container in this case but if we had any other things we wanted to render, we would do it in there too and so we could always quickly see what we're doing with our DOM in our component and all the other places and all the other methods of our component are only responsible for updating data, which is then

getting used in render to update the DOM correctly, like we're using tooltip visible to update the DOM correctly by either adding or removing our tooltip container and we're only setting the data here and then of course we always have to call render when we know that we changed something that should trigger a re-render. We can also call render initially here, even though we don't require it for this component but we can call it initially here in the connected callback to say hey when this component gets loaded for the first time, we also want to render it for the first time.

Now if I reload here, this of course has no special effect because we don't show the tooltip because initially we have the tooltip visible status set to false but we do render it as soon as I hover over this, now it's not getting removed anymore if I hover away, let me quickly check that, yes this makes sense, this check here and also the way we removed this will not work, tooltip container always gets re-initialized to an empty, to an undefined variable when render gets called, the old state is of course not carried over so this will not be set if we call render after changing tooltip visible to false.

So what I should do instead is I should initialize this with my loaded tooltip container if available, so I will simply access my shadow root here and there, I'll query for either a div because I know my tooltip container will be the only div or of course we could also assign a class to our tooltip container to query by that or an ID but here I'll do it by this and now if this is set, then I can remove it and I do load it whenever render is called.

So with this change in place, if I now reload this, still everything works, no errors here, if I hover over this get shown, I can hover away and this now all works with this central render method. Again, not something we need so much for this trivial component but the more complex your components get, the more different parts of your shadow DOM you might be updating, the more sense it makes to do all this updating in one central place where you can then quickly see all your updating logic instead of having it distributed across your entire component and all the methods in your component.

lectures.title: The Next Steps
lectures.text:
With all the core basics out of the way, let's dive into building more complex components or one more complex component in this module. We'll build a modal component, so like this pop-up, this overlay inside of a page with a nice backdrop behind it where we can pass our own content into it and which we can also configure, for example where we can control from outside whether it's shown or not. We'll also learn how we can dispatch our own events from inside our web component, so that we can react to these custom events outside of it and we'll see a lot of the features you already learned about in the last modules in action too.

So a great practice as well as many exciting new features, let's dive in.

lectures.text:
So let's start building that modal component and for that I have a brand new project, just an HTML file with that basic HTML5 skeleton, no script files, nothing. There, I will now add my modal.js file where I want to create that code for that modal web component. Now throughout this module, always feel free to pause the video and try something on your own, if we're working on a certain feature where you feel like hey I can do that on my own, definitely pause and try it on your own, otherwise just code along and you will see many of the things we covered in the last lectures and modules and this module should therefore also help with really understanding all these pieces and see how they come together.

So in modal.js, I will start by creating a new component class with the class keyword and I will name it modal and I will extend the HTML element, so I'll not extend an existing HTML element like a div or anything like that, I'll start from scratch here. Now before I add any content here, any logic, I will also register this with custom elements define, I'll name it uc-modal, that will be my tag and I point at this modal class. Now with that added, I'll go to the index.html file and there as before, add the script import to the modal.js file and thereafter we can add it here, uc-modal adds our own HTML tag in the body of this template and later we'll also add some logic so that we have to click a button to show it and height it but that will all come later, for now let's start adding some content to this modal and I'll start with the constructor where we always have to call super first and now in here, I will set up this general template for this modal and for that as you learned, we want to create a shadow DOM.

Now as you also learned, this is of course not a hard requirement, we can create custom elements without the shadow DOM but the shadow DOM gives us many advantages and therefore I definitely want to use it here. So I will call this attach shadow and set the mode to open as always and now we can use the shadow root to start setting our innerHTML, so the template so to say, the HTML code of this custom component that is hidden away from the light DOM.

Now I want to create a modal and this will actually consist of two major parts, for one I will have a div with a CSS class of backdrop, could also be an ID of backdrop if you prefer that and this will be the part behind the modal which will gray out the rest of the page whilst a modal is in the foreground and the other part therefore is of course the modal itself and again here I'm using a class of a modal, actually let's use the ID because we can be that specific here and selecting an ID is actually a bit faster than selecting a class, so from a CSS perspective, this is a bit better and now let me also add style tags here so that we can style all the components or all the elements we'll have in the modal and I will start with some rough styling and with the rough layout and later we'll add more and more feature to that modal, like different slot areas and so on, something we haven't covered yet, we'll learn it in this module.

So let's start building that modal and first of all here I'll select the backdrop and I'll set a style for that backdrop. Now the style for this backdrop will be that it has a position of fixed from the top of the page and the way this is positioned in the index.html file directly in the body, this will refer to the overall document, to the overall page as a container. So from the top I want to have a distance of zero, from the left as well and then this backdrop should cover the entire page.

So I'll give it a width of 100% and for the height, this would not work unless we also set the height of our body and the HTML tag to 100% but here we can use 100vh which stands for viewport height and also is about the entire height of our window basically. Now I'll give it a background of RGBA and then a transparent black color, maybe 75% opacity so 25% transparency here and with that, we should have a backdrop in place. Now since we already import this and we use our tag here, we should be able to reload this page and indeed, we now have a gray background and that is the modal background, it's not obvious here but we can confirm this if we simply inspect this in the developer tools, it's this background, this div here that is responsible for that.

If I uncheck the background, it's gone. So we see the modal background here, that's great and if we had other content on this page and I will add something here, please confirm your choice and then we have a button which maybe says show details and confirm whatever you want, if I now reload, this is hidden behind the modal or behind the backdrop. I'll get rid of the margin actually, let's give this a margin of 2rem instead so that we have a little bit of margin on the body, yes. Okay, so this is the general styling, the backdrop is in place. Now let's also add the modal style itself in the next lecture.

lectures.text:
Let's add some content in the modal, so inside of my modal div there, I actually want to have three sections. I want to have a header in there which holds a title and for now I'll simply have a dummy title there, h1 tag please confirm. Below the header here, I want to have a section, maybe with the ID main, whatever you want and in there, I'll have a slot because I want to be able to pass the content that is displayed as a message into this modal from outside and actually you're of course not limited to passing in some text here, you can pass in anything here - you can pass in an image, buttons, a form, inputs, whatever you want.

With that, we got a nice looking modal in my opinion, let's now ensure that we can also open and close it and we want to open it when this show details and confirm button here is pressed.

lectures.title: Adding Some General App Logic
lectures.text:
So we want to be able to show that modal and for that, we need a way to control the visibility of the backdrop and the modal. Now there are various ways of doing so in CSS - we can set the opacity, we can set the display property, anything like that. What we will need in the end is some way to pass in the information whether this should be visible or not from outside, so from our main document because one possible way would be to set let's say an open attribute, either set this to true or as you also see it on some built-in elements, just open, for example the built-in button element has a disabled attribute which you also add just like this. So when open or opened maybe is added let's say, then we want to show the modal, if it's not added we don't want to show it and now I'll add a script tag here and you could outsource this into a different file too of course where I want to do something when this button is clicked and I want to add this opened attribute when we click it.

So I will now get access to my confirm button here maybe by using document query selector and I can select a button here because another advantage of the shadow DOM, we will just fetch this button because the buttons in our modal are part of the shadow DOM and therefore we are in no danger of accidentally selecting these from outside. So that's another advantage of the shadow DOM here, when we select something in our main document, we only select buttons in that main document and in this case we only have one button, so I can use this query selector and then I'll add my event listener here for the click event and here, I want to add the opened attribute to my uc-modal element.

For this, I'll get access to my modal with document query selector and now we can simply use uc-modal as a selector because this is a valid tag by which we can select it and then we could say modal set attribute opened and now we need to assign a value here and I'll set this to an empty string. Now in order to be able to see that effect, we have to make sure that we're not showing the modal by default, which we currently are and especially its backdrop is blocking us from clicking anything, so to hide it by default, we got a couple of possible ways of solving this; one way of making sure we can show and hide this is to set the opacity to 0 by default which will hide this but then we'll face a problem actually because now if I reload this, it is hidden but we still can't click this because even though it's invisible, it's fully opaque, it's still in front of us. Now we could change the z-index but we can also set the pointer events here to none and this will not accept any clicks on the backdrop but let them through instead and we do the same on the modal and we just have to change this later when we show it so that we then really block clicks through it but here we want to allow them.

So now if I reload, I can click this and if you watched, you saw opened was added here on the right, let me show this again. If I reload, this modal here doesn't have the opened attribute but if I click this button, watch it here on the right, here it is, there it opened. So this is working and now in the next lecture, we can work on doing something in our component when this opened attribute is added.

lectures.title: Opening the Modal via CSS
lectures.text:
To act when we add this opened attribute, we need to listen to changes in attributes obviously and you learned how that works right. Thus far we have all the logic in the constructor, now it's simply time to add more methods here and I will add the attribute changed callback here and you remember that you here get the name of the attribute which changed, the old value and the new value and then this will trigger for any observed attribute which changed.

For this we also have to add our static getter here, observed attributes, and make sure you get the naming right here otherwise it will not work and there you have to return square brackets and then the name of the attributes you want to watch and here it's the opened attribute and if you chose a different name, that will be added here outside of your component, then you also have to listen to a different name in here of course. Now for the addition of the opened attribute, this should be triggered and then when this runs, maybe we also have other attributes, so here I will check if name is equal to opened and if that is the case, we know that something happened on the opened attribute so we probably want to show our modal but I can simply add another if check and see if this has an attribute of opened now because if that is now available, then we know it has been added and then I know I want to change the styling to set the opacity to 1 and to set pointer events to all, so to react to clicks on my backdrop and my modal again and there are a couple of ways of doing that.

One thing we can do is we can access our shadow root and there of course, query for our backdrop and set the style of the backdrop and here, simply add opacity or set opacity to 1 and then also the style of the backdrop pointer events should be set to all, to react to all clicks on the backdrop and then we do exactly the same here for our modal. So there we also set the opacity to 1 and the pointer events to all and if you save that and you reload that page and you click that button, indeed both shows up here and now we can't click this button here anymore because the pointer events are on, we now catch any clicks with the backdrop and with the modal.

This is one possible way of doing this, there are other possible ways too but I will actually comment this out. It might seem like the obvious way of reacting to the opened attribute but if all you want to do is change some styling, then there is a way easier approach to do that, to get there. You don't need attribute changed callback for that, you don't need to listen to these changes even, so I will comment all of that out, it's nice knowing that and you would need that if you had any other logic you wanted to execute, like start a timer, change some text, add an element but if you just want to change some styles, you can do that with CSS only because what happens when the opened attribute is added to our tag here?

Well then it looks like this here right, our tag and then the opened attribute and you might remember that in CSS, there are attributes selectors. So we can simply write a CSS rule that changes the style when the opened attribute is available on our root element, on our host element. So what I'll do is I'll add a new rule here, :host, with the condition that the opened attribute is there and this is all I need to write for this, this now means for the host element, which is our custom tag, when the opened attribute is available and this is the normal attribute syntax you know from CSS, then I want to change the style and I want to change the style of my backdrop, so I can still combine these selectors and this just means select the backdrop if my host has the opened attribute and then I want to set the opacity to 1 and I want to set pointer events to all and I can now of course do the same for my modal by simply repeating this with #modal. And with this change in place, please keep in mind that I commented out my attributes changed callback, so with this change in place up here, we can go back and reload our page and still click that button and see the modal and the backdrop and this is now the more elegant way of solving this

if you only need to change styles. If you needed to do anything else, like add an HTML element, then of course you would need to listen to that and then run whichever logic, add whichever element you want to add in your attributes changed callback.

lectures.title: Public Methods & Properties
lectures.text:
The implementation we're currently using is absolutely fine, it opens the modal but we could also add another way of using our modal. We get access to it here in code, in our Javascript code and it's always important to remember that what you get here is a full Javascript object, the Javascript object representing this DOM node and this object can be used to set the attribute, we could also set the classes there, we could even remove it from the DOM and since it is an object, it is an object based on our class here.

This is in the end the object that was generated for us by the browser, it has all the default properties of HTML element which we extend here and it has its default methods and actually set attribute is just a default method of every HTML element and since we extend HTML element here, our own modal object also has set attribute available but this means that if we add any new properties or methods in our class, we can also access these from outside and therefore one thing we could add here is an open method.

Now please note that I did not add an underscore at the beginning here because I don't want to mark this as private, it should indeed be accessible from outside and what I do in here is here, I add some code to show my modal and again this could be the code we use here before or I set my attribute inside here. Now what this allows me to do with this open method added is that I go back to my index.html file and instead of setting the attribute here, which I absolutely can do, I can call open here on my modal object because I just added this open method and if you're wondering why I would do it like this, well I can abstract complexity away from my main document, from me as a component user and manage it inside of my component.

Now obviously, the complexity is not very large here but if we were adding different elements or anything like that, then all we have to do outside is call open and we do all the magic inside of this open method, inside of our component. So this is not a strictly better approach than setting the attribute manually as we did before outside of the component, it's just an alternative, an alternative of which you should be aware and actually it's perfectly fine to handle both cases, the case that we add opened manually from outside or that we call open and you do find built-in elements where you can call a method to something or where you can call a method from outside to do something.

Now with this adjusted, I can reload my page and still open a modal because it has still the same mechanism, still the opened attribute gets added but now we're not doing this manually with our own code, we're calling open outside instead and this is just one alternative I wanted to show you here. Also be aware that you can not just call methods from outside, if you had some public properties, so any other properties like let's say this is open and you set this to false initially and we change this to true here, then you can access this from outside too.

So now we have is open here and now after calling modal open, if I console log modal is open here from outside my component, you will see that if I open the console and I reload and I click this button, we see false here because I should set it to true in open and not leave it as false, so let's give this another try, reload, now we see true here. So we can also access properties from outside our component and we might have some useful information in there which we now can extract and use programmatically from our main document, from our main application logic which would be this one and which we still manage inside of our modal.

Now a little side note, if we do expose this is open formation, then we all of a sudden need to readd our attribute changed callback, not change the styles here but certainly change this is open to true here and on the other hand, if we don't have that opened attribute, we want to change is open to false here. By the way we can get rid of that outer check, we can always check for the existence of this attribute, even if this attribute change callback was triggered due to the change in some totally different attribute.

So now, this is totally optional, just to show you that you can access properties from outside too but now we have this extra functionality added, where we can always access this information too through this public property. Now with this is open property exposed, we can actually enhance our logic out here and we can check that if this button gets clicked, we only want to open a modal if modal is open is not true, so if this is not true hence an exclamation mark at the beginning, otherwise we don't have to call open because it already seems to be open.

Not sure how we could click this but if we did something fishy, then we would block this. So here I can show console log opening and now if I reload, we see opening here but now if I hack this and I manually remove the backdrop, now I all of a sudden can click this button again but now you will see if I do so, we don't see opening again because of this extra check. So now we have this extra check which is a little bit useful here but it's easy to imagine other components where you would need to get some information from inside to prevent strange logic from running outside, so in your main application and then public properties like is open can be very helpful.

lectures.title: Understanding Named Slots
lectures.text:
So now that we got this open button working here, we got our basic, our very basic modal functionality in place. Now a next step that would be great is if we could customize the content of this modal a bit more. Right now we can pass in our own body, our own main content but what about the title, would be nice if we could pass in the title too and first setting the title, there are of course two possible routes we could take; one option would be to have like modal title attributes here which we can set.

We could certainly do that and we could set this attribute here and then in modal.js in the connected callback which we don't have yet because we don't need it, we could add it of course, we could extract the that attribute and we could then initialize our h1 tag content here with the title we set up in our attribute and of course we could then also listen to changes in that title, so in that modal title attribute and possibly update it in the modal when that changes. There would be nothing wrong with that but I actually want to show you how to use multiple slots because maybe, we also have a modal where we don't want to force the user into using a h1 tag here, instead we want to let the user pass in any header the user wants and it could for example also be a h1 tag with an h2 tag below it, so to have a title and subtitle and for that, I want to use a slot here in my component too. The problem now of course is, I now got two slots right, I got one in the header and I got one in the main section.

Now if we do that and we then go into the modal and we have let's say our h1 tag here, please confirm, if I do it like this and I reload this page and open the modal, then it might look right at first but if we inspect this, we actually see this is not really working out the way we want it to work, if we have a look at our modal, then in the header, well both is inserted - the paragraph and the h1 tag and the main section, there the slot basically is empty because what essentially happens here is that the first slot catches all the content we pass into the component and that makes a lot of sense because how would Javascript know which part here should end up in which of our slots.

What we need is some kind of identification for each slot, some ID we assign to a slot which we then can use when we pass in some content to target a specific slot and we can actually do that, we can give our slots names and that is totally optional but something we can do and here I will give my slot a name by adding the name attribute, this is how you do assign names to slots and I'll name this title and down there, we now could give this a name of main or we leave it unnamed and then any content which we pass in, which does not target a specific name will automatically go in here.

Now let me show you how this works. So we get this slot named title here, now back in the index.html file, the content which should go into my name slot will receive an extra slot attribute and there I simply point at the name, so in my case, title. So I use title here on the slot attribute of the content that should go into that title slot because I have title as a name here. The second slot has no name and therefore the content which has no slot attribute automatically goes to that default slot and I can show this to you if I now reload this page, here if we now inspect this, we see the header slot has the h1 tag and if I go into the main section, this slot has the paragraph tag and now we got a modal with more options for us to customize it because now we got multiple slots where we can pass in content and of course we can also still assign a default value here, so for example for this named slot just as we can do it for the unnamed slot, I will add a default content of please confirm payment in case we would not pass in content for this slot.

Now in our case we do, so when I reload, we should still see please confirm instead of my default content of please confirm payment and indeed we do and now all the things you already learned apply. So we can now style this content which we do pass in from inside our main app so to say, from our main document, we can style that here in the light DOM or in our modal with the slotted special selector. So here, this style in particular has no effect anymore because we can't target the h1 tag that's passed into the shadow DOM from outside, if we would want to target anything that gets passed in, we would have to use the slotted attribute like this.

So now here, I simply add my condition and say I want to style slotted h1's and now if I reload this, we have that smaller text here. So this is something we can still do, basically what you already learned about slots.

lectures.title: Listening to Slot Content Changes
lectures.text:
Now with named slots explored, let's dig a bit deeper into slots and let's see how we could actually get access to the content we pass in our slot in our code in the component and with that I don't mean get access in the sense of render it, what we do here automatically by simply using the slot but what if we would need to kind of read our list of data, our list of HTML nodes that gets passed into our slots. Now for that let me first of all show you something else, after setting up my innerHTML template here, so the next line after this statement basically. I want to get access to all my slots and I'll store them in a constant and we can easily query for them on our shadow root with the query selector all method and then querying for the slot element because this is a normal HTML tag by which we can query of course.

Now here we can access our slots, this will basically be an array or a node list of HTML elements and we have two slots - the first one will be at index 0, the second one at index 1. Now let's say we want to have a look at our second slot, so the one with index 1 and then we can add an event listener here and the event to which we can listen is the slot change event and that will be triggered whenever new content arrives, which will happen at least once when our shadow DOM basically is used to render our component into the real DOM and we project the content we pass into our component into our slot, this will be the first time this triggers but then also if we would update it programmatically from outside and the content we pass in would change, then slot change for this given slot would also trigger again and in this function which then triggers, we get an event object and in here most importantly, we'll be able to analyze the content that's inside of our slot.

So here I will actually console dir, dir prints an object in the console which we can inspect instead of the HTML element console log with print and there, I will print that slot we're listening to. So now if I save this and I reload, you see we now have a slot output here and that gets printed by this line, so that means that the slot change event did indeed fire, which it as I mentioned does when we render this component to the screen because that is when the slot here will be replaced with the projected content for the first time and if we now have a look in the slot here, we can see a couple of interesting elements but some very interesting data can be seen if we call the assigned nodes method on our slot, so this is not a property, this is a method.

If we do that and we go back, if I reload, then we see an array of all the content that was projected into our slot. Now you might be wondering why we have four elements instead of just one paragraph tag, the reason for that simply is that the whitespace in front of the paragraph tag and after the paragraph tag also is treated as text. In the end we have this paragraph tag we're interested in and if we would optimize our code here and basically write this all in line which is harder to read but gets rid of all the excess whitespace, if we would do that here for our component in the HTML file, then you would see we only have the paragraph element in there and this is now the paragraph DOM node which gets projected into our slot, so this is also not part of the shadow DOM but still of the light DOM, just the content at which our slot points so to say. Now I do now restructure this again to make it easier to read but now if I reload, I get these four elements again but again it is the paragraph tag which we get in the end here and if you ever need to get access to the content that is projected into your slot, then this is how you can do it, you can use assigned nodes and as a little side note, on the protected element, you also find this assigned

slot property here which you can on the other hand used to find out into which slot this was projected. So this also may be an interesting information depending on which kind of application you are writing. So slot change combined with assigned nodes can be very helpful if you for example also have an application where the content in your slot might change at runtime too, so not just this initial change which we have here but also a change at a later point of time maybe because you loaded some data from the web and you want to change something in your modal when that is done.

So this is just another thing I wanted to show you which can be helpful when you're working with slots.

lectures.title: Closing the Modal
lectures.text:
So now that we covered a lot about slots, let's finish up this modal by tweaking some of its styling again but most importantly and first of all, by making these buttons work. Right now I can click cancel and okay and nothing will happen. Now I want to close the modal in both cases but I want to dispatch my own events to which I can listen from outside my component, so from inside my main application, my main Javascript logic which runs int my main document so that I know whether the user has confirmed this modal or cancelled it because right now what I want to be able to do in the end is that I add an event listener here to my modal object and keep in mind, my modal object is really just my own custom component and there, it would be nice if we had like a confirm listener and confirm is not a built-in event, so right now this will never trigger where I can do something, so most of the time in my application I would probably want to do something like create a payment request which I sent to some backend once the user confirmed or where I also can do something if the user declines this, so if the user cancels this, then maybe I want to reset some state in my application.

Of course here I'll not focus on the application logic, I want to focus on the component and how we add our own events there but I just want to give you some ideas of what you could do there in a real application, so outside of your web component will focus on making these customer events work here now, so confirm and cancel is the go. For that let's dive into our modal again and there we have these buttons. Since these buttons are part of the shadow DOM, we have to create listeners to these buttons inside of our shadow DOM.

So for that, I'll add another constants here in the constructor below my slots listeners I added in the last lectures and there I'll have the cancel button and for this, I'll give this button an ID of cancel button, maybe like this, confirm button and now I can select by that ID, so I'll access my shadow root, use the query selector, you could also use get element by ID of course and then select the cancel button ID here and then I'll duplicate this to also select my confirm button here with the confirm button ID.

So now that I have access to these two buttons, I can register listeners here in my component. So let's maybe start with the cancel button here and on the cancel button, I want to hide the modal and I want to dispatch this custom cancel event to which I'm listening from outside. Therefore, I'll first of all add a new method here and I'll name it hide, I could turn this into a private method by adding a leading underscore and always keep in mind, it's not really private, you can still call it from outside, I just add this to show hey this should only be used from inside, if you then don't follow that rule, well you can do that but here I want to keep it as a public method because even though we're not doing it in our app, you could of course definitely imagine an application where you want to hide a modal from outside, so from your main application instead from inside of the component. Now how do we hide it?

Well in the end it's all about setting our open attributes to none or to remove it and we do that not with set attribute but with remove attribute and there, I want to remove my opened attribute. We can add an extra check here to see if this has the attribute opened before we then try to remove it of course. Besides that, I want to set this is open to false of course to update this property as well and with that, the modal will already be closed because of that opened attribute which we use in our CSS styles here.

So therefore we have that functionality, the custom event is missing but I'll come back to that later. So for now let's continue with the event listener on the cancel button in the constructor, there we want to listen to an ordinary click which of course is a built-in event, built into core Javascript and the browser and upon a click, I want to trigger this hide, so this hide method and of course I'll bind the this keyword here to ensure that this inside of hide refers to the class and not to the button which is the event trigger. Now I'll duplicate this to also hook up my confirm button and there, I also want to hide this modal.

Now we already see a problem here, I definitely don't want to run the same logic two times. So what I will do instead is, I'll add a private method here which I'll name cancel and I'll add one which I'll name confirm. Now in both, I will call this open and here we don't need to bind this because if we're calling it like this from inside the class, the class itself is calling a method and therefore this in the called method will refer to the class too, so I'll also call hide here, sorry here it should also be hide of course, not open. So it should be hide in both but now we can dispatch different custom events here. So let's tweak that and go up and for the cancel button, I will now actually call my private cancel method and for confirm, my private confirm method and right now, they will both just call hide but that will change soon.

So now with that, we should already have a working modal, such that when I click cancel, it gets hidden and if I open it again, I can also hide it and close it with okay and you can see I can reopen it even though I have an extra check here in my main app, in my index.html file where I check for whether it is not open yet with the is open property and I can still reopen it after closing it because I do update this is open property in my modal as well.

So this is the first important step but the more important and more interesting step of course now is to emit our own custom event, let's do that next.

lectures.title: Configuring Custom Events
lectures.text:
So it would be really great if we could listen to our own event from outside our component and not just from inside because that kind of defeats its purpose, right? Well the good thing is when you create such an event, we can specify an object as a second argument where we can add some information about how this event should behave and there, we basically got three configurations. Bubbles allows us to define whatever this event should bubble up or not, this means if it should only be available on the element we dispatched it on or if it is not handled there, if it should go to the next element in the DOM tree.

So in our case, for this button, the cancel button, if we don't add an event listener there, it would bubble up and event listeners on the section would handle it and if we had no event listeners there, it would bubble up and event listeners on this div would handle it and if we have no listeners there, it would bubble up and so on. So this doesn't sound too bad, right? If I set this to true, let's see, now theoretically we should be able to listen to it from other places too and not just on event listeners on this button.

So maybe now our event listener on our custom component, which in the end wraps this button, works. So let's go back and reload and click cancel, still no output. The reason for that is that there is another important argument and that is the composed arguments here. Composed when set to true now suddenly ensures that this will work, if I now click cancel, you see cancel here and the reason for that is that composed, which by default is false just like bubbles, composed means that if you set it to true, then this event may leave the shadow DOM in which it is, if it is in one and here of course, it is triggered inside of our shadow DOM.

If you set composed to false, then the event must not leave our shadow DOM tree, so it will bubble up but only inside our shadow DOM tree, so we could add a listener to modal and handle it but not outside of our component. So we need to set both to true, bubbles and composed, to handle our event outside of our component and now we can listen to it. Now this is one way of doing that, of course there is a simpler way too, I just show you this way because sometimes you need to take that route, but of course for confirm and we could have done that for cancel too, we can also just refer to this, which is our component, so our own custom element in the end, remember our modal extends the HTML element, so this really refers to our own custom HTML element in the end and therefore our custom element itself also has the dispatch event method.

So here, our confirm event can also be holding a new event, here the confirm event, so the name is confirm and you can pick any name you want but of course it should match the name we are listening to outside and then here, I will use this confirm event and now if I save this without any extra config and I click okay, we still get confirmed because now we're triggering this event on our element itself, so not inside the shadow DOM, not on some nested element in the shadow DOM but on our custom element itself and therefore listeners on our element will of course receive that event.

It will not bubble up there now though, so if we would want to listen to it on the body in our main document, this should not work but we also don't need to manage composed and so on because this is now simply not required. So this is of course the shorter alternative and the one you would typically use but I found it important to mention how you can use bubbles and composed to also let events triggered inside your shadow DOM, on some nested element, bubbles up through the shadow DOM and potentially even leave it with composed.

So these are the custom events and how we can handle it and now we have the full flexibility we might need, we're closing the modal and in our main application, which we typically would run or import in our main document, like this index.html file, there we can now also find out which button the user pressed without having to kind of dig into our component and try to attach listeners to the buttons in the component from outside, instead we use these convenient listeners on our custom element itself.
